Police in Santa Barbara, California, are investigating after nearly 30 people had to seek medical care at a half-marathon running event held in the city on Sunday.
In a statement provided to the BBC's US partner CBS News, officers said they received a report from Santa Barbara Cottage Hospital about race participants who sought medical treatment "for unusual symptoms" after the race ended.
"The cause of the reported symptoms has not been confirmed," the statement added.
Cottage Health, which operates the hospital, told CBS it had seen "a larger than expected number of emergency visits" from those who ran the race.
"There is no specific action recommended for the public at this time; however, participants who feel unwell should seek medical attention and follow guidance from healthcare professionals," police said.
Cottage Hospital said it treated 27 people from the half marathon at emergency rooms in Santa Barbara and the nearby city of Goleta.
The vast majority of them - 24 - were discharged after treatment, while three people were still in hospital as of Monday in stable condition.
Several thousand people ran the half marathon on a hotter-than-usual day in Santa Barbara along the Pacific Ocean. Temperatures reportedly reached 86F (27C) by midday, compared to a typical early November temperature of low 70s.
One of the runners who went to hospital told local news outlet KEYT-TV that they had lost consciousness and could not remember parts of the race.
"It is awfully suspicious," said the runner, who declined to be identified. "We had people saying they were hallucinating."
"I am not too familiar with heat exhaustion but I have never seen anyone not remembering a long portion of their run," the runner added.
Event director David Monico told US media that 15 people were taken from the medical tent to local hospitals because of dehydration and overheating.
The BBC has contacted the Santa Barbara Police Department, Cottage Health and the half marathon organisers for further comment.

Sovereign wealth funds, including some of those in the Gulf, are among the big losers from the AI sell-off, with their listed portfolios slumping $30.5 billion since the end of June. Globally, sovereign wealth funds and public pension investors hold about $335.5 billion of exposure to AI companies, according to consultancy GlobalSWF. Gulf funds have been a big part of that, both domestically and around the world, backing AI firms in private funding rounds and as they list on public markets.
Among those with some of the highest disclosed exposures is Abu Dhabiâs Mubadala, which may have seen its portfolio shrink by $17.5 billion, mostly due to a more than 50% slump in chipmaker GlobalFoundries stock. Saudi Arabiaâs PIF is estimated to have seen its AI exposure fall in value by $5.64 billion, mostly attributed to its SpaceX holding.
Despite the stock market slump, it is unlikely to change how sovereign funds bet on AI. âWe would not expect strategic investors to retreat wholesale from AI,â said Daniel Brett, head of research at GlobalSWF. âLower valuations could create opportunities for long-term funds to increase exposure selectively, although this does not imply an imminent rebound.â

Silicon Valleyâs bet that billions of agents will be out ordering food, booking travel, and filling up their humansâ shopping carts is running into an (admittedly early) reality check.
Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky said Friday that the site was seeing âvery, very low numbersâ of bookings by Metaâs Muse and Instinct AI agents, while DoorDash has received âmaybe several hundred orders in totalâ from personal AI assistants, CEO Tony Xu said. âThe adoption of these horizontal personal agents may be much slower than is anticipated,â Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel said.

A word of caution for Wall Streeters planning how to spend their year-end bonuses: This may be as good as it gets for a while.
Bonuses at big banks and investment houses are set to grow again thanks to a blockbuster year of historic IPOs, AI financings, and zippy markets, according to pay consultancy Johnson Associates, whose annual bonus report is required reading across the financial industry. But the AI trade is now starting to sour, interest rates are rising, and last weekâs Democratic gains may darken the backdrop for 2027.
Even this yearâs bumper crop will be shared unevenly, tilted more heavily toward the best performers rather than spread âpeanut-butter-likeâ across and within divisions, Alan Johnson told Semafor. âFirms now value the best people more than they ever have, and value the average person less,â he said. âNobody is going to wring their hands if an average performer is complaining â âdonât let the door hit you on the way out.ââ
Financial executives are keen to avoid the trap of 2021, when their efforts to gift-wrap the fruits of a banner year as special, one-time bonuses got baked into expectations anyway, with predictable howling in 2022.

Wall Street giants have hundreds of billions of dollars riding on Jensen Huang, but sound remarkably unfazed by the trouble the company is in.

e401a3e93ad1.text: By — Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press By — Ben Finely, Associated Press Ben Finely, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-hegseth-holds-news-conference-as-house-impeachment-vote-looms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Hegseth says House impeachment push is about 'policy disagreements' not high crimes Politics Updated on Nov 10, 2026 8:54 AM EST — Published on Nov 10, 2026 8:00 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dug in for a fight Tuesday against his potential impeachment in Congress, telling reporters that a rogue lawmaker is targeting him over "policy disagreements" and not the high crimes or offenses the nation's founders intended. Watch Hegseth's news conference in the video player above. The embattled Pentagon chief spoke at his first press briefing from the five-sided building in six months, launching a counteroffensive against outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie's effort to impeach him over his handling of the unpopular war against Iran and other actions. WATCH: Rep. Massie speaks after filing Hegseth impeachment resolution "In the 250 years of our American republic, no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations," Hegseth told reporters. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The briefing was Hegseth's first since May even as the U.S. military has kept up intermittent operations against Iran as well as fatal strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America. WATCH: Hegseth speaks at the Naval War College as possible impeachment vote looms Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, filed the impeachment resolution in the House on Monday. It sets the stage for a dramatic vote on whether to remove a prominent Trump administration figure following sweeping losses for Republicans in last week's midterm elections that many at least partly blamed on the Iran conflict and its economic impact. The resolution largely focuses on the war in Iran but also includes references to Hegseth's role in military actions in Yemen against Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela. Massie said Hegseth's actions amount to "high crimes and misdemeanors" and his leadership at the Pentagon "warrants impeachment." What constitutes "high crimes and misdemeanors" is not spelled out in the Constitution, leaving it to lawmakers to decide what are impeachable acts. A vote in the House could come by midweek, putting pressure on Republicans — many of whom blamed their election wipeout on the Iran war — but next steps are highly uncertain. During his news conference, Hegseth framed the impeachment effort as an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes while undermining American forces "in real time." "This is not patriotism," Hegseth said. "This is sabotage." Hegseth said that Massie's effort "tells our enemies -- Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching -- the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations." Trump has backed Hegseth, pointing to the raid to capture then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January as well as military operations against Iran that he asserts have "obliterated" its navy and air force. In a briefing Monday, President Donald Trump addressed the impeachment threat that looms for his defense secretary. Watch his remarks in the player above. Iran, however, has been able to keep striking U.S. military bases in the Middle East and has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz during the course of the more than 8-month-old conflict, driving up global oil prices. Trump told reporters Monday that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over" and repeated his often-made claim that Iran "would love to make a deal." Hegseth also has been defending his stewardship of the U.S. military. "There's a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success," he told reporters Monday after a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island. He added that "if we want to litigate" the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, "I'm happy to do it all day long." He also released a video on social media last week that argued impeachment would be "all about the politics of personal destruction" and that "won't work with me. You can rest assured of that." Afterward, scores of Pentagon political appointees posted images of Hegseth emblazoned with the words, "Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic." Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesman, released a statement saying that "despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats," Hegseth is "100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump's term in office." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. e2d23d726dc0.text:
Timâs view
In the decade since the Paris Agreement, the annual round of UN climate summits has seemed like a parallel universe, increasingly out of touch with geopolitics and the real economy.
Between the idealism-bordering-on-naivete, and the impenetrable thicket of acronyms, jargon, and obscure treaty provisions, âsometimes I come into negotiation rooms and the contrast with the real world cannot be any bigger,â Ali Mohamed, Kenyaâs special climate envoy, told me here. There are still many people here at COP31 in Antalya, TÃ¼rkiye, this week who would love to see the oil and gas industry shuttered tomorrow, energy access and prices be damned. Fossil fuel companiesâ record-breaking profits this year are proof that, like it or not, the world still needs a lot of this stuff.
While the Iran war certainly did drive some countries to accelerate their adoption of renewables, the global reprioritization of energy security means âthere is no doubt weâre backslidingâ on the goal adopted at COP28, in Dubai, to transition away from fossil fuels, Mohamed said. And needless to say, nothing that happens at COP has any real legally binding force on any country.
So whatâs it all for? Iâve asked myself this question a lot in the past 48 hours, while navigating Antalyaâs maddeningly overwhelmed transit system (although I will say the COP venue itself, if you can manage to get inside, is the nicest one weâve had in years). One answer is that pragmatism was never the point. Idealism is a feature of UN summits, not a bug, Eurasia Group analyst MarÃa JosÃ© Valverde said: âCOP goals arenât designed to be achieved. Itâs about where we want to take humanity.â Another answer is that, while it may not get headlines, âthereâs still all kinds of shit happening behind the scenes,â as one diplomat put it to me this morning, from deals on clean cooking stoves in Africa to negotiations among European countries to remove bureaucratic barriers between their rail networks that force more commercial traffic onto dirtier highways.
And while it may not be happening at activistsâ preferred pace, clean energy adoption is already driving a tangible transition away from fossil fuels. Thatâs in spite of a surge in overall energy demand that has made it harder to displace any one source. In the absence of all renewables that have been built since 2010, the International Energy Agency reported last week, global fossil fuel demand in 2025 would have been 8% higher, âan amount equivalent to Indiaâs total energy consumption.â
The big goal for this particular COP is to drive this trend forward by getting countries to agree on a target to raise the share of total global energy demand served by electricity from 23% today to 35% by 2035. Thatâs basically another version of the fossil fuel transition goal, viewed through the opposite end of the kaleidoscope, which could be more palatable to the oil-producing countries that are usually the spoilers here. Whatever is negotiated here will, again, be nonbinding. And itâs impossible to say precisely what role COP, per se, has had in the pace of the clean energy rollout up to now. But to the extent that these meetings mainly serve to send long-term political signals that buttress â if not dictate â the economic signals companies use to make energy investment decisions, the best outcome for COP is to put itself out of business, as clean energy projects increasingly beat fossil fuels on merits unrelated to environmental ideology.
âIn the real world, things are happening and not waiting for the negotiations,â Mohamed said. âThe transition is going to happen whether you want it to or not.â
Notable
- In December, new US Commerce Department rules will make it costlier to import Chinese manufacturing components for solar panels, as part of an effort to make it harder for US solar firms to rely on China.

0595e684b842.text:
The FBI is investigating the CEO of Nvidiaâs affair with an alleged Chinese spy, US President Donald Trump said, widening the fallout from the scandal engulfing the worldâs biggest chipmaker. Nvidia shares fell following Jensen Huangâs admission of infidelity with an executive tied to Chinese intelligence, while lawmakers in a soon-to-be Democrat-controlled Congress have pledged investigations into the episode, and the US Commerce Department has reportedly begun readying a new set of semiconductor export controls.
Pressure is mounting on Huang, but he appears unlikely to lose his job, at least for now: Trump has publicly backed the executive, and Nvidia is highly dependent on him, with no clear successor in view and a board that is relatively low on heft.

d69e71123784.text:
Andyâs view
Nobody outside the Oval Office has been more influential on US policy toward chip sales to China â and, by extension, the superpower race for AI supremacy â than Jensen Huang.
The Nvidia CEO had Donald Trumpâs ear. And he used his privileged access to make the case that keeping China hooked on Nvidia hardware and software was critical to maintaining the US technological lead. Cutting off sales to Americaâs chief strategic rival, he cautioned, only encouraged Beijing to speed up development of its own AI technologies that would, over time, become the global default.
Whatever the merits of that argument, the events of the past 48 hours have almost certainly doomed his central contention.
Huangâs admission of an affair with a woman who, according to US intelligence, is a Chinese spy plays directly into the hands of hawks in Washington pressing to clamp down on tech transfers to China. This camp has insisted all along that Huangâs advocacy was not only self-serving â a thin justification for his pursuit of profits â but, on its face, absurd. Under Chinese leader Xi Jinping, China is going all out for tech self-sufficiency precisely to escape the kind of dependencies that Huang envisages.
Indeed, Xi has been cool on Huangâs marketing pitch. Although Trump greenlit sales of Nvidiaâs H200 chips to China (taking a cut of revenues for the US government), Beijing is strictly limiting imports.
Huangâs defenders insist heâs been arguing in good faith. Ben Thompson, the author of the influential Stratechery newsletter, argues that âit is entirely rational â and defensible â for Nvidia to want to sell chips to China.â By doing what he thinks is right, Thompson contends, Huang and Nvidia have âachieved unimaginable success.â It also needs pointing out that Huang stands by his patriotism. In a letter to staff, he insisted, âI love our country and our company.â
But having allegedly been compromised in a Chinese âhoneytrap,â one of the central figures in US technology and co-founder of one of the worldâs most valuable companies, will be hard pressed to convince US congressional investigators heâs always put US national interests first.
Theyâll want to know whether Alice Huang extracted any Nvidia secrets in the course of their affair. Did she have access to his unguarded laptop? Or his cellphone? Did she garner any insights into White House strategy during their assignations?
Of special interest to lawmakers looking at potential conflicts of interest: The Nvidia CEOâs relationship with the Singapore company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was an executive and that was under investigation by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it formed part of a clandestine supply chain shipping Nvidia chips to China and Southeast Asia data centers. The issue is whether the romance influenced his business decisions. (The New York Times reported on Monday that the Commerce Departmentâs inquiry was suspended following outreach from an Nvidia executive. The department denied wrongdoing, and Nvidia said the company regularly consults with officials.)
This drama will run and run. For the new Democrat-controlled Congress, the scandal offers multiple lines of attack against Trump. Iâve been predicting a backlash to the presidentâs China policies, widely criticized by politicians in both parties as weak and feckless â particularly his relaxed approach to tech transfers, but also on Taiwan, human rights, and military readiness in the Asia Pacific. The onslaught has now been brought forward.
Chris Coons, the incoming chair of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, signaled the start of hostilities in a post on X. âThe more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires,â he wrote âthe more Iâm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isnât corrupt.â
Whether Huang will keep his job or not is an open question. Those who claim that heâs irreplaceable may be underestimating the political storm thatâs about to break.
In any event, heâs lost the debate on chip sales to China, with significant commercial consequences for Nvidia, and even larger implications for superpower rivalry. He may well feel wronged, but as Thompson, the Stratechery analyst, put it, âhe has only himself to blame.â
Notable
- WIRED reported that in October 2025, around the same time he was first linked to Alice Huang, Jensen Huang hired consultants from the crisis communications firm Heller, which is known for managing sex scandals.

- Published
Israeli forces have shot dead a 14-year-old Palestinian boy during an operation in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say.
Moataz Daghlas was killed on Monday evening in the village of Burqa, north-west of Nablus, according to the Palestinian health ministry.
The Israeli military said soldiers identified "several terrorists who intended to hurl stones" in an area where stones had previously been thrown at Israeli vehicles. The soldiers fired towards them "to remove the threat", it added.
The Palestinian Red Crescent said its teams treated two people with gunshot wounds, but that Israeli forces blocked their access to a third wounded person and detained three volunteer paramedics.
Moataz Daghlas's relatives said Israeli authorities were withholding his body.
Meanwhile, Palestinian news agency Wafa identified the two Palestinians wounded during the raid as a 17-year-old child, who it said was shot in the abdomen and pelvis, and a 19-year-old man, who was shot in the hand.
According to the UN, at least 98 Palestinians, including 22 children, have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year.
Six Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank over the same period, it says.
The rules of engagement for Israeli forces were reportedly broadened after the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, allowing soldiers increased discretion to use lethal force against a perceived threat.
In June, the UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory said it had verified the killing of 241 Palestinian children by Israeli security forces and settlers in the West Bank since then.
Most of the children were teenage boys and, in many cases, Israeli authorities accused them of having engaged in stone-throwing as justification, it found.
The UN office said its assessment was that none of the children killed while involved in confrontations with Israeli forces had posed an imminent threat to life, which it said was the only legal justification for the use of lethal force in the West Bank under international law.

5030b51e9b3b.text: President Trump, with the clock ticking and congressional investigators closing in, plans to govern even more imperially , hell-bent on stretching executive power, targeting those on his enemies list, pardoning allies, and daring the courts and Congress to slow him down. Why it matters: Trump and his allies are exploring executive action on new tariffs and immigration restrictions, and asserting greater control over spending. On X over the weekend, Trump discussed targeting and perhaps jailing Democrats who investigate administration officials. He claimed politically motivated harassment . Trump is retooling his White House by elevating the one official who's synonymous with his all-gas-no-brakes style: Stephen Miller, who took over for Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff on Monday. Watch Miller and Russ Vought , the White House budget director, to understand how this approach will unfold. Both are architects and advocates of vastly expanding presidential power, believing there are virtually no restraints on what Trump can do as president. The Swamp can expect tougher sledding: Miller, unlike most of his predecessors, is driven more by ideology than by meetings with lobbyists or industry groups. "Stephen gives zero f*cks what K Street thinks," a Trump confidant told us. Between the lines: Midterm losses pushed Presidents Clinton and Obama to the center. Trump's instincts are the opposite: Assert maximal power. The playbook: Restore MAGA. Two years ago, MAGA — mostly its network of podcasts , YouTubers and online activists — was a powerful, united force in media and politics. Today it's a hot, divided mess. Trump's attention to his base drifted. Now Vice President Vance and Miller desperately want to rebuild and rev up MAGA. That's why ending the Iran war , curtailing aid to Israel and pushing harder on RFK Jr.'s MAHA agenda are suddenly top-tier topics. Rule by pen. Miller, Vought and White House lawyers have been drafting executive actions to govern without Congress, with Justice Department opinions ready to defend them, Reuters reported just before the election. Remember: Vought was an architect of the Heritage Foundation's Project 2025 blueprint for maximizing executive power in Trump II. Target enemies. Before, it was pure payback. Now, it's also a preemptive warning that the Trump administration will target anyone, including elected members of Congress who target them. Trump ally Roger Stone told us: "Many Democrat lawmakers are going to find themselves under indictment and fighting conviction. Watch." Purge the "deep state." The Supreme Court's ruling in a case about independent agencies, Trump v. Slaughter , widened the president's power to remove officials. "The Slaughter case gives the president tremendous powers," Trump said in an Election Day phone interview with CBS News' Robert Costa. The June ruling handed Trump the power to fire the heads of the FTC and other independent regulators ( like FERC ) for any reason or no reason. More monuments. Trump's pharaonic need to gild the White House, build a ballroom, erect a triumphal arch and slap his name on buildings is also an exercise in raw power. He told New York Magazine's Ben Terris why he's honoring himself: "Nobody will do it once I'm gone. When I leave here, nobody will." No one can stop him. The Republican resistance: Expect very little inside the new Congress. The reason: Most of Trump's Capitol Hill critics are gone. What's left is a much smaller, but more Trumpian, band of middle-aged and older white Republicans with margins too small to matter much. The Trump bet: Congressional Republicans will quickly feel Democrats are overreaching and unify in solidarity with Trump, even if it's forced or begrudging. Yes, but: One of Trump's most predictable attributes is his unpredictability. He said on election night that he'll " work together " with Democrats. What that may look like (with a heavy emphasis on "may"), based on reporting by Axios' Marc Caputo: Soften aspects of immigration enforcement, particularly regarding masked agents harassing U.S. citizens. Find common ground with MAHA's healthy food agenda, which has become the subject of vicious post-election infighting among Trump insiders. Sign legislation from the new Congress that would undo massive Medicaid cuts in his "One Big Beautiful Bill." The bottom line: Trump is still Trump. He's 80 and it shows. But he meets force with force and he'll go down swinging the more Democrats attack him. "Trump and his team are at our best when our backs are against the wall," one adviser told Caputo. "Trump comes out fighting. We're full-throated and full-throttle." Go deeper : Texas, Texas, Texas.

97a004069c98.text: House Republicans voted Tuesday evening to block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , shielding a top Trump administration official from a politically embarrassing rebuke. Why it matters: The vote marks a victory for Hegseth, the Trump administration and Republican leaders, who were bracing for the prospect of a rebellion within their own ranks. But the reprieve is probably short-lived: Democrats are all but guaranteed to force the issue again when they retake majorities in the House and Senate in January. The vote to refer the impeachment measure back to committee passed 211-204, with Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), the measure's sponsor, the lone "no" vote. Driving the news: Massie forced a procedural vote on his resolution to impeach Hegseth, alleging he has defied Congress and illegally continued the U.S. war in Iran. The Trump administration has been vehemently defending Hegseth , including through a statement opposing the impeachment effort issued shortly before the vote. "Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes? The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not," Vance said Tuesday on X . "Like so much of Congress , impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking. Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements," Vance added. Axios' Marc Caputo and Alex Isenstadt previously reported that Hegseth is on " thin ice " with Trump officials. Between the lines : Republican leaders protected their members from having to go on record on the politically difficult issue before Election Day after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) sent lawmakers home early to campaign. What's next: Tuesday's vote effectively kills any effort to impeach Hegseth this Congress.

EL PASO, Texas—Border communities voted in overwhelming numbers for Democratic candidates in the midterm elections last Tuesday.
Come January, every U.S. House member representing the U.S.-Mexico border—from San Diego to Brownsville—will be a Democrat. After a three-decade drought, Democrats swept all 18 statewide races in Texas.
Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa and Sen.-elect James Talarico were among the Democratic candidates who vowed to fight the border wall in Big Bend. Now comes the challenge of delivering on their campaign promises.
While Democrats chalked up major victories in the election, the Trump administration still has the funding and statutory authority to continue border wall construction through ecologically sensitive areas, including Big Bend. For more than a decade, Donald Trump has vowed to complete border wall construction from the Pacific to the Gulf of Mexico. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act turbocharged these efforts, appropriating $46.5 billion for border barriers.
Advocates on the border said in interviews that Democrats must seize the tools at their disposal to push back on border wall construction.
With majorities in the U.S. House and Senate, Democrats will have the authority to investigate Department of Homeland Security officials and compel them to provide contracts for border wall construction that have been confidential. In Austin, state legislators have already introduced bills for the upcoming session, when Democrats will control the state House for the first time in 24 years, to prohibit border wall construction in state parks. Incoming Texas Land Commissioner Ben Flores, a Democrat, told Inside Climate News he would not grant access to land managed by his office in the Big Bend sector for border wall construction.
“There is a renewed sense of hope and optimism,” said Martin Castro, watershed science director at the Rio Grande International Study Center in Laredo. “We had been telling landowners to please hold out until the midterms to potentially turn the tide against this project.”
Castro is part of a coalition opposing border wall construction in Laredo and surrounding communities, including landowners who are fighting construction on their property. He hopes incoming state officials will help landowners defend their private property rights.
Border wall construction, halted under former President Joe Biden, resumed and expanded to new areas after Trump returned to office last year. In February, DHS waived dozens of federal laws to fast-track construction in the Big Bend region of Texas, setting off a national outcry. Texans have spoken out against construction in the remote region that includes Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park and numerous privately owned tracts.
An injunction temporarily paused construction in the Big Bend sector last month. But the Supreme Court overturned that injunction Monday, allowing construction to resume. Elsewhere in Texas, contractors have continued working in the El Paso area, South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley to close gaps in the wall and line the Rio Grande with buoys.
While Democrats will hold a majority in the Texas House, Republicans will retain control of the Senate. But some Texas Republicans have spoken out against the wall in Big Bend, opening the possibility for bipartisan action.
On Monday, the first day to file bills for the upcoming legislative session, state Rep. Eddie Morales (D-Eagle Pass) and Sen. César Blanco (D-El Paso) introduced companion bills that would prohibit border security infrastructure on state park property. They both represent the Big Bend region.
Several Texas state parks are in the planned path of the border wall, including Big Bend Ranch, Seminole Canyon and Bentsen-Rio Grande Valley. Federal officials have already sought access to these parks for the wall, as reported by Inside Climate News.
Outside the parks, the border wall is slated to cross large swaths of land in West Texas managed by the Texas General Land Office. Land Commissioner-elect Flores previously told Inside Climate News that he would not voluntarily authorize border wall construction on GLO land and is “prepared for a prolonged legal battle.”
If Texas were to block construction on state park or GLO land, the federal government would have to condemn the property to proceed with the project. Condemnation would undoubtedly stall any construction plans.
In Washington, Democrats will hold the majority in the House and Senate and have vowed to take on corruption in the Trump administration. Advocates are urging them to weave the border wall into this broader effort. Talarico has called the border wall in Big Bend “a monument to corruption” and questioned billion-dollar no bid contracts.
DHS waived contracting and procurement laws in every border sector, allowing the agency to rapidly issue contracts for billions of dollars without going out for bids.

Castro, of the Rio Grande International Study Center, said that the sweeping authority DHS has to issue waivers under the 2005 Real ID Act must be reexamined.
“The waiver authority is so far-reaching that, until that goes away, the threat to these communities is never going to go away,” he said. “Can we work with a bipartisan delegation on the repeal of the waivers?”
Adam Isacson, an analyst at the Washington Office on Latin America, said that with Democrats leading the House and Senate Committees on Homeland Security come January, they could investigate these contracts.
“Transparency is where the Democrats have the biggest short-term power right now,” Isacson said. “[The contracts] could technically be legal. But they could be very embarrassing.”

- Published
Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.
Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe.
The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (Â£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday.
Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools.
It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race.
Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.
Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked.
Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern.
According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington earlier this year warning that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Beijing has rejected claims that the Nvidia chief has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China".
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang, who had said he had "no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed him.
However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing.
The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. The committee has the authority to subpoena Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before it, if deemed necessary.
When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe.
Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce.
Joon Kim is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focusing on fraud and other criminal acts.
The Nvidia investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with the company.
He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity.
It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang.
A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI.

d16e41542597.text:
The Scene
Joon Kim has taken down mobsters, pursued a congressman, and investigated sexual harassment claims that toppled a New York governor. His latest assignment will decide the fate of a $4 trillion dollar company the global economy depends on.
The former acting US Attorney for the Southern District of New York was tapped to investigate whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, following Huangâs bombshell admission Sunday that the chief executive had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Kim, a 55-year-old prosecutor who joined Wachtell Lipton last month, will lead an internal probe overseen by a committee of independent directors, into whether Nvidiaâs Huang compromised trade secrets or more pressingly, the USâ national security interests. The company has said it has confidence in its CEO and has âno reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.â A spokesperson for Wachtell declined to comment on the firmâs and Kimâs behalf.
Shares in Nvidia have dropped 10% since Huangâs admission, knocking $500 billion off the companyâs market value and stoking worries about the future of a company that underpins an AI financing buildout that has ensnared most of the global financial system. It comes against a fraught national security backdrop in which US officials have been warning for months of foreign influence campaigns and corporate espionage.
A tangled web
Huang, a close confidant of US President Donald Trump, has pushed Nvidia to take stakes in hundreds of companies across the AI boom it supplies. The company has also entered into billions of dollars worth of financing deals up and down Wall Street.Â
Even Kimâs own employer, Wachtell, Lipton, is not immune: OpenAI is one of Wachtellâs highest-profile clients, and the law firmâs M&A advisors are working on the companyâs pending IPO, according to people familiar with the matter. Nvidia is a major OpenAI investor and the primary supplier of the chips that underpin the data centers (which Nvidia also finances) that power OpenAIâs models.
Corporate probes can range from window dressing to essentially prosecutorial in nature, and Nvidia has $4 trillion reasons to limit its damage. Itâs unclear how far Nvidiaâs board will let Kim roam, but the board has already drummed up corporate governance concerns: The unusually long-tenured board lacks the experience and stature typically found at companies as large as Nvidiaâs and has let Huang run the company with no clear successor and more than 50 direct reports.
Mob bosses
Kim began his career at New Yorkâs Southern District more than two decades ago, working in the organized crime unit before leaving for Cleary Gottlieb in 2006. The son of a South Korean diplomat, Kim traveled around the world, including in Jordan and the UK.
In his first stint as a federal prosecutor, Kim took on mob boss John âJuniorâ Gotti in a federal racketeering trial, trying him for the kidnapping of future New York mayoral candidate Curtis Sliwa. âHis entire adult life, John Jr. has thought himself special, entitled to everything, accountable for nothing,â Kim said at the time.
His former colleagues describe Kim as dogged, citing his time at the Southern District in 2013, under Attorney Preet Bharara, where Kim pursued a successful case against disgraced former Congressman Anthony Weiner and briefly ran the Southern District after Trump fired Bharara.
Kim returned to Cleary in 2018, where he led a number of internal investigations into allegations of executive wrongdoing at large corporations, including Nissan Motorsâ probe into former CEO Carlos Ghosn. But among his most defining cases was New York Attorney General Letitia Jamesâ investigation into sexual harassment allegations against then-Governor Andrew Cuomo, which led to his 2021 resignation. Cuomoâs office was ârife with bullying, fear and intimidation,â Kim said when announcing his findings.
A sensitive assignment
Before Sunday, Huang and spokespeople for the company had publicly denied that the Nvidia CEO had an affair with Alice Huang. The company abruptly changed tack on Sunday, when Huang wrote a letter to employees admitting to the affair and announcing a plan to initiate an independent probe.
The company had assembled an independent committee to oversee the investigation and was on Sunday leaning toward tapping former Cooley CEO Stephen Neal, the Financial Times reported and Semafor can confirm. Some Nvidia directors also suggested tapping Cooley to run the independent probe, other people familiar with the matter said. Cooley is Nvidiaâs longtime outside counsel and would have exposed the company to criticism that the probe wasnât independent, especially since Cooley is best known for its tech and IP practices, and isnât considered by white-shoe lawyers to have a top-tier white-collar investigations practice.
Nvidia declined to comment on either the nature of the independent committee or on whether directors considered tapping Cooley.

24de1952662e.text: By — Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/the-time-is-now-for-change-bernie-sanders-wont-support-schumer-for-senate-democratic-leader Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 'The time is now for change.' Bernie Sanders won't support Schumer for Senate Democratic leader Politics Nov 10, 2026 5:26 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he would not be supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer as the Democratic majority leader in the new Congress, setting up a seismic confrontation after the party's sweep to power in the midterm elections. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Sanders was joined by Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan at a news conference at the Capitol, and together they said there needs to be a new generation of leadership and a vigorous debate about the party's direction and future. A number of incoming Democratic senators have echoed the call, signaling that they would support another candidate over Schumer. "The time is now for change," said Sanders, the independent from Vermont and essentially the father of modern progressivism in the U.S. "And I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader." Slotkin, who said she is not actively seeking the job herself, explained that she wants to see potential Senate leaders present a full plan about the priorities for the new majority. "I'm a no until and unless I see that from anyone," she said. The showdown has been building as Democrats marched across the Senate map to flip Republican-held seats far beyond those that were initially competitive, including in Texas, Kansas and South Carolina. READ MORE: Democrats plan to use new power to rein in Trump's education agenda. But their tools are limited Schumer recruited high-profile candidates that helped secure the majority, including Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Sen.-elect Roy Cooper in North Carolina. But his preferred candidates also lost primaries in Michigan and Maine, with the progressive candidates prevailing and then going on to win their general elections. Democrats, particularly in the party's progressive wing, have been bombarding congressional offices with phone calls saying it's time for new leadership. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and other progressives have pushed for Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland as a potential contender. Van Hollen, who has previously said he is considering a run for president in 2028, is now also considering a run for Senate leader. It is not clear how much backing he would have. "I am in the process right now of calling my colleagues," Van Hollen said at a Washington event Tuesday. Schumer, 75, has shown few signs of stepping aside, especially after he just led his party to power. New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, gave a full throated defense of Schumer on Tuesday, saying "this caucus is grateful for the work of Senator Schumer." "I'm confident I will be elected," Schumer said at the Capitol. Pressed about his own future in an interview with AP shortly after the party's election wins, Schumer said he was focused on the year ahead. "The focus has got to be on getting things done," he told AP. While Republicans have been meeting behind closed doors Tuesday to choose their party leaders for the next Congress, the Democrats in the Senate have just begun those conversations ahead of elections expected later this month. Associated Press writer Steven Sloan contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. The unfolding Nvidia saga has intensified scrutiny of the legal means by which top Chinese firms are able to access advanced American compute.
While Megaspeed, the Singaporean firm at the center of the scandal, is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, Washingtonâs export controls have spawned lucrative opportunities for Asian cloud operators that get their hands on the most advanced Nvidia chips, offering a legal loophole to Chinese hyperscalers.
Singapore-based DayOne is worth roughly $15 billion and counts ByteDance as its top customer, while Moonshot has looked to tap Nvidia chips hosted in Europe, highlighting âthe nonsensical nature of our export control regime,â a Carnegie Endowment expert said. âNo administration has had the cojones to do something about it.â

Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents.
Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning.
US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show.
Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device.
The BBC has contacted his representatives.
Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court".
He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician".
"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday.
"We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.
Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.
Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.
In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.
Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention.
He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.
FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".
Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".
He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.
The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

266794cec38b.text: By — Larry Neumeister, Associated Press Larry Neumeister, Associated Press By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/u-s-charges-3-men-with-plotting-terror-attacks-including-planned-assault-on-uk-airbase Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. charges 3 men with plotting terror attacks, including planned assault on UK airbase Nation Nov 10, 2026 5:11 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — Three men, including one already jailed in the United States, were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S. as well as a planned assault on a British airbase used by the U.S. Air Force. READ MORE: British police rearrest 2 men on suspicion of assisting Iran over suspected plot at a U.S.-run air base Charges against Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court. Only al-Saadi is in custody. U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed. "These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members," McDonald said. "The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real." Attorney General Todd Blanche said: "Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government." The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight on Sept. 27 on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England. A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested several days later. All the men were released on bail. British authorities linked the incident to Tehran, and though Iran denied involvement, the arrests prompted the U.S. to withdraw its bombers that had been stationed there. The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States. RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East. According to the indictment, al-Saadi used coded language in communications with relatives from jail to direct that money be passed along to others who could carry out attacks. The indictment alleged that the three men conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah. In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran. He called himself a "prisoner of war." He has been held without bail since. His lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday on the latest development. Both Kata'ib Hizballah and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say Al-Saadi was a Kata'ib Hizballah commander. Tucker reported from Washington. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. In a Mexican restaurant in north-east Australia, the nacho bowls are served by staff from France, Italy, Ireland and Argentina.
Cairns has long attracted a young and transient international crowd, who enjoy the tropical lifestyle while earning money for travel.
But one nationality is in shorter supply than it used to be.
"You get far fewer British backpackers looking for jobs here these days," says Mexicairns owner Peter McLeay.
It's a trend McLeay has noticed since mid-2023, when a free trade deal between the UK and Australia kicked in.
That agreement - as well as tariff-free trade in Tim Tams and Penguins - included special treatment for Brits on working holiday visas: exemption from having to find jobs in regional or remote places if they wanted to remain beyond a year.
That, along with an increase in the age limit from 30 to 35 saw backpacker visas issued to Brits surging from 47,200 in 2023-24 to just over 77,000 in 2025-26, according to the latest Australian government data.
Without the incentive to go regional, many are choosing to base themselves in the big cities, or, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, "Bondi or Coogee" - two of Sydney's most famous beachside suburbs.
Now though, with Brits making up almost a quarter of all 323,000 backpacker visas issued last year, his government wants the free trade deal to be revisited.
A privilege not enjoyed by others
"Many Brits don't treat it as a working holiday anymore. It's more a three-year career break," says Dan McConnell, general manager of the Mad Monkey backpacker hostel chain.
He says Brits used to be the largest clientele at its Cairns accommodation but "now French outnumber British three to one".
"We see the Brits get to Sydney, decide it's the coolest place in the world, and stay there," he adds.
It's a privilege not enjoyed by working holidaymakers from other countries who must do at least 88 days of "specified regional work" in industries that need a seasonal or temporary workforce - including agriculture, fisheries, tourism and hospitality - if they want to quality for a second year extension, and six months to stay a third year.
Barely a month ago, Albanese ruled out forcing British backpackers to do the same, accepting it as part of the trade deal.
But, under pressure from businesses here in Far North Queensland and other regional Australian communities, who are concerned about a lack of labour, the mood music has changed.
Last week Albanese met UK counterpart Andy Burnham at the meeting of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.
And alongside AI, gender violence online and the AUKUS defence pact, backpackers were on the agenda.
Despite speculation in the Australian media, no immediate announcement was made. Albanese instead told reporters that he had pushed for a change in the rules on backpackers and that Burnham had been "very constructive about it".
"We'll work those issues through over coming weeks," he said adding that the free trade agreement was not set in stone and tweaks could be made "if there are good policy reasons".
Backpackers make up one in seven farm jobs across Australia, with about 52,000 people on working holiday visas doing jobs in horticulture each year, according to the National Farmers Federation.
It welcomed Albanese's discussions with Burnham, but said the issue of worker shortages in agriculture was far broader than the UK deal.
Of greater concern are wider proposals, announced in September, to cut net migration into Australia, under political pressure from the resurgent right wing populist One Nation party and the opposition coalition.
That includes an overhaul of the working holiday visa system, introducing a ballot for backpackers wanting to extend their stay â capped at 45,000 for people wanting a second year in Australia (down from 57,000 who qualified this year) and just 5,000 allowed to remain for a third year (compared with 31,000 this year).
This, the federation says, is "a low blow".
Those plans are still out for consultation, but immigration officials have slowed processing rates for some working holiday visa applications and paused them from several countries.
Tourism Tropical North Queensland chief executive Mark Olsen has also been among those lobbying Albanese in Canberra - telling him that backpackers brought both the spending power and the temporary labour needed to fill seasonal roles in a region famed as a gateway to the Great Barrier Reef and the Unesco world heritage listed Daintree rainforest.
Young Brits temporarily living and working in this region peaked at around 20,000 he says. Now it's closer to 11,000.
"Numbers have dropped significantly since the UK free trade agreement kicked in when border arrangements returned to normal [after the pandemic] in 2023 ," he said.
A two-way street
Cairns restaurateur Fintan Rafferty says that of about 180 staff on his payroll across four venues, only five are British. Prior to the visa rule change, that was closer to 25.
UK workers came with good skills in hospitality and "were willing to work, and to work flexible hours", he told the BBC.
And, he said, it was a two-way street. "The pay is very good, the conditions are very good. And one of the great things about the 88-days rule is that it forces people to travel. It's enriching their experience."
Bucking the trend, at the bar of Gilligan's backpackers, Paige Tomlinson serves vodka and soda with plenty of ice and a broad South Yorkshire accent.
The 27-year-old, from Barnsley, has been in Cairns for four months, attracted by the "chilled" lifestyle and local waterfalls.
"Most people prefer Sydney and they question me all the time why I'm here," she laughs. "But I got to Sydney and I just didn't like it. It was too busy, too much like London and I don't like London."
She says she'd like to see the regional work requirement brought in for all Brits, "getting them out their comfort zone".
"If every other country's got to do it, why should we not?"

25b898aa2c84.text: Federal Reserve Bank of New York ; Note: Not adjusted for inflation; Chart: Axios Visuals Americans' credit card balances hit a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter, according to a new report released by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Why it matters: Falling behind on credit card payments can trap struggling households in a cycle of fees, damaged credit and increasingly expensive borrowing. The latest figures show that financial pain is concentrated in lower-income communities, even as delinquency rates improve nationally. By the numbers: Consumer credit card balances rose by $22 billion in the third quarter, an increase of 1.7%. That's $52 billion higher than a year earlier. The figures aren't adjusted for inflation, meaning some of the increase reflects higher prices rather than greater borrowing in real terms. Total household debt, including mortgages and student and auto loans, rose $334 billion, reaching a record $19.1 trillion in the third quarter. The total is up $5 trillion since 2019, just before the pandemic. Yes, but: Fewer credit card balances are becoming seriously delinquent, a sign of some improvement in Americans' ability to keep up with payments. The rate at which credit card debt becomes seriously overdue edged down to 6.9% in the third quarter, though it remains notably above the 5.2% recorded before the pandemic. Between the lines: A separate report from the New York Fed on Tuesday showed Americans in lower-income neighborhoods are having a harder time keeping up with credit card payments relative to their wealthier counterparts. Delinquency rates remain above pre-pandemic levels across all neighborhood-income groups, with the gap between the richest and poorest areas increasing since 2022. In the lowest-income neighborhoods, 10.3% of credit card balances became seriously delinquent over the past year — more than double the 4.4% rate in the wealthiest neighborhoods. The big picture: Average credit card balance per borrower is now $6,678, according to TransUnion's Q3 insights report. Borrowers under 30 had the highest rate of credit card debt newly becoming at least 90 days overdue, the Fed's report found. What we're watching: Democrats won the midterms promising to lower prices — but delivering relief that voters can actually feel in their household budgets will be difficult to fulfill.

John Thune as leader of the GOP conference after a tense day of discussions about steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority. But Senate Republicans vented their frustrations in three separate meetings on Tuesday after an election wipeout that cost them at least seven Senate seats. Some Republicans had tried to delay the leadership decision, but the conference voted to proceed, said Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson, who had pushed to postpone. He walked out of the room as the voting began. West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice said after the first meeting that "we want to be thoughtful and do the right thing." Justice said there was a "legitimate argument that, good gracious, if we lost as badly as we lost, why would we continue on with the same leadership?" At the same time, the current GOP leadership "didn't cause this problem to happen," Justice said. "They do a good job." The angst — and the indecision — comes as frustrated Republicans are just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for their future. Two additional Senate races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers. Several senators had already called on Republican leadership to delay the elections, which include contests for other party leaders as well and are held in the small Old Senate Chamber. Josh Hawley said he isn't aware of anyone else running for leader, but "maybe there would be" if they waited. "I just think that we've got a lot of things that we've got to think through, and I think that to just rush into this and just ratify all of the same leadership, what message does that send?" Hawley told reporters after walking out. "If you don't think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don't know what planet you're on," he said. Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, said before the meeting that they would have a "very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here and then we'll see what the consensus of the conference is." No alternative to Thune has emerged Hawley said the discussion was a "frank" and "honest" open microphone meeting and some senators discussed their own races this year — some who won, and some who lost. Republicans in the meeting were also pushing Thune to stay in session around the clock in the coming weeks to push through war spending and other party priorities before they lose power. "We need a plan to get the Republican agenda done," said Florida Sen. Rick Scott. Before the meeting, Johnson, the Wisconsin senator, had circulated a letter asking for the delay. He said the conference needs to do some "real soul-searching" but conceded that there's no one else on the ballot. "That's part of our problem, who would want the job?" he said, turning to a reporter and joking, "Do you want it?" Oklahoma Sen. Jim Lankford said that there is "widespread support" among Republican senators for Thune, who has made it a point to hear out different viewpoints before he makes major decisions and has maintained close relationships with the rank and file — a different approach from his predecessor, McConnell. Lankford said he supported having the elections on Tuesday because many of the new GOP senators are already in town for freshman orientation. "It's a pretty complicated role to be able to manage," Lankford said of Thune's leadership post. "No one wants that job." Walking into the meeting, South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds said most senators are ready to move forward. It is time to have "leadership in place," he said. Thune has navigated Trump in his first two years as leader Thune has spent much of the last two years navigating President Donald Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate. While backing Trump on most policies, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president's political base. READ MORE: Trump-backed redistricting sought a midterm edge for Republicans. It didn't work But Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is "a very fine man." The election is "up to the Senate," Trump said. The soul-searching comes as lawmakers are trying to wrap up the year's work — funding the government and seeing if there are some issues where they can work together, including an energy permitting bill that moved forward on a bipartisan vote Monday evening. When he gets the chance to speak at the meeting, Thune is expected to emphasize his collaborative approach to his colleagues and point out what they did get done in the last year — including the tax and spending cuts legislation and an attempt at reining in the chaotic annual spending process. 5d05e1edf79b.text: House Republicans elected Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) as their new leader Tuesday, handing the reins of the battered GOP conference to one of its most prominent conservative firebrands. Why it matters: Jordan's victory marks a major shake-up in House Republican leadership, elevating a founding member of the hardline Freedom Caucus who campaigned as an alternative to the leaders who presided over the GOP's crushing midterm defeat . Jordan bested Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.), who had served as the No. 2 House Republican since 2014, in the conference-wide secret ballot for minority leader. Scalise trailed Jordan by 33 votes. Jordan's victory signals an appetite among House Republicans for a more confrontational approach as they prepare to enter the minority. State of play: Jordan and Scalise entered Tuesday's election locked in a tight race, with both camps expressing confidence in their chances of winning. Jordan drew public support from some of the conference's most conservative members, who argued Republicans needed a change in direction after their devastating midterm losses. Scalise leaned on his longstanding relationships across the conference and his decade-plus of experience in leadership. The big picture: Jordan's ascent represents a remarkable turnaround for a conservative agitator who spent much of his career challenging the Republican establishment before becoming one of President Trump's most vocal allies. He'll be tasked with uniting a fractured Republican conference and leading the party's efforts to reclaim the House majority in 2028. Zoom out: Beyond the top job, current whip Tom Emmer (Minn.) beat back a challenge from Rep. August Pfluger (Texas) to stay on as minority whip. Conference Chair: Lisa McClain (Mich.) won a three-way race with Reps. Erin Houchin (Ind.) and Greg Steube (Fla.). Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional vote results.

Hudson lost North Carolina's 9th district to Richard Ojeda, a former Army major who became a liberal social media phenomenon during President Donald Trump's first term. He ran multiple races in West Virginia then moved back to North Carolina, where he had served at Fort Bragg, and successfully ran against Hudson. "Our victory is not just impressive because of how many seats we gained — although we did gain a lot — what was incredible last night was how far we reached into deep red territory," said Rep. Suzan DelBene, chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. Ojeda arrived on Capitol Hill this week, one of several new members who pulled off upset victories this year. Here's a look at some of them. Colorado 5th district This district is home to NORAD, Fort Carson and the Air Force Academy, as well as the evangelical group Focus on the Family. Although Colorado Springs has been a conservative stronghold for years, the city has been slowly turning more moderate as young families move in. Its veteran population has also been unsettled by Trump's approach to the military and the Iran war. Jessica Killin, a Democrat and former Army captain, capitalized on this to run as a moderate against Rep. Jeff Crank, who had previously run the Colorado chapter of the conservative group Americans For Prosperity. She hammered him for falling in line behind Trump once he got into the House. Nevada 2nd district Former state lawmaker Teresa Benitez-Thompson made history as the first Democrat to win Nevada's 2nd Congressional District after her Republican opponent David Flippo's campaign was muddied by accusations of exaggerating his military record and failing to release his required financial disclosures on time. READ MORE: Nevada is set to have one of nation's premier races for governor as Democrats seek to reclaim seat Benitez-Thompson campaigned as a moderate with longtime northern Nevada roots, contrasting herself with Flippo, who aligned himself closely to Trump and moved from southern Nevada to join the race after longtime Republican Rep. Mark Amodei announced his retirement. Amodei refused to endorse Flippo, calling him a fraud. For the first time ever, all of Nevada's congressional seats will be held by Democrats. Before him, former House Speaker Paul Ryan held the seat for two decades, and no Democrat had won since 1993. All of those factors made it improbable that Democratic newcomer Mitchell Berman, running his first campaign for any office, would come out on top this year. But Berman, an emergency room nurse, tapped into voter anger and leveraged his middle-class background to beat Steil by nearly 4 points. The outcome will ripple through Wisconsin politics because Steil was widely considered as a likely candidate for U.S. Senate down the road. Texas 23rd district The race opened up when Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales announced he wouldn't run for reelection after admitting to an affair with a former staff member who later died by suicide. Primary voters chose Brandon Herrera, a gun enthusiast YouTuber with some 4 million subscribers and a history of caustic commentary, to run in his place. Democrats put up Katy Padilla Stout, a lawyer and former teacher, but she was believed to have little chance. The district hadn't elected a Democrat since 2012. She ended up winning by 8 points. Texas 9th district This district used to be considered so blue that Republicans didn't even put up a candidate to run there in 2024. But a year later at Trump's urging, the state legislature redrew the congressional map, making it far more conservative. Democrats and their donors figured the seat was a lost cause as Democrat Leticia Gutierrez, who had previously worked in Houston city government, went up against Republican Alex Mealer, a well-financed military veteran who was active in conservative politics. Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia were among those who have attended a memorial service in tribute to the 69 victims of last month's deadly train crash.
The accident occurred when one train, travelling at high speed, ploughed into the back of another that was stationary on the Madrid-Seville line, near the small town of Urda, about 40 miles from Toledo.
It was the worst rail tragedy in Spain since 2013. Twenty-eight people remain in hospital.
"The tragic accident in Urda has left our families, our towns and our society with a pain that is difficult to accept," Archbishop Cerro Chaves told those present.
Representatives of those killed carried lit candles to the front of the cathedral and placed them next to the main altar. The first reading of the service was by Ana BenÃtez, sister of David BenÃtez, a 38-year-old father-of-two who died.
The king and queen were met with applause by bystanders as they entered the cathedral and at the end of the service, after Catholic Mass, they spoke to relatives of the victims.
Senior politicians also attended the service, including the leader of the opposition People's Party, Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano GarcÃa-Page, and Transport and Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo.
Cuerpo took on the transport portfolio following the resignation last week of Ãscar Puente from the post.
Puente had come under mounting pressure following the crash, Spain's second major rail tragedy this year after 46 people died in a collision on the same high-speed line in January.
Some local people from the town of Adamuz in Andalusia, where that accident happened, as well as residents of Urda, were present for the memorial service.
The investigation into the recent accident is still in progress. Puente suggested that human error combined with a glitch in the safety system may have been the cause.
The tragedy happened a month before the 29 November general election and is seen as likely to hurt Socialist Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez's attempts to secure re-election.
The ceremony took place on the same day as a nationwide strike by train drivers, who are demanding greater safety on the rail network.
Rail services were also expected to be affected across the country on Wednesday due to a general strike, led by housing activists calling for urgent measures to control rental costs.
