Crimes committed by the late disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein after 2005 could have been prevented were it not for "failures" by federal investigators and prosecutors, a congressional investigation has concluded.
The Republican-led US House Oversight Committee on Tuesday released its final report into what it described as the "decades-long" mishandling of the criminal investigations into Epstein and his long-term associate Ghislaine Maxwell.
The report's findings are based on interviews and depositions with witnesses, government files, and financial records over a 15-month period.
Epstein died in 2019 as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.
"While some of these failures involved an exercise in poor judgement by the USAO, others appeared to be the result of Epstein's pervasive and wide-reaching influence," the report reads, referring to the US Attorney's Office.
It states that, rather than fully investigating allegations in other states, the USAO for the Southern District of Florida entered an agreement with Epstein in 2007 allowing him to evade federal prosecution.
Regarding Epstein's death in a New York prison, investigators concluded this was a result of "a series of institutional failures at the facility," which included staffing shortages, overworked employees, poor recordkeeping, and lax security practices.
Testimony the panel solicited was "unable to definitively dispel certain theories" surrounding Epstein's death, the report states, including accounting for a lapse in surveillance footage.
It found the justice department (DoJ) failed to communicate about document releases and that deficient redactions exposed survivors' sensitive personal information.
The DoJ has released millions of pages of Epstein-related files in response to legislation from Congress.
Earlier this year, the department had to remove thousands of documents related to Epstein from its website after victims said their identities had been compromised.
The report also alleges that financial institutions like American Express enabled human trafficking and immigration fraud, by allowing Epstein to use decoy flights and dummy itineraries to transport foreign workers across borders. The BBC has contacted American Express for comment.
The investigative panel recommended that Congress should pass legislation to prevent the weaponisation of non-disclosure agreements, which they said Epstein used to silence survivors.
"Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims," said James Comer, the Republican chairman of the committee.
He called upon the DoJ to "interview or re-interview key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records.
The department remains under bipartisan scruntiny regarding the Epstein files.
In the state of New Mexico, where Epstein had a ranch, the top state prosecutor accused the DoJ of stonewalling their criminal investigation.
"With all due respect, the Chairman's recommendations have already been addressed," a spokesperson for the department said in response to Comer's report.
"The Attorney General has repeatedly said that the Epstein case is not closed and there is no statute of limitations on human trafficking."
The report accuses Democrats of being "obsessed" with trying to implicate US President Donald Trump and that an "unfounded witch hunt continued without regard for the interests of survivors".
Trump has previously said he was friendly with Epstein before they fell out in 2004. The president's name has appeared thousands of times in the Epstein files but there is no suggestion that appearing in the documents implies any wrongdoing.
The committee's review of documents did not identify any that would implicate Trump, the report concluded.
In a statement, Rep Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, alleged his Republican colleagues "released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein".
Garcia accused the justice department of withholding "over 2.5 million pages of documents".
"We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation," said Garcia, who is expected to lead the committee when Democrats take control of Congress in January following the recent midterm elections.
The family members of one of Epstein's most prominent accusers, the late Virginia Roberts Giuffre, thanked Comer for releasing Tuesday's report.
"A sentence from the report stands out to us: 'Questions remain as to whether the DOJ has released all its relevant documents.' We could not agree more and urge that all 7 million-plus files be released," Sky and Amanda Roberts said in a statement.
"There are many more individuals who have yet to be identified and brought to justice," they said.

Watch: E-bike battery explodes into massive fireball inside Oregon home
Home surveillance footage shows the moment an e-bike battery burst into flames and exploded inside a home in Troutdale, Oregon. After investigating a strange smell, a mother and son notice smoke coming from the battery before it erupts into a huge fireball, followed by smaller explosions.
A second angle shows the battery charging moments before the blast, as occupants rush to escape. All six people in the home got out safely, though a cat died in the fire, according to local reports.

5ceda6872c0b.text: By — Kevin Freking, Associated Press Kevin Freking, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/house-republicans-pick-ohio-rep-jim-jordan-to-lead-them-in-the-minority Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter House Republicans pick Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan to lead them in the minority Politics Updated on Nov 10, 2026 4:18 PM EST — Published on Nov 10, 2026 2:52 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio won the race Tuesday to serve as House Republican leader as the GOP prepares for its new role in the minority. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Jordan, who serves as chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, defeated Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana in a secret ballot election of Republicans who will serve in the next Congress. The vote was 106-73. Jordan, 62, is a co-founder of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus and served as its first chairman. His candidacy appealed to those looking for new leadership in the wake of last week's election debacle and to those who like his hard-hitting political style. Jordan as minority leader will inherit a historically small House Republican conference that is only beginning to grapple with its loss of power as President Donald Trump serves out his final two years in office. Leading the party back to the House majority in 2028 is sure to be a stiff climb, given the scope of Democratic victories in the midterms. Jordan warned of the coming Democratic efforts on oversight, with numerous investigations of the Trump administration expected. "Our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democratic Party is — offense, not defense, wins elections," Jordan said, a nod to his pugnacious reputation in committee hearings. Trump said he was staying out of the race. Scalise and Jordan were a familiar match-up Scalise and Jordan had faced off before, both running to serve as House speaker after Kevin McCarthy was ousted from the job a little more than three years ago. Neither was able to rally the support necessary to secure the position, which eventually went to Mike Johnson, who is stepping aside from the leadership in the new Congress. Scalise, 61, has held key GOP leadership positions going back to 2014, serving as party whip and then as majority leader. In 2017, he was critically wounded when a gunman opened fire at a baseball practice where several Republican lawmakers and staffers were preparing for an annual charity baseball game against Democrats. In 2023, he was stricken with multiple myeloma, a blood cancer that was successfully treated. WATCH: Hegseth says House impeachment push is about 'policy disagreements' not high crimes "Overcoming adversity is nothing new to me," Scalise said in his pitch to colleagues. He also emphasized his fundraising prowess, noting he raised $67.9 million for this year's midterms, with about a third of that going directly to individual House campaigns and the National Republican Congressional Committee. But the majority of Republicans opted for Jordan, who emphasized his experience battling with Democrats in committee rooms. "I am battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats' playbook," Jordan said. Other positions are also up for grabs In addition to the race for minority leader, Reps. Tom Emmer of Minnesota and August Pfluger of Texas are vying to serve as Republican whip, the No. 2 position in the leadership hierarchy. Three candidates are seeking to serve as conference chair: Reps. Lisa McClain of Michigan, Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida. The Republicans who will serve in the next Congress will hear from the candidates in the morning, followed in the afternoon by voting through secret ballot. Democrats will hold their leadership elections next week. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York is expected to become the next House speaker, the first African-American to hold the job, and Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts is expected to become the next majority leader. She would be the first woman to hold that position. Associated Press writer Joey Cappelletti contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 94120362c558.text: By — Brian Melley, Associated Press Brian Melley, Associated Press By — Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press By — Emma Burrows, Associated Press Emma Burrows, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/u-s-soldier-arrested-in-britain-accused-of-espionage-linked-to-russia Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. soldier arrested in Britain accused of espionage linked to Russia Nation Updated on Nov 10, 2026 4:30 PM EST — Published on Nov 10, 2026 2:41 PM EST LONDON (AP) — A member of the U.S. Army was arrested Tuesday in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police said. The arrest comes during heightened concern over threats to American forces stationed in Britain and tension between Moscow and much of Europe. The 41-year-old man, who was not named, was arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of violating two sections of the National Security Act 2023: assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information. READ MORE: 5 men arrested near UK air base used by U.S. in Iran war on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act U.S. Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of the Army's Counterintelligence Command, described the suspect as a senior soldier but offered no other details on his identity in a news release. When asked for more details, U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command declined to provide more information about the case. The Metropolitan Police said its counterterror forces worked closely with the FBI and U.S. military. In the news release, FBI Director Kash Patel called it an "important arrest" dealing with allegations of espionage that are of "utmost concern" for the U.S. and its allies. "This FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners," Patel said. The suspect was in custody at a London police station, officials said. Searches were conducted at two locations in Gloucestershire, a county about 90 miles (140 kilometers) west of London. Police said the arrest was not related to other counterterrorism investigations, indicating no connection with a suspected terror plot linked to Iran in September at a U.S.-run base in Britain, RAF Fairford, near Gloucester. After the threat, the U.S. Air Force withdrew bombers that had been used to strike Iran from RAF Fairford. The Air Force this week also relocated aircraft from another base in Britain — RAF Mildenhall — because of a threat, which The Wall Street Journal reported was related to Iran. Tuesday's arrest near Gloucester appears to be separate from those incidents, with authorities saying the case was related to Russia. Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine, The Associated Press has tracked around 200 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe blamed on Russia by Western officials that included organizing plots to set fire to warehouses, launching drones and trying to kill enemies abroad as well as stealing defense technology and carrying out cyberattacks on critical European infrastructure. One of the most recent incidents was an attempted drone attack on a German airport in August that officials blamed on Russia. It prompted Germany to shut a Russian consulate. Toropin reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Ben Finley in Washington contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Police in Bangladesh have fired tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse supporters of the deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who are demanding her return to the country.
A police vehicle was set on fire in Gopalganj district, where the banned student wing of Hasina's Awami League party clashed with security forces.
Nationwide protests by pro-Hasina activists started a day after the former leader said she had requested a passport to return to Bangladesh from exile in India.
The demonstrations by the student wing, called Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL), are seen as the first organised show of force by Hasina's supporters since she was ousted in August 2024 following a huge uprising against her rule.
Traffic was disrupted in some parts of the country as protesters tried to set up roadblocks using burning tyres.
Several passenger vehicles were also set on fire in various parts of Bangladesh in the run up to the protest.
A 60-year-old driver of a passenger bus was killed by smoke inhalation after people set fire to the vehicle in the city of Faridpur early on Tuesday.
Elsewhere, about 200 protesters briefly blocked traffic on the 6.2km (4 mile)-long Padma bridge across the Ganges, that connects the capital Dhaka with the south-western region.
Bangladeshi local media said dozens of crude bombs exploded in the past few days in Dhaka and elsewhere.
"Any attempt to worsen the law-and-order situation or create instability through any conspiracy within the country from across the border (India) will not be allowed to succeed," Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.
"Our supporters were not responsible for the violent incidents. They were carried out by unknown miscreants. We believe in peaceful protests," a senior leader of the BCL, who is now in exile in a foreign country, said.
Hasina fled to neighbouring India two years ago following a massive uprising, bringing an end to her 15-year reign.
Opposition parties accused Hasina of jailing political rivals, supressing dissent and overseeing widespread human rights abuses. She always denied the charges.
The United Nations has estimated up to 1,400 people were killed, most by gunfire from security forces, during the anti-government protests in 2024.
The activities of the Awami League were banned soon after she fled the country and it was not allowed to contest the February general election.
A special Bangladeshi tribunal last year sentenced her to death in absentia after being found guilty of crimes against humanity.
She has denied all the charges, calling the trial "biased and politically motivated".
Despite the death penalty threat, Hasina said she wanted to return to Bangladesh in December and requesteded the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi to issue her with a passport.
But the Bangladeshi government said the country would not provide a passport to her and called her "a terrorist".
"She is a fugitive criminal. We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's junior foreign affairs minister, said.
"Should we treat her like an ordinary commercial traveller and tell her to come and visit her in-laws' residence?" Kobir asked.
A state prosecutor in Bangladesh on Tuesday said the verdict would be executed if she came back, saying she had missed the opportunity to appeal.
Awami League leaders allege that in the past two years hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces.
Dhaka officials reject accusations that Awami League supporters are being systematically targeted.

6ad5bf4b7cea.text: By — Ignatius Ssuuna, Associated Press Ignatius Ssuuna, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/genocide-suspect-deported-by-u-s-will-stand-trial-in-rwanda Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Genocide suspect deported by U.S. will stand trial in Rwanda World Nov 10, 2026 2:24 PM EST KIGALI, Rwanda (AP) — A Rwandan man suspected of participating in the country's 1994 genocide has been deported from the United States and will stand trial for his alleged crimes, according to local authorities. Jean Léonard Teganya, who arrived in the East African nation on Monday, faces charges related to genocide, said Justin Nkusi, a spokesperson for the prosecution. Teganya is currently being interrogated by police before prosecutors receive his file, Nkusi said. Teganya, 55, was indicted in 2014 over his alleged involvement in genocidal crimes in several areas in the district of Huye, in Rwanda's south. Rwandan authorities say he allegedly committed some of his crimes at a university campus and a medical school in Huye. The 2014 indictment triggered an investigation into Teganya's presence in the U.S., with Rwanda seeking his deportation. At the time, Teganya denied playing a part in the genocide, in which an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed by extremist Hutus. Jean Leonard Teganya, a Rwandan man who U.S. prosecutors said participated in the African nation's 1994 genocide and who was convicted in April of lying in hope of gaining asylum in the United States, is seen in this undated photo provided by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Massachusetts, U.S., July 1, 2019. Courtesy U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Massachusetts/Handout via REUTERS READ MORE: Rwanda says 7 deportees arrived from the U.S. in August under agreement with Washington Teganya fled Rwanda in July 1994 and later sought asylum in Canada. According to the U.S. Justice Department, he evaded a Canadian deportation order and crossed into the U.S. in 2014. In 2019, a federal jury in Boston found that Teganya had committed immigration fraud and perjury after seeking asylum in the U.S. One survivor of the genocide told The Associated Press in Kigali, the Rwandan capital, that she welcomed the decision to send Teganya home to face justice. "Genocide crime and crimes against humanity are never time-barred and perpetrators will be hunted, arrested, deported and prosecuted," said Yolande Mukakasana. "As survivors, we remain hopeful that justice will be done no matter how much time has passed." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. e61db9f4b81f.text: By — Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/oil-shock-from-iran-war-led-to-drop-in-carbon-pollution-scientists-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Oil shock from Iran war led to drop in carbon pollution, scientists say Science Nov 10, 2026 2:05 PM EST Global carbon pollution dropped this year ever so slightly, but it's more because of oil shocks reverberating from the Iran war than anything the world has done to fight climate change, scientists said in a new study. In 2026, the world emitted 42.2 billion tons (38.2 billion metric tons) of heat-trapping carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas. It's a 0.4% decrease from last year, according to the scientists of the Global Carbon Project. "It's downwards which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said study co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway. "So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons." The war in Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping artery for petroleum products, pushing up global prices of gasoline and oil. They found oil emissions dropped nearly 2% and natural gas fell 0.3%, while coal was up 0.6%. The international team of more than 140 scientists uses data from around the world to calculate the yearly emissions figure, with estimates for the last few months of the year, and then present them at the U.N. climate negotiations in Antalya, Turkey. Their findings were also published in the journals Earth System Science Data Discussions and Nature Climate Change. Peters said they are certain that this was related to the war-triggered energy shocks because of both the timing and type of fuel emission drops. If the overall carbon dioxide emission drop were due solely to a rise in renewables and a systemic drop in fossil fuel use, oil emissions "would slowly come up to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, whereas what we see this year is oil emissions are going up and then suddenly BANG, down 2%," Peters said. Previous carbon pollution drops This is the third time global carbon pollution dropped in the 21st century. The other two times were because of the global recession in 2009 and the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. In those past two crises, people hoped the recovery from the shocks would emphasize clean energy, Peters said, "but at the end of the day, we seem to go back to where we were before." Outside experts greeted the figures with a mix of hope and skepticism that it will last. Niklas Höhne, co-founder of Germany's NewClimate Institute, said "permanent shifts are happening" especially with skyrocketing switches to electric cars and trucks, especially in Asia. So he thinks the global peak of carbon emissions is near or here. But Malte Meinshausen, a climate science and policy expert at the University of Melbourne in Australia, said oil producing nations and companies not affected by the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz reaped "tremendous windfall gains," and it boosts their efforts to look for oil outside the Middle East. That, he said, will dampen any short-term effects of reduced carbon emissions from the war. More than 1,000 tons per second of pollution The 42 billion tons of carbon dioxide emitted this year comes to about 1,335 tons (1,211 metric tons) of the transparent, heat-trapping gas going into the air every second. "We shouldn't lose sight of the bigger picture. The world is still pumping more than a thousand (metric tons) of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere every second," Mohamed Adow, director of the environmental group Power Shift Africa, said in an email. READ MORE: Inflation runs hotter than expected as higher prices extend beyond the gas station "It's very abstract to think about the magnitude of stuff we throw in the atmosphere every year, but it's a ginormous number," Peters said. "If it was black and not transparent, the sky would be dark." And even though the amount of heat-trapping gases from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions went up 1%. That's because of land use changes, such as deforestation and human-caused peat fires, that increased faster than fossil fuel burning decreased, the study said. China's emissions drop raises eyebrows and hope Most of the world's biggest carbon polluting nations — China, the United States, Europe, Japan — showed about a 1% drop in emissions this year, but Peters attributed it to the oil shock. India's fossil fuel pollution went up 4.4% this year, the study found. China's emission drop raised eyebrows and hope for some experts. Experts have been waiting for China's ever-growing emissions to start dropping. "China is giving us real reasons to be optimistic that its emissions may have peaked," Adow said. "It's building the world's first major electrostate, investing at extraordinary speed and scale in solar power, wind energy, electric vehicles and the infrastructure to support them. This isn't a temporary response to an oil crisis. It's a fundamental transformation of China's economy that is steadily reducing its dependence on fossil fuels." University of Michigan environment dean Jonathan Overpeck said, "We're not phasing out fossil fuels fast enough, but some progress is better than no progress." The News
By Corbin Trentâs estimate, heâs spending 15 hours a day on a cause that has animated the left ever since Democrats won huge majorities in the House and Senate: urging them to dump their leaders.
Trent, a former spokesman for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, has some well-known allies in his long-shot campaign to oust Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. They include actor Mark Ruffalo, former Ocasio-Cortez chief of staff Saikat Chakrabarti, and countless progressive influencers.
But they donât include Ocasio-Cortez, who underscored on Tuesday that sheâs backing Jeffries. Even Trent acknowledged that what legions of online progressives are asking for â the rejection of leaders who just presided over Democratic landslides â is unlikely to happen.
âI reckon itâs about a 10% chance on Schumer and a 3% chance on Jeffries,â Trent told Semafor. âWhat matters, and matters a lot, is making it loud and clear that voters asked for something else. That it is being denied to them. If youâve ever got a chance to beat these folks, you need votes.â
Theoretically, the votes to shake up leadership are at least within reach. Informal whip counts and hallway interviews confirm that dozens of newly elected Democrats are interested in challengers to the two New Yorkers who occasionally break from the left. But realistically, the battle to replace Jeffries and Schumer was built for a disappointing election, not a landslide.
And the obstacles of the anti-leadership campaign are revealing the limited reach of a progressive movement that wants to pick the next presidential nominee. Critics of Schumer havenât given up on enlisting Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen to challenge him, but no Democrat has stepped up to take on Jeffries.
Even if Van Hollen mounts a campaign, it will be a massive uphill climb for progressives to deny Schumer the votes in next monthâs closed-door vote. The leftâs chances of defeating Jeffries are even lower.
But by forcing the question, progressives hope to either pull off a miracle â or at least, keep an argument going. Activists believe that they, not Schumer and Jeffries, put in the work to win the biggest Democratic victories in decades. The progressive media outlets that exploded after the partyâs 2024 loss to Trump are now watching the leaders take credit for what they think their movement built.
Their message is consistent: That voters who want âchangeâ and support progressive ideas will stay engaged only if the leadership changes and President Donald Trump is forced to veto big progressive bills.
At last weekâs post-election Crooked Con, a gathering of progressive activists, strategists, influencers, and podcast addicts, the demand for new leaders hung in the air. Attendees walking up to the Washington Convention Center on Saturday were offered leaflets about stopping bipartisan permitting reform moving through the Senate, warning that it would speed up the building of âimmigrant detention centers.â (The bill advanced two days later.)
Inside, there were excited murmurs whenever a Democrat was asked about replacing Schumer or Jeffries.
Pressed by Pod Save America co-host Jon Favreau on whether she would challenge Schumer, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin gave a winding answer that didnât rule it out â but suggested that Schumer could win her over.
âLook, if he wants to be majority leader, what is your plan for the first 100 days?â she said. âHow are you going to do things differently so that Democrats get their sh*t together?â
That got muted applause from an audience ready to join an insurgency. There was much more excitement when Rep.-elect Milat Kiros of Colorado said there had been a âmandateâ for change, not for current leadership; Kiros unseated Rep. Diana DeGette in one of the leftâs biggest primary wins.
Everywhere he went, Van Hollen was asked if he would challenge Schumer. In a short interview with Semafor, he disputed the idea that the leader had earned the job already by electing between seven and nine new Democratic senators.
âIâm glad that the DSCC and Senate Majority PAC raised a lot of money,â Van Hollen told Semafor. âI mean, their Republican counterparts raised even more money. I think the lesson from this election was, this was people power over money.â
The scale of the Democratic wins has made the entire push trickier.
âLook, we had a wonderful, wonderful outcome,â said Maurice Mitchell, the president of the Working Families Party, which clashed with DC Democrats over primaries in the Midwest and California. âItâs almost like it would be greedy of me to want better outcomes. But I know there were elections that could have been won if we were able to move as a united front.â
Davidâs view
The modern left is at its most powerful inside the Democratic Party after the party screws things up.
Hillary Clintonâs defeat convinced many Democrats, even his Senate colleagues, that Sanders would have won the presidency, and his populist ideas were more popular than whatever it was she ran on. Kamala Harrisâ defeat was even more empowering for Sanders, whose âFight Oligarchyâ rallies brought out hundreds of thousands of people.
After victory, the leftâs challenge is twofold. One: Schumer and Jeffries didnât blow it. They are no longer the brittle wimps who were protesting outside of federal buildings last year and insisting theyâd âfightâ Trump. They beat him.
Two: Democrats really did listen to them. Last yearâs government shutdown fight, while it did not end as progressives wanted it to, was about healthcare funding â the sort of life-or-death economic issue the left wanted to focus on. The eventual Democratic themes of the election were âcosts, chaos, and corruptionâ and âfighting for an affordable America.â
Whatâs worth watching most closely right now is how upstart progressive media â Hasan Piker, Drop Site, Lever, Majority Report, and other influencers â approach all this. Left-leaning media has a much larger reach than it did

Delgado, Associated Press By — Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Sibi Arasu, Associated Press By — Suzan Fraser, Associated Press Suzan Fraser, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/at-un-climate-talks-5-nations-back-plan-to-double-rooftop-solar-panels-by-2030 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter At UN climate talks, 5 nations back plan to double rooftop solar panels by 2030 Science Nov 10, 2026 1:57 PM EST ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Five countries have backed a plan to double the number of homes with rooftop solar panels worldwide by 2030, as U.N. climate talks in Turkey focus on expanding access to electricity and transitioning away from fossil fuels. The new Global Rooftop Solar Declaration launched Tuesday on the second day of this year's climate talks, known as COP31. The aim is to double the number of homes with rooftop solar panels from about 150 million today to at least 300 million by 2030. "This is the future of affordable energy," said Sonia Dunlop, CEO of the Global Solar Council. "This is the way we can help average working people insure themselves from future price rises to come." COP31 comes after a year of deadly climate-related disasters and as concern grows that governments are not doing enough to curb global warming. Recent energy shocks from the Russia-Ukraine war and Iran war have also increased interest in renewables. The U.N. climate talks have been criticized in the past for making promises that later fall flat. For rooftop solar goals to actually make a dent in the emissions contributing to climate change, experts said policies to upgrade power grids and subsidize solar panels and batteries must quickly follow. "The pledge is a pledge," said Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance. "We now need to see national policies and frameworks in place." More rooftop solar may help regular people Bangladesh, Kenya, Nigeria and Vanuatu joined Australia by endorsing the rooftop solar declaration in the Turkish resort town of Antalya, where COP31 is being co-hosted by Turkey and Australia. Lawmakers from 21 other countries — including the United Kingdom, South Africa and Sri Lanka — have also endorsed it. So has Indonesia's state-owned electric power company Perusahaan Listrik Negara. The declaration is voluntary and non-binding, like many of the agreements made at U.N. climate talks. "We know the world is currently facing the greatest energy cost of living crisis the world has ever seen," Dunlop said. "We know that families all over the world are struggling to pay their bills and what we are saying with the Global Rooftop Solar Declaration is that we have a solution that will bring down your bills." Electrification is a cornerstone of this year's talks, with Turkey pushing for electricity — preferably from renewables like solar and wind — to make up 35% of global energy consumption by 2035. "Electrification by itself is incredibly beneficial because of the efficiency gains. Renewables by themselves, again, very beneficial. Put the two together and it is really a killer combination," Douglas said. Nations lean on fossil fuels, despite solar gains Turkey's electrification pledge and Australia's rooftop solar declaration put a spotlight on the energy mix of both nations, which still rely heavily on fossil fuels. In Turkey, home to one of Europe's largest solar farms, solar and wind make up nearly 23% of energy generation. But coal was still the country's largest source of electricity last year, accounting for 33% of generation, according to Turkey's Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources. In Australia, one in three homes has rooftop solar and more than 700,000 homes have batteries to store excess energy. But coal still makes up more than 40% of electricity generation in Australia, which is also one of the world's largest coal exporters. "Setting ambitious renewable targets without addressing grid capacity, storage and the continued role of coal risks undermining energy security, reliability and affordability," said Michelle Manook of FutureCoal, an industry-backed group formerly known as the World Coal Association. READ MORE: Outdated power grids a major hurdle in renewable energy transition The tension between renewable rollouts and continued coal use is mirrored in the world's most populous countries, China and India. They have both installed record-breaking amounts of renewables, but sometimes lose the energy because of insufficient transmission and storage capacity. "Energy storage deployment must catch up with the speed of renewables deployment," said Nikit Abhyankar, with the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley. "Otherwise, it creates massive operational challenges for the grid, resulting in significant curtailment," he said, referring to the practice of limiting electricity output because the grid cannot handle it. Solar spreads, but barriers remain Rooftop solar panels are often decentralized from power grids, meaning that electricity is generated, stored and managed near where it is consumed, rather than coming from distant power plants. This makes solar ideal for remote communities and hard-hit areas, like refugee camps and disaster zones. Renewables, largely driven by solar from China and India, generated more than a third of the world's electricity last year, overtaking coal for the first time. The Iran war's energy shock has also spurred solar interest in energy-hungry regions, like Southeast Asia, which was hit hard by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sent into a state of energy triage. Indonesia pledged to install 100 gigawatts of solar power by 2029. Thailand and Vietnam are offering subsidies for rooftop solar installations, and the Philippines became the second-largest destination for Chinese solar exports in the first quarter of 2026. e10cbab3af36.text: By — Sophie Austin, Associated Press Sophie Austin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/california-voters-reject-tax-on-net-worth-of-billionaires Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter California voters reject tax on net worth of billionaires Politics Nov 10, 2026 1:48 PM EST SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California voters have rejected a first-in-the-nation tax on the net worth of billionaires following a contentious ballot fight that generated huge spending by some prominent tech leaders eager to stop their taxes from going up. The measure's failure is a win for Democratic leaders who opposed it, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who may run for president in 2028. Critics of the tax, known as Proposition 40, said it would have prompted ultrawealthy taxpayers to leave the state. Most Californians vote by mail, and any ballot postmarked by Election Day that arrives within a week is counted, meaning it often takes days or even weeks for close races to be settled. The Associated Press determined Monday that 'no' had received enough votes to win. The "no" side raised roughly 10 times as much as the "yes" side. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone dumped more than $100 million into a political action committee working to defeat the measure. The measure would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. Most of the money would have been used to backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare, and 10% would have gone toward education and food-assistance programs. SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, which backed the tax, said it was necessary to replace an estimated $100 billion the state will lose in federal healthcare funding over five years. Proposition 40 was the nation's biggest test yet on an idea progressives have long championed: raising taxes on the ultra-rich by targeting the main way they make their money — through their investments as opposed to the paychecks they receive from work. Proponents say they could put the measure back on the ballot in 2028 The measure attracted support from liberal leaders beyond the state, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who rallied in cities across California in the race's closing weeks to urge voters to pass it. The "Yes on 40" campaign said the measure sought to protect healthcare for Californians and that they will put a tax back on the ballot in 2028 if patients are not protected. "Buying an election is not the same as winning the debate," the measure's proponents said in a statement on Monday. "The billionaires may have bought themselves a temporary victory at the ballot box, but they have not bought themselves an end to this debate, and this is only round one." Billionaires donated millions of dollars to a political action committee, Building a Better California, working to defeat the measure. The committee, which backed other measures on the ballot designed to nullify the tax, raised more than $333 million, nearly a third of which came from Brin. READ MORE: Newsom urges a national 'billionaires' tax' while fighting one in California The AP Voter Poll indicates that the majority of young voters in California — those younger than 30 — voted "yes" on Proposition 40. Older voters were far less supportive, with roughly 7 in 10 voters who were 65 and older saying they voted "no" on the ballot measure. About half of voters with a household income under $100,000 annually said they were in support of the initiative. Closer to 6 in 10 California voters with an income of $100,000 or higher said they were opposed. Brin, along with his fellow Google co-founder Larry Page, was among the billionaires who started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the possible tax. Another tech mogul, Mark Zuckerberg, said he would remain in the state for eight years and made a deal with Meta to help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company. Some feared the measure could drive wealthy taxpayers out of state Some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association, were part of a coalition opposing it. They were concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state's budget if there was a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California's budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state's richest residents. "Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state's economy with little regard for the harms it would cause," the coalition said in a statement. Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who's politically independent, said before voting concluded Nov. 3 that he planned to vote against it. "Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do," he said. "But I don't believe taxing them out of existence is going to work." Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million. Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month, Newsom told reporters that the senator's focus on wealth inequality was "spot-on." But he said that "on this issue, we fundamentally disagree." Supporters of the California tax started running ads recently in New Hampshire, New Mexico and Virginia, states that will vote early in the Democratic presidential primary in 2028, that criticize Newsom for his opposition to the measure. ffb6ec3ce31a.text: By — Sylvia Hui, Associated Press Sylvia Hui, Associated Press By — Brian Melley, Associated Press Brian Melley, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/british-comedian-and-childrens-author-david-walliams-accused-of-sexual-misconduct Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter British comedian and children's author David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct World Nov 10, 2026 1:43 PM EST LONDON (AP) — British children's author and comedian David Walliams used his fame to groom girls and young women for sex, two British news outlets reported on Tuesday. ITV News and the Guardian newspaper said their joint investigation featured interviews with multiple women who gave first-hand accounts of Walliams' conduct. One woman alleged he sexually assaulted her at his house when she was 15, while others accused him of grooming them when they were teens. Walliams, 55, denied the allegations. He had sought a court injunction to bar ITV News and the Guardian from identifying him in their reporting. His lawyers claimed that publication of sexual misconduct allegations would lead him to take his own life. A judge rejected his injunction request last week, but protected his identity until late Monday. "I am not a sexual predator," Walliams said, according to ITV. "I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me." "Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did," he added. Walliams' lawyer, Sara Mansoori, earlier told the High Court that he had made a suicide attempt when he received letters from ITN and Guardian News and Media seeking his response to the allegations. He later made another attempt, she said, and he was recently admitted to the hospital for psychiatric care. READ MORE: Russell Brand is sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault The case drew widespread attention in Britain because it highlighted questions over public figures' right to privacy and what media can report on the basis of public interest. Gavin Millar, representing the media companies, has said that the allegations were gathered after "a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation" and that there was a strong public interest in publishing them. He told the court that the investigation involved speaking to more than 100 people, and alleged that over a period of years Walliams "used his status and influence as a well-known public figure to establish contact with young women, some considerably younger than him, and that he engaged or sought to engage in seriously inappropriate conduct," according to a summary of the court judgment. Some of the alleged conduct could amount to criminal offenses if proven, it said. Walliams was dropped last year by publisher HarperCollins after allegations were made of inappropriate behavior. Few details were published at the time, but the Guardian reported Tuesday that there were concerns about his behavior for years, including an allegation that he had an inappropriate sexual relationship with a junior female employee. Walliams is best known for comedy sketches on "Little Britain," a hugely popular British TV show in the 2000s, but he's also a celebrated children's book author with some 40 published titles that sold more than 60 million copies worldwide, according to his website. Several of them, including "Gangsta Granny," have been adapted into BBC comedy dramas and stage productions. He was also a judge for years on "Britain's Got Talent," though in 2022 he stepped down after apologizing for making "disrespectful comments" about auditioning contestants. The BBC said Tuesday it was removing some programmes, including "Little Britain," while it carried out a review of "all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms." The literary agency Independent Talent Group also said it was dropping Walliams following the new allegations. In dismissing the injunction bid by Walliams, Justice Matthew Nicklin said such a legal measure would mean "an exceptionally serious interference" with the rights of the media companies. He noted that Walliams had a "serious and longstanding psychiatric vulnerability" which must be taken seriously, and said a decision allowing the allegations to be published will substantially increase his risk of suicide. However, he added that the evidence did not "establish that suicide is inevitable." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) told makers of popular weight-loss GLP-1 drugs that they must add warning labels about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness.
Manufacturers of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound must warn about nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). The disorder happens when vessels supplying blood to the optic nerves become blocked, depriving the nerves of oxygen.
The condition can cause painless decreased vision in one eye, which can be permanent, the FDA said.
In a statement to the BBC, the American Academy of Ophthalmology said "any added risk appears small, and it has not been established that these medications cause NAION".
"GLP-1 medications offer important benefits for people with diabetes, obesity, and heart disease, so our message to patients is simple," the group said. "Don't stop your medication without talking to your doctor, and if you notice sudden, painless vision loss in one eye, see an ophthalmologist promptly."
There is no known treatment to reverse vision loss caused by NAION. It is the most common cause of acute optic nerve injury in people over 50 years old, according to the academy.
The FDA said it conducted a detailed review of reports of NAION in GLP-1 users as well as a review of other studies and concluded there is an "increased risk of rare NAION events" in people taking the drugs.
In a statement, Novo Nordisk, the manufacturer of Wegovy, one of the most popular weight-loss medications, said the company believes the data "do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship".
"We recognize that NAION can have a profound impact on patients and their families. Patient safety is a top priority for Novo, and we continue to monitor the safety of our medicines," the manufacturer said.
Some research was challenging to review because people taking GLP-1 drugs for obesity and type 2 diabetes may already have risk factors for NAION separate from the drugs, according to the regulator. The FDA said it was not known why those taking GLP-1 drugs may be more at risk for the eye condition.
The drugs already have warning labels for several other conditions including pancreatitis and gallbladder disease. Some of the most common symptoms for semaglutide - a key ingredient in many GLP-1 drugs - include nausea, vomiting and stomach pain.
â Last year, a safety arm of the European Medicines Agency, a part of the European Union, said up to 1 in 10,000 people taking semaglutide may be affected by NAION.
In a study published two years ago analysing 17,000 patients, US researchers found those taking semaglutide were four times more likely to be diagnosed with NAION than those not taking the drug.
But one of the authors of the study, Harvard Medical School ophthalmology professor Dr Joseph Rizzo, said the findings were "significant but tentative", and more research was needed on the relationship between the drug and the eye condition in a more diverse population.

Meet the Peaky Blinders, Ukraine's drone unit protecting a devastated front-line city
The BBC's Jonathan Beale reported from inside Slovyansk, one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.
The town has become almost uninhabitable and has been under heavy bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.
Members of a Ukrainian drone unit that call themselves Peaky Blinders, named after the cult BBC TV series, have taken on the task of intercepting Russian drones.
Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.

Malaysia's disgraced former Prime Minister Najib Razak has arrived home to begin serving the rest of a jail sentence for corruption under house arrest.
There was a big media presence at his Kuala Lumpur residence to see the 73-year-old return from prison in an SUV late on Tuesday night, escorted by a heavily armed police convoy.
Najib's return ended a four-year prison stint after he was found guilty over the embezzlement of billions of dollars from the country's sovereign wealth fund.
The 1MDB scandal brought down his government and made headlines around the world when it came to light a decade ago, embroiling prominent figures from Malaysia to Goldman Sachs and Hollywood.
Investigators estimated that $4.5bn (Â£3.3bn) was siphoned from the state-owned wealth fund, which Najib co-founded, into private pockets, including his own. More than $1bn allegedly ended up in accounts linked to Najib, according to prosecutors.
Najib's lawyers claim he had been misled by his advisers - in particular the financier Jho Low, who has maintained his innocence and remains at large.
Najib's mansion in one of the capital's most exclusive neighbourhoods was declared a federal prison ahead of his homecoming on Tuesday.
Critics said his release from jail undermined efforts to fight corruption and questioned its legal basis, saying Malaysian law made no provision for house arrest.
Najib, who was prime minister from 2009 to 2018, denied wrongdoing but was convicted at two separate trials.
In the first trial he was sentenced in 2020 to 12 years in prison and jailed in 2022. The term was later halved on appeal.
In September, the King of Malaysia granted him a conditional pardon to see out the remaining two years of his sentence at home.
The transfer to his mansion was to take place on Friday but put on hold after the attorney general sought clarification of the royal decree. On Tuesday the high court ruled the house arrest was effective immediately.
Najib's party paid a $12m fine as part of the terms of the royal pardon allowing him to serve the rest of his term at home.
He was sentenced after being convicted of abuse of power, money laundering and breach of trust over 42 million ringgit ($10m; Â£7.7m) transferred from SRC International - a former unit of 1MDB - into his private accounts.
Najib is appealing against a 15-year prison sentence, handed down at a second trial in December 2025, in a case involving much larger sums of money. In that case he was convicted of misappropriating nearly 2.3 billion Malaysian ringgit ($569m; Â£422m) from the nation's sovereign wealth fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
He is due to start serving that sentence after his house arrest ends, which is expected in August 2028.

7fa114fe35d2.text: By — Kelvin Chan, Associated Press Kelvin Chan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/nvidia-and-huang-face-lawsuit-alleging-investors-were-misled-about-spy-affair Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Nvidia and Huang face lawsuit alleging investors were misled about spy affair World Nov 10, 2026 1:32 PM EST A shareholder has sued Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, accusing them of deceiving investors in their responses to media reports about Huang's affair with a purported Chinese spy that threatens national security. The complaint comes after President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating the affair, which Huang has acknowledged and apologized for. Trump said Monday that Huang told him he had no idea the person could be involved in espionage. The affair, which is also being scrutinized by Nvidia's board, has raised concerns that Beijing is using nefarious means to gain access to Nvidia 's cutting-edge microchips which power the development of artificial intelligence but face export restrictions to China. The complaint filed Monday in a California court says the company misled investors about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who news reports said is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, and the national security implications. The news reports said that the Commerce Department was investigating Alice Huang's company, Singapore-based Megaspeed, on suspicions that it was helping to sidestep U.S. export restrictions blocking Nvidia chips from being sold to China. But Nvidia said then that its compliance team checked and determined that Megaspeed wasn't doing anything illegal. But, according to the complaint, the statements were misleading because they were made when Jensen Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang, who is "suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products into China." It accuses Nvidia and Huang of failing to disclose the affair and issuing false statements about Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed, which posed a "material risk" to Nvidia's reputation and business prospects. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. WATCH: What China stands to gain from Nvidia's CEO's alleged affair with spy The complaint, filed by retail investor Mark Kistenmacher, seeks unspecified damages and a jury trial. It seeks to represent in a class-action lawsuit anyone who bought shares of Nvidia from October 9, when The New York Times first reported about the pair socializing in Taiwan, until November 8, when the company said it was investigating reports that Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." Shares of Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, fell $7.97, or 4.3%, on Monday, wiping out about $190 billion in market value. Shares were down again Tuesday before the opening bell. "As a result of Defendants' wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company's securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages," the complaint said. Had investors known the truth, they wouldn't have purchased Nvidia's shares "at the artificially inflated prices that they did, or at all," the complaint said. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that Alice Huang, a former executive of Megaspeed International, was gathering information for Beijing. Huang is a common Chinese surname and the two are not related. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to The Times. Trump said in a White House briefing that the FBI is "looking into" the affair, but added he doesn't think Huang needs to worry, saying "he'll be in good shape." The episode is also starting to attract congressional scrutiny, with top Democrats Sen. Mark Warner and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries saying Monday they are interested in investigating it further. Huang is a singular figure in the technology landscape and one of the world's wealthiest people thanks to booming demand for his company's microprocessors, which are in huge demand for cloud computing and data centers that underpin the AI boom. He apologized to his wife, family and the company for the affair in an open letter posted on Nvidia's website. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security," Huang said in his letter. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 5ce95021760d.text: A federal judge took sharp aim at FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday, ruling in favor of The Atlantic and freezing most discovery in his defamation lawsuit against the publication. Why it matters: The ruling shields The Atlantic from potentially intrusive demands for its reporting materials and confidential sources while the court weighs dismissing the case entirely. What they're saying: " Plaintiff misrepresents Defendants' argument, the court's reasoning in Moldea, and the standard applicable in this District," U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan wrote in his 16-page ruling . "The Court concludes that discovery should be stayed at this juncture because of Defendants' legitimate First Amendment concerns and because discovery may be unnecessary," Sullivan wrote. Catch up quick: Patel sued The Atlantic after the magazine reported in April that he allegedly drinks excessively and is sometimes unavailable or difficult for his staff to wake because he was seemingly intoxicated. The story also alleged that Patel had grown increasingly worried about losing his job. Patel denied the reporting and sued the publication shortly after the story aired. Zoom in: The judge paused most discovery until he rules on The Atlantic's motion to dismiss the lawsuit, but both sides may request government records. The Atlantic says it needs Justice Department and FBI records to assess the truth of its reporting and Patel's reputation. Patel complained the requests were too broad, seeking everything from his medical and travel records to his calendar and records about personnel decisions. Sullivan rejected Patel's objection that the arrangement was unfair. The intrigue: The Atlantic warned that discovery could involve "the sitting FBI Director invading Defendants' newsgathering and editorial processes," potentially exposing confidential sources to retaliation. The Atlantic called Patel a "serial defamation plaintiff" and warned that he "may seek to wield governmental power" in connection with the lawsuit and broader criticism of his FBI leadership. Sullivan agreed that the magazine had "legitimate First Amendment concerns" and found it would face "substantial prejudice" if discovery proceeded now. Worth noting: Sullivan didn't rule on whether the Atlantic's reporting is true or whether Patel was defamed. Neither The Atlantic nor the FBI immediately responded to Axios' request for comment. e2903792730a.text: By — Bassam Hatoum, Associated Press Bassam Hatoum, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/russia-and-ukraine-hold-nearly-4-hours-of-u-s-mediated-talks-in-abu-dhabi Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Russia and Ukraine hold nearly 4 hours of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi World Nov 10, 2026 1:09 PM EST ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates (AP) — Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday held their first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months on ending their war, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling the meeting "very productive" and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the session was "constructive and quite substantive." Hopes of ending Europe's biggest conflict since World War II are tempered, however, by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks earlier this year. READ MORE: Russia-Ukraine peace talks led by U.S. will look at security guarantees for both sides There's nothing to suggest a new posture that would lead to a breakthrough, but circumstances surrounding the talks have been changed by the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections as well as increased pressure on Russia's wartime economy. Moscow also is seeking to break Ukrainians' will as winter sets in by ramping up its battering of the country's power grid. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Neither Rubio nor Zelenskyy attended the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. The session lasted four hours and another is scheduled for a second day Wednesday. Delegations from Moscow and Kyiv met as Washington, represented by U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff, renewed its push to stop the fighting. READ MORE: The Kremlin hopes the U.S. election shake-up won't shift Trump's negotiations on Ukraine "It looks like the talks in Abu Dhabi were very productive," Rubio said in Paris at the Group of Seven meeting, though he urged patience. "There's a lot of work to be done in that regard. It's not like something that's on the verge of being solved in the next 24 hours or anything like that." Zelenskyy said the talks were largely about humanitarian issues, including prisoner exchanges and returning Ukrainian civilians in captivity, as well as children taken from the country. Security guarantees also were discussed, he added during an appearance at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark. A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to comment publicly said Ukraine and Russia talked about a large scale prisoner swap, although the details will be discussed in the coming days. The 3-way meeting was the first since February The two-day session is the first such meeting since February on the war, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians. Kushner said he believed there were "some good ideas how to bridge" the differences between the two sides. Trump, whose stance on the war has varied, must reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. elections. Democrats could demand more support for Ukraine. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told ZDF television on Monday night that "I don't have overly high expectations" for the talks. There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks come against a backdrop of new long-range strikes by both Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line. Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's air force said. Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces downed 155 Ukrainian drones overnight in eight Russian regions, as well as over the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed from Ukraine in 2014. Kushner says the U.S. aims to build on past experience Kushner said in opening remarks that the goal of the talks is to "create a new framework and a new understanding building upon the different institutions and understandings of the past." "We take what's worked, we try to identify what's failed, why we're in this position and hopefully create a new framework that leads us for decades, if not centuries, of peace," he said. NATO commander U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who was also present, said that the U.S. delegation looked forward "to working with both sides as we seek to advance the progress we've made in the past and continue this pursuit to set the foundations for a lasting peace." Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service who leads Kyiv's delegation, thanked the U.S. for its efforts to end Russia's invasion. "Our people are waiting to end this war. And we hope that we will achieve the lasting peace for Ukraine," he said. Ukrainians meet first with European and NATO officials The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, expressed hope the meeting "will allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine." Umerov said the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the U.S. envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission. Russia has objected to the Europeans' involvement in the three-way talks, but said EU representatives could join at a later stage. Russia and Ukraine hold to their demands The Russian and Ukrainian governments remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal. Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from four regions of Ukraine that Moscow annexed in September 2022 but has never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO and accept strict limits on its military, among other issues. At least two arrests have been made following a surprise visit from former US President Joe Biden to Trinity College in Dublin on Tuesday.
Biden was accompanied by former first lady Jill Biden as they attended a ceremony where their son Hunter was awarded the Gold Medal for Outstanding Contribution for Public Discourse.

A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.
London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."
The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."
Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.
It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.
Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws.
Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.
The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.
Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.
The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.
Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".
Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular.
"They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."
Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

1a30ef3f8c21.text: By — Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/inflation-runs-hotter-than-expected-as-higher-prices-extend-beyond-the-gas-station Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Inflation runs hotter than expected as higher prices extend beyond the gas station Economy Nov 10, 2026 12:59 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation was higher than expected last month as the rising prices that powered sweeping Democratic victories in last week's midterm elections appear likely to pose ongoing challenges for the White House and the Federal Reserve. The consumer price index rose 0.4% from September to October, the Labor Department said Tuesday, down from 0.6% the previous month. The government did not report a yearly inflation rate because last year's government shutdown meant no data was released for October 2025. READ MORE: Voters demanded economic relief. Trump and Democrats face tough choices on how to deliver But excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the preceding month. Both figures were a tenth of a point higher than forecast, and at an annual rate would be well above the Fed's 2% target. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The new inflation data heightened concerns that strong consumer and business spending, combined with higher gas prices and supply disruptions stemming from tariffs and global turmoil, are creating increasingly stubborn inflation that could extend beyond temporary spikes in prices at the gas pump. The economy expanded at a 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, mostly driven by consumer spending. "It's worrisome. There is a sense that inflation is broad, persistent, a little bit everywhere," said Riccardo Trezzi, founder of Underlying Inflation, a consulting firm, and a former Fed economist. "The Fed should be very worried." Using rough estimates for last October's data, Trezzi calculates that consumer prices rose 4% in October from a year ago, up from 3.7% in September. Core prices rose 2.8%, he estimates, up from 2.6%. Americans' struggles with high prices were evident as they ousted Republican majorities from the House and Senate last week. With historic gains in both chambers, Democrats in Congress will soon face the same challenges. President Donald Trump has acknowledged voter anger over the Iran war and gas prices but has shown no sign yet of changing course. The AP Voter Poll, a survey of 100,000 voters, found about two-thirds blamed Trump's policies for higher costs. About 9 in 10 said the cost of living was a "crucial" or "major" factor in their vote. Federal Reserve may become more aggressive about raising borrowing costs The persistence of elevated inflation makes it highly likely that the Fed will raise its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. It kept rates unchanged late last month, after raising them in September. The Fed increases borrowing costs in an effort to cool spending and bring down inflation. Earlier Tuesday, Fed governor Christopher Waller, an outspoken member of the central bank's rate-setting committee, said that a hike of a half-point next month was possible, double the size of the usual quarter-point increase. "Economic activity is strong, the labor market is stable, but inflation is too high, well above" the Fed's 2% goal, Waller said. Stock prices fell in early trading Tuesday, and Treasury yields rose, on expectations of more persistent inflation and higher rates from the Fed. Higher gas prices may have begun to spread through economy Gas prices rose 1% from September to October, the government said, a stiff increase but still much lower than in previous months. Gas prices have soared more than 37% from a year ago. Still, oil prices have fallen sharply in recent days on hopes that the Iran conflict is fading, and gas costs have declined this month. Yet there are signs higher energy prices are spreading into other parts of the economy, with air fares, public transportation, and delivery services all jumping in price. Electricity prices rose 0.9% from September to October, the most since April, and grocery prices jumped 0.4%, a painful rise after years of increases. Beef prices rose 0.9% last month, after jumping nearly 14% in the first half of this year. Restaurant prices rose 0.5% from September to October, the most since January 2024. Rising shipping prices, driven up by more expensive gas, have lifted costs for restaurants and grocery stores, which may be passing them on to consumers. Inflation has also been worsened by the massive investments flowing into artificial intelligence, which has contributed to higher prices for computer chips, electricity and consumer electronics. Voters swept dozens of candidates into office who had pledged to slow data center construction. Computer prices jumped 0.5% last month, the government report showed, after rising nearly 10% in the year ending in September, lifted by more expensive chips. The cost of computers had been retreating for years as semiconductor chips became more efficient. That trend reversed course this year as prices rose sharply. Prices are rising, and it's not just gasoline Prices are also rising in some sectors that have little to do with oil and gas or AI. Streaming video services have recently gotten more expensive, with Disney raising prices last month for its ad-supported Disney+ and Hulu streaming bundle to $12.49 a month from $11.99. The ad-free version rose by $2.50 to $21.49. Prices also increased last month for an Apple TV/Peacock streaming bundle, to $17.99 from $14.99 a month. Small businesses are bracing for a spending pullback by customers. An artist has set a record for the world's largest soil painting as he bids to raise awareness of how important the material is.
The UK-based Official Record Breakers has verified that organisation Save Soil had surpassed the previous best of 59,458 sq cm (about 64 sq ft), with the new painting measuring 61,000 sq cm (about 65 sq ft).
Phil Lambert, who lives in Cardiff, used four types of soil and an upcycled wooden frame and canvas supplied by Oxford Wood Recycling.
The artwork was created to raise awareness of the movement's call for soil regeneration to be prioritised at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP).
Save Soil is pushing for improvement of soil health around the world and works with governments to shape policies on the subject.
The painting, which Lambert created at University College London (UCL), follows its new report, which outlines the importance of healthy soils and steps for their restoration.
Lambert said he had been using soil for about 10 years and painting with it "is something I've been very familiar with".
As well as using soil from his garden and some from his mother's home, the artist also received donations from the James Hutton Institute in Scotland.
"I did have a motive in my mind of this tree and hedge and field," he said.
Through his work with scientists, Lambert said he had been taught about the "perils and the needs of soil".
"If you go back to the fields you were walking in when you were young, you will notice that there is a thinner soil on there and there's more rock on the surface," he said.
UK Save Soil spokesperson Henry Asplin called the painting "a visual call to action".
"Soil is the planet's quiet infrastructure and one of our greatest climate solutions, yet it remains largely invisible in national climate plans," he said.
Mark Maslin, climate scientist and professor at UCL, said healthy soils "regulate water, store carbon, and underpin biodiversity and food systems".
"...protecting and restoring soil must sit at the heart of every nation's climate strategy if we are serious about limiting warming and securing a liveable future," he added.
Jennifer Robinson, from Abingdon-based Oxford Wood Recycling, said looking after the environment was "at the heart" of its work.
She said the company collected wood from several sites across Oxfordshire.
"I myself come from a farming background, so ... I think [Save Soil]'s cause and what they're trying to do is absolutely crucial," she said.
Robinson said she had been noticing changes in the colour of soil locally.
"We're all seeing massive cracks as we're out walking and the areas where there are more plants and more trees, the soil is less exposed and evidently healthier."
