If neither candidate wins a majority, the race will proceed to ranked choice tabulation on Nov. 18. The state's "target date" for certifying the election results is Nov. 25. READ MORE: Will ranked choice voting affect timing of Maine and Alaska's Senate race results? Here's what we know Recounts in Alaska are automatic only in the event of a tie vote. Candidates may also request a recount within five days of the state's certification. More than a dozen House races are still up in the air In most of the House races that have not been called, the margin between the leading candidates was less than 1 percentage point among votes counted as of late Tuesday afternoon. In North Carolina, four races remain undecided, the most of any state, and Republican incumbents were being challenged in all. There are no automatic recounts in North Carolina, but candidates may request a recount if the margin between candidates is 1% or less of the total votes. The state must receive the recount request by noon Eastern time Nov. 17, two business days after the county canvass in the state. The state is scheduled to certify its results Nov. 24. WATCH: Roy Cooper speaks after flipping North Carolina Senate seat for Democrats In California, only one of the remaining House races, in the 23rd District, will affect the chamber's balance of power. The other uncalled race is between two Democrats. Mail ballots must be received by Tuesday and counties must certify their results Dec. 3. The state will certify its results Dec. 11. In South Carolina's 2nd District, a recount is ongoing in the race between Republican incumbent Joe Wilson and Democrat Zyon Khalia. Wilson led Khalia by only about 3,000 votes in the original tally by late Tuesday afternoon, when 99% of the votes had been counted. WATCH: South Carolina wins give Democrats hope to expand reach in Deep South In Minnesota's 1st District, the race was still undecided late in the afternoon Tuesday, with about 300 votes separating the top two candidates and an estimated 99% of votes counted. Recounts are not automatic in Minnesota, but a candidate can request a publicly-funded recount if the margin between the winning and losing candidates is less than 0.25% of the vote. In Tennessee's 4th District, about 300 votes lay between Democrat Victoria Broderick and Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais as of late afternoon Tuesday. FAYETTEVILLE, N.C.— North Carolina environmental regulators this week sent a scathing critique to Chemours, which is responsible for contaminating at least 10 counties with toxic “forever chemicals,” arguing that the company’s cleanup proposal violates the terms of a consent order.
The state Department of Environmental Quality detailed multiple inadequacies in the company’s plan to remediate widespread, decades-old groundwater and soil contamination from PFAS chemicals in southeastern North Carolina.
“Today’s direction to the company makes clear that DEQ expects Chemours to clean up all the areas they have polluted,” said DEQ Secretary Reid Wilson in a prepared statement. “DEQ will hold Chemours accountable no matter how long it takes.”
The company’s predecessor, DuPont, is responsible for some of the contamination emanating from the Fayetteville Works plant, but it shielded itself from liability when it spun off Chemours in 2015. An international company, Chemours manufactures chemicals used to make Teflon cookware, data center coolants and grease-, water- and stain-resistant consumer products.
DEQ’s letter said the agency also determined the company could not justify how it assessed the public health and environmental risk of PFAS exposure. The letter cited numerous instances of what DEQ described as missing data, substandard sampling methods and flawed analyses in Chemours’ reports. In some cases, these errors led the company to reach conclusions that lacked a factual, scientific or legal basis, according to the letter.
The groundwater and soil remediation must be detailed in a corrective action plan, a key component of a 2019 consent order between the company, DEQ and the nonprofit Cape Fear River Watch. The agency rejected the company’s draft corrective action plan in 2020, calling it “inadequate” and lacking a “thorough technical basis.”
Progress on the plan stalled for six years until September, when the state announced it had reached a half-billion dollar settlement with Chemours that included a provision accelerating progress on its completion. The settlement required DEQ to provide written feedback to Chemours.
A Chemours spokesperson told Inside Climate News that with DEQ’s formal feedback to its 2019 corrective action plan, risk assessment and other studies “now in hand, we can move forward. We are reviewing the comments in detail and will respond through the established process.”
Because of shortcomings in Chemours’ data and analysis, DEQ wrote, neither the company nor the agency knows the full extent of the PFAS contamination in the Lower Cape Fear River Basin, nearly 10 years after the public first learned of it through media reports.
Over 36 pages, DEQ rebutted the company’s conclusions about the extent of the contamination and the public health and ecological risks.
Chemours told DEQ that current concentrations of the PFAS chemical GenX near the Fayetteville Works plant were unlikely to harm human health even without treating the groundwater. However, the state said, Chemours failed to evaluate all PFAS originating from the plant, as legally required. DEQ said the company also used outdated toxicological data for GenX, one of 15,000 types of PFAS compounds.
What Are Forever Chemicals?
There are more than 15,000 types of PFAS—per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, the so-called “forever chemicals.” They are found in many consumer products, such as microwave popcorn bags, pizza boxes, stain- and water-resistant clothing and furniture, and lithium-ion batteries, including those used in electric vehicles.
They’ve been linked to many serious health conditions, including several types of cancer.
PFAS also disrupt the ocean’s ability to sequester carbon, a driver of climate change. PFAS manufacturers emit thousands of tons of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere each year.
In 2022, the Chemours Fayetteville plant emitted 52,000 tons of greenhouse gases, according to EPA data.
Chemours’ health risk assessment excluded people who regularly fish in the Cape Fear River for food, and the company didn’t account for other ways people could become exposed, such as eating contaminated vegetables, touching water or soil that contains PFAS or inhaling the compounds, the state added.
DEQ also requested that Chemours complete its investigation about biosolids—sewage sludge—that could have originated from the plant and have been applied to farm fields. The agency requested comprehensive information about where and when the biosolids were shipped offsite and their quantities.
Sewage sludge is often used to fertilize farm fields. When the sludge is contaminated, the PFAS can seep into the soil, groundwater and drinking water wells.
“The agency is asking the company to look into how their contamination is truly going to harm communities,” said Jean Zhuang, senior attorney for the Southern Environmental Law Center, which represents Cape Fear River Watch. “It demands much more of Chemours than the company has ever done so far.”
Over the past six years Chemours has spent about $1.2 billion on complying with some provisions of the consent order. The company installed a thermal oxidizer to remove 99.9 percent of all PFAS emissions from the air, offered free water filtration systems to more than 10,000 homes with contaminated wells and built a mile-long underground barrier wall to prevent contaminated groundwater seeping from the site and into the Cape Fear River.
These projects have reduced, although not eliminated, the amount of PFAS entering the environment. Contaminated groundwater continues to seep from the Fayetteville Works plant into the river and other surface waters; PFAS are still entering the air.
The magnitude of the contamination is so vast that Chemours has previously told DEQ it is “technologically and economically infeasible” to comply as closely as possible with the state’s groundwater rules.

c91cd19fd939.text: By — Josh Boak, Associated Press Josh Boak, Associated Press By — Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press By — Chan Ho-him, Associated Press Chan Ho-him, Associated Press By — Eileen Ng, Associated Press Eileen Ng, Associated Press By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/how-nvidia-ceo-jensen-huangs-extramarital-affair-could-cause-collateral-damage-in-washington Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter How Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affair could cause collateral damage in Washington World Nov 11, 2026 3:26 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Extramarital affairs are usually private matters. Jensen Huang's has global implications. The 63-year-old is the leading face of the artificial intelligence revolution with his black leather jackets and fluff of gray hair. He runs the company Nvidia, which produces highly coveted computer chips. That's landed him on a late-night-phone-call basis with President Donald Trump, a promoter of the industry. READ MORE: Nvidia and Huang face lawsuit alleging investors were misled about spy affair But Huang was also liaising with a Chinese businessperson who has allegedly fed intelligence — as well as advanced chips — to China. Alice Huang is a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News It's a saga of personal betrayal, corporate espionage and high-tech development, and the fallout is spreading across Washington. There are bipartisan calls for investigations on Capitol Hill. The Department of Justice has opened its own investigation. Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, is conducting an internal review. Some expect the technology to reshape human civilization by imbuing computers with the vast powers of creation and analysis, and Trump has repeated that "whoever wins AI, wins." Nvidia is the backbone of America's plans for dominating the field. When asked about Jensen Huang's affair, Trump said this week that he had spoken to the tech executive as the scandal grew. "I think he'll be in good shape," Trump said, adding that "he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy." As for when the president first learned about the concerns involving Alice Huang, Trump brushed off the question. "They could have been mentioned," he said. "Certainly it didn't make much of an impact on me." Authorities are investigating Megaspeed and Alice Huang With the AI race between the U.S. and China often framed as a fierce and consequential rivalry, the Justice Department has persistently warned of the espionage threat posed by Beijing. That includes efforts to cultivate well-placed relationships in government and private industry, as well as to acquire sensitive technology such as AI chips developed in the United States. READ MORE: What we know — and what we don't — as Nvidia investigates an alleged spy plot involving its CEO Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. Commerce Department over its alleged skirting of U.S. export laws and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese users. The company denied those allegations. U.S. intelligence officials eventually concluded that Alice Huang had spied for China, according to The New York Times. The Commerce Department's investigation was handed off to the Justice Department, and its National Security Division is investigating whether Megaspeed violated export control laws in an inquiry that will also include scrutiny of Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing law enforcement inquiry. Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday, and The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang. Jensen Huang has apologized to his company about the affair, saying he hurt his wife and their children, but he didn't address reports that Alice Huang was a suspected spy. Nvidia's board said that it had "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, and that Huang would remain in charge while cooperating with the investigation. Beijing has said the "Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated" and called it "nothing but smears." Trump has been close with Jensen Huang After their first dinner together at Mar-a-Lago in early 2025, Trump latched onto Jensen Huang as a tech titan positioned to deliver on the president's own promises of an economic renaissance. The computer chips produced by Nvidia would essentially turn data centers into factories that made raw intelligence, which could then be applied across the economy to produce cars, new pharmaceutical drugs, advanced weapons and seemingly unparalleled wealth. Trump would regularly phone Huang to discuss this future. "From the moment that I met him, the only thing that he's ever talked to me about is creating more jobs, reindustrializing the United States, of protection, of national security," Jensen Huang told AP in an interview this summer. "He knows that if America is wealthy, we have a lot of tax revenues. We can fund the military, we can fund our economy, we fund our communities, create more jobs." Trump saw his political fortunes — and that of the country — in Huang's Nvidia. Huang joined Trump on Air Force One for a state visit to Beijing earlier this year. Just last month, Trump awarded Huang with a National Medal of Science. WATCH: Trump says FBI is looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese agent The president called him "a man whose determination laid the foundations for the explosion of super intelligence and put America at the front of the race, an amazing man, gotten to know him so well." Nvidia also donated $25 million to help fund the construction of Trump's White House ballroom. Multiple estimates suggest that more t

cdf10059d309.text: The U.S. has asked Russia to submit a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe that includes Russian steps to ease tension with the continent, two sources with knowledge of the matter said. Why it matters: For years, Russia has sought a European security deal that limits NATO expansion and scales back its military presence in Eastern Europe. The U.S. has rejected those demands in the past, but now appears open to them in some form as part of a broader agreement to end the war in Ukraine. But many European governments are deeply suspicious of the administration's approach. State of play: President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday to reiterate the request. They also want Putin to allow European representatives to join the next round of Russia-Ukraine peace talks, a U.S. official said. From Moscow, Kushner and Witkoff are expected to travel to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday night. Catch up quick: The talks on Tuesday and Wednesday were the first time Ukrainian and Russian officials met with U.S. mediators present since February, when they were suspended due to the war in Iran. In recent weeks, Witkoff and Kushner met with both Putin and Zelensky, creating a bit of momentum. Putin agreed to resume peace talks and release U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was detained by Russia in 2022 . Together with First Lady Melania Trump and her team, Witkoff and Kushner also brokered a humanitarian ceasefire in the city of Oleshky. Driving the news: The talks in Abu Dhabi started on Tuesday with Witkoff, Kushner and commander of the U.S. European Command Gen. Alexus Grynkewich mediating between the Russians and the Ukrainians. The parties agreed to a prisoner exchange deal that Kushner and Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said could be the biggest since the war began. U.S. and Ukrainian officials said the exact number of prisoners to be released will be decided during meetings with Putin and Zelensky on Thursday. Before and after the talks, the U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams briefed a delegation of senior diplomats from Germany, the UK, France, Italy, the EU and NATO. Behind the scenes: The meetings between the Russians and the Ukrainians on Tuesday were tense and at times emotional, with both sides airing grievances after nine months of not talking directly, according to a source in the room. Kushner and Witkoff tried to lower the temperature, telling Russian and Ukrainian negotiators that the goal is to end this round of talks with options for the leaders on both sides. Eventually, after each party made its case, the discussion became more constructive, the source said. "We had pretty tough discussions," Kushner said at a press conference after the talks concluded on Wednesday. "The Russians came with strict directives. It was very hard to soften it, but it ended productively," Arakhamia said. Zoom in: The U.S. proposal to secure a deal on a new Europe-Russia security architecture as part of an agreement to end the war in Ukraine was a key focus of the Abu Dhabi talks. Russian negotiators said Putin launched the invasion of Ukraine because then-President Biden did not reply to his 2021 letter laying out his security concerns, two sources with knowledge of the talks said. According to one of the sources, Kushner and Witkoff told the Russians that the world has changed a lot since 2021. They proposed that Russia draft a new proposal that includes its security concerns and demands, but also lays out what "symmetrical steps" it's willing to take to de-escalate and reassure Europe that it will not attack in the future. Kushner and Witkoff also told the Russians that in order to seriously discuss security issues in Europe, they need to agree to allow European representatives to participate in future peace talks. "We told the Russians, they have their desires and fears, but they have to provide different de-escalation and different proposals as well, if they want Europe to be able to receive those proposals in a good way," Kushner said at the press conference. The other side: So far, Russia has been unwilling to allow Europeans to be part of peace talks with Ukraine. "As for the leadership of a number of European countries, they are essentially engaged in a collective deception of the Ukrainian people and contributing to the mass deaths of civilians," Putin adviser Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation, said at a press conference after the talks. "Therefore, I don't understand what can be discussed with them." Still, Medinsky said that Russia wants to reach a broader security deal with Europe as part of an agreement to end the war. "In Ukraine, an abscess has simply burst. The entire body needs to be treated — a Band-Aid won't do the trick," he said. What to watch: The Trump administration wants to negotiate a new Europe-Russia security architecture and a Russia-Ukraine peace deal simultaneously. But the implementation of a security arrangement would only happen after a deal to end the war is reached, according to a source familiar with the White House's thinking. The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said before the talks in Abu Dhabi that Europe will discuss a new security architecture only after the war in Ukraine ends. But two sources with knowledge said European officials who were in Abu Dhabi this week agreed to engage on both tracks simultaneously, while stressing that final decisions on European security architecture would be made only after the war in Ukraine ends. The U.S. hopes giving European representatives a seat at the peace talks will make their governments more willing to discuss and agree on a broader security agreement before the war ends. The Caine Prize for African Writing has said that after an internal review it has found no evidence that Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza had used generative AI to write his winning short story and confirmed him as the winner of this year's Â£10,000 ($13,000) award.
Ellah Wakatama, chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees, said the matter had been investigated following an article in US magazine The Atlantic with the headline, Yet Another Literary Prizewinner Seems to Be AI.
"From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human written," she said in a video posted on X.
The accusation had caused a social media uproar and Kundizeza had denied the allegation.
The Atlantic article by journalist Vauhini Vara alleged that AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.
Her allegations followed rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author ThÃ©lyson OrÃ©lien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies.
Following the publication of her article last month, Vara had told BBC's Front Row programme that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".
The backlash on social media included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.
Wakatama said the Caine Prize organisation had considered Vara's allegations "carefully and fairly".
"We chose to take a human-centred approach to the investigation. Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel, and the Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published," she said.
"It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author."
In a statement, the Caine Prize explained further that the analysis had been conducted by an independent cyber security and digital forensic investigator, external.
The day after winning the prestigious Caine Prize award earlier in October, Kundizeza had told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.
He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began.

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.
Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.
Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.
Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.
The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.
The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.
This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.
The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.
Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

A ship that was once the fastest in the world and is longer than the Titanic will be sunk off the coast of Florida and turned into the world's largest artificial ocean reef.
The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will soon become a home for sealife and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.
Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.
Instead, after being purchased by a Florida county, it will be added to the dozens of artificial reefs off the coast, as a land-based museum detailing the ship's history is also planned.
Before its retirement, the SS United States was known for carrying royalty and celebrities from the US the Europe, beginning in 1952 and ending in 1969.
A young Bill Clinton, before he was president, used the ship to cross the Atlantic. Former presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John Kennedy also travelled on the vessel.
The ship was moved from Philadelphia to Alabama last year for cleaning and remediation work. On Monday, it took its final journey from Alabama to the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will be sunk on Wednesday in a precision operation without explosives.
Stars including Marlon Brando, Coco Chanel, Duke Ellington, Salvador Dali, Walt Disney, Judy Garland and Cary Grant also boarded the ship during its sailing lifetime.
Before its purchase by the municipal Florida government, a number of proposals that would have seen the ship live a second life as a museum or a floating hotel failed.
Instead, the famed ship sat at various docks with various owners as legal battles played out.
The SS United States Conservancy group repeatedly attempted to keep the ship above water, but was unsuccessful.
Conservancy President Susan Gibbs - whose grandfather helped design the SS United States - said she was glad that the story of the ship would live on.
"[The ship] has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together," Gibbs told CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father.
Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him.
The baby was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours.
The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery.
Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father.
The search for baby Koah began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house.
Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Koah.
Comer was seen travelling to multiple locations without the baby and was later arrested in Lexington County without Koah. A search party of 100 police and fire department officials were then sent to search for the child, the sheriff said.
He added that when they asked Comer where his son was, he "did not have much to say" about his whereabouts.
Koon said that rescuers searched the woods near Comer's house and saw some "freshly disturbed dirt". As they began to dig, they heard a baby crying - something the sheriff described as "the most joyful sound you ever heard".
"The race was on. Everybody was getting down there trying to get him out," Koon added.
He said the crate was wrapped in a towel that probably provided enough air for Koah to survive for as long as he did, while the cold weather kept him from getting too hot.
"The crate was, probably, I'm guessing about a two-foot [61cm] by two-foot dog crate. So, I think, once that crate hit the ground, he was probably up at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground," Koon explained.
Of the parents' relationship, the sheriff said there were "obviously some issues". Comer had previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges, court records show.
Comer's mother, Patricia Comer, told NBC News that Koah's mother had full custody of him but allowed her to supervise while her son watched him. She said her son had watched the baby before unsupervised without any problems.
"Honestly, I'm his mother, and I never expected this from him," Patricia Comer said.

Jack Zhang isnât worried about AI taking over global finance, but he is concerned about cybersecurity.
Zhang co-founded Australian fintech unicorn Airwallex, which allows businesses to make cross-border payments and manage finances in dozens of countries, and is now morphing into an agentic finance company.
Zhang joined Future Proof to discuss how his company is using AI to build systems to help companies handle their finances âÂ essentially building an AI-managed CFO office. The company currently relies mainly on ChatGPT and Claude, but Zhang also said itâs looking at developing proprietary models using open-weight solutions.
Zhang doesnât think AI will get so good that it can entirely replace humans, at least not in his field. âThe laws still require you to have somebody sign off as auditor, and how the auditor does that sign-off can be assisted by agents,â he said. âI donât think we can completely get rid of the human in the loop.â
What Zhang is âvery, very, very, very worriedâ about is cybersecurity. With news about cyber breaches emerging almost daily, the company is tackling the issue by using behavioral monitoring and hiring experts from the Australian Department of Defence and Palantir, among other strategies.
âWeâre moving hundreds of billions of dollars today ... Weâre constantly paranoid about how good our defense [is] against this type of threat,â he said.

Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.
Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.
However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.
Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."
"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.
Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said.
After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.
The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.
For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.
For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.
Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.
That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.
Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.
Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.
There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.
Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.
Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security.
Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said.
Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.
Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again.
"These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."

CHEEK—On a rural road outside Beaumont, a Texas energy giant is preparing to pump carbon dioxide underground to permanently store it and keep the gas from contributing to global warming. The project could be the first of its kind to start operating in the state.
It’s a long-awaited milestone for the oil and gas industry, which has touted carbon capture and storage as an important tool for cleaning up industry emissions. Texas lawmakers threw their support behind the technology, while state regulators spent years seeking permitting authority from the federal government to try to clear projects faster.
The Texas Railroad Commission, which oversees the oil and gas industry, won that authority late last year and approved this ExxonMobil project in September. But the nearby community of Cheek has asked commissioners to reconsider the permit decision.
The area close to the project is predominantly Black, and many residents are working class or elderly. People there don’t trust the company’s assurances that it will keep residents and their groundwater safe.
Only a small number of carbon storage wells have been permitted so far across the United States, and some CO2-related accidents have already happened. Experts and community advocates have warned of the risk for pipeline accidents and potential underground leaks. Leaders in Cheek are concerned the injected carbon dioxide could contaminate groundwater or get into the air and suffocate them. They worry emergency responders won’t be equipped to rescue them.
“We’re just shocked that they would want to do this so close to homes,” said Douglas Cormier, the 67-year-old president of the Cheek Texas Community Association, who grew up in the rural town and lives there with his wife near his daughters and grandkids.
Residents explained they don’t want to be the test subjects for the technology, and some experts argue it’s more distracting than effective in fighting climate change. Harvard University History of Science Professor Naomi Oreskes, who studies disinformation and climate change, has called carbon capture and storage “mostly a dangerous distraction.”
A recent investigation by Drilled and ProPublica showed it would take more resources than feasible for carbon capture and storage to reduce emissions enough to avoid extreme warming. Companies have canceled or paused nearly a third of 19 proposed carbon storage projects in Texas so far.
But carbon capture supporters argue that storing emissions is an important part of an “all of the above” approach to fighting climate change. Federal tax credits support carbon capture projects. Locally, East Texas remains attractive because of its existing carbon dioxide pipeline network (owned by ExxonMobil), its geology and nearby industrial facilities that might pay for their carbon to be stored.
ExxonMobil has seven agreements with companies to store the greenhouse gas. The volume of carbon dioxide injected underground through those agreements will equal emissions from 2 million cars.
“The community’s concerns around safety of any sort of an injection project are valid and real and need to be taken seriously,” said Nichole Saunders, senior director and lead counsel for energy transition with the Environmental Defense Fund. “At the same time, the need for more carbon management infrastructure to get to where we want to go on climate is also real.”
So far, the case has raised questions about whether companies and the Railroad Commission are doing enough to address community concerns as a backlog of projects awaits approval.
Agency watchdogs say the commission has a history of failing to keep communities safe from industry risks. It’s also facing pressure from state Rep. Drew Darby, leader of the House’s energy resources committee, who told the agency at a September hearing that carbon-capture projects needed to be moving at “utmost pace while protecting the public.”
In a statement to the Tribune, Railroad Commission spokesperson Bryce Dubee said the organization has a record of protecting drinking water while regulating injection wells. Winning the authority to regulate carbon storage “speaks volumes to this expertise,” Dubee said.
ExxonMobil held early meetings with community members in Cheek. The company’s permit requires it to install automatic shut-off systems for the injection wells, monitor the underground carbon dioxide plume and post a phone number where the operators can be reached around the clock.
The permitting program requires coordination with local emergency officials, according to the commission. ExxonMobil sponsors emergency training programs through the Texas A&M Engineering Extension Service in College Station.
“We want community members to know they can count on us to operate responsibly, communicate openly, and put safety first every day,” senior vice president Dominic Genetti wrote in a blog post.
But the day following Darby’s comments, after hearing ExxonMobil hadn’t talked with the community since the residents hired lawyers, Railroad Commission Chair Christi Craddick scolded ExxonMobil for not supporting residents enough. Some people from Cheek had taken a bus to be there to voice their concern.
“Give them information,” she said. “Be there for their safety. Give ‘em a fire truck if that’s what they want.”
Then Craddick voted for the permit.
Community Distrust
Photos and posters about the area’s decades-long history hosting local rodeos hang in 81-year-old Preston Frank’s self-made museum in Cheek. Like many who live here, Frank, an upholsterer, inherited the land from his family. He considers it an important way to build generational wealth.
“That’s the reason why we’ve been fighting ExxonMobil,” he said. “We don’t want them coming in here and diminishing the value of the land.”

Reedâs view
Nvidia has been battered over the past couple of days, but it could get worse.
That is, if founder and CEO Jensen Huang is forced or chooses to step down, or if investigations pin him down for doing something illegal.
In most sectors of the economy, CEOs are expected to run businesses well, but they are generally interchangeable parts â albeit expensive ones. Google and Apple show that founder CEOs, which are harder to replicate, can be replaced. But even among founder CEOs, Huang stands apart for bold bets that helped him endure short-term suffering in return for long-term gain. Most people know Nvidia for the climbing stock in their portfolios, or the GPUs on every tech companyâs Christmas list. But his creation of the CUDA platform in 2006 is perhaps the best example of how heâs been able to step ahead of the industry for decades. Nvidiaâs computing platform and programming model, the software that essentially underpins the modern AI industry, created one of the most valuable moats in business history.
A half dozen years later, seeing the progress in neural networks, he pivoted to AI. Huang realized AI would require massive data centers with interconnected chips, and concluded that networking would become the bottleneck. He bet billions on the development of NVLink, a nervous system that allows discrete GPUs to act as one massive supercomputer, and the $6.9 billion acquisition of Mellanox Technologies, the Israeli networking company, in 2019. He funded neoclouds so he wouldnât be reliant on a few customers and acquired Hugging Face to stay ahead of the game on open source.
Huang is 63, and while he has said he could run the company for decades to come, the current investigations raise questions about the future of one of the worldâs most consequential companies. Even if he does ride out the turmoil, will he still have the same bold personality that got him here?
Nvidia may still mint money, as demand for the companyâs products shows no signs of slowing down. But itâs difficult to imagine anyone stepping into the role with the strategic vision and gravitas to match Huangâs.
The next handful of years are going to be even trickier. China is ascendant. Once it gains independence on semiconductors, it will be able to scale faster than the US. There wonât be any data-center red tape and China will have abundant energy compared to the US.
Because Mooreâs law is dead, AI chipmakers are no longer making exponentially better chips every year. Now, they must design entire systems with compute and cooling crammed into server racks like the worldâs highest-stakes game of Tetris. They involve immensely complex supply chains colored by geopolitics, big personalities, and vast sums of money.
Nvidia will be a crucial player in the effort to stay ahead of China. Without Huang, it will be fundamentally weakened. It may be already.

4f06b70962b1.text: By — Katie Marlow Katie Marlow Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/watch-live-ss-united-states-once-worlds-fastest-ocean-liner-sinks-to-become-reef-off-florida Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: SS United States, once world's fastest ocean liner, sinks to become reef off Florida Nation Nov 11, 2026 12:54 PM EST The historic ocean liner SS United States will be intentionally sunk Wednesday off the coast of the Florida panhandle. Live coverage of the sinking of the SS United States is expected to start at 1 p.m. EST, with the sinking expected at 2 p.m. EST. Watch live in the video player above. In its heyday, the SS United States crushed the trans-Atlantic speed record, which it still holds. The luxury ocean liner took only three days to cross from New York to Europe on its maiden voyage in 1952. Carrying presidents and Hollywood stars, the nearly 1,000-foot vessel was a technical marvel of its time. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News However, the rise of air travel and high operating costs sunk its economic viability, and the ship was pulled from service in 1969. The ocean liner sat at Philadelphia's Pier 82 for nearly 30 years. After a contentious back and forth with a pier landlord over rent and docking fees, Okaloosa County in Florida eventually stepped in to purchase the ship and bring it to the Gulf of Mexico to become the world's largest artificial reef. The multi-million dollar project is also aimed at creating an economic development opportunity as a major diving attraction. WATCH: Why the military is creating artificial reefs to protect U.S. shorelines "It was our goal to make sure that she wasn't lost forever," said David Lawrence, a member of the board for the SS United States Conservancy, the group that sold the vessel to the Florida county. Like the ship's unconventional life, it will also have an unconventional sinking. Federal environmental and explosives rules prevent the county from using explosives. Instead, tanks inside the ship have been removed and large holes were cut into the decks. Once the valves are opened, water will flood the hull, sinking the ship. Resting at 180 feet below the surface of the water, the SS United States will join more than 500 artificial reefs in Okaloosa County, which the county relies on to support the underwater ecosystem. The News
Progressive Democrats are trying a tricky feat as their party takes power: endorsing Medicare for All while quietly pushing for smaller steps toward it.
Their dilemma began with the partyâs remarkable midterm success. Democrats are united in attributing their electoral triumph in part to voter backlash against GOP healthcare moves â and this year, even purple-district candidates won while backing Medicare for All.
But now, the left is split on how to make it happen. Without a filibuster or veto-proof majority in Congress next year, Democrats are calibrating their expectations for change based on what can potentially pass through the maneuver known as reconciliation, which requires only a simple majority.
Some progressives are calling for a unified drive to lower the Medicare eligibility age, add guaranteed coverage up to age 19, and add dental and vision coverage. That could offer a middle ground for party leaders who are looking to stave off fights over bills likely to be vetoed by President Donald Trump.
Embracing a big step toward pure Medicare for All could also hand a victory to progressives who have long pushed for legislative action â if they can settle for something less than the litmus test they set up.
âItâs the perfect way for us to get ready for the next trifecta if we pass those three bills, and then if we mark up the entire Medicare for All bill,â said Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., the lead sponsor of the Houseâs Medicare for All bill.
Others on the left may not be content with pushing off action on the marquee policy until later. An incoming cohort of progressives want to push their party to vote on the full government-run healthcare package now. Rep.-elect Melat Kiros, D-Colo., said the program was âone of our number one priorities.â
âIâll never let perfect be the enemy of the good,â she added. âBut if weâre not fighting like hell to actually get healthcare to every single American, then I donât know what weâre doing here.â
Centrists wanted the party to work towards consensus â a tall order for Democrats. Quite a few in the caucus want the party to focus on the underlying drivers of healthcare costs before considering a system where taxpayers pay for all healthcare.
âI think we should talk more about cost and less about coverage,â said Rep. Jake Auchincloss, D-Mass.
Democratic leaders have said they would need to have a âfamily conversationâ on their path forward; a working group led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., laid out a menu of options that included Medicare for All alongside many other proposals.
âAre we messaging or are we getting something done?â said Rep. Adam Gray, D-Calif., a member of the moderate Blue Dogs. âWe know that we have broad agreement that we want healthcare to be affordable, that we want it to be accessible â¦ and that every American should have it, and so what are the solutions we can get agreement on to do that?â
The Plan
Democrats across the ideological spectrum have coalesced around their healthcare agenda in the near term. After relentlessly campaigning on reversing GOP-enacted Medicaid cuts and restoring lapsed health care subsidies, Democrats plan to put those up for a vote.
They may even use the issues as leverage in the looming December government funding fight.
âI think everything should be on the table,â said Rep. Glenn Ivey, D-Md. âItâs important for us to make sure we listen to and respond to the message of the voters, and I think they want to really get relief.â
Rep. Kim Schrier, D-Wash., said that she wants both of those priorities to advance, but cautioned that âwe still have the same president in the White House.â
The View From The Senate
Across the Capitol, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is pushing to use reconciliation to immediately advance his bill to lower the Medicare eligibility age to 55, add dental, vision and hearing coverage to the federal health insurance program for seniors, and ensure universal coverage for children through age 19.
Sanders already has one powerful ally: Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., the expected chair of the Senate Finance Committee, said he wants âto push for the boldest, best bill possible.â
âIâm not taking anything off the table,â Wyden said, when asked about whether he supported using reconciliation to advance the legislation.
Other senators are already calling for a more moderate approach.
On Tuesday, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., introduced a bill that would lower the Medicare eligibility age to 50 and allow adults to buy into traditional Medicare or Medicare Advantage plans.
The legislation would allow adults eligible for Affordable Care Act cost-sharing subsidies and premium tax credits to continue to use such assistance to help make Medicare plans more affordable. But it would not give adults taxpayer-funded Medicare before they turn 65.
Nicholas and Davidâs View
Democrats are going to eventually grapple with what exactly âMedicare for Allâ means to the disparate factions in their caucus.
While Republicans will be quick to paint any effort as a first step toward implementing a single-payer healthcare system that replaces private insurance, the truth is more complicated. The reality is that very few Democrats on the campaign trail explicitly called for the enactment of a single government-run insurance plan.
But with dozens of Democrats expected to launch presidential campaigns over the coming year, supporting universal healthcare coverage may quickly become, yet again, an up-or-down question for primary voters.

The News
In the fall of 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was riding high on the wave of the AI boom. He also landed at the center of an ideological war over chip exports that the $4 trillion company and its allies now think played a pivotal role in his undoing.
On one side were the China hawks inside the Trump administration â and circling outsiders â who worried Huangâs chips were helping fuel Chinaâs AI ambitions. On the other side were Huang, David Sacks, and other technologists that argued for spreading US tech around the globe to ensure American-backed AI became the world standard.
Huangâs long-held, pro-trade views were already unpopular with many of the think tankers, academics, national security staffers, and US government officials that make up a loosely held group of anti-China ideologues. But in a podcast interview with influential venture capitalists Bill Gurley and Brad Gerstner, Huang took things further, arguing the term âChina hawkâ is a badge of âshameâ and that those who wear it are not âpatriotic.â
The slight did not go unnoticed, drawing the ire of anti-technology voices like far-right podcast host Steve Bannon and other critics who had railed against Huangâs lobbying against strict China export controls.
âLetâs just say this â China hawks are patient and have long memories,â wrote Eric Sayers, a former Congressional defense staffer and current managing director of lobbyist Beacon Global Strategies, a firm that has done work on China policy, according to people familiar with the matter.
Sayers re-upped his year-old X post again on Nov. 2, days before Huang admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, on the back of weeks of media coverage digging into Megaspeed, an AI data center company based in Singapore that US government officials allege might be smuggling Nvidia chips into China. The implication was clear: Huangâs fate was not simply a result of the Nvidia CEOâs own personal failings or bad judgment. He had also made powerful enemies at the highest echelons of government that Nvidia now believes has all but stopped the companyâs ability to lobby for the export of chips to China, according to a person briefed on the matter.
Although thereâs no evidence to suggest they are connected to any leaks, among the most prominent of the China hawks that have been mentioned, these people say, are Sayersâ former colleague, Ivan Kanapathy, who serves as senior director for Asia at the National Security Council, and Tarun Chhabra, who served as deputy assistant to the president and coordinator for technology and national security on the National Security Council, and Landon Heid, an NSC staffer who nearly became assistant secretary of commerce for export administration at the Bureau of Industry and Security.
Chhabra now works for Anthropic, another vocal critic of chip sales to China, with CEO Dario Amodei comparing the practice to selling nuclear weapons to North Korea. Anthropic has also accused Chinese AI companies of stealing its intellectual property in order to train open weight AI models.
Spokespeople for Nvidia, the White House, Commerce Department, State Department, NSC, Marco Rubio, and Beacon Global didnât immediately respond to requests for comment.
Itâs unclear who was responsible for leaking national security documents that were used to discredit Huang. And whether the Nvidia CEO was the target of an espionage plot, or if there was any wrongdoing on his or Nvidiaâs part, will be determined by investigators in the months ahead. But the damage has already shaved about $280 billion off the market value of the $4.2 trillion company. Huangâs now facing a board probe, shareholder lawsuits, Congressional questioning, and the near-certain prospect of details leaking out in drips and drabs.
Several people familiar with their China policy agenda say the group of hawks wield considerable power and influence in DC, and the elimination of Huang from the other side of the debate will make the upcoming fight over export controls being added to the National Defense Authorization Act significantly easier.
Reedâs view
Huang obviously walked into a scandal, but the US government bears some responsibility for clearing up whether or not itâs investigating the founder of the countryâs most successful company, potentially harming a company with massive strategic value and shaving off billions of dollars of a stock thatâs in most peopleâs investment accounts.
Nvidiaâs success and failure has direct and indirect impacts on almost everybody in the US, and many around the world. We should get a full accounting of the impacts of an extrajudicial action against a US citizen by the government with enormous economic implications, positive and negative. Either something is classified or itâs not. Now that itâs been leaked, the rest of the information should be made public.
Room for Disagreement
From James Czerniawski, head of emerging technology policy at the Consumer Choice Center. âThe government shouldnât be able to weaponize a surveillance file against an American and their business. It should concern every American whenever intelligence is selectively surfaced and leveraged to advance certain policies, whether that means tighter chip export controls or building support for reauthorizing a deeply flawed surveillance program. When the government wields this kind of power, it isnât just disrupting an individualâs life; it can put a target on an American company and create economic uncertainty in the marketplace. That kind of power demands real limitations and accountability. Protecting our national security is important, but giving the government carte blanche to use its surveillance capabilities is a recipe for disaster that will ultimately leave everyone worse off.â

f82e9c2e4ab0.text: By — Darlene Superville, Associated Press Darlene Superville, Associated Press By — Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/white-house-sends-warning-to-democrats-about-investigating-the-trump-administration Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter White House sends warning to Democrats about investigating the Trump administration Politics Nov 11, 2026 12:06 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the Trump administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress -- may amount to "blatant criminality." White House counsel Will Scharf issued the warning in a letter dated Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee. WATCH: Rep. Garcia says voters gave Democrats a mandate to pursue accountability Garcia most likely would chair the powerful panel in the new Democratic-controlled Congress that is seated in January. Garcia warned Trump officials to "lawyer up" after his party's stunning victories in last week's midterm elections. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News In response, Scharf wrote in Monday's letter that "threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality." The letter's existence was first reported by Punchbowl News. Garcia said in response to the letter that "it appears Donald Trump has something to hide" and stressed that Congress's investigative powers do not need the "permission of the White House." "Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate," Garcia said. "The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse." Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing. Garcia also wants to look at the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations. Other targets include Trump's White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family's role in mineral deals and Trump's crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a CNN interview that aired Sunday that "there could be" a crime to investigate if rhetoric from Democrats turned threatening. He appeared to strike a more conciliatory tone during an appearance in Missouri this week, saying "Congress has oversight authority. It always has, it always will. The Department of Justice, the federal government, works with Congress to address questions they have — whether it's through subpoenas or letters — so we're not going to stop working with Congress." "Nothing I've said this weekend, or in the past, should suggest otherwise," he added. Associated Press writer Eric Tucker contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The Signal Interview
An 11-item menu board from the 1950s still hangs in McDonaldâs Chicago headquarters, recalling the era when Ray Kroc struck his franchise agreement with the McDonald brothers and began building the worldâs best known fast-food chain. The 10-cent root beers are long gone, but Chris Kempczinski, who marked his seventh anniversary as CEO this week, is having to pay new attention to its value proposition.
The business is facing a âchallengingâ US consumer environment, he told investors this week, with comparable sales falling 0.2% in the three months to September. Kempczinskiâs assurance that the company had started to turn things around in the last month of the quarter helped revive a stock that had fallen a jarring 32% between February and October. But to reverse the drop in customer visits, he has had to put more marketing dollars behind potentially slimmer-margin deals, like a $2 breakfast sandwich with free fries for loyalty program members.
âOur goal is straightforward,â Kempczinski told Wall Street: âCustomers should see a clear and compelling value proposition every time they consider McDonaldâs.â
Few companies see as many consumers each week as McDonaldâs does, and it has seen growing numbers of lower-income Americans staying home for breakfast or skipping it altogether, Kempczinski says in an interview for The CEO Signal.
âHousing, medical care, childcare, utilities, transport â all of those things are putting, I think, a lot of pressure on peopleâs disposable income,â he says.
McDonaldâs sometimes benefits in tough economic times, as higher-earning households trade down from pricier restaurants. But the US economyâs current âK-shapedâ nature means that wealthier households are still eating out in pricier restaurants, rather than trading down to eat burgers and fries.
Reserving the right to get smarter in a franchised system
Kempczinskiâs $8.5 billion game plan, announced in June and dubbed âMcDonaldâs > NEXT,â is the second strategic overhaul of his tenure. Designed to update the groupâs menu and modernize restaurants, he expects it to lift sales and margins by making McDonaldâs âmore customersâ first choice more often.â
The complication is that about 95% of the worldâs 46,000 McDonaldâs restaurants are owned and operated by franchisees â and some have pushed back against a proposal that could require $650,000 to $800,000 of investment per store.
There is tension in any business where customers want better value, franchisees want healthier returns, and shareholders want faster growth. McDonaldâs relies on its 5,000 independent partners to execute its strategy, Kempczinski notes, which means he must operate âthrough influence, not through direct control.â
A clear focus on growth can unite his disparate stakeholders, he believes. âIf you have growth and the pie is expanding, itâs amazing how harmonious everything is,â he says. âWhen the pie isnât growing, then everybody starts to think about their share â¦ and then a system can turn on itself.â
Restaurant upgrades are essential for driving that growth, he says, because âyou canât sell a $5 burger in a $1 lobby.â But he knows he canât influence franchisees who think heâs not listening to them, and he says the headline number McDonaldâs put on its proposals âfor sure is going to get knocked downâ in response to their feedback.
He wonât be so âdogmaticâ about the details of his strategy that he wonât learn from their feedback, he says. âWe have a saying here at McDonaldâs: We reserve the right to get smarter.â
This week, he told analysts he feels âoverall, goodâ about franchiseesâ willingness to roll out the upgrades his strategic plan requires.
Changing a risk-averse culture through âpositive shamingâ
Kempczinski, who grew up in a Catholic household in Cincinnati and would visit McDonaldâs after Friday night football games, admits to some Midwestern conservatism. When he was invited to pick art for his office from the McDonaldâs archive, he chose an all-American Norman Rockwell painting.
But the former Procter & Gamble brand executive says he balances those instincts with a restlessness that he is trying to bring to McDonaldâs. âThe company is never going to go faster than the pace that the CEO sets,â he says, and he is pushing people to take more risks and make faster decisions.
McDonaldâs is âawesomeâ at testing new offerings and ideas, Kempczinski says, by way of example. With thousands of restaurants, âwe can do A/B testing forever â¦ but you can also test for too long.â The danger in a collaborative culture like at McDonaldâs is that âeverybody owns it and nobody owns it,â he observes. âYes, we all need to work together, but at the end of the day, there needs to be a person or a group whoâs actually held accountable for the results.â
A CEO can do that by appointing people to senior positions who model the behavior they want others to adopt, he says. And, instead of shaming people for their mistakes, he believes âpositive shamingâ â praising top performers who set the right example â gets better results.
The lessons of a Big Arch and a little bite
McDonaldâs menu now ranges from Cookie Butter Iced Coffee to the Red Bull Dragonberry Energizer drink, and includes far more chicken than it once did. Demand for chicken has been surging for several years, and the home of the Big Mac already sells more of it than KFC or Chick-fil-A.
But Kempczinski sees âa lot of headroomâ to sell more still, he says, with a push to add KFC-style breaded chicken to the menu. McDonaldâs already commands more than 40% of the beef business in its 10 biggest markets, amounting to about $50 billion, he explains â but it has only 20% of the $130 billion chicken market. His strategy is about more than building on the power of McNuggets and McCrispy Strips, he says. âItâs just simple math.â

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports.
CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal.
Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade.
While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials.
"After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.
Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents.
Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area.
In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans.
The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".
Other US officials reportedly on Iran's list of potential targets include former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Advisor John Bolton and Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Milley and Bolton's security teams were taken away by the Trump administration shortly after he returned to office last year.
Bessent is one of a number of administration officials that live on military bases. The White House's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, was moved to a base in late 2025 - before the conflict with Iran began.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both live on military bases, as did former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard.
The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.
In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a blockade targeting Iranian ports.

Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.
It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.
The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.
Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.
Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.
Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.
It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.
Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.
On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.
Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.
Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.
His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.
Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.
Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.
Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.
All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.
On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

1e0caadefc7b.text: By — Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-weighs-lawsuit-brought-by-peltola-campaign-over-absentee-ballots-in-alaskas-us-senate-race Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge weighs lawsuit brought by Peltola campaign over absentee ballots in Alaska's Senate race Politics Nov 11, 2026 11:01 AM EST JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — A state judge said Tuesday that he expects to issue a swift decision in a lawsuit filed by the campaign of Alaska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola, which is seeking a list of absentee voters whose ballots have been rejected in one of the most closely watched races of the midterm elections. LIVE RESULTS: Alaska Senate midterm election Peltola's campaign also said it wants to know the reasons for the rejections and said its intent is to ensure that all qualified voters have their ballots counted. Attorneys for the state say the information requested would violate voter privacy. The campaign sued Friday, three days after the ranked choice election in which Peltola and two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan are the main contenders. Absentee, early in-person and other ballots are still being tallied. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Alaska's is one of two U.S. Senate races, along with Mississippi's, that remain too early to call. In arguments before state Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews, Peltola attorney Abha Khanna said the campaign isn't seeking to disrupt the ongoing ballot counting process and it has seen no cause for concerns. READ MORE: Alaskans are waiting for more votes in Senate and governor's races. Both could go to ranked tabulations "As far as we can tell, the absentee ballot review process is going incredibly smoothly and we plan to keep it that way," she said. But Khanna argued the information the campaign seeks is a matter of public record and is in line with what campaign observers have access to in locations where absentee review boards are meeting. The campaign wants access to that information in a more centralized way, she said. Absentee review boards meet at the state Division of Elections' regional offices, and campaigns and parties can have observers on hand to watch the process. State law includes provisions for challenging absentee ballots if there is "good reason to suspect" that a challenged voter is ineligible to cast a ballot. In a court filing, attorneys for the state said daily reports generated by the division with lists of absentee ballots to be reviewed are not public records because they contain confidential information and are "ephemeral working documents that are not meant for preservation." The final word on whether to accept or reject an absentee ballot comes from the state review board, which goes over the work of the regional absentee review boards. The version of the report that observers, such as those affiliated with the campaigns, receive does not include as much confidential information but does include home addresses that many voters seek to keep private, said Michaela Thompson, who manages absentee ballot review boards for the elections division. The state's "old, inflexible" voter database cannot produce a report that excludes confidential addresses, she said. The observers must sign confidentiality agreements and cannot keep, copy or record information in the report, she said. No absentee ballot is rejected until after the state review board process finishes and the results are certified, she said. Assistant Attorney General Margaret Paton Walsh told the judge that state law sets out timelines for notifying voters if their absentee ballot is rejected. Voters can check the status of their ballot through an online system, but the information isn't posted until at least 10 days after certification, she said. It doesn't make sense that a campaign would have access to that information before a voter does, she said. Alaska does not have a process that allows voters to fix problems on absentee ballots that can cause them to be rejected, such as forgetting to sign the envelope. The state accepts ballots up to 15 days after general elections from overseas voters, making Nov. 18 the final day to receive them. That also is the target for the Division of Elections to conduct ranked vote tabulations if no candidate wins more than 50% of the first-choice votes. The division has announced vote counts for Tuesday and Friday this week, with the potential for additional days, as well as the Nov. 18 count. An attorney for Sullivan's campaign, Stacey Stone, filed a motion in support of the state. But the campaign said that if the judge ordered any production of data or documents, it's asking that such information be made "equally and simultaneously available to all candidates in the affected race." Matthews said he planned to issue a written ruling within a day of Tuesday's hearing. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
