Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.
Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be elected to the US Senate in more than 140 years.
Fewer than five thousand votes out of nearly a million counted separated him from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The result means the Democrats will hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.
Colom, 43, won with 49.2% of the vote, while Hyde-Smith received 48.7% and an independent candidate got 2.1%, according to figures from CBS.
Hyde-Smith congratulated Colom in a video posted on X on Wednesday evening and wished him well.
"While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said.
Dozens of people were gathered at the Mississippi HQ of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in Jackson on Wednesday when Colom's victory was announced.
The room burst into deafening applause and cheers.
"This is an amazing result," said Leon Russell, chairman of the NAACP board.
"This is purely the work of particularly the black community," he continued. "There was not a whole lot of money, but there was a whole lot of organising.
"This is a historic election."
Across the room, filled with people embracing, Amber Thomas sat, revelling in the victory.
"When you fight, you win," Thomas said. "Right now, I am overwhelmed with joy."
The result wipes away a Republican winning streak in the Magnolia State that dates back to 1982.
The contest was never expected to be this close, with Hyde-Smith running for re-election in a state that President Donald Trump won in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.
But Democrats have scored a series of major wins in these midterm elections, taking control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
The party flipped Senate seats in Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa.
Polls suggest this was due in large part to voter frustrations with the economy and the Iran war under President Trump.
Colom appeared to a ride a national wave of resentment against Republicans.
Voter backlash against Trump's Republican party has been driven in large part by economic woes, blamed on his administration's tariffs and war with Iran, according to exit polls.
Colom, a local prosecutor, used the national mood to his advantage, highlighting his opponent's support for Trump's tariffs and giving her the nickname "Cindy High Prices".
The Democrat campaigned aggressively, visiting all of Mississippi's 82 counties.
Hyde-Smith's campaign assailed Colom as a puppet of billionaire liberal donor George Soros, whose family has helped fund the Democrat's political campaigns.
The 67-year-old Republican was criticised for a lack of public appearances.

Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.
The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.
Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.
Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.
The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.
Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms in Africa's largest oil producer.
"That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.
The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians.
"Fuel prices went up, and everything that Nigerians consume skyrocketed," Osiyemi told the BBC.
"Most Nigerian families are saying they cannot survive on 10,000 naira [$7.40; Â£5.50] a day," he said, referring to a survey conducted by his organisation.
Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including beans, garri (cassava flour) and bread, also recorded substantial increases.
In a sign that the reforms might be starting to pay off, SBM Intelligence, a security risk consulting firm, found that the cost of preparing a pot of jollof rice fell by 11.5% between June and September 2026, the sharpest decline it had recorded in the 10 years it has been running its Jollof Index.
However, this has not translated into significant relief for most households.
"Nigerians spend more and more of their income on basics," said Ikenna Okonkwo, head of research at SBM Intelligence.

- Published
Levels of the two most toxic "forever" chemicals in England's rivers have dropped by nearly a third over the last decade, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA).
The decline in the chemicals, PFOS and PFOA, has been put down to stricter restrictions on their use in products after increasing evidence emerged of their damaging impact on human health and the environment.
One expert studying the impact of the chemicals said it was "brilliant" to see how far the UK has come on this issue.
Thousands of other forever chemicals, known officially as PFAS, remain in use but the regulator said its report showed the need for them all to be better monitored and regulated.
PFAS were first developed in the 1930s in the US and became popular with companies making products like frying pans and firefighting foam because of their useful, oil-resistant, water-resistant and electrical properties.
They are called forever chemicals because their natural resistance means they take a very long time to break down naturally.
The earliest types of these chemicals were called PFOS and PFOA. But two decades ago researchers started to find that they were linked to tissue damage in animals and increased rates of certain serious health conditions such as testicular cancer., external
As a result, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010 and PFOA in 2020.
The latest data from the regulator, published on Thursday, shows that the concentrations in English rivers of PFOS and PFOA over the last ten years have now fallen by 30% and 29% respectively.
Levels in fresh-water fish have fallen 49%.
"It's brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years," said Dr David Megson, reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University.
There are thought to be around 15,000 other PFAS, although only around 200 are frequently used.
The EA said that despite increasing research into these compounds, "uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS". It said its findings "reinforces the need" for regulating all PFAS rather than one by one.
The chemicals industry has long opposed such an approach, arguing that there is currently no, or limited, evidence to suggest that other PFAS are toxic and that some have vital uses such as in life-saving medical equipment.
The regulator is now regularly testing for 60 other PFAS to build a picture of contamination across the country, and earlier this month the government announced it would begin monitoring levels in people's bodies.
The EA report acknowledged that while concentration levels have fallen, because the chemicals take so long to break down, the overall amount still in the environment is likely to have remained unchanged - they have simply been diluted and been washed into the sea.
"There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused," said Megson.
One of the few ways to permanently destroy PFAS is by high-temperature incineration - there are just two such suitable sites in the country currently.

d432a054b7d5.text: Iran's top national security official warned that it would strike American bases beyond the Gulf, including in Europe, if the United States resumes air strikes against the Islamic Republic. The warning comes one day after indictments in New York against three men who allegedly conspired to attack U.S. Air Force planes at a base in England. Nick Schifrin reports. Amna Nawaz: Iran's top national security official today warned the U.S. that it would strike American bases beyond the Gulf, including in Europe, if the United States resumes airstrikes. Geoff Bennett: The warning comes a day after three men were indicted in New York for allegedly plotting to attack U.S. Air Force planes at a base in England. One of the suspects with deep ties to Iran allegedly directed the plot from a federal detention center in New York. The threat prompted the U.S. to relocate bombers from the British base back in September. Nick Schifrin has more. Nick Schifrin: The attack was livestreamed and set to propaganda music, a man throwing a Molotov cocktail at a media company critical of the Iranian regime, as, 1,500 miles away, one of the organizers watched and recorded. It was one of multiple terrorist attacks across Europe in March and April, including the stabbing of two Jewish Londoners and another arson attack on a Jewish-owned charity that the U.S. now says was orchestrated remotely by this man, Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, seen here in 2024 with machine guns behind him. The U.S. accuses Al-Saadi of working on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iranian proxy group Kataib Hezbollah based in Iraq. Earlier this year, the U.S. alleges he planned or promoted 18 terrorist attacks in Europe, as well as a plot against a New York synagogue. He was then arrested in August by Turkey and extradited to the United States. But that didn't stop his plots. The U.S. alleges that, while behind bars in Brooklyn, he directed and paid fellow militants in the United Kingdom to drive these white vans to a British air base. The vans pretended to be from a gas delivery and swimming pool supply business, but were actually surveilling the Royal Air Force base at Fairford. The U.S. alleges the plotters had bought shrapnel and chemicals that could be used for a bomb. The plot forced the U.S. to evacuate B-1s that had been used to bomb Iran. And the U.S. alleges Al-Saadi initiated the attack while he was in the Brooklyn prison while speaking to his immediate family using code words. Colin Clarke, The Soufan Center: This is something that really hearkens back more to things like gangs or the mafia, right? So, allowing mafia members or gang leaders to have conversations that are then monitored, surveilled, and acted upon. Nick Schifrin: Colin Clarke is the executive director of The Soufan Center, which focuses on terrorism. He says the plot against Fairford highlights Iran's willingness to use terrorism and other asymmetric attacks to fight what it considers a decades-old war against the U.S. and Israel. Colin Clarke: It just shows that the Iranians are going to continue to be relentless in their pursuit of what they see as revenge, even if we were to reach a deal tomorrow, which, by the way, is highly unlikely. Nick Schifrin: And in response to the 2020 U.S. strike that killed powerful Iranian commander Qasem Soleimani, the U.S. has long accused Iran of trying to assassinate senior American officials. Colin Clarke: The United States killed Qasem Soleimani in January 2020 and helped the Israelis find and kill the supreme leader of Iran. And so all bets are off when it comes to Iranian vengeance. This is something we're going to see for the foreseeable future. Nick Schifrin: And this week's indictment shows, to seek that vengeance, Iran will increasingly turn to proxies, including the Iraq-based Kataib Hezbollah. Omar Al-Nidawi, Atlantic Council: Most of the Kataib Hezbollah operations in the past have been crude military operations, lobbing rockets, short-range rockets against American bases. Nick Schifrin: Omar Al-Nidawi is with the Atlantic Council's Iraq Initiative. Omar Al-Nidawi: This is the first foray of -- by Kataib Hezbollah into attacks, terror-style attacks, sophisticated-style -- sophisticated attacks on European soil. Nick Schifrin: And why is that significant? Omar Al-Nidawi: It definitely pulls Iraq closer into the conflict. It also highlights Iran's increasing reliance on these factions. Nick Schifrin: A plot thwarted this time that American officials fear Iran could try to repeat. For the "PBS News Hour."

c7b7da7d21f0.text: Shares in Nvidia sank Wednesday night after the New York Times reported CEO Jensen Huang had a second affair with a senior executive who reports to him. Why it matters: The report adds to mounting scrutiny of Huang, already under investigation over an affair with a purported Chinese spy. The potential impact goes beyond one man and one business, though. Huang is arguably the world's most powerful CEO at the moment, his company serving as the beating heart of the AI revolution. He also has no obvious successor . Driving the news: Huang, 63, had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, 48, Nvidia's vice president of health care, according to the Times. Both are married to other people. The two were reportedly seen being affectionate at a hotel during Nvidia's annual developer conference in San Jose in March. A bystander recorded the interaction, and Huang's security team made an offer to the person to sign a nondisclosure agreement, per the Times. The paper reported that Nvidia declined to issue a statement, and Powell did not respond to a request for comment. By the numbers: Nvidia shares fell nearly 8% in after-hours trading as of 6 p.m. ET Wednesday. The company's lost about $1 trillion in market cap since the Times first reported on Oct. 29 that Huang had a "close relationship" with a suspected spy. On the prediction market Kalshi, the odds of Huang being out as CEO as soon as this weekend skyrocketed. Zoom out: This new report comes after Huang confirmed in a company email that he had been unfaithful in his marriage. Nvidia has an independent panel investigating, and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to handle the probe. Between the lines: Peter Jaworski, a business ethics professor at Georgetown University, said it will be hard for Huang to keep his job after this. "You can't have a relationship like this with a direct report," Jaworski tells Axios. "Does the CEO get fired? In this situation that's probably the move to make." Jaworski said the situation could also raise questions about what the board knew and when it knew it. At a minimum, he says Nvidia's board needs to place Huang on administrative leave immediately while it conducts an investigation into both relationships. What we're watching: How Nvidia handles the growing scandal could have effects far beyond just its walls. Editor's note: This story has been updated with new details.

37e339ac5774.text: Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a stunning Mississippi upset , becoming the first Democrat elected to the state's Senate delegation since 1982, AP projects. Why it matters: Colom's victory marks another extraordinary breakthrough for Democrats in the Deep South, extending the historic blue wave that handed the party control of both chambers of Congress. Colom also becomes Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction. Hiram Rhodes Revels became the nation's first Black senator in 1870. Mississippi's last Black senator, Blanche K. Bruce, served until 1881. Catch up quick: Colom's victory expands Democrats' 55–44 advantage over Republicans in the Senate. Worries of a recount — which requires a court order, as Mississippi has no recount law — seemed moot as Hyde-Smith posted a video message to X shortly after AP called the race, appearing to concede to Colom. "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Cologne and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state," she said. Hyde-Smith also addressed another worry from Mississippi voters following a significant purge of the state's voter rolls, saying that her campaign "has worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election." "I am proud of what we have accomplished together, but I want to make one thing very clear: an election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will," she said. The big picture: Colom's victory followed a late surge of Democratic spending and organizing in a state Trump carried by 23 points in 2024. Hyde-Smith faced warning signs in the campaign's closing months, when Colom raised twice as much as the GOP senator despite her overall cash advantage. She was also outspent on TV advertising , with a flood of ads from left-leaning PACs and super PACs pushing support for Colom and attacking the senator for her vote not to release files related to the convicted human trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. Hyde-Smith's campaign also faced criticism over an interview she gave to WLOX-TV in Biloxi, Mississippi, where she fumbled an answer about the price of beef, saying that Mississippians had "so many other proteins to choose from." Colom's campaign capitalized on her blunder, creating a viral campaign ad urging voters to "choose another senator." The GOP made a late push to help Hyde-Smith, including President Trump speaking at a rally for her in Alcorn County, where he won by 68% in 2024. But it wasn't enough. Hyde-Smith's term will end after eight years. She was appointed to the Senate in 2018 by then-Mississippi Gov. Phil Bryant, and ran for a full term in 2020, where she bested her Democratic challenger Mike Espy by 10 points. Zoom in: Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney from Columbus, campaigned on lowering the cost of living, raising wages and protecting rural hospitals. His campaign also drew in heavy Democratic hitters to stump for him, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock. The bottom line: Colom's win adds Mississippi to a growing list of Republican strongholds where Democrats broke through in the midterms, including Texas and South Carolina. It also reinforces the role of Black voters in the Democratic comeback, after the party rebuilt support among a crucial voting bloc that showed signs of shifting toward Trump in 2024. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated. This story has been corrected to show that Hyde-Smith's interview was conducted in Biloxi (not Jackson, Mississippi).

4565df3c4c84.text: With Democrats set to take control of Congress, the White House is threatening them over investigations into the Trump administration. The top White House lawyer warned that aggressive oversight of the administration “may cross the line into blatant criminality.” It comes amid a wave of resignations within the Justice Department. Amna Nawaz discussed more with Devlin Barrett of The New York Times. Amna Nawaz: As Democrats gear up to take control of Congress, the White House is threatening them over planned investigations into the Trump administration. In a letter this week, the top White House lawyer warned the likely incoming House Oversight chair, Robert Garcia, that aggressive oversight of the administration -- quote -- "may cross the line into blatant criminality." It comes amid a wave of high-profile resignations within the Justice Department following last week's Democratic wins and reporting that there are more to come. Here to discuss this is Devlin Barrett. He's a New York Times reporter who covers federal law enforcement. Welcome back. Good to see you. Devlin Barrett: Thanks for having me. Amna Nawaz: Let's start with this letter. Is there any basis for the White House to be threatening members of Congress for their oversight? Devlin Barrett: Look, as a legal document, it doesn't mean very much. As a political document, it's quite important, because it's sending the message about how much the White House plans to fight these investigations. We have already seen the administration fight even judicial inquiries about what the administration has done. So I take this letter to basically mean, we intend to fight every subpoena you send us. Amna Nawaz: Related to that, we saw the attorney general, Todd Blanche, over the weekend say that Democrats' talk about investigating some of the administration was akin to outright threats and that some of those could be considered a crime. Do you see the attorney general launching probes into Democratic lawmakers who are engaged in oversight? Devlin Barrett: Well, we have already seen them launch probes into Democratic lawmakers for very shaky premises. For example, there was an attempt to get an indictment on lawmakers who made a video talking to military officers about not following illegal orders. I don't think there's any reason to expect they will stop launching investigations of Democratic lawmakers. But I think, when it comes to this particular fight over investigations, they're going to be very hard-pressed to craft a sort of criminal theory of why a congressional investigation is in any way a crime. They haven't articulated that certainly. The letter really doesn't, nor does Blanche in his comments. Amna Nawaz: Devlin, let's talk about some of those resignations, several high-profile folks leaving their jobs in the last week, and some were very strong enforcers of the president's agenda, among them Harmeet Dhillon, who was the president's former personal lawyer and led the Civil Rights Division to DOJ, Jason Quinones, who oversaw investigations into the president's opponents. Brett Shumate was central in attacking DEI programs, and John Eisenberg oversaw national security at the Department of Justice. What do we know about why they're leaving and why now? Devlin Barrett: First of all, it's not completely out of the ordinary for senior DOJ officials to leave after an election, to leave after two years. But, obviously, this is a very different type of Department of Justice in the Trump administration. And I think what you're seeing here in a lot of these cases is senior officials who, for very different reasons, each sort of unique to their own jobs, did not live up to some of the expectations that the White House set for them or even that Todd Blanche set for them, particularly when you look at the U.S. attorney in Miami, who's in charge of this grand conspiracy investigation of former officials. There's been a lot of disappointment by the White House that that hasn't produced more in the way of criminal charges or accusations. Amna Nawaz: You think that they were forced out of these rules or asked to leave? Devlin Barrett: Our reporting shows that there is a significant amount of displeasure from senior officials with the U.S. attorney in Miami who just left. And there were significant disagreements in some of these other issues like national security, like civil rights. Amna Nawaz: Permanent replacements for those roles would require Senate confirmation. With the incoming Democratic majority, how do you see that playing out? Devlin Barrett: Well, that's why these departures are categorically different than many other administrations, because it's going to be extremely hard to confirm someone in these top jobs that the president would like to have in these top jobs. So it may be that, for the people who stay in the Trump Justice Department, they may be in a sense locked in for a long -- for the rest of the ride. Amna Nawaz: There's also this reporting that the DOJ warned its field office leaders in a meeting earlier this week to prepare to be on -- quote -- "wartime footing" when Democrats take over or to leave if they couldn't do that. When you hear that, combined with these resignations, what do you think we should expect to see from the Department of Justice? Devlin Barrett: So one thing is, this happened in the type of call where the person -- the senior official doing these calls does a lot of this sort of rhetoric. Like, to many of the career staff, it comes across as wild rhetoric. But this kind of rhetoric is not that unusual for this senior official. But what's really interesting here is, the elections had consequences for the Justice Department. And one of those consequences is states like Texas are now going to be run by Democratic officials. Until now, states like Texas have been very cooperative with the Trump administration on issues related to ICE and immigration. You have already seen local officials in Texas say they ar

e17267fb1039.text: As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, Delaware Sen. Chris Coons is poised to become chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, succeeding retiring Democrat Jeanne Shaheen. A staunch supporter of Ukraine and a critic of President Trump’s war with Iran, Coons would take the helm at a consequential moment for American foreign policy. Coons joined Geoff Bennett to discuss more. Geoff Bennett: As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, Delaware Senator Chris Coons is poised to become chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. A staunch supporter of Ukraine and a critic of President Trump's war with Iran, Coons comes to the role at a consequential moment for American foreign policy. And Senator Coons joins us now. Welcome back to the program. Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE): Thank you, Geoff. Great to be on with you again. Geoff Bennett: So, as we said, you are set to chair Senate Foreign Relations with the U.S. at war with Iran, with Russia's war in Ukraine continuing. There is growing national concern over artificial intelligence. As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, what are your top foreign policy priorities? And where do you most want to change the administration's course? Sen. Chris Coons: So, Geoff, as I was campaigning up and down the state of Delaware in the last few months, I heard over and over that folks' top concern was their costs. And when I asked, why do you think your costs have gone too high, they would say Trump's tariff war with Canada and Trump's illegal or immoral war against Iran. I heard that over and over from voters. So finding a way that we can deliver on that to lower their costs by repealing Trump's tariffs, by ending the war in Iran, by improving wages and the way that wages are growing and rebuilding our alliances globally will be among the top priorities for me. So, to me, we need to both have some oversight and investigations about recent developments in Nvidia and China and AI, actions by Elon Musk to control whether or not Ukraine can defend itself using his Starlink system, and we have to knock down the tariffs that have raised people's costs. The underlying American economy has been quite weak. In fact, some have argued it's in a recession, except for the investments in AI.So the central role that Nvidia and Nvidia designed and manufactured chips play is a core concern for me, in particular the urgency of putting limits on exporting Nvidia's chips to China. I have a bipartisan bill with Senator Ricketts that would put guardrails on those exports. It is called the SAFE Chips Act. And part of what is so concerning to me about these recent allegations about Nvidia -- look, I'm not that interested in the salacious details of the private life of the CEO of Nvidia. I'm very interested in why credible reports of a national security threat were not acted on, and Jensen Huang was allowed to continue advocating for the export to China of some of his most advanced chips, in particular to the company represented by the Chinese spy. Geoff Bennett: I want to ask you about this effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which failed yesterday in the House. Should Democrats revive that effort when you take control of both chambers next year? Sen. Chris Coons: Look, Geoff, my hope is that President Trump will read the tea leaves, recognize that Secretary Hegseth, more than anyone, is responsible for giving him bad advice about the war in Iran and the current situation we find ourselves in, with no easy or positive way to get out of the war with Iran, and fire him and replace him. I do think that there will be another effort in the House to impeach and remove Secretary Hegseth. But, frankly, what would be best for our country is to just move on to new leadership. Secretary Hegseth has fired dozens of senior flag-rank officers across the Pentagon with no justification or explanation in a way that has demoralized and weakened the senior ranks of the American military at exactly the moment when we can least afford that. I think it's time for those firings to move to the secretary level and for Trump to find a next secretary of defense who can be confirmed by the Senate. Geoff Bennett: Speaking of new leadership, I want to ask you about your party's own leadership. The midterms delivered this overwhelming vote for change, and you have senators as far apart ideologically as Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin Democrats, obviously, both calling for Chuck Schumer to step aside a Senate Democratic leader. Our audience is seeing a press conference they held yesterday over in the Senate. Do you believe that Senator Schumer is the right person to lead your caucus in the next Congress? Sen. Chris Coons: So, we're in the middle of vigorous caucus discussions a

Economics correspondent Paul Solman explains how that technology is transforming the prices we pay. But as the military's reach has grown, fewer Americans are serving in uniform. Judy Woodruff explores what that means for the country in her series, Crossroads: America at 250. Geoff Bennett: Over the last 250 years, the U.S. military has helped shape the nation's history from the fight for independence to its emergence as the world's leading military power. But, as our military reach has grown, fewer Americans are serving in uniform. This Veterans Day, Judy Woodruff explores what that means for the country in her series Crossroads: America at 250. Judy Woodruff: So this is your first deployment. Former Cpl. Jeremy Villanueva, U.S. Marine Corps: My wife had made these nice illustrations, and she listed right here all the things that I had missed. Daniel being born was a big one. Judy Woodruff: Jeremy Villanueva had been a U.S. Marine for just a year when the 9/11 attacks happened. Former Cpl. Jeremy Villanueva: The idea of being in the United States Marine Corps as an infantryman suddenly became very, very real. Judy Woodruff: He was newly married with a baby on the way. Former Cpl. Jeremy Villanueva: They put us on a boat and we sailed out December 1, and my son was born December 17. And I didn't get to see him until he was 6 months old. Ensign Daniel Villanueva, U.S. Navy: I always wanted to join the Amphib Navy, so Marines would be on board, and I could feel a little bit closer to my dad and what he went through when he was on board a Navy ship. Judy Woodruff: Today, that son is a Navy officer and has served aboard the same kind of ship that once carried his father overseas to fight the war on terror. From the Revolutionary War, when Americans took up arms to fight for freedom to today's war with Iran, military service has helped shape what it means to be an American. But today's military looks dramatically different. From small localized forces that relied heavily on volunteers, it has grown into six branches with more than two million uniformed personnel. Col. Greg Daddis (Ret.): We're moving from a regional power to a global power. Judy Woodruff: At the National Guard Memorial Museum in Washington, we talked about that history with retired Army Colonel Greg Daddis of Texas A&M University and Katherine Kuzminski of the Center For a New American Security. Katherine Kuzminski: While there was a U.S. military, the concept was much more localized at the state level. We shifted from a mixed force of conscripts and volunteers to the all-volunteer force. Judy Woodruff: But as the country expanded, so did its military reach. Col. Greg Daddis (Ret.): I think, from a historical standpoint of thinking of Native Americans as being national threats, but, in fact, we were invading other nations, and that impulse continues after the late 1890s as we move into Spanish colonies and Cuba and the Philippines, and then just continue that outward expansion, especially with the two World Wars. Judy Woodruff: Fighting wars on a much larger scale required more troops. The draft brought millions of American men into military service. Katherine Kuzminski: The beginning of World War I, we saw the first real melting pot of the entire U.S. Army specifically thinking about the United States as a fighting force in the world. We, of course, had to induce a draft to make that happen in World War I and then again in World War II. We saw that draft take us through the Vietnam War. Judy Woodruff: But, eventually, it went away. Katherine Kuzminski: It wasn't politically tenable to the American population that we are sending our sons, because the draft was only for men, to fight the nation's wars without the broader public say in the use of those forces. Judy Woodruff: But after the war in Vietnam, there was a big shift. The military became a smaller, all-volunteer professional force. Katherine Kuzminski: We're able to have a smaller force because we rely on a number of factors of national power, to include our economy, our ability to raise and develop ambassadors and diplomats, and we lean on all of those measures of national power, and then we can leverage this professional military. Judy Woodruff: And the backbone of that military is increasingly made up of families like the Villanuevas, who pass down the tradition of service from one generation to the next. According to Pentagon data, more than three in four new Army recruits had a family member who also served. Col. Greg Daddis (Ret.): Serving in the military itself has become a family business. When I'm teaching at West Point and the cadets that I have in class, their mothers have gone to West Point, their fathers have gone to West Point, and there's just now a very strong tradition of those who are serving, that their sons and daughters will follow in their footsteps. Former Cpl. Jeremy Villanueva: My dad worked until the day he died in a factory, so that I could go and I could serve my country, and I didn't have to worry about the same things that they had to worry about. And I went and enlisted in the military so that my son could go ahead and commission into the military. Ensign Daniel Villanueva: Family service was encouraged throughout my childhood, both from my father and my uncles and my cousins. So joining the military wasn't that big of a question when I was a kid. Judy Woodruff: But that tradition may be weakening. A 2025 Blue Star Families survey found just 37 percent of active duty family respondents would recommend service to a young relative, down from 55 percent in 2016. Former Cpl. Jeremy Villanueva: Unless you have lived through it, you can't fully appreciate what that sacrifice actually is. The hardest thing for that parent is that we know exactly what that person is going to have to sacrifice. And to see your own child make that same sacrifice, it's hard. Judy Woodruf

(AP) — Democratic nominee Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, and it will echo through the country as well. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom's favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi. The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43 year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state's large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith's missteps as she sought a second full term. Please check your inbox to confirm. "They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through," Colom said in the campaign's closing stretch. Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society. "It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better, and we don't come up with excuses as to why we can't do it," he said. A race Washington once viewed as a longshot The contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, drawing attention from Democrats who belatedly infused cash into Colom's candidacy. The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith's vulnerabilities crystallized. Colom attracted particular notice for some of the year's most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith, 67, seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they'd "pick another senator instead." WATCH: Mississippi voters reflect on surprising Senate race as count continues When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities. Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: "Is this not the best president in our lifetime?" Then she stepped away. Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. "I love that," Trump replied when he continued his 80-plus minutes at the microphone. "Sometimes they get up and they talk for 10 minutes." The appearance tracked Colom's tactic of criticizing Trump's policies — especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a non-entity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state that has been accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi. There is some irony to Hyde-Smith finding herself flat-footed against Colom. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi's senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination. Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom's confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president's choices for federal judicial positions in their home state. Colom said his Senate bid was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith. Colom called on Mississippi's history The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family. "In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection," Colom said, telling the story of Evers' military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction. Hopes had been low for any significant development in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped POWs but have remained far apart in their demands for accepting a peace settlement. READ MORE: Russia and Ukraine hold nearly 4 hours of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi U.S. officials say they are determined to revive Washington's peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results. Along with postwar security guarantees for both countries, other key hurdles are the fate of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory and what role European countries will play in an eventual settlement. U.S. envoys to meet with Putin and Zelenskyy The sides last met in February on Russia's invasion, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians. The talks lasted just under two hours Wednesday, after a four-hour session the previous day. "One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalize the numbers tomorrow," said Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, after the Abu Dhabi talks ended. Alexander Zorin, a deputy chief of the General Staff's information department who attended the talks, told Russian state TV it would be one of the biggest such swaps since 1,000 soldiers from each side returned home last year. The latest exchange could take place in the next two or three weeks, he said. WATCH: Zelenskyy on his 'emotional' relationship with Trump and fighting Russia Kushner said he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin, Ireland, to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Ukrainian leader gave a muted welcome to the outcome of the talks, saying a proposed prisoner exchange was a positive step. But he said Ukraine will not give in to demands that it cede its territory that has been occupied by Russia in exchange for peace. Medinsky said he felt the talks helped Moscow and Kyiv edge closer to peace, while Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov described them as "substantive and quite useful." Russia opposed European officials in the talks Umerov said Kyiv's delegation was expected to meet later Wednesday with representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO who were in the capital of the United Arab Emirates but did not attend the three-way talks. Moscow doesn't want European countries, which are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. Kushner said one of the goals of the Moscow meeting is to try to get Europeans added to the talks. In Dublin, Zelenskyy said it was positive that security advisers and senior officials from European governments, the EU and NATO were in Abu Dhabi, even though they were not a part of the talks. Despite that. he said there had been a "change in temperature," with Washington warming to the idea of a European role. "Ending this war without Europe's participation would be unjust, and it would be impossible," Zelenskyy said through an interpreter. READ MORE: Zelenskyy pushes for 'clear' postwar security guarantees in Ukraine Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said European representatives could eventually join peace talks but added their current statements "don't indicate any desire on their part to contribute to movement along the path toward peace." Moscow complains that Europe is financing and supplying weaponry to Ukraine. Kushner said both Ukraine and Russia needed clarity on postwar security arrangements. He said European countries, the EU and NATO have to be involved in those discussions to build consensus on next steps. Ukraine wants to ensure that Moscow doesn't invade again, and EU officials say any discussions on Europe's security arrangements could only start after a ceasefire. Many in Europe see the inclusion of Russia in those plans as a concession to Putin, who has described NATO's eastward expansion as a top security threat to his country. Moscow has demanded that the alliance's troops be pulled back its troops from Russia's borders. Russia's security concerns were discussed at the talks, Kushner said, adding that Moscow was told it needs to provide different de-escalation proposals acceptable to Europe. "The reality is, is there's no trust right now between the sides. And that's to be expected after a conflict like this," he said. But he posted on X later that the POW exchange "will reunite families, build trust and create momentum toward peace." The talks were held in a new political atmosphere The context of the negotiations has changed since the February meeting in Geneva. The Trump administration now must reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections, and they could demand more support for Ukraine. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and members of his team were admonished by an Army guard at the Arlington National Cemetery after he and his entourage appeared to violate the solemn war memorial's rules for decorum.
A video of the Veterans Day observance event shows Hegseth, his wife and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
The Army sentinel on duty then steps towards Hegseth and his group and yells: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
Rules on etiquette at the cemetery dictate that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.
The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.
A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the Tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.
"While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum," Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement.
"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoredâand will always honorâthe sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."
Earlier, President Donald Trump, Vice-President JD Vance and other top officials attended the annual wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery.
During his speech at the ceremony, Trump offered his gratitude to uniformed service members who have fought for the country. He also touted what he sees as his administration's success in the Iran war.
"Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back. All of us fought back," he said.
"And we won," Trump said of the Iran war. "It's just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory."
Trump also pointed out Hegseth during the ceremony, saying he's done a "fantastic job" as defence secretary.
Trump has repeatedly defended Hegseth amid Democratic lawmakers' push to impeach him. On Tuesday, an effort to impeach the defence secretary under accusations that he waged war on Iran without congressional authorisation failed on Capitol Hill.
Hegseth has called the impeachment efforts a "farce" and a "stunt".

Cacti are among the toughest plants on the planet, withstanding scorching temperatures and parched conditions that would wilt a more sensitive sprout. But climate change may threaten these hardy plants more than previously thought, a new study suggests.
Scientists in recent years have raised some concerns over the effects of rising temperatures on cactus species, which span nearly every type of ecosystem on the planet—from tree-hanging Christmas cacti in tropical rainforests to the mighty saguaros standing tall in the harsh Sonoran Desert. However, few studies have incorporated the potential risk of another climate-change side effect: extreme drought events.
It turns out these combined factors aggressively crank up the threat level, according to a study published Wednesday in the journal Nature. Integrating new spatial data on severe drought with climate models, the researchers tracked how future conditions could affect the suitable climatic area for nearly 1,000 species of cacti. They found that more than a quarter of the analyzed cactus species could lose most of their suitable habitat by the end of the century, more than 80 percent in all. That’s far more than when only rising temperatures and projected average precipitation were considered.
The habitat declines identified in the paper are associated with substantial losses in cactus diversity in some regions.
These findings challenge a long-standing assumption for cacti that “in a warming world, they’ll likely be winners,” said study co-author Brian Enquist, a professor at the University of Arizona. “Even in these really hot, dry environments where you see cactus species, the climate now is shifting into a new climate regime that these species haven’t encountered in their evolutionary history.”
The study analyzed nearly 650,000 records of cacti around the world, including community science data from the app iNaturalist, which more than doubled the number of species analyzed. Models showed that droughts and heat are poised to have the worst impacts on species in some of the world’s most concentrated cactus hotspots, including Chile, Argentina, Peru, Ecuador and countries in Central America.
Some regions, such as the Mexican Pacific coast, saw modest gains in cactus species diversity, but these were offset by large losses in neighboring areas.
Cacti are already some of the world’s most imperiled plants, with more than 30 percent of species considered threatened. That’s largely due to habitat loss and illegal trade, which has helped supply the collector and houseplant industry as cactus popularity spikes around the world.
On top of this, unprecedented droughts in recent years have fueled widespread die-offs of species such as Copiapoa cacti in Chile’s Atacama Desert and saguaros around Phoenix and Tucson. That’s a precursor of what’s to come if climate change continues to fuel longer, more intense periods of heat and dryness, said study co-author Michiel Pillet, a postdoctoral researcher at University of South Florida.
“We were extremely surprised by how intense our results were,” Pillet said. He added that the impacts are likely an underestimate due to insufficient data on rare species—and the disproportionate impacts they face from climate change. “Think about a cactus species that only lives right at the coast in a single spot, and a hurricane comes in and wipes out that entire population.”
The study’s authors say their modeling approach could be applied to other plant species.
That was echoed by David Williams, a botany professor at the University of Wyoming who was not involved in the study.
“The findings extend well beyond our understanding of the climate vulnerability of cacti,” he said over email. “The work will guide future studies that uncover species-specific ecological, demographic and physiological processes that shape persistence across shifting climatic conditions.”

The researchers say their method could also help experts develop more targeted cacti conservation efforts in a warmer, drier world. For example, artificially dispersing seeds into new environments that fit a cactus’ climate niche—a process called “assisted migration”—can establish more stable populations for at-risk species.
Even just raising awareness for the cacti species most at risk and the need to gather more data on them can help determine where to spend “very limited conservation resources” to “get the best bang for our buck,” Pillet said.
Enquist was encouraged by the widespread public interest in cacti, which has generated an abundance of citizen-science observations that helped make the research possible.
“There are a lot of people that care about these plants,” he said. “What’s wonderful then about that is that there’s a lot of opportunity for intervention.”

Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.
The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.
It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this.
Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust, external, which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.
Despite 90% of the country being used for agriculture, external, only about 0.1% is currently being used for horticulture, external.
Growers at Fisher's Wern Farm, near Newtown, Powys, said this must change if the country is to survive climate change, wars and other global disruptions to the supply chain.
"We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires, and overheating," said Fisher.
Food security has become a hot topic, with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.
Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets".
He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways.
"That is a security hazard because it's very vulnerable to cyber attacks.
"If the system goes wrong, there's no resilience in it. The food just runs out straight away."
Fisher and Sue Holbrook launched Our Food Trust about 10 years ago with the aim of growing more produce locally for local markets.
They found one of the main barriers was stable housing for farmers.
As Fisher explained: "If there's a high wind during the night, they need to get out there and protect things.
"If a sheep gets in, they have to get the sheep out before the entire thing is destroyed in an hour. So they have to live there."
But he said planning regulations have made it really difficult to build homes on farmland.
However, by working with Powys council and Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Authority, they have been able to build three temporary homes for farmers on 36 acres of council-owned land.
They are currently building three more.
One of the growers at Wern Farm is Lydia Dibben, 28, and she agreed access to land is one of the biggest barriers to new farmers.
She said if her home was not provided she would have to get another job to be able to afford rent, and then would end up without enough time to farm.
"I'm only growing on about just over an acre this year, and we're now doing 50 veg boxes a week," she said.
"We've been doing four farmers' markets a month up until the beginning of October. We're also supplying into regional and national wholesale as well.
"I don't know how many people we're feeding, but it's got to be hundreds of people on just a couple of acres."
She believes there are lots of people who want to do similar work, and they should be given access to land and affordable housing to do so.
Dibben said she believed people in the UK thought it would be able to "avoid many of the real challenges of climate breakdown" and "just be able to grow grapes and peaches" but the reality is very different.
"We're going to have to really think a lot harder about how we're producing food, even in this country," she said.
This includes looking at which vegetables work best in hotter climates.
Dibben described the past summer as the hardest she had experienced in five years of growing.
"The hours I was keeping were just insane," she said.
"I was getting out to the field at 05:00, and then working until it got just too hot to be outside, which was like 11:00 some days, maybe even earlier."
She said working in polytunnels was impossible by 09:00 due to the heat.
When it became too hot to work, she had to go indoors and "just survive until it was cool enough to go back outside at probably 17:00".
She then worked until midnight to try and get everything watered.
Dibben said she did not usually have to worry too much about not having enough water, but this year was completely different.
"Even the things that you felt like you were giving as much water as you could were still not growing as much as they should be," she added.
"Everything was slower and stunted.
"We've not had the water bill yet for this summer, but I dread to think.
"We've just not had the crops to make it worth it."
She does not believe it will necessarily be as bad every year, but Dibben accepts there will be more hot summers and unpredictable weather such as flooding.
Dibben thinks there will always be a need for bigger scale farms producing wheat, barley, beef or sheep.
"But I think if there was a farm like ours every 10 miles throughout Wales, that would be a pretty great future in my eyes," she added.
The Welsh government said "significant progress" had been made on its plans to create a national food strategy to "target a more resilient, integrated and sustainable food system".
"There will also be a focus on how to grow more fruit and vegetables in Wales, and we have already begun mapping the current position of the sector with key stakeholders," said a spokesperson.
The UK government's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: "We recognise the hurdles that our vital fruit and vegetable growers face, which is why we are slashing planning red tape and investing Â£200m to help farmers trial crop boosting technology.
"The prime minister has made clear that food security is national security, and we're working across the farming sector to make supply chains more resilient."

Lego has taken its online marketplace BrickLink offline after detecting what it described as unusual activity on the platform.
BrickLink is used by Lego collectors worldwide to buy and sell secondhand Lego sets, source new bricks and purchase limited edition releases.
It was originally set up by a fan, but Lego acquired it in 2019. In a homepage message, the firm said that before restoring BrickLink, it wanted to "fully understand" what had happened.
"That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues," Lego said. It did not provide any further detail about whether the site has been breached or hacked, and whether any customer data was affected.
After being contacted by the BBC, Lego published the update.
BrickLink has been offline for the last three days, with a previous message saying it was down for maintenance.
Cyber-professional Melanie Hoskin has been collecting Lego for 45 years and is a regular user of BrickLink.
She told the BBC she had received multiple links for payment for a limited edition release she had pre-ordered on the platform, after she had already paid for it.
She said Lego did not believe that the payment had been taken and at one point said it would ban her from BrickLink.
The problem has now been resolved and Lego said it was not aware of wider payment issues.
It is unclear if the payment glitch had any connection to the issue that led to the website going offline.
Hoskin said she felt like she had been accused of theft.
"Lego is my stress relief," she said. "Lego is what I grew up with as a kid, it's what bonded me with my sisters.
"I've got a Lego room and I've not even been able to walk into it this past couple of weeks because it just angers me."
Earlier today, a message on BrickLink said the platform would be back online by Wednesday evening, but that message has now been deleted and there is no longer a time frame given for its return.

e28e3148a615.text: By — Bill Barrow, Associated Press Bill Barrow, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/biden-says-he-wouldnt-have-run-for-a-second-term-in-2024-if-he-knew-he-had-cancer Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Biden says he wouldn't have run for a second term in 2024 if he knew he had cancer Politics Nov 11, 2026 5:04 PM EST ATLANTA (AP) — Joe Biden says he did not know he had cancer while he was president and would not have sought a second term if he already had been diagnosed. The former Democratic president's comments came in an interview with People magazine before the release of his White House memoir on Tuesday. "If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer," said Biden, who turns 84 on Nov. 20, "I would've not gone forward" with a 2024 reelection bid that ended after a disastrous debate performance against Republican Donald Trump. Biden was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer months after leaving office in 2025. READ MORE: In memoir, Biden says Trump should carry the weight of Jan. 6 riots 'to his grave' "I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running" for president, Biden said in the interview. Still, he argued that the June 2024 debate, less than five months before Election Day, was not a seismic event even if it accelerated Democrats' concerns about his age — he was 81 at the time — and his ability to defeat Trump. "First of all, I thought there'd be another debate, which there wasn't," Biden said. "But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn't another debate, it didn't disturb me because it wasn't consequential." Within weeks, Biden announced he was ending his campaign and endorsing his vice president, Kamala Harris, who secured the nomination and lost to Trump in the general election. Biden insisted he was able to perform his duties while he was in office. He said age itself was not disqualifying and meant he had experience and deep personal relationships with world leaders. "I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job," he said. His son Hunter told the BBC in August that the cancer had spread and was causing his father pain. "It's very painful and it's very debilitating in many respects," he said. READ MORE: Joe Biden's prostate cancer has spread and is causing him pain, Hunter Biden says Since Joe Biden left office, his son has become a higher profile public presence, sparring with Republicans on social media, posting lengthy thoughts on the nation's direction and launching his own cryptocurrency. Joe Biden defended his son's public persona and his decision to pardon Hunter Biden after the younger Biden's 2024 conviction on federal felony gun charges and his guilty plea to federal tax charges. Hunter Biden also had faced years of scrutiny and withering Republican attacks over his international business dealings. Hunter Biden has said the pardon damaged his father's legacy, but the former president said Trump's penchant for vengeance made it necessary. "He goes after people without any basis, whether they're viewed as an enemy. I knew what he would do," Joe Biden said. "If I hadn't pardoned — not just some of my family members, anyone who's dealt with me — he would go back and try to do harm to them." Biden called his son "one of the brightest men I know," adding, "I'm really proud of him." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned that the consensus on both science and climate change has "gone".
Addressing other world leaders and delegates at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, he said that despite this, the UK was ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on the climate change issue.
But environmental campaigners at the summit said the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions.
In recent months, the UK government has announced policies which critics say have weakened its green credentials, such as reducing support for heat pumps, approving the Jackdaw gas field and doubling down on support for Heathrow Airport's expansion.
Burnham opened his speech on Thursday by talking about the heat experienced in the UK this past summer.
He said "it was not normal" - in fact it was the hottest on record, made 130 times more likely because of climate change, according to the Met Office.
Hundreds of schools were closed, cereal harvests were down 11%, and ambulance services were inundated with calls beyond levels seen during the Covid-19 pandemic.
As a result of the threat to people's health and homes, the PM said he was creating the UK, and the world's, first climate security envoy, Dame Madeleine Alessandri.
Alessandri, the former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee, said: "Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates."
As a result this was "placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world", she added.
This will be seen as a strong indication of the focus of the UK's priorities when it takes up the G20 presidency next year.
The current president is the US, which has been a notable absentee from the COP process over the last two years since President Trump withdrew the country from the most important global climate treaty - the Paris Climate Agreement.
Professor Lord Nicholas Stern, who identified 20 years ago that climate change could cost the global economy up to 20% of GDP if left unchecked, praised the PM's words.
"The Prime Minister was right to identify climate change as a threat to security around the world, and the importance of investments in clean electricity generation as the best way of protecting households and businesses from the high prices and volatile markets for fossil fuels," he said.
On tackling the causes of climate change, Burnham said his government remained committed to meeting the country's target of net zero by 2050 whilst also getting bills down.
He said key to this was cutting our "dependence on fossil fuels" and increasing electrification - the amount of our energy needs met from renewable electricity.
Turkey, the co-hosts of COP31, wants a key outcomes of this year's summit to be a commitment by countries to meet 35% of their energy supply from electricity by 2035. Currently, it is around a fifth.
But Burnham has been accused of having double standards.
"The Prime Minister simply cannot call for clean power across the world while saying yes to more fossil fuels in the UK," said Beth John, climate adviser at Oxfam.
Last month, the government approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on the grounds that it provided energy security.
And in the budget last month Chancellor John Healey announced a funding cut to the Warm Homes Plan, which provides grants and loans to support the installation of heat pumps.
Whilst this week there has been media speculation that the government is considering watering down electric car sales targets, although the government insists no decision has been made.
Successfully switching petrol and diesel cars to EVs and moving from gas boilers to electric-powered heat pumps are key ways to achieve the 35% electrification target, external.
Fire and Floods: Our Extreme Weather
The BBC's climate editor, Justin Rowlatt, investigates the impact of the changing climate on our weather.
Watch on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One (BBC Two in Northern Ireland) at 20:00 on Monday 9 November.
Although there was no royal presence this year, King Charles III sent a message ahead of Burnham's speech.
"As the world gathers for Cop31, I can only hope that this same spirit of partnership and common purpose can help inspire the collective action that our planet â and future generations â so urgently need.
"Our children and grandchildren will not judge us by the promises we made, but by what we chose to do."
Burnham was the only G7 leader to speak at this year's conference in a sign of faltering support for the COP process - something he acknowledged in his speech.
In an almost word for word copy of Sir Keir Starmer's address last year he said: "The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate has gone, and the reality is now the world will reach 1.5 degrees."
Other leaders expected to speak on Thursday include many island states like Tonga, Tuvalu and the Solomon Islands.
For these nations, the impact of climate change is already at their front door. With most of their land just metres above sea level, rising water levels have caused many to abandon their homes in recent years.
Last year, Australia - the co-host of the COP31 summit - opened up the world's first climate visa for Tuvalu citizens wanting to evacuate.
The first intake was massively oversubscribed, with more than a third of the population entering the ballot.
As glaciers continue to melt and oceans expand, average sea levels are expected to keep climbing and potentially accelerate. The World Meteorological Organisation said on the opening day of this conference the global mean sea level was at its highest level since records began.

de1edcc66cc7.text: Scott Colom 's path to a historic U.S. Senate upset ran through the Mississippi Delta — where Emmett Till was abducted, Fannie Lou Hamer fought for the ballot and the blues became an American art form. Why it matters: Nearly 150 years after Reconstruction, Mississippi sent a Black American to the U.S. Senate for the first time since 1881. The votes pushing Colom toward that milestone came from communities where Black residents spent generations fighting for the ballot. Driving the news: The Associated Press projected the race for Colom on Wednesday, handing Democrats a historic upset over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. By the numbers: An Axios analysis of AP county returns found Colom ahead in 16 of the 18 counties in the Mississippi Delta National Heritage Area . Colom collected roughly 100,000 votes to Hyde-Smith's 62,000 — a 38,000-vote advantage. In 2020, Democrat Mike Espy carried 15 of those counties by about 25,000 votes, according to Mississippi's certified county returns . Colom's share of the two-party vote climbed from about 56% to 62%. Statewide, Colom led Hyde-Smith by about 4,700 votes out of more than 962,000 counted when the AP called the race Wednesday — a margin of roughly half a percentage point. What they're saying: "Mississippi voters made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out," NAACP president Derrick Johnson said in a statement. Johnson said Mississippi voters showed up despite efforts to remove voters from the rolls . Zoom in: Colom's electoral map traces some of the most painful and defining chapters of Black American history. Coahoma County: Home to Clarksdale and the famed crossroads associated with the legend that bluesman Robert Johnson sold his soul to the devil. Colom led with about 4,700 votes to 1,300. Leflore and Tallahatchie counties: Emmett Till was abducted near Money in Leflore County in 1955. His body was recovered from the Tallahatchie River in Tallahatchie County, where an all-white jury acquitted his killers. Colom led by about 4,200 votes in Leflore and 1,300 in Tallahatchie, according to AP returns . Sunflower County: Fannie Lou Hamer, who lived in Ruleville, challenged Mississippi's racist voting restrictions. As late as the spring of 1965, only 155 Black residents had registered to vote in the county, according to the Mississippi Department of Archives and History . Colom led with about 5,300 votes to 1,700. Washington County: Robert F. Kennedy visited Greenville during his 1967 tour of Delta poverty . 29.4% of Washington County is still in poverty per the Census Bureau's 2020–2024 estimate . Colom led with about 8,700 votes to 2,400. Zoom out: Colom didn't suddenly turn the Delta blue. Espy won most of it in 2020. But Colom widened the Democratic margin. In DeSoto County, which falls within the heritage area but outside the Delta's historic heartland, Colom led by about 3,300 votes. Hyde-Smith won there by roughly 12,100 in 2020. Colom also swept the Golden Triangle counties of Lowndes, Oktibbeha and Clay, his home region in northeastern Mississippi. He won all three by double-digit margins and improved on Espy's 2020 performance. Between the lines: The historical symbolism stretches beyond the Delta. Colom led with about 12,100 votes to 9,700 in Forrest County, named for Confederate Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest, the Ku Klux Klan's first grand wizard. Hyde-Smith faced criticism during her 2018 race against Espy after saying she would sit in the front row if invited to a public hanging . She later apologized to those offended. The bottom line: The region where Black Mississippians fought some of America's fiercest battles for voting rights helped elect the state's first Black U.S. senator in 145 years — and raised a new question. Can political representation finally bring economic change to the Delta?

- Published
At least two people have died and more than 17 others are injured after a building in New York City collapsed into an open construction site, officials have said.
It sparked a massive search-and-rescue operation, with more than 250 first responders at the scene in Brooklyn, trying to find survivors who may have been trapped under the rubble of the three-storey building.
Hours later, aerial video showed firefighters pulling a survivor, covered in dust, out of the debris on a stretcher. She was later said to have been a pregnant woman. Officials say they do not know how many others are missing.
An investigation is under way into what caused Wednesday afternoon's sudden collapse.
Witnesses described a terrifying sound as the building came down at about 16:00 local time (21:00 GMT).
"I live literally right behind the building," one woman, Emmanuella Carilus, told the New York Times. "It sounded like a big boom and you just heard a bunch of screaming."
The newspaper published images showing a crowd of fire trucks and police vehicles at the same, and wrote that the noise of sirens had not stopped in the area.
"I've never seen anything like this," said another witness, named only as Dashik, who spoke to local television station PIX 11.
Officials are yet to identify those who died or were injured.
Locals have gathered at the scene to await news of those feared to have been caught in the collapse.
The rescue mission has been described as "extremely dangerous" by New York City Fire Department (FDNY) Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore.
She added that people from the collapsed building and also the construction site had been trapped.
"Members have been working methodically and haven't stopped since they arrived this afternoon," Bonsignore said.
The woman who was filmed being rescued from the rubble was identified by her husband.
Speaking to a reporter from CBS News New York, he described his relief after an anxious wait: "She is alive. She is still alive. I'm very happy. I'm very happy. I'm very happy. I thank all of you guys. She's pregnant, six months."
Rescuers have used search dogs, drones, axes and chainsaws to carry out their work. They say they anticipate the effort will last for several days.
Some pictures of the collapsed building, on Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn, show an entire side of it gone, with bedrooms and closets exposed. Among the debris, smashed concrete and twisted metal, are household items and clothes.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani joined emergency responders at the scene, praising them for their rapid response.
They "arrived in under a minute and have spent hours working in dangerous and highly technical conditions to rescue New Yorkers," he later wrote on X.
The Brooklyn building was built in 1930, city records show, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.
At the adjacent construction site, where plans have been approved for a new building, active work was going on when the incident occurred, according to FDNY Chief of Department John Esposito.
The activity was described by another official as "excavation work". It was not immediately clear whether the work had anything to do with the collapse of the neighbouring building.
