3c160034bb57.text: President Trump is turning the federal government into an investor in dozens of private companies, and some Democrats are considering following his lead as their party emerges emboldened from the midterm elections. Why it matters: Democrats are gaining new power to scrutinize Trump's corporate investments, even as his approach gains traction within their own party. They're looking at investments and aid for clean energy and other priorities, like support for energy infrastructure. State of play: The Trump administration's investments in energy, critical minerals and other industries are already drawing calls for congressional investigations . "The Trump administration has widened the aperture for industrial policy," Jennifer Granholm, who served as President Biden's Energy Secretary, said at a gathering of energy and climate experts Axios attended in Berkeley, Calif., last month. "You're not going to have state ownership of enterprises," Granholm told Axios in an interview afterward. "But maybe you do take a little bit of an ownership slice" for national security or global competitiveness reasons, she said. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) has also expressed openness to federal ownership stakes, while raising concerns about the Trump administration's lack of transparency and accountability, he told Semafor . Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) has argued that the U.S. needs to consider a more aggressive industrial policy to compete with countries like China, while warning against direct government ownership. "We are long overdue for having a conversation about, 'should the United States even have an industrial policy?'" Casten said at a recent University of Chicago event . "For a long time, we viewed industrial policy as something that socialists do." Casten said he would support the U.S. ensuring domestic manufacturing of certain parts of supply chains, like electronic control systems that operate energy infrastructure, and even pursuing "smart tariff policy" to have competitive markets. The big picture: The Biden administration spent billions subsidizing clean energy and semiconductor manufacturing. Trump has taken government intervention a step further by acquiring ownership stakes in companies ranging from Intel to critical mineral producers. It's been a striking reversal for a president who has repeatedly criticized Democrats for government overreach. How it works: The Trump administration has announced more than $30 billion in investments across nearly 50 deals involving government ownership and related financial arrangements, according to a Council on Foreign Relations tracker . The investments span semiconductors, critical minerals and energy — strategically important industries where high costs and long development timelines can make private financing difficult. Flashback: Washington has taken ownership stakes in private companies before, including during the 2008 financial crisis. But those investments were intended as temporary measures to rescue struggling businesses, unlike Trump's national security-focused investments. What they're saying: "Equity from the U.S. government can act as patient capital that helps derisk an investment with a long time horizon or technological risk that would otherwise not attract sufficient private investment," said Jonathan Hillman, a Council on Foreign Relations fellow behind the tracker. Hillman said the deals announced since January 2025 have also mobilized $28.5 billion in private capital. Yes, but: Some politicians and energy leaders warn that direct government ownership could open the door to political favoritism and market distortions. "Government is not a venture capital fund. It's not a private equity fund. It's not well suited to pick winners and losers in the marketplace," said Tim Pawlenty, former Republican governor of Minnesota who now leads the Solar Energy Industries Association, at the same University of Chicago event. "If it starts to go down the slippery slope of 'it's just the flavor of the day company because we like it' or they're well connected or whatever, then you got problems." Threat level: "Buying stakes in public companies is so, so, so dangerous," Casten said. "I have no idea how a future president unwinds our stake in Intel without totally tanking Intel stock," he added, referring to the administration's roughly 10% stake in the semiconductor giant. To avoid such concerns, Hillman suggests creating a federal chief investment officer to oversee investments and eventual sales. The other side: The White House defended the investments as a way to rebuild American manufacturing and secure critical supply chains, emphasizing that companies participate voluntarily, spokesman Matthew Middleton said. What we're watching: Democrats could spend the next two years scrutinizing Trump's investments — while debating whether a future Democratic administration should make similar deals of its own.

c5fce0e7186a.text: Newly elected Democrats from ruby red states are leading a charge to take on corporate health care and some business practices that they say drive up health care costs. Why it matters: Democrats may not be anywhere close to agreement on Medicare for All, but they're relatively united around confronting Big Health Care after campaigning hard on the populist theme. Driving the news: While expanding Medicare, reversing GOP Medicaid cuts and reviving enhanced Obamacare subsidies are getting most of the attention, there's a subtle shift in rhetoric and policy positions toward blaming big health companies for the affordability crisis. It reflects the reality that a substantial expansion of the federal government's role in health care isn't in the cards while President Trump is in office, but populist themes could unite the rank-and-file and even draw in some Republicans. Even candidates who didn't constantly rail about drugmakers or insurers have adopted policy ideas that, until recently, were confined to left-leaning think tanks. Case in point: Incoming Texas Sen. James Talarico ran on breaking up big health care companies and "stop[ping] hospitals and insurance companies from overcharging patients." (He also supports allowing Americans under 65 to join Medicare.) South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews ran on limiting insurer profits per enrollee, expanding the number of drugs subject to Medicare drug price negotiations and banning private equity-owned hospitals. Incoming Kansas Sen. Adam Hamilton supports expanding Medicare drug price negotiations and extending the negotiated prices to private health plans, as well as addressing Medicare Advantage overpayments from the federal government. Other targets include medical debt, pharmacy benefit manager practices and caps on out-of-pocket drug costs. Many of these ideas already have buy-in from more-senior progressives. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) has sponsored the Break Up Big Medicine Act, which is co-sponsored by Republican Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, which would prohibit common ownership of health plans and providers. Incoming Michigan Sen. Abdul El-Sayed, an avid Medicare for All supporter, ran on support of the Warren-Hawley bill, as well as expanding Medicare drug price negotiations. The House's health care working group , made up of both progressives and moderates, pitched capping "excessive" hospital prices and enacting site-neutral payments. The big picture: Voters have made clear that they want lower health care costs. So while a broad overhaul of the health system may not immediately be on the table, Democrats are looking for ways to deliver. Powerful health industry groups are poised to push back, arguing that the populist policies would threaten patient care and access in some communities. But the ideas under discussion could gain favor with some Republicans. What they're saying: When asked at an Axios event on Tuesday whether Congress should address ownership ties between insurers, PBMs and pharmacies, Rep. Morgan Griffith — the top Republican on the House Energy and Commerce's Health Subcommittee — said, "I've only heard the case for breaking them up." "There's just something in your gut that bothers you when your pharmacy, your PBM and your insurance company are all owned by the same people," he added. What we're watching: Forcing drugmakers to lower prescription drug prices could be a particularly compelling target, given Trump's demonstrated interest in the topic. He has previously called on Congress to codify the "most-favored-nation" deals he made with pharmaceutical manufacturers that require the companies, in some cases, to offer Americans prices on a par with what's paid abroad. The Senate Finance Committee's top Democrat, Ron Wyden of Oregon, told reporters this week that he's open to a deal codifying those agreements in exchange for an expansion of the number of drugs Medicare can negotiate on, according to InsideHealthPolicy . The bottom line: It was only four years ago that Democrats struggled to find enough votes for the modest drug price negotiations that exist today, marking the first successful legislative attempt to directly lower health care costs in any sector by either party. Now, they're more willing to push for change and confront big industry players.

821d9fd67181.text: New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is shaking up her team for the second time in the past few months as she prepares to make the biggest decision of her political life. Why it matters: The overhaul comes as the democratic socialist leader is debating whether to run for president in 2028 — or Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's seat, which is up the same year. Zoom in: Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with her longtime digital fundraising firm, Middle Seat, according to three people familiar with the decision. At the same time, sources said, she's brought on Aisle 518 Strategies — the company led by Democratic strategist Tim Tagaris, who oversaw Bernie Sanders' record-breaking online fundraising strategy in his two presidential campaigns. Middle Seat has been key to Ocasio-Cortez's operation. Over the past two years, she has paid the firm more than $6 million — about a quarter of her operation's disbursements during that period. AOC is close with Sanders, and if she decides to run for president, progressives say, she would be able to quickly staff up with his former advisers. But Ocasio-Cortez's latest move doesn't necessarily signal that she's leaning toward a presidential run or a Senate bid. Tagaris' firm has helped power the small-dollar fundraising operation for California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who's widely expected to run for the White House. It also has worked with other Democrats who are potential contenders for president — Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Vice President Kamala Harris, according to the company's website . Middle Seat, the firm AOC is leaving, has Sanders roots as well: It was founded by alumni of the Vermont senator's 2016 campaign. Flashback: Ocasio-Cortez's reorganizing follows several changes she made to her staff this year, as Axios previously reported . They included parting ways with her longtime campaign manager and creative director, as well as bringing aboard a few former aides. The Washington Sun reported this week that AOC had hired Freeland Ellis, a Sanders alum, as a communications aide. What they're saying: A spokesperson for Ocasio-Cortez declined to comment. Tagaris declined to comment, and Middle Seat partner Kenneth Pennington did not respond to a request for comment.

3a5558395dfd.text: Note: Figures compare average daily sentiment readings over the seven days before each election with the five days after. Election Day is excluded; Data: Morning Consult; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios There was an unusually sharp partisan mood shift in the wake of the midterms, according to sentiment data from Morning Consult that was shared exclusively with Axios. Why it matters: While big partisan swings in consumer sentiment are typical after a presidential election, they have been much smaller in midterm races. The latest numbers show just how tightly Americans' views on the economy are now intertwined with politics. By the numbers: Democratic consumer sentiment rose 6.5 points in the five days after the election compared with the week before, while Republicans' mood fell 6.4 points. How it works: Morning Consult's index considers survey responses from approximately 5,000 U.S. adults. They're asked five questions, including on people's personal finances and financial outlook, as well as their views on overall business conditions. Zoom in: The biggest shifts in sentiment were in respondents' feelings about the future. Republicans' outlook across all five metrics fell after the election. Their confidence in business conditions over the next five years plummeted 12 percentage points. Democrats, meanwhile, had a jump of 9 percentage points in confidence about business conditions (although they remain negative about it) and an even bigger increase — 12 percentage points — in optimism that their own finances would improve over the next year. Of note: Both sides were more negative about their own finances compared with a year ago. Zoom out: Overall sentiment, which includes Independents, barely moved — ticking up less than one point, per Morning Consult. The opposing partisan shifts appear to have canceled each other out. Reality check: It's early days, and sentiment could shift quickly. Between the lines: Consumer sentiment was once a telling measure of how people would actually spend their money: Good vibes meant more spending. Lately, it's looked more like a political measure. "Sentiment matters because it's vibes," says Eli Yokley, a U.S. politics analyst at Morning Consult.

c0a5ea394eab.text: Data: Major Cities Chiefs Association (MCCA) ; Note: Tulsa Police changed crime-reporting systems, which may affect year-over-year comparisons.; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios Homicides fell 15.2% across major U.S. police jurisdictions through the first nine months of 2026, extending a retreat from pandemic-era violence that began under President Biden and continues under President Trump . The big picture: A new Major Cities Chiefs Association report found declines in all four major violent-crime categories among 66 reporting U.S. large law enforcement agencies from January through September, compared with the same period last year. Homicides dropped 15.2%. Robberies fell 9.1%. Rapes declined 3.5%. Aggravated assaults decreased 3.4%. State of play: Combined, the four categories fell 4.9% — or 13,822 fewer reported offenses. Fifty-one of the 66 agencies reported overall declines. Homicides dropped in 49 jurisdictions, increased in 15 and remained unchanged in two. Zoom in: Some of the nation's largest cities recorded striking homicide declines. Memphis: Homicides plunged 36.5%, from 156 to 99. San Antonio was down 36.5%, Indianapolis down 33.6%, Philadelphia down 21.2%, Aurora, Colorado down 65.2% and Newark, New Jersey down 59.1%. The other side: New York City was a major outlier and reported more violent crime in all four categories, including 24.5% more homicides and 14.2% more robberies. Its combined violent crime total was up 5.1%. San Diego reported 45.2% more homicides and Las Vegas recorded a 23.4% jump. Washington, D.C., saw homicides fall 29.9%, but robberies surged 41.1%, pushing its combined violent-crime total up 9.7%. The caveat: The figures remain preliminary. Houston reported no data because of a records-system transition, and Tulsa recently transitioned to a new crime reporting system, the report notes.

A British woman has gone missing from a cruise ship while it was crossing the Atlantic, travel operator Tui has said.
The 72-year-old was last seen aboard Tui's Marella Voyager on Monday while the vessel was en route to the Caribbean. The ship could have travelled hundreds of miles in the time between when she was last seen to when she was reported missing.
Staff realised the passenger was missing on Tuesday, when they noticed her bed had not been slept in. The alarm was raised and a search carried out, Tui said in a statement.
It is understood the missing guest was then reported to the US Coast Guard, which asked the ship to continue to its crossing rather than reverse course and search for the woman.
Holidaymakers were told to abandon dinners, drinks and entertainment as the crew carried out an emergency headcount on Tuesday evening, the Daily Mail reports.
Passengers stood in lines of four while staff scanned boarding cards to verify the identity of every person on the ship, according to the newspaper.
The USCG Rescue Co-ordination Centre in Norfolk, Virginia has issued an alert calling on any ships nearby to "keep a sharp look out" for the woman, the Mail reports. The BBC has contacted the USCG for comment.
The Marella Voyager, carrying around 2,000 passengers and 800 crew, left Malaga on 4 November and is due to arrive in Antigua on Friday before calling at Dominica and finishing its voyage in Barbados on Sunday.
A spokeswoman for Marella Cruises said it was "deeply saddened" by the disappearance, adding: "Our thoughts are with the guest's loved ones at this very difficult time.
"We're supporting the authorities with their enquiries, and out of respect for the guest and their family, we won't be commenting further at this stage."
A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: "We are supporting the family of a British national reported missing on a cruise ship in the Atlantic Ocean and we are in touch with the relevant authorities."
In a separate case, a cruise ship pianist was found treading water on Sunday around 20 miles off the Californian coast after falling overboard.
Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have arrived in Moscow for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, a day after the latest talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.
Videos shared by Russian media showed Kushner and Witkoff disembarking a plane and being welcomed by Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev with handshakes and hugs.
The American negotiatiors were due to meet Putin at 12:00 local time (09:00 GMT), and will then fly to Dublin to speak to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
On Tuesday, Kushner said the US had seen "some openings and some opportunities" and that they would try to "make some progress" at the meeting with Putin.
The in-person talks with the Russian and Ukrainian presidents were only announced on Wednesday after two days of talks which were framed as centred around the postwar security architecture of Europe.
Nearly five years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow shows no sign of backing down from its maximalist demands for sovereign Ukrainian territory and for Western countries to give up any future commitment to protecting Kyiv in case of further attacks.
During the first years of the war, Europeans cut communications with the Kremlin and refused to engage with Russia directly.
However, in recent times many have grown concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin, and have been pushing for a seat at the negotiating table.
The talks in Abu Dhabi were led by the Americans and only included Russia and Ukraine, but Kushner said he and Witkoff would ask Putin to "give his blessing" to invite European representatives in future discussions - particularly with regards to the future configuration of their continent's security architecture.
Kushner also urged Europe to "identify one person to speak on their behalf" in the negotiations.
But the Russians have been opposed to the idea, citing Europe's support for Kyiv as an obstacle.
Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi, said he thought all parties had "moved closer to achieving peace" but that now "a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the United States, and on whether Europe comes to its senses".
As Witkoff and Kushner were meeting Russian officials in Moscow, Zelensky said Ukraine's military was again facing news of "systematic" restrictions to Starshield satellite internet, Elon Musk's SpaceX service which plays a key role for frontline communications. Connectivity issues in October lasted about a week. Musk denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection.
The restrictions have made it more difficult for Ukrainian forces to intercept Russian jet-powered drones, Zelensky said in a statement.
"This is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine," he said.
"We are trying to clear up all circumstances with the American side."

9e07f0745d86.text: Jensen Huang's potential ouster from Nvidia has plunged the AI industry into uncharted territory — a corporate earthquake that dwarfs even the chaos unleashed by Sam Altman's temporary firing from OpenAI in 2023. Why it matters: Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy , with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars. At the center of that vast financial flywheel is Huang, who spent 33 years making himself synonymous with Nvidia — and Nvidia synonymous with the AI revolution. "This is no ordinary CEO. This is no ordinary company. This is no ordinary sector. This is no ordinary time," economist Mohamed El-Erian wrote on X , warning of contagion across the AI industry. Zoom in: As recently as two weeks ago, the notion of Nvidia without Jensen was unthinkable. Even after his affair with a suspected Chinese spy came to light, President Trump and Nvidia's board stood behind him, Silicon Valley's elite rallied to his defense and betting markets suggested he would survive. It took revelations of a second affair — this time with an executive who reported directly to Huang — to shatter that consensus and bring his storied reign to the brink of a stunning end. Driving the news: After that second affair came to light Wednesday night, Nvidia's board reportedly met to settle Huang's fate, though there was still no decision as of early Thursday morning. The White House was read in. The market reaction has been brutal. Nvidia had already shed more than $1 trillion in market value since the initial scandal erupted, and shares plunged further in after-hours and pre-market trading overnight. One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang. Zoom out: Huang's rise was the stuff of Silicon Valley legend: The Taiwanese immigrant went from cleaning toilets at a Kentucky boarding school and waiting tables at Denny's to building one of the most valuable companies in history. Huang and two fellow engineers hatched the idea for Nvidia at a Denny's booth in 1993, launching a chipmaker that would revolutionize gaming, transform modern computing and ultimately power the AI revolution. Clad in his trademark black leather jacket, Huang became a global AI rock star — with a cult of personality that drew adoring crowds, calmed markets and commanded the attention of world leaders. The big picture: Huang's apparent downfall comes amid mounting anxiety over the AI industry's future, as new financial, political and regulatory risks threaten one of the largest infrastructure buildouts in history. The timing is especially fraught for Anthropic , whose historic IPO — backed by a $10 billion commitment from Nvidia — looms as a referendum on Wall Street's faith in the AI trade. Huang spent years defending the industry's soaring valuations and dismissing warnings of a speculative frenzy. Now his own scandals could help burst the bubble he insisted didn't exist. What to watch: The blast radius could extend far beyond Silicon Valley and Wall Street, threatening to engulf the Trump administration in a scandal over its handling of sensitive technology exports to China. Huang forged a close alliance with Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who loosened restrictions on chip sales even as other officials raised concerns about Chinese espionage and smuggling. Top Senate Democrats are already demanding that Lutnick and other senior officials preserve records of their dealings with Nvidia and Huang, laying the groundwork for a sweeping investigation. The bottom line: As veteran China watcher Bill Bishop wrote after Huang acknowledged his first affair: "There is rarely just one lie."

4c0d106ffc04.text:
State and local governments spent about $3.7 billion in opioid settlement funds last year. That’s more than the median annual income of 42,000 American families combined.
The money comes from companies that were sued for aggressively pushing painkillers and fueling the opioid crisis.
Large amounts went to addiction treatment, recovery housing, and other initiatives that many public health researchers and families affected by the crisis agree fit the spirit of the settlements — to save lives and remediate the problem.
But other expenditures had tenuous ties to addiction, including:
- $150,000 for street lighting in Camden, New Jersey.
- $130,000 for Flock cameras in Carmel, Indiana.
- At least $84,000 for city insurance, building utilities, vehicle repairs, and other standard city expenses in Mullens, West Virginia.
- $36,200 for a pickleball court in Gilmer County, West Virginia.
KFF Health News uncovered these expenditures among about 17,500 examined through a yearlong investigation with the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and Shatterproof, a national nonprofit focused on addiction. The team filed public records requests, scoured government websites, and extracted expenditures, which were then sorted into categories such as treatment or prevention. The result is the most comprehensive national database documenting how opioid settlement money was used (or left unspent) in 2025.
The pot of settlement cash, which many addiction survivors and their advocates consider “blood money,” is expected to total about $60 billion over nearly two decades. It is split among state governments, counties, cities, and specially created opioid settlement councils in some places.
Although there are some spending guidelines within the settlement agreements, there is considerable flexibility, a vacuum of leadership and oversight, and significant gaps in how the public can track the dollars.
Much of the questionable spending — ranging from law enforcement gadgets to mundane municipal needs — happens at the county and city level, where local leaders often have no background in addiction policy and sometimes award the money to the first people who ask for it.
Nationwide, local decision-makers control nearly half the money, according to OpioidSettlementTracker.com, a site dedicated to following this cash. Proponents of local control say these officials know their communities best and are closest to the problem. But as dubious expenditures mount, some recovery advocates question if county and city officials are equipped to handle this once-in-a-generation opportunity.
“It shouldn’t be run by these politicians,” said Elizabeth Burke Beaty, a person in recovery and a New Jersey-based advocate who’s been following the opioid cash for years.
She said people directly affected by the crisis understand gaps in their local community care systems best and have the most insight into how funds can be used effectively. “This whole opioid settlement should be run by the people who’ve lost everything,” she said.
As executive director of the Sea Change Recovery Community and Harm Reduction Center in Ocean County, Burke Beaty sees those people daily. A woman who lost her brother and father to addiction and later landed in the hospital herself. An 11-year-old boy, holding his grandfather’s hand at an overdose awareness event, as they mourned a family member.
“This is money from dead people and people left behind,” Burke Beaty said.
Of course, many local officials have lost friends and family to the crisis as well, and many care deeply about putting the money to good use.
Unlike state officials, who have access to health departments with specific expertise and staff whose entire job is writing policy, local decision-makers often work with bare-bones support. They may juggle other jobs alongside their official duties and can be bombarded by aggressive sales tactics from companies that view the settlements as a gold rush. They must determine how to make an impact with opioid settlement cash while facing the sober reality of needing to balance a government budget, keep public schools running, and ensure roads are maintained.
Burke Beaty acknowledges these challenges and offers to work with many local leaders in her area, often writing letters, showing up at public meetings, and creating reports with detailed feedback on how localities spent the money.
But when these efforts go ignored, she wonders if it’s because of a lack of resources or “a lack of willingness to do the right thing,” she said. “Did this come from a place of ignorance or an ‘I don’t care’ place?”
Who Should Control the Money?
It can be tempting to suggest state governments should oversee all the cash, especially as some debatable spending patterns emerge at the local level.
But that’s been tried before.
In the Tobacco Master Settlement of 1998, cigarette companies paid hundreds of billions of dollars to states, typically without county or city involvement. Ultimately, much of the money went to plugging budget gaps, and, over 20 years, less than 3% of tobacco settlement and tax-related revenue was directed to anti-smoking programs.
“It is not likely that whatever model we pick is going to work flawlessly,” said Philip Rutherford, who leads substance use strategy at the National Council for Mental Wellbeing, a nonprofit representing community mental health and addiction treatment organizations.
Splitting the opioid money with local governments offers some advantages, he added. They spend less on administrative costs, can pivot more quickly as the drug landscape changes, and can test innovations.
It’s also not unusual for local officials to involve themselves in areas in which they lack personal expertise, said Annie Qing, who oversees health and human services work at the National Association of Counties.

Jason Fazekas has spent most of his adult life on the street or behind bars. He was addicted to heroin for decades and often stole to support his habit. On rainy days, he slept in building stairwells to stay dry. On winter mornings, he woke up with fingers too numb to bend.
That all changed in September when he moved into a one-bedroom apartment in East Haven, Connecticut.
“I never knew what it was like to have your own apartment, to live on your own, until this,” said Fazekas, 49.
Now he attends a daily treatment program and virtual “Sober at Seven” meetings. He makes grilled cheese and cold-cut sandwiches; works occasional jobs, such as cleaning out a truck; and is in bed most nights by 8:30.
This simple life is “the best thing in the world,” said Fazekas, who celebrated nine months of recovery in October.
That life has become his reality thanks to a housing program the state of Connecticut funded with about $59 million in opioid settlement cash, money paid by companies accused of aggressively pushing painkillers and fueling the opioid crisis. The housing program provides people with substance use disorders a rental voucher, a case manager to help them find and keep their home, and money to cover the costs of settling in, such as a security deposit or basic furniture.
Nationwide, state and local governments invested more than $340 million from opioid settlements into housing-related initiatives in 2025, according to an analysis by KFF Health News, the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, and Shatterproof, a national nonprofit focused on addiction. Some projects, like the one in Connecticut, are aimed directly at helping people most affected by the opioid epidemic. But others lack a clear connection to the crisis, leading to criticism by recovery advocates that the money is at risk of being squandered.
Opioid settlement cash, expected to total about $60 billion over nearly two decades, is considered a once-in-a-generation opportunity to address an overdose epidemic that has claimed more than 1 million lives since 2000. Although there are some spending guidelines, there is a lot of wiggle room, little oversight, and large gaps in the public’s ability to track the money.
To shed light on where funds are flowing, KFF Health News and its partners annually file public records requests, scour government websites, and assemble a database of expenditures by state and local governments, which are then sorted into categories such as treatment or prevention.
The result is the most comprehensive national resource of its kind: a catalog of more than 17,500 ways settlement cash was used (or left unspent) in 2025.
Of the roughly $3.7 billion publicly reported as spent or committed last year, about 9% went to housing initiatives, ranging from permanent housing like the Connecticut effort to temporary recovery housing and assistance in navigating complex applications and other social services.
Many public health researchers, recovery advocates, and families affected by addiction are excited about the investments. Housing can stabilize people’s lives enough to get them into treatment and increase their chances of maintaining long-term recovery.
Settlement funds also provide flexibility at a time when the Trump administration opposes federal funds for efforts to house people before they’re sober — despite evidence that such policies are effective.
However, some people closely tracking settlement money worry that the lines will be blurred between general homelessness initiatives and those that focus specifically on people with substance use disorders. As jurisdictions continue to grapple with people living on the street and public backlash over encampments, they may be tempted to use opioid dollars to reduce the visibility of homelessness with little or no programmatic link to addiction.
“The most important piece” of investing settlement dollars “is maintaining that connection to opioid remediation and the populations impacted by opioid use disorder,” said Dan Kelly, who worked in housing and homelessness initiatives before joining the Michigan Association of Counties, where he guides local governments on settlement spending.
Blurred Lines in Local Spending
In Connecticut, Fazekas and other participants must have a verified substance use disorder to be eligible for the housing program.
Elsewhere, it’s less clear-cut.
For example, New Brunswick, New Jersey, spent $520,000 of its settlement funds on “homeless services.”
That may include crucial services for the general homeless population, recovery advocates say. But unless the money is targeted specifically to homeless people with substance use disorders, it may do little to address the overdose crisis. To some, that violates the spirit of the settlements.
J.T. Miller, a city spokesperson, did not answer questions about what specific services were funded or how they related to addiction. Instead, he wrote that settlement money was used to “support staff and services who actively engaged with the homeless population addressing ongoing assistance, prevention and drug addiction programs.” He shared a link to the city’s community services website, which did not mention addiction.
In a report to the state, the city wrote that the money was for “budgetary offsets and allocations” in its Department of Human and Community Services.
Recovery advocates have long feared that governments would use the opioid money to simply replace general taxpayer funding for existing services, rather than enhancing those services or creating new ones.

The Democrats’ sweeping success at the national level in last week’s midterms was mirrored in major swings at the state level as well. In Pennsylvania, where Democrats flipped the state Senate, the party will control both chambers of the legislature and the governor’s office for the first time since 1993.
After four years watching bills clear the state House of Representatives only to stall in the Republican-controlled Senate, the party’s leaders say they plan to seize the moment. That’s especially true on the Energy Committee, chaired by Rep. Elizabeth Fiedler of Philadelphia. She knows voters will be looking to her committee to address two pivotal issues that helped decide the midterms: rising utility bills and controversial data center development.
The trifecta in Harrisburg represents “a huge opportunity and a huge responsibility” for Democrats, Fiedler said in an interview a few days after the dust settled.
“We’ve got to act quickly,” she said. “What we saw in the results of Tuesday’s election made clear that people are not happy with the status quo. People want to see change. People do not want excuses.”
With that in mind, she said her colleagues on the Energy Committee have about 15 bills that have already passed the House and will be reintroduced “first thing” in the new session, aimed at addressing “what’s on people’s minds.”
In this interview, which has been edited for length and clarity, Fiedler discussed the party’s approach to affordable utility bills, renewable energy development and an issue that hung over the elections both nationally and locally: data centers.
BEN SEAL: Post-election, what have the early conversations among your Democratic colleagues focused on?
ELIZABETH FIEDLER: At the very top of the list is affordability. We have to find a way to lower people’s bills. We have already passed quite a few bills in our committee and also in the House that would do just that.
[Lancaster Democrat] Nikki Rivera’s battery storage bill would allow us to store energy at a time when it’s abundant and then release and use that energy during times of peak demand, like during a heat wave. Return on equity reform is a bill I introduced last session that the governor himself talked about in his budget address. That’s focused on making sure that the shareholders of utility companies are not making excessive profits.
We’ve got to take a careful look at everything we can do right now to help people. And that definitely includes lowering the cost of energy, lowering utility bills and getting more renewable energy online. So [Berks County Democrat] Jacklyn Rusnock’s solar on warehouses bill is a great example. [Allegheny County Democrat] Arvind Venkat has a geothermal bill.
SEAL: A lot of the legislation that’s been sitting in the Senate has been described as “low-hanging fruit.” Are there more ambitious proposals that you think might gain traction?
FIEDLER: I’m all for bold and ambitious ideas. Now is a great time to go on the offense on renewable energy and, in particular, solar. The technology has made huge steps forward over the last couple of years.
I am excited for the future of Solar for Schools. The more we can do to spread the word about it to more schools the better, because then schools can save millions of dollars by installing solar panels, and they can put that money back into kids’ education. That’s a real win-win-win. I also plan to introduce legislation to offer a residential solar tax credit.
A lot of the work that we want to do is making up for changes that were made at the federal level. The [Inflation Reduction Act] and other federal programs were supposed to support the construction of renewable energy projects across the U.S. When the president decided to dismantle and defund those programs, it had a huge impact.
With a relatively modest appropriation, the Pennsylvania Energy Development Authority could do huge energy infrastructure projects. So I am hopeful on the appropriations front. We’re talking about hydropower on state dams, and there’s also huge potential for both geothermal and solar.

SEAL: Clean energy advocates often point to the Alternative Energy Portfolio Standards as a limitation in moving the state forward. Do you think there might be updates that would accelerate the state’s timeline for renewable energy adoption?
FIEDLER: Yes. A resounding yes. It’s been a very long time since it was updated. All reports and expectations are that in just a few years we’ll be facing significant power outages. We’ve got to take that into account while we also take into account the climate crisis and global warming, more extreme weather, changes in seasons—all the stuff that is our reality now.
SEAL: How do you think the legislature will respond to the strong public sentiment against further expansion of the state’s data center build-out?
FIEDLER: We have already passed [in the House] a number of bills that would change the landscape and place much more stringent regulations and requirements on data centers. House Bill 1834 is a great example, focused on making sure regular people do not subsidize the build-out of energy systems and transmission for data centers. That to me feels like the absolute bare minimum of what we should be doing.
I’ve worked with my colleague Kyle Donahue, [a Lackawanna County Democrat], on a model ordinance bill [guiding municipalities on standards for data center development], and an interconnection bill [ensuring ratepayers don’t bear the costs of energy generation and transmission]. As House Democrats debate the future of the select committee on China, some in their party are arguing for keeping it around.
âIf you want to be able to look at the comprehensive issues facing the US-China relationship, there is not a single committee that covers all of it. Itâs spread all over. So this puts it in one single committee,â said Rep. Greg Stanton, D-Ariz., who hails from a more centrist wing of the party and sits on the select panel now.
Some progressive groups led by Just Foreign Policy are mobilizing to defend it, too, after Semafor reported some lawmakers were lobbying to kill it.
A letter from the groups shared with Semafor praises the âdifferent approachâ from Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., its current top Democrat.
âWe believe Democratic leadership now has an important opportunity to build on this progress and demonstrate a more responsible and constructive approach to US-China relations,â it states.
Thereâs a bipartisan push to save the committee as members consult House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries on its future. He told reporters Wednesday the discussions with committee leaders and the caucus on the future of the China select panel and a proposed AI select committee were âongoing.â
Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat, who favors folding the select panel under his committee, has been pushing to make it a âspecialâ committee under House Foreign Affairs, a person familiar with the talks said. Some top Democrats want to pump the brakes on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth next year after this weekâs attempt came up short.
âWe have a very difficult set of decisions to make and I donât think we should hastily make them,â said Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the top Armed Services Democrat.
He worries the party could get stuck in internecine conflict after a sizable number of Democratic absences on the impeachment procedural vote caused hand-wringing this week, which could take attention away from cost-of-living issues that powered their midterm gains.
âStrategically and tactically, whatâs going to best advance our agenda? And I worry that what you saw yesterday is a preview of one of our biggest challenges,â Smith added.
With plenty in the caucus pushing for a Hegseth impeachment, though, another lawmaker could force a vote next Congress â whether Democratic leaders want it or not.
House Minority Whip Katherine Clark told Democrats in a closed-door meeting Wednesday morning that the party had disappointed the American people by not having all of the members there for the impeachment vote, and that it was their job to show up for the people who sent them there, according to people familiar with her comments.
Still, Democrats, including Clark, note that they likely couldnât have won the vote, given the lack of GOP defections beyond Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who introduced the resolution. Nearly a dozen Democrats missed the vote Tuesday referring the impeachment articles to the Judiciary Committee, with Democratic lawmakers blaming traffic and scheduling conflicts, among other issues.
Looking ahead to the next Congress, top Democrats plan to conduct investigations into Hegseth on their own terms, rather than letting their hand be forced early. âI think we should do oversight and investigations under our own timetable, not Tom Massieâs,â said Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., the top Intelligence Committee Democrat. âAnd Iâd really like to see affordability stay at the center of the agenda.â
Still, others wanted to keep impeachment in mind. âEverythingâs on the table there. I donât think thereâs a single Democrat or a lot of Republicans that think that Hegseth is qualified for the job and has done the job well,â said Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat.

Some Democrats say they wonât vote for Chuck Schumer to be Democrat leader. Others are declining to endorse him publicly as Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., weighs a challenge and dials up colleagues.
But a confident Schumer is acting like heâs staying put. And many of his colleagues are itching to skip the Democratic infighting altogether and reach the moment when Schumer is reelected Democratic leader on Dec. 1.
âSchumer has been an unpopular figure among people who donât understand the role of the Senate party leader. And I think it probably helped them on the trail,â Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., told Semafor. âItâs not the first time that a Senate leader has helped elected members who have opposed his leadership.â
He said he was confident when all is said and done, Schumer will emerge as the victor. Schumer is, too.
The New York senator has asserted repeatedly heâll be the majority leader again next year. And in a sign of that confidence, heâs already plotting out a unified Democratic agenda with House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries. He spent his Wednesday doing things that only a returning leader would: meeting with incoming newly-elected senators like Rep. Chris Pappas, D-N.H., and Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., to discuss their priorities and what committees theyâd like to serve on.
Schumer is not acting like a guy who is short of the votes. Hamilton has called for new party leadership and told Semafor that Schumer didnât ask him to reconsider that demand during their sitdown on Wednesday: âNo, he didnât at all, actually.â
âWe talked about being overwhelmed when youâre first getting into this and talked about stories, things that matter, committees,â Hamilton said.
Path to victory
Schumer recruited a number of strong Democratic candidates, including former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina, and former Rep. Mary Peltola of Alaska (who is ahead of Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, in a race that has yet to be called). Still, thereâs no question that the core of the Democratic Caucus is changing and Schumer has to adapt to it.
Whitehouse is from the class of 2006, the year of Schumerâs first big Senate triumph, when he flipped the chamber as party campaign chair. He then achieved a stunning 60-seat majority two years later. Those Democrats were the bulwark of Schumerâs political power as he became leader in 2017, and his support remains strong within the caucus even as his reputation has eroded outside the Capitol.
And despite Schumerâs relentless fundraising on candidatesâ behalf and candidate recruitment, the class of 2026 has its own ideas. The Schumer-aligned Senate Majority PAC and its affiliates spent $67 million in Michigan, $65 million in Maine, and $14 million in Kansas, only to see those senators say they do not support him.
âWe have a lot of new voices coming into the Senate and folks who have been on the ground hearing directly from their constituents about how frustrated they are. So we just have to make sure that leadership recognizes the urgency of this moment,â said Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan, D-Minn. âWeâll see who decides to step in,â she added, calling Van Hollen âfantastic.â
Schumer also has moves to make to reshape his caucus. He may elevate progressive Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., to a more prominent leadership position as Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., prepares to be sworn in as governor of her state. Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., a vocal critic of President Donald Trump who was elected to the Senate in 2024, is also making calls about a position in leadership.
So far, no one besides Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., is raising their hand to be chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee â a position appointed by the party leader. Gillibrand just enjoyed a wildly successful 2026 cycle.
And most importantly, Schumer will have to decide whether he will run for another six-year term as senator in 2028.
Votes in hand
Even as a number of Democrats like Sens. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., and Mark Warner, D-Va., decline to publicly back Schumer, Democrats believe Schumerâs private commitments range far beyond his public ones. The long windup to the Dec. 1 leadership election, which is conducted by secret ballot, offers little upside for members with national ambitions to endorse Schumer early.
But even so, a number of Democrats are still publicly backing him. Brown, who was first ushered into the Senate in 2006, says heâll support Schumer after Schumer-aligned groups spent an eye-watering $150 million in Ohio. Sen. Angus King of Maine, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, said on CNN that expects the caucus to unite around Schumer.
Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., said sheâll back Schumer, as did Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn. âWhen the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract,â added Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz.
And Schumer is already plotting out next yearâs schedule. Senate and House Democrats are planning fast legislative action on potentially bipartisan bills by picking up the four or more Republican Senate votes they need to pass legislation. If Republicans block those bills, Jeffries and Schumer would move more quickly to party-line budget reconciliation legislation that can reach Trumpâs desk.
If Schumer were somehow dislodged as leader, the new Democratic majority would be way behind the eight-ball.
Room for Disagreement
As Gallego and Gillibrand lauded Schumer this week, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., announced he canât support him, while Sen. At least six people have been killed and about 20 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital, the biggest in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.
Eyewitnesses told the BBC that a single missile fired by a warplane hit a building containing the surgical wards and intensive care units overnight.
The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizk Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".
The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.
Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".
Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.
Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.
Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.
In a video posted on social media, a paramedic from the Civil Defence agency who arrived at the building after the strike early on Thursday said the missile penetrated the five-storey structure and hit a room in the surgical department.
A spokesman for the Civil Defence, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry, initially said that five people had been killed and 20 others injured.
Videos shared by activists showed thick smoke inside the building and extensive destruction on the second floor, where medical equipment and beds had been scattered by the blast.
Local activists have also circulated claims that the strike may have targeted a senior Hamas security figure who was hiding inside the building.
Speaking to reporters in the aftermath of the strike, the director of Nasser hospital said the building had been hit in a vertical strike, causing extensive damage.
Nasser hospital was hit by a double Israeli strike in August 2025, which killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers.
Israeli strikes on Gaza have continued despite a ceasefire agreement in October last year.
More than 1,620 people have been killed since then, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire.
The humanitarian crisis in Gaza has recently worsened as a result of heavy rains that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Daryna Kulchytska is a mum under pressure. A single parent in a seventh floor flat in Kyiv trying to feed two lively kids and ensure they do their homework. But Daryna also faces the added strain of a deadline she can't even be certain of.
All she knows is soon the lights will go out, the sockets will lose power, the wi-fi will drop, and the taps will run dry. Tonight, the electricity has kept flowing an hour longer than advertised, but Daryna's still racing to serve dinner and finish her own work from home.
"The last few days it was only four or five hours we had power, but it's not at the same times. For two hours we have electricity, then for eight hours we don't."
As peace talks continue, with US envoys meeting the Russian and Ukrainian leaders on Thursday, Ukrainians are facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts because of intensified Russian attacks on their energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.
Officials are concerned that life will quickly become unsustainable for millions of Ukrainians if power supplies cannot be maintained for at least four hours per day. Some privately warn that's close already, as some families are living with outages of up to 20 hours in Kyiv.
The power cuts were introduced earlier this year than last winter, and they're already lasting longer - making homes like Daryna's darker and colder. She's wrapped in layers of clothing and a heavy coat - the temperature is dropping, indoors and out.
Just before 7:30pm, there's a click and that's it - darkness until dawn.
The lift doesn't work, the water will stop flowing because electricity is needed to pump it to their flat. So the torches and LED candles come out and Daryna, her son Kyryll and daughter Olena gather for a card game of Uno before an early night.
Twelve-year-old Kyryll, speaking perfect English learned during two years living in the US, is frank about the disruption.
"There's no light, no water, no heat, no electricity. And no fun. All the fun got sucked out with the electricity," he says. "We have a lot of board games. We have a whole shelf, but we've played them like a hundred thousand times already."
Many families sit in the shadows as blackouts sweep entire neighbourhoods, smothering homes and streets in darkness.
"You look outside and sometimes you see nothing. You have a big city around but you see nothing because there's no light," Daryna says.
Kyiv has been worst hit - its metro trains and trolleybuses at times brought to a standstill. Nationwide, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians have gone without power in recent weeks.
We saw why on a visit to one of Ukraine's largest power stations, barely standing after a recent ballistic missile strike - the most powerful and devastating attack of Russia's campaign against Ukrainian energy targets.
The enormous plant - which we've been asked not to name for security reasons - has been reduced to a pile of twisted metal and broken pipes, its turbines buried in rubble, taking the site completely off line.
Volodymyr Kovalenko was on duty in the control room keeping the plant working when the missiles hit at 3am.
"It was a very powerful attack. We'd never experienced anything like it. We'd had strikes before â part of the roof had collapsed, it was pretty grim. But this time it was particularly severe."
Kovalenko, who followed in his parents' footsteps and has worked at the site for 25 years, says the damage is heartbreaking, though he's confident it can be repaired.
But the work is being hampered by air raids every 15-30 minutes â seven times during our four-hour visit. Each warning of drones and further missiles forces teams to down tools and dive for cover, though during our visit all were shot down or flew on towards other targets.
If there isn't time to reach the site's main shelter, the workers hide in the foundations of its towering chimneys.
"It's very difficult," says Vadym Bobyr, who is leading the recovery effort. "You've mentally prepared yourself to do a particular job, and thenâ¦ the air raid siren goes off, and you have to get out as quickly as possible."
The 39-year-old, who has worked here half his life, is dwarfed by the mangled ruins and daunted by the challenge of rebuilding the plant.
"It's emotionally difficult, because we've already repaired all this, got it running again, and now it's happened all over again. It hurts, but we keep working and getting things done."
As we speak there's another alert - an incoming Banderol cruise missile.
The workers dart through the maze of passages and pipework but there isn't time to reach a shelter - one of the plant's thickest walls will have to do for cover. The missile was eventually intercepted 5km (3 miles) away.
Energy workers are at enormous risk. Since August there have been almost daily attacks on power facilities, claiming several lives every week. And it's getting more dangerous.
On the edge of the site, with the latest threat over, a team returns to reinstating the power lines feeding the national grid. But they won't be carrying electricity from the shattered plant before the end of this winter, at least.
President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine still has enough generating capacity to meet electricity demand - the problem is getting it to homes and businesses when so many power lines and substations have been hit. Russia is using "waiter drones" that cling to pylons and cables and go undetected until Russia decides to detonate them.
Maxim Timchenko, CEO of DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, said Russia was already putting the degraded electricity grid under even greater pressure than last year, and that overstretched air defences were unable to protect all of Ukraine's critical infrastructure.
"What is different is the scale of attacks and the different types of weapons used in these attacks. This is what is the difference - they've doubled in power and in scale".

Ugandan police are investigating the deaths of four pupils at a school in the capital Kampala which they suspect may be the result of poisoning.
The four girls, aged between nine and 11 years, died on Tuesday. Three of the pupils died at home while the fourth passed away while receiving emergency treatment at a hospital.
The head teacher at the school, Ta'aliim Primary School and Quran Memorisation Centre, has been arrested to assist with investigations.
According to the school, eight pupils had eaten oranges shared by a fellow pupil.
Five pupils, including the four who later died, started vomiting. The fifth is still in hospital.
Post-mortem examinations are being carried out to determine the exact cause of death.
A police spokesperson was quoted by local media as saying that detectives would visit the village where the oranges the pupils ate came from.
The centre has been cordoned off as a crime scene.
Ugandan media shared videos of grieving parents describing their children's final moments, with some accusing the school of failing to provide clear and timely information.
The police have offered condolences to the bereaved families and affected community and say more information will be provided in due course.
The tragedy comes at a time when concerns are mounting over health and safety conditions in schools across Uganda.
Previous cases involving suspected contaminated food and exposure to harmful substances have left pupils hospitalised with symptoms including stomach pain, vomiting and breathing difficulties.
The incidents have intensified calls for authorities to strengthen monitoring of school feeding schemes, improve hygiene standards and ensure safer learning environments for children.

The Scoop
Some members of Nvidiaâs board favor appointing Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO at the beleaguered chipmaker if CEO and founder Jensen Huang is ousted, according to people familiar with the matter.
The full board has yet to make a decision. But the companyâs directors are scheduled to meet Wednesday evening, these people said.
Nvidiaâs board has debated whether, as part of its potential replacement of Huang, to introduce a chief operating officer to serve alongside the interim chief executive, some of the people said.
Semafor earlier confirmed that Nvidiaâs board is preparing to oust Huang as soon as Wednesday, after media reports detailed that he had a second extramarital affair. The Nvidia board briefed the White House on its planned meeting, according to a senior administration official.
Nvidia has tapped an outside search firm to find the companyâs next CEO, Bloomberg reported. One person being considered for the top job is Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who was among the executives considered for Intel CEO in 2019, according to another person familiar with the matter.
Whirlwind Saga
Nvidiaâs stock fell more than 8% in after-hours trading, hitting a 52-week low. Spokespeople for the company didnât immediately provide a comment.
Huangâs firing would cap a whirlwind saga thatâs seen the global frontman for the AI boom admit to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The $4 trillion companyâs long-tenured board announced a Wachtell Lipton-led probe into whether Huang may have divulged corporate secrets or endangered US national security.
In addition to providing many of the most advanced chips for hyperscalers, Nvidia has entered into billions of dollars worth of financing deals underwriting the AI buildout.
Democrats Move In
Sens. Chris Coons, D-Del., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., sent a letter to members of President Donald Trumpâs Cabinet on Wednesday asking them to preserve documents related to Nvidiaâs chip exports to China or entities that could divert such chips to the country. 
They also asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller to preserve documents and communications concerning Huang and the suspected Chinese operative he had an affair with, as well as the correspondence between Huang and Trump.
âThis incident raises significant concerns about the federal governmentâs ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,â the senators wrote in the letter. âReports suggest that officials within the government â including at the White House, State Department, and Commerce Department â were aware of concerns about NVIDIA, its relationship with Megaspeed, and the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips.â
Brendan Ruberry contributed to this report.

After a successful campaign getting parkland protected, residents in a Norfolk town are asking for more space to be given the same safeguards from development.
Seven acres (2.8 hectares) of land known as Harding's Pits, beside the River Great Ouse in King's Lynn, will be preserved after it was given "village green status" by the county council.
The Harding's Pits Community Association had campaigned for the past 30 years to keep the area as leisure space.
Next, the group wants the protection to be extended to the east side, which has been earmarked for up to 50 houses in King's Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council's local plan, external. The authority has been approached for comment.
Alexandra Kemp, an independent councillor, said she was asking her authority to amend its local plan.
She said: "I want to protect the east side of Hardings Way as a village green. To take out the 50 houses earmarked for Harding's Pits east from the borough's local plan, and provide community sports facilities, more trees and places for wildlife instead.
"Any development along Hardings Way risks more general traffic which would be devastating to the peace, quiet, safety, and amenity and wildlife."
The local council has been given a target to build more than 10,000 new homes by 2040 by the government.
Harding's Pits was turned into a public space in the early 1960s, but was originally a 19th Century clay pit which was then used as landfill.
The site is currently used for dog walking and as pedestrian access to King's Lynn town centre.

A new public art trail will mark the arrival of Asiatic black bears, Jersey Zoo has said.
Sculptures of bears and bees would be put up across the island's wild landscapes, coastal spots and urban spaces to celebrate the arrival of the new species in their new enclosure next year, said bosses.
They said the installation, which launches in July next year, aimed to shine a light on "connections that sustain the natural world, from its largest inhabitants to its smallest".
Artists will be invited to submit designs to turn the sculptures into "distinctive works of art" while schools and community groups will also be encouraged to participate.
It is hoped the sculptures will then be sold a fundraising auction at the end of the summer.
Rebecca Brewer, chief executive of Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust, said: "We want everyone who connects with our work, whether at Jersey Zoo or through our conservation projects around the world, to feel they can make a difference for nature.
"Our public art trails are a wonderful way to bring that belief to life."
She said previous Go Wild Gorillas and Tortoise Takeover trails "brought so much joy to Jersey, encouraging people to explore parts of the island they might never have visited, walk new paths, meet new people and create lasting memories".
An auction of the 54 tortoise sculptures raised Â£720,000 for a new tropical house.

Research into the effects of a microplastic spillage on sea-birds and marine life will be carried out for the next year after funding was secured.
A team working across Tyneside is doing tests to discover the impact the pellets, known as nurdles, have on animals, birds and fish, as well as the overall spread.
Tonnes of microplastics were spilled into the River Tyne on 19 July following a collision between ships at the Port of Tyne.
North East England Beached Bird Surveys co-ordinator Dan Turner, who is leading the research on dead sea-birds, said: "This will be a long-term issue, securing the grant now gives us room to conduct more research not just in the North East but worldwide."
The research, which has been funded by The National Environment Research Council (NERC), will focus on the effects of the spillage on the River Tyne and at the coast.
Necropsies have been carried out on dead sea-birds at the Dove Marine Laboratory in Cullercoats, North Tyneside, for the past six weeks. The current stage is focusing on stomach rinsing, which will check if nurdles have been found in the birds' stomachs.
"We haven't found any evidence of plastics in the stomachs just yet but we have more to check and have evidence that nurdles have been found in regurgitated material," Turner said.
The research was prompted over concerns birds could "starve" if they confuse the nurdles for food and fill their stomachs.
"It's concerning plastics can also break down over time which could have a big effect on the wider food chain as well," Turner added.
Denmark coast research
The research team is being led by a team of scientists and experts at Newcastle University and the University of Liverpool.
They are also being assisted by volunteers and other regional organisations such as Environment Agency, Tyne Rivers Trust and Groundwork North East and Cumbria.
Over the course of the year the research will also look to map the travel of the plastic pellets.
The nurdles have been found in beaches across Tyneside, Wearside and Teesside, with experts suggesting they may have reached the coast of Denmark.
Dr Geoffrey Abbott, a reader in geochemistry at Newcastle University, said: "We hope to visit Denmark to determine if the pellets found are the nurdles from the Port of Tyne spill.
"There have been cases where they can travel great distances, for instance a spill in South Africa led to nurdles washing up in Perth, Australia, in no time at all."
Members of the public are being asked to continue to send pictures of nurdles to help with the research.

A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive.
William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria.
Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search.
He was located on Thursday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life".
Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up.
The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy.
"He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added.
"He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive."
Joking, she added: "He's never leaving the house again."
Police have said officers were emotional to have found the teen alive.
"It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said. "I'm sure he's got a story to tell us soon, which we're very keen to hear," he added.

ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming.
Climate Action Tracker, a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5 degrees Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus.
“This striking change suggests that global warming has accelerated in recent years,” the EU scientists wrote. Even without understanding every aspect of the recent rapid global temperature increase, “It is clear that the ever-growing concentrations of greenhouse gases emitted by human activity in the atmosphere remain the main driver of this trend.”
The current level of warming has already triggered deadly and destructive floods, wildfires and catastrophic glacier collapses, said Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, who is attending the U.N. “Conferences of the Parties” climate talks, for the first time since 2021.
“The climate crisis is a matter of life and death,” she said. “The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.”
Sarah Heck, a climate policy analyst with Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute, said governments have failed to meaningfully improve the outlook for end-of-century warming.
“Our message is a stark one,” Heck said. “Collective government action on climate change has stalled for the fifth consecutive year.” Efforts to speed up the shift away from fossil fuels have been negated by new oil and gas drilling projects and governments that are “delaying, weakening or rolling back their climate policies.”
Even under the most optimistic scenario, assuming full implementation of existing policies and promises, global temperatures would rise 3.4 degrees Fahrenheit above preindustrial levels by 2100, an increase climate scientists consider extremely dangerous.
While there has been progress on developing renewable energy sources, the “brutal truth is that these positive developments have not yet added up to bend the curve fast enough,” said Niklas Höhne, a researcher with The New Climate Institute. Developing new oil and gas projects is a bit like discovering your food is burning and then turning up the stove instead of turning it off, he added.
Getting into the specifics of the current negotiations at COP31 surrounding global renewable goals, he noted that conference co-hosts Turkey and Australia have so far opposed including the word “clean” in connection with electrification targets.
“It’s very hard to understand, and the only explanation I can think of is their interest in fossil fuels,” Höhne said.
Australia is one of the world’s biggest coal exporters, and Turkey is a major coal consumer, with its power sector still highly dependent on the most climate-damaging fossil fuel. Even as they host this year’s climate conference, neither country has offered any specific plans to transition away from fossil fuels.
Bill Hare, the CEO of Climate Analytics, called out wealthy, developed countries for their lack of leadership on climate action, noting that European Union Commission President Ursula von der Leyen failed to mention anything about transitioning away from fossil fuels during her speech this week at COP31.
“Governments … at this COP have a stark choice,” Hare said. If they continue supporting fossil fuels, “it would consign humanity and our ecosystems to insurmountable economic damage and irretrievable loss.”
About This Story

We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.
That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.
Some 3,778 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported similar threats to one that created chaos on Wednesday - even though no explosive devices have been found.
The government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated". Unlike a day earlier, only 77 schools were evacuated on Thursday, authorities say.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says her government will come up with "sector-specific" advice to help those facing this kind of threat.
Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.
On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.
The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.
Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.
Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".
Some officials say it originated in Taiwan.
A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.
Many parents, though, are concerned and have been demanding clarity and action from the government.
La Repubblica newspaper reports that protests have been held against a decision by the headmaster of a secondary school in Rome who did not take any action, saying she had realised the threatening message to contain typos and therefore be "fake".
According to the newspaper, protesters want new national guidelines to be issued.
