Lieb, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-plans-to-make-it-harder-to-get-grocery-assistance Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration plans to make it harder to get grocery assistance Politics Nov 12, 2026 2:02 PM EST President Donald Trump's administration is planning to make it harder to get food aid through the federal government's big grocery assistance program that serves about 1 in 10 Americans. READ MORE: More than 1.2 million children have lost SNAP benefits since last July. Experts explain why The administration says the proposed rule would close a loophole by no longer allowing some people who receive benefits under the federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program to automatically qualify for the separate Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program too. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News About 6.3 million people could lose eligibility for SNAP by the 2029 fiscal year if the proposed change takes effect, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which administers the program. That is on top of 5.5 million people who already have lost SNAP benefits over the past year. The plan is laid out in a proposed rule published Tuesday on how to run SNAP, and the government is seeking public comment until next month. If it is accepted, the rule would not take full effect for about two years. The proposal addresses the link between 2 federal programs At issue are two separate federal programs. The TANF program provides federal grants to states, which set their own eligibility rules for distributing cash and other benefits to low-income families with children. The incomes of recipients vary by program and state. WATCH: Millions lose SNAP benefits as One Big Beautiful Bill's stricter requirements kick in Federal guidelines generally limit SNAP food benefits to those earning less than 130% of the poverty level, a little over $1,700 monthly for an individual or nearly $3,600 for a family of four. To reduce duplicative paperwork, the federal government allows people who already receive TANF benefits to automatically qualify for SNAP — though they still have to apply. Some states have used that automatic eligibility to expand SNAP benefits to people who might not otherwise qualify. In 2009, President Barack Obama's administration encouraged states to provide people a minimal TANF-funded benefit, such as an informational pamphlet or telephone hotline, as a way of qualifying them for the food program. Forty-one states and the District of Columbia have some form of broad-based categorical eligibility for SNAP, according to a USDA report from last year. Trump's team put forth a similar plan 7 years ago The first Trump administration proposed to clamp down on such tactics in 2019. But that proposal was withdrawn by President Joe Biden's administration in 2021. "Simply put, we did not want to remove millions of people from the program, particularly working poor or children," said Stacy Dean, a former USDA official under Biden who now is executive director of the Global Food Institute at George Washington University. The latest proposal is more sweeping and could prevent states from basing SNAP eligibility on TANF-funded benefits such as job-related counseling or one-time vouchers for vehicle repairs so that people can get to work, said David Super, a law professor at Georgetown University who has studied the food aid program. "The administration here is basically proposing to eliminate the flexibility that Congress gave the states to serve working poor people," Super said. SNAP is also connected to other programs for low-income people Being in a household that receives SNAP benefits also makes school children eligible for free meals. The Agriculture Department says that nearly 1.8 million children would lose eligibility with their family losing SNAP — but that 97% of them would still qualify for free or reduced price school meals through another process. But the government says some of the children would not get the lunches, even if they are eligible, if their families don't apply. The proposal comes at a time when the number of people receiving the aid has fallen sharply — and on the heels of sweeping election gains for Democrats across the country. "The public indicated they want their elected officials to focus on making life affordable," the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning policy research institute, said in an analysis of the proposal. "Yet the Trump Administration is doubling down on making it harder for people to feed their families." It has been a period of flux for the food aid program As of July, the Department of Agriculture, which runs SNAP, said 36 million people were receiving the aid. That was down by 13% from a year earlier. Over that time, another federal requirement expanded a work requirement to more enrollees, including those ages 55 to 64 and to parents whose youngest children are at least 14. Trump's big 2025 tax and policy law that broadened the work requirement also requires states to start shouldering about three-fourths of the cost of running it, up from half. And they will also have to pay some of the costs of the benefits if their error rates exceed certain thresholds. Congressional Democrats are pushing for a delay in implementation of that change. The newly proposed rule from the Trump administration "is just one of many things right now that states are grappling with that would reduce access to SNAP," said Carolyn Vega, director of policy analysis for the advocacy group Share Our Strength. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities is concerned that the eligibility change may result in higher error rates for states — making them have to pay for more of the cost of

Over the loud noise of her radio, Ann Marie did not hear the sound of the Brooklyn building behind her home collapse on Thursday night, but she soon saw the flashing lights of fire department trucks rushing to the scene.
When she made her way out to the wreckage, workers were still searching for bodies. One of the building's walls had torn off, exposing the inside of several apartment homes, and the rubble had collapsed into a construction site next door.
At least eight of her neighbours died in the accident - six adults and two children, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.
"Right now, I'm really scared," Marie told the BBC. "Now that I'm seeing exactly this side of the building, you can imagine the fright of those people, what happened to them."
On Thursday afternoon, Mamdani said he had visited survivors in hospital. Eighteen people were injured, including four firefighters. One person is in critical condition.
"I want to take a moment to remember those we have so senselessly lost," Mamdani added. "These were our friends and our neighbours, parents and children, young families building their lives in our city, immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Trinidad and beyond."
It was around 16:00 EST (21:00 GMT) on Wednesday when residents heard a loud boom as the 1930s building collapsed into a neighbouring construction site, where crews were working, according to fire department officials. Two construction workers were among the dead.
The New York City Fire Department was on the scene within one minute of the emergency call, Mamdani said.
Patricia Starek was waiting for her son to come home from school last night when she saw the helicopters near her home. The surge of the emergency responders initially brought back memories of New York during 2001 terrorist attacks. She has lived in Flatbush for 26 years, including during 9/11.
"How does a building just fall into a pit? We all live here with the assumption that stairs are stable, floors are stable, that you can be on your third floor and not have the earth fall below you," she said.
Mamdani said search conditions would grow more difficult with the rain on Thursday, but responders will continue their efforts. Workers have been looking through the wreckage with drones, sniffer dogs, cranes and other equipment.
Officials said they would continue to search the wreckage until they were entirely certain there was no one left trapped, saying they still had big pieces of debris to remove.
The mayor pledged a "comprehensive and thorough" investigation into the construction site and the building. He said city officials had identified the companies running the construction site, and were examining 100 other sites operated by the same groups to ensure they are safe.
Dozens of residents gathered around the building on Thursday morning as debris floated through the air, and they watched in horror as workers tried to find more survivors or recover remains.
The incident has rattled their calm and quiet neighbourhood, a melting pot of many New York immigrant communities including Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic and Asian residents.
Joyette Kerr had been at the scene since midnight, praying with family members who were missing loved ones.
At 1:30 EST (6:30 GMT), Kerr watched emergency responders pull a survivor from the wreckage.
At the church across the street, she consoled the wife of a young construction worker who died when the building fell on him. Rescuers recovered his body, Kerr said.
"His wife was very hysterical," said Kerr, who has lived in the neighbourhood since she was a teenager. "She couldn't take the pain."
She said another man had been frantically going to all the nearby hospitals to try to find his two nephews, but still had no answers.
Footage showed another woman who was six-months pregnant being rescued from the rubble.
"She is alive. She is still alive. I'm very happy. I'm very happy," her husband told the BBC's US partner CBS News. "I thank all of you guys."
Starek, the longtime Flatbush resident, said she was heading to the local YMCA where some family members were gathered to see if she could help - and many others in the neighbourhood were doing the same.
"People look out for each other," Marie said. To lose eight of her neighbours, she said: "I can't believe it. There's a pain."
Kerr said she hoped her hours with the victims' families brought them some measure of comfort after one of the deadliest building collapses in recent New York history.
"It's going to be very profound," she said of the impact the accident will have. "Hopefully this will bring the community together."

33c416988943.text: By — Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/hegseth-presents-award-to-soldier-who-scolded-him-and-his-aides-at-tomb-of-the-unknown-soldier Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Hegseth presents award to soldier who scolded him and his aides at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier World Nov 12, 2026 1:35 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has given a top award to the service member who scolded him and his staff at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery. Watch the video from Wednesday when Spc. Thomas Iglesias reprimanded Hegseth and a group of his staffers in tne video player above. On social media Thursday, Hegseth posted photos that show him pinning the award and shaking hands with a soldier. His post says, "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist." WATCH: Trump marks Veterans Day with wreath laying, remarks at Arlington National Cemetery Hegseth welcomed to the Pentagon the Army unit that guards the tomb and awarded Spc. Thomas Iglesias with the Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026," the Pentagon said. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Iglesias reprimanded Hegseth and a group of his staffers when a loud laugh was heard after they took photos at the site following a ceremony that included President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. Video showed Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb on Wednesday with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh. READ MORE: House approves bill to boost compensation for many veterans, with some floor drama The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from World War I, World War II and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock — rain or shine — by a soldier from the Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," since 1948. The Joint Service Commendation Medal is considered to be one of the higher awards in the military and is not typically issued to junior enlisted service members. Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesman, said soon after video of the reprimand emerged that the soldier "correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum." The scolding drew attention once more to the embattled defense secretary, who had survived an impeachment attempt the day before. The effort was led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats. While Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed a bid to impeach him. With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed. Hegseth rebuked the move Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal and framing the effort as an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes. "This is not patriotism," Hegseth argued. "This is sabotage." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. a3ce5ef3f17a.text: By — Kevin Freking, Associated Press Kevin Freking, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/house-approves-bill-to-boost-compensation-for-many-veterans-with-some-floor-drama Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter House approves bill to boost compensation for many veterans, with some floor drama Politics Nov 12, 2026 1:28 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The House passed a major package of veterans bills Wednesday on Veterans Day — but not without confusion and controversy. Watch the House floor from Wednesday in the video player above. The centerpiece of the package is an effort to boost compensation for an estimated 58,000 veterans who are medically retired because of combat-related injuries. That objective has broad, bipartisan support in Congress, but lawmakers and veterans groups aren't on the same page about how to get there. WATCH: Trump marks Veterans Day with wreath laying, remarks at Arlington National Cemetery The dilemma lawmakers are trying to resolve is this: Under current law, combat-injured retirees with less than 20 years of service give up a portion of their military retirement pay when they also receive Department of Veterans Affairs disability compensation. Lawmakers from both parties are trying to change that so that those retirees get all of their injury compensation and military retirement pay. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The change would lead to an average compensation boost of about $1,450 more per month, according to the Congressional Budget Office. Republicans brought to the floor a bill that would help pay for the income boost for those retirees by changing how the department rates tinnitus or sleep apnea. Those changes would lower disability compensation for some future veterans, though they would not affect current veterans receiving compensation for those conditions. Democrats overwhelmingly opposed that trade-off and denounced the measure as the bill was debated. READ MORE: Trump says the towering arch he wants to be build might be dedicated to military veterans "It does not take care of veterans. It takes from them," Rep. Raul Ruiz, D-Calif., said of the Republican bill. Republicans had to pull the bill from consideration earlier this year because they didn't have the votes to pass it. This time, Democratic leaders again encouraged their members to oppose the measure because they said cutting benefits for one group of veterans to fund new benefits for another is not the answer. The House chamber was packed and noisy as lawmakers talked among themselves following an earlier vote. As is the normal course of business, the House clerk read the title of the veterans bill and then the presiding officer, Rep. Addison McDowell, R-N.C., said the question for the House was on passage of the bill and that those in favor should say aye and those opposed should say no. "The ayes have it," McDowell said. "The bill is passed." Normally, Democrats would interject and ask for a roll call vote. But none came. And Republicans simply put the onus on Democrats, with Rep. Mike Bost, chairman of the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs, calling Democrats "asleep at the wheel." "If nobody calls for the vote, it's passed, which is a good thing," said House Majority Leader Steve Scalise. "If a few of them want to go voice their objections, they can go and make it clear on the House floor why they are against our veterans on Veterans Day. But I was proud to support it," Scalise said. "I'm glad it passed." Rep. Mark Takano, the ranking Democratic member of the Veterans' Affairs Committee, said there was no opportunity for the minority to ask for a recorded vote. "The intention was to sneak this through," Takano said. "Well, all I can say is, I think it's a shallow, a hollow victory because it will go nowhere in the Senate." Cory Geisler, the national commander-in-chief at the Veterans of Foreign Wars, blasted the voice vote in a statement. "If congressional leaders believed this proposal was worthy of passage, they should have had the courage to let every member's position be recorded for the country to see," Geisler said. "Playing political games with veterans' benefits while avoiding public accountability is cowardly and dishonorable." Democrats have their own bill dealing with the issue that is expected to be voted on Thursday. Supporters used a discharge petition to get around Republican leadership and force a vote on the floor. But the Democratic measure does not include offsets. Takano said that while some Republicans have voiced concerns about the price tag of his bill they also have no problem sending soldiers to war and approving the Pentagon budgets that come with it, or in passing tax breaks that primarily benefit the wealthy. "Why then do they insist on balancing the budget on the backs of our veterans?" Takano said. If the Democratic-led bill passes, the Senate could pick the one it favors, or neither, leaving it for a Democratic-controlled Congress to take the issue on next year. Six adults and two children have died after a three-storey building collapsed in New York, the city's mayor Zohran Mamdani has said.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission this week issued permits for construction of four next-generation nuclear reactors at a petrochemical complex on the rural Gulf Coast of Texas.
The Long Mott Generating Station, developed by chemical giant Dow and nuclear startup X-energy, is one of two flagship projects selected by the U.S. Energy Department in 2020 for its Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program, intended to kickstart a new era of growth for the nation’s nascent nuclear sector.
“This milestone marks a significant step forward,” Mike Goff, principal deputy assistant secretary for nuclear energy, said in a press release Monday. “The NRC’s approval demonstrates meaningful progress toward deploying advanced reactors.”
The Texas project is at the leading edge of a new generation of reactor designs that could revolutionize the commercial model for atomic energy. They replace the gargantuan construction projects currently required for nuclear power plants with small, modular units that can be produced in factories and then shipped and assembled onsite at industrial installations, from data centers to petrochemical plants.
“We understand that owning a nuclear facility is a different kind of responsibility,” said Kreshka Young, North American business director for energy and climate at Dow, during a public meeting on the project’s construction permits in the town of Port Lavaca in September. “We do not take that lightly.”
Dow plans to install four 80-megawatt reactors by X-energy at its Seadrift Operations complex, on the Gulf Coast between Houston and Corpus Christi. The units won’t require the towering, concrete containment structures characteristic of existing nuclear reactors, nor the 10-mile emergency planning zone, thanks to what scientists describe as revolutionary safety features inherent in new reactor designs.
X-energy CEO J. Clay Sell, a former deputy energy secretary, has described the company’s Xe-100 unit as “physically impossible to melt down.”
Diane Wilson, a retired fourth-generation shrimper from the tiny nearby town of Seadrift and director of San Antonio Bay Waterkeeper, a local environmental organization, remains deeply skeptical. “Frankly, it’s outrageous,” she said. “This is outrageous.”
Spent fuel from the reactors will be stored indefinitely on-site as nuclear waste, she noted, as the U.S. still lacks a permanent national disposal site.
In 2025, Wilson’s organization filed legal challenges to the project’s permit application over safety concerns, which were ultimately dismissed by the NRC. The agency approved Dow’s reactor construction permit after an expedited review under executive orders from President Donald Trump aimed at accelerating the national energy sector.
“We delivered on the 18-month schedule, proving we can do rigorous safety reviews on predictable timelines that move advanced nuclear technology from design to construction,” said NRC Chairman Ho K. Nieh in a press release.
Dow still needs to make a final decision to proceed with the project, the company said in a release. If it does, construction could begin before 2030.
If the project proves successful, it would “provide a pathway other industries can emulate” to install dedicated, onsite power generation, said Martin O’Neal, general counsel for the Nuclear Energy Institute, at the September meeting in Port Lavaca.

Donate Now
The NRC hosted the meeting to take questions and comments from the public on the Long Mott Generating Station.
“The nuclear industry is watching this project very closely,” O’Neal said.
In the last three decades, the U.S. has built just one new nuclear power plant, but federal authorities have pushed in recent years for an industry revival based on new reactor designs. The NRC issued its first permit for construction of an advanced test reactor in 2023, and its first permit for an advanced commercial reactor in March 2026.
While typical nuclear reactors use water to cool, advanced designs use alternatives, from molten salt to gas. The Xe-100 uses helium gas. Rather than traditional fuel rods, the Xe-100 uses a pelletized fuel form in a moving bed of pebbles.
“These are new technologies,” said Mehdi Reisi Fard, deputy director of advanced reactors at the NRC, during the public meeting in Port Lavaca in September.
The innovations add up to a feature known as “functional containment,” where the natural resilience and circulation of fuel pebbles prevents the kind of runaway warming that could lead the reactor to meltdown.
Compared with current control systems, functional containment is “less reliant on pumps or human intervention to mitigate anomalies,” Fard explained.
It works thanks to a new kind of pelletized nuclear fuel, called TRISO fuel, which has been developed in Energy Department labs over decades.
“Simply put, TRISO particles cannot melt in a commercial high-temperature reactor,” a DOE webpage says.
The new technology enables developers to skip the big, expensive safety features, like the massive concrete casings, that are required for traditional water-cooled reactors.
“The argument these developers are using is that they don’t need a physical containment because the reactor is so safe,” said Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety with the Union of Concerned Scientists, in an interview earlier this year. “Nuclear designers have been trying to reduce the costs of containment, and one way to do that would be to eliminate it entirely.”
But Lymann doesn’t consider the fuel to be as safe as authorities say.
“It’s just a myth that this fuel is indestructible or meltdown-proof,” he said. “This fuel has vulnerabilities.”

Major economies representing 58% of the worldâs GDP have adopted at least one measure to restrict the import of clean energy technologies, many targeting Chinese goods, according to data published by the Oxford Climate Policy Monitor. In contrast, a large number of small economies outside China, accounting for about 8% of world GDP, are liberalising imports of EVs, batteries, along with wind and solar equipment, creating a de facto free trade area for clean tech.
Analysis by the Blavatnik School of Government at the University of Oxford found that restrictions are making the transition slower and more expensive, but they may also be needed to balance effective climate policy with industrial development and economic security. âOpenness and protection can be combined, rather than traded off wholesale,â it said. Large economies could pursue more selective trade restrictions instead of trying to build entirely self-sufficient industries, while smaller countries could specialise in particular stages of manufacturing. âOur findings show that many countries have begun to implement this strategy,â said Claas Mertens, the briefâs co-author.

a48b2b70b55b.text: By — Harriet Morris, Associated Press Harriet Morris, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/u-s-envoys-meet-with-putin-in-moscow-on-ukraine-talks-then-head-for-dublin-to-see-zelenskyy Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then head for Dublin to see Zelenskyy World Nov 12, 2026 12:22 PM EST MOSCOW (AP) — U.S. envoys met Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin and then left for Ireland to talk with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as Washington sought new momentum in its peace efforts. Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump's son-in-law, brokered talks this week between delegations from Moscow and Kyiv. The meeting in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, brought the first direct discussions between Ukrainian and Russian representatives in nine months as the push for a settlement stalled. READ MORE: Russia and Ukraine agree to a large prisoner exchange as talks end with no major breakthrough The two days of talks that ended Wednesday produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Kushner and Witkoff met with Putin in a meeting that lasted about two hours. They then headed for Dublin for talks with Zelenskyy as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark. Europe seeks a place at the negotiating table Kushner said one of the goals of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader's blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent's broader security arrangements. The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow. READ MORE: Russia and Ukraine hold nearly 4 hours of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi Russia, meanwhile, doesn't want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine's military effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent. But Washington and European capitals have sometimes seemed at odds in their diplomatic efforts. Trump has repeatedly sided with Putin, last month waiving sanctions and striking a deal to import Russian diesel, in moves that dismayed Ukraine and European leaders. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov argued that for Europe to join peace talks, it first must name a representative. "The Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar. If someone takes the initiative to establish contact with the Russian side, such people are facing ostracism." Many in Europe also see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO's eastward expansion as a main security threat to Russia. Putin has demanded the trans-Atlantic alliance's troops be pulled back from Russia's borders. READ MORE: The Kremlin hopes the U.S. election shake-up won't shift Trump's negotiations on Ukraine Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO's strategy in return for peace in Ukraine — a possibility that alarms European leaders. The Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi "agreed on many of the principles, but are still apart on some of the ways to accomplish" peace, Kushner said in Moscow. Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys that any European troops sent to Ukraine after a ceasefire would be "absolutely unacceptable" and Russia would regard the deployment as a security threat and legitimate targets. "In other words, the war would resume immediately," he said. He also said Russia regards its border with Ukraine to be sealed by a prospective peace deal as now extending to cover the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully controlled. Zelenskyy sees a political 'window of opportunity' Zelenskyy is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte. Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are "very much aligned" on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January. "But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire," Rutte said. Zelenskyy said political changes, including Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following midterm elections and balloting in France next year, could bring "a window of opportunity" for a peace deal. "The political landscape in Europe could change in 2027. … We also see changes already taking place in the United States," Zelenskyy said in Dublin late Wednesday. He called the proposed prisoner exchange a positive step but also insisted Ukraine won't surrender Russian-occupied territory in return for peace. Russia and Ukraine have occasionally swapped prisoners, but both sides remain far apart in their terms for accepting a settlement. Fighting continues as another bitter winter approaches Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line. Russia's bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow's drone and missile strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies to Ukrainian cities, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a "weaponization of winter." Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. Its forces struck a drone-manufacturing plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said. Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered drones, at Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian air force said. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, it said. One person has been killed and four others injured after a gunman opened fire in Washington DC.
The shooting began on Thursday morning local time inside a gym in an apartment building in the Logan Circle neighbourhood, which is about a mile (1.6km) north of the White House.
Police said the male suspect was "contained" after barricading himself in one of the apartments. They later confirmed he had died.
Of those injured, one is in a critical condition and the others have non-life-threatening injuries.
While the suspect was barricaded, "he did fire through the door at officers at least on two occasions", Jefferey Carroll, the interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department, said at a news conference.
Negotiators had been on the phone with the suspect when they heard a gunshot and he stopped communicating with them, according to Carroll.
Officers forced their way into the apartment and saw the suspect had what appeared to be a "self-inflicted gunshot wound", he said.
Carroll added that police "believe there was a fire that was set", which has been contained.
Authorities are still working to understand the exact timeline, suspect's motivation, and other details of the incident.
"We believe there was some sort of a conflict with the apartment building, but we don't have much more than that," Carroll said.
Washington DC Mayor Muriel Bowser called it a "senseless act of gun violence" and said the White House had been briefed.
A BBC producer who lives in the building where the shooting happened, Jonathan Csapo, said a fire alarm went off. Then, as he came out of a fire escape, he heard gunshots very close by.
"I could see the smoke, I could see the flash. We just all started running. That was our first instinct," he said.
"We immediately ran and took cover behind a barricade, a little brick structure just near the building."
Csapo said he was then taken back inside, to a safe room, by a building manager.
"And then everybody started screaming," he said.
Michael Carney told the Washington Sun he was on a treadmill at the Vida Fitness gym when the shooting started.
He says he heard "one pop" which he assumed was an exercise ball bursting before seeing a victim on the floor who had been shot.
"Everyone was kind of just hiding behind planters and stuff," he said, adding a fire alarm was pulled.
Once outside of the gym, Carney says he heard five or 10 shots that seemed to be coming from a nearby alley.
Another witness told the Washington Sun that she heard "an enormous, loud thing" in the fitness centre and more shots outside the gym after being evacuated.
"I thought something had crashed or fallen," she said. "I didn't know it was a gunshot until later."
Were you in Washington DC this morning, or do you live nearby? Share your story.

Jensen Huang, known for sporting a black leather jacket to shareholder events, appeared to have it all. He was courted by leaders in the US and China alike, worshipped by investors and seen as a loyal family man. But a rockstar approach to his personal life has ultimately led to his resignation.
The 63-year-old has been married since 1985, long before the foundation of Nvidia, the company that propelled him to tech stardom.
He is known as a workaholic and a demanding manager, with high standards for those who worked for him, which included his own children, promoted within the company. But he has seen his personal reputation go into freefall this week, undone by romantic entanglements that throw doubt on his focus and his judgement.
On Thursday, he resigned following back-to-back revelations of two affairs. News of the first - a relationship with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy - ricocheted around the world, raising eyebrows among investors. It was followed on Wednesday by reports that the tech boss had also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague.
His departure creates uncertainty in the global stock market, which was already knocked-off balance in recent weeks. Nvidia is a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China.
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.
But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.
The company, which is still valued at nearly $4n (Â£3.02tn) despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.
His remarkable rise to the top of his profession has led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" and seen him amass an estimated fortune of $145bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.
The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.
Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.
So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.
"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".
But while the former Nvidia CEO is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said.
Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him".
"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," Witt added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."
First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.
After the revelations of the first affair, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.
Trump, as well as other leaders in the AI tech industry, initially backed Huang to continue in his role at Nvidia. The president described him as "honourable".
But the reporting of a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare who has worked at Nvidia for 18 years, prompted a board meeting, followed by the announcement Huang was stepping down.
In the aftermath of that news Trump said Huang had done "a fantastic job" and proposed Tim Cook of Apple as a suitable replacement at the head of Nvidia.

266e9a0c5a63.text: The Ukrainian government has asked the Pentagon and SpaceX to explain new restrictions it says are disrupting the satellite system its military uses to intercept Russian drones. Why it matters: This is the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine reported that Starshield, made by Elon Musk's SpaceX, was impeded. The Ukrainian military uses Starshield — the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system — to control and operate its reconnaissance and to intercept drones. The other side: SpaceX respond Axios: "This is false. There has been no change." Driving the news: Ukrainian President Zelensky said Thursday he was briefed by the minister of defense and the commander of the Ukrainian military that "units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations" along the entire front line and in the parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia. "The Ukrainian military have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions," he wrote on X. "We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side." Zoom in: A Ukrainian official said the restrictions have been happening for three days. "On the first day there were 10% limitations, on the second day 50%, and today 100% of the missions fail because of restrictions," the official said. Ukraine's charge d'affaires to the U.S., Denys Sienik, said the Starshield system shuts down when drones fly at more than 100 miles per hour. "We don't have clarification from SpaceX or Pentagon at the moment," he said. State of play: Zelensky said the new restrictions began shortly before President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met at the Kremlin with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday. Kushner and Witkoff are expected to meet Zelensky later on Thursday in Dublin. What they're saying: The bipartisan Congressional Ukraine Caucus said in a statement that it was "extremely alarmed" by the reports of a Starshield slowdown and "demanding a full accounting" from the Trump administration and SpaceX. Catch up quick: Ukraine relies on two SpaceX satellite services. Starlink, the commercial service, supports battlefield communications and logistics. Starshield is designed for government and military customers. Ukraine accesses it through a U.S. government agreement and uses it to operate reconnaissance drones and intercept Russian attack drones. The Defense Department and SpaceX did not immediately return requests for comment.

7c0e45bd90c5.text: A gunman killed one person and injured four others in Logan Circle on Thursday morning before fatally shooting himself, police say, prompting a massive law enforcement response in one of D.C.'s busiest neighborhoods. The latest: The suspected gunman died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound while barricaded in his apartment, said D.C. interim police chief Jeffery Carroll . Residents were told to shelter in place until around 11:35am, but police are still urging people to avoid the area while the investigation continues. The big picture: A gunman fatally shot one person inside VIDA Fitness, a popular neighborhood gym at 15th and P streets NW, police said at a Thursday morning press conference. Four others were injured, including one seriously, police say. Police said some victims were injured at a construction site across the street, but their exact locations remain under investigation. Zoom in: MPD announced around 11:10am that the barricade concluded and the scene was safe. Earlier, police said officers reported hearing a gunshot during negotiations with the suspect, and had not heard communication since. Mayor Bowser said the lone gunman had been "contained." People stand behind police tape in Logan Circle early Thursday. Photo: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Zoom out: The massive law enforcement response blocked off nearby streets and the neighborhood Whole Foods. Nearly a dozen DC Public Schools in the vicinity, from Columbia Heights to Adams Morgan, went into lockdown . DCPS tells Axios the schools have resumed normal operations after police gave the all-clear around 11:15am. Police helicopters circled overhead throughout the morning, rattling windows in surrounding neighborhoods. U.S. Park Police and other federal authorities could be seen speeding down 18th Street and other major thoroughfares in response. A U.S. Park Police helicopter flies above the scene. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images U.S. Marshal officers move position at the scene of the Logan Circle shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Residents cross a street as law enforcement responds to the shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images What's next: Police say 14th Street traffic has now reopened. This is a developing story. Check back for details.

b6f66424a8c4.text: Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Inflation is no longer confined to a handful of trouble spots. Now, Federal Reserve officials are starting to question whether raising interest rates gradually will be enough to contain it. Why it matters: Fed officials had hoped that a relatively modest series of interest rate hikes would be enough to bring inflation under control — more a recalibration than a tightening campaign. But stubbornly high — and increasingly widespread — price pressures are raising the possibility of a more prolonged tightening campaign, with no clear endpoint in sight. That would leave the Fed facing a more difficult balancing act: raising rates enough to contain inflation without unnecessarily damaging the economy. What they're saying: "We have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing — and we're going to have to deal with that," Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee, who called the inflation data "borderline disturbing," said late Tuesday . Driving the news: Treasury yields are surging after Tuesday's hot inflation report and hawkish commentary from Fed officials — including governor Christopher Waller, who raised the prospect of a supersized rate hike next month. Short-term yields have risen more sharply than longer-term yields, a sign that investors expect the Fed may need to raise rates more aggressively than previously anticipated. The yield on the two-year Treasury note is still marching higher after surging 17 basis points on Tuesday, which was the biggest one-day surge since April 2025 — when markets were reeling from the "liberation day" tariffs. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note jumped about 8 basis points, putting it back above 5%. Financial markets see a December rate hike as virtually certain, according to CME FedWatch. Expectations for next year are trending higher, with traders now pricing in two additional quarter-point hikes by June. The big picture: Measures designed to strip out unusually large price swings suggest that underlying inflation pressures are gaining pace. The Cleveland Fed's trimmed-mean Consumer Price Index —which filters out unusually large price swings to give a clearer picture of underlying inflation — rose 0.4% in October, the largest monthly increase since May. The Atlanta Fed's sticky-price CPI , which tracks prices that typically change, slowly accelerated to a 4.7% annualized pace in October, its fastest since February 2025. More than three-quarters of the consumer price basket saw prices rise at an annualized rate exceeding 2% in October, the largest share since August 2022, Charles Schwab's head of macro research Kevin Gordon posted on X . Yes, but: The Fed may have reason to proceed cautiously even against the backdrop of stubborn inflation. Rising bond yields and a sell-off in technology stocks (revived again by the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ) are already tightening financial conditions — potentially doing some of the work of higher interest rates. Fed governor Michelle Bowman said in a speech that falling stock prices, higher borrowing costs and a stronger dollar could weigh on economic growth, particularly in sectors already struggling with high interest rates. Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who dissented against the decision to hold rates steady last month, said she still supported a more gradual approach to raising rates. "It's less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements," she said Thursday morning . What to watch: Some of the forces driving inflation higher this year — including tariffs and the Iran war — were expected to be temporary. But the risk that they will prove more persistent keeps resurfacing. President Trump threatened on Thursday morning to double tariffs on Mexican imports unless the nation stops a caravan of migrants from reaching the U.S. border. Trump also said the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran , raising fresh questions about how soon the conflict (and the disruption to global energy supplies) might end.

8f9a0b337d05.text: By — Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press By — Jennifer Peltz, Associated Press Jennifer Peltz, Associated Press By — Kathy McCormack, Associated Press Kathy McCormack, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/brooklyn-building-collapse-death-toll-rises-to-8-as-rescuers-search-for-survivors Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Brooklyn building collapse killed 2 children and 6 adults, mayor says Nation Updated on Nov 12, 2026 12:49 PM EST — Published on Nov 12, 2026 11:34 AM EST NEW YORK (AP) — A pair of excavators scooped up rubble Thursday where a three-story apartment building in Brooklyn collapsed at the edge of a construction site, killing at least eight people, New York City's mayor said. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani held a news conference Thursday about the building collapse and rescue efforts. Watch in the video player above. Two of the people killed were children, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said during a news conference Thursday. READ MORE: Suspected gunman shoots 5 people in D.C., killing 1, before dying by suicide Emergency workers spent the early morning peering into crevices and sifting through debris during a desperate search for survivors. At least 18 people were injured, including four firefighters, Mamdani said. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The building gave way Wednesday afternoon while construction workers were digging at a neighboring lot, a city official said. The cause was still under investigation. Speaking as torrential rain drenched the area, Mamdani said the weather would hinder but not stop the search. "Conditions will get more challenging today with the rain, but operations will continue," he said. New York Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said crews were still searching for survivors Thursday afternoon. "We have not shifted from rescue to recovery," Bonsignore said. "We are still in the search and rescue phase." "We always assume there are more people there until we can access the ground," Bonsignore said. ""So until we remove some of the bigger debris and are able to search beneath them, this will remain a rescue operation" Witnesses describe the immediate aftermath and destruction James Williams, who works at a deli across the street, said he heard loud banging at the site all day Wednesday and looked outside to see bricks falling from one of the buildings. "Two minutes later, the building collapsed," he said. As the building crumbled and exposed the neighboring building, Williams spotted a woman on a staircase. "There wasn't anything I could do," he said, his voice cracking. Customers and stylists at a nearby hair salon jumped up and ran onto the sidewalk as the building fell. "We heard the boom and we all rushed outside and saw smoke and dust everywhere," said hairstylist Brigitte Anama. She saw emergency workers pulling people from the rubble, including what appeared to be a child. "People were saying, 'Pray for the baby, pray for the baby,'" Anama said. Authorities said late Wednesday that at least seven children were among the injured or dead. "There are no words for a loss of this magnitude," Mamdani posted on X. "My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we have lost, those who are injured and everyone grieving today." This was the second high-profile structural problem with a building in New York in the past five months. In July, several buildings in Manhattan were evacuated after support columns buckled inside a skyscraper that was formerly the headquarters of Pfizer. Rescuers with dogs searched through the night Flatbush Avenue, a busy thoroughfare in Brooklyn, remained at a standstill Thursday morning as firefighters picked through the rubble. Hundreds of firefighters and police officers wielding pickaxes and power saws worked through the night, clambering over the rubble, punching holes in the ruins to pull out dust-covered survivors. Rescue dogs sniffed piles of twisted wood and brick that were dotted with brightly colored clothing and vinyl record albums. Two excavators removed large chunks of debris. Firefighters filled buckets with debris, passing them down a line. Heavy rain was forecast for Thursday afternoon, and Fire Department Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore cautioned that could hinder search-and-rescue operations. "It'll turn to mud," she told WNYW-TV, vowing firefighters would work through the rain if necessary. Building records showed there were four apartments on the upper two floors and a commercial unit on the ground floor of the collapsed building. Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with shoes and clothing. On Wednesday night, firefighters pulled a pregnant woman from the rubble, hoisted her up on a stretcher and rushed her to a waiting ambulance. Other survivors were rescued as the night wore on. Bonsignore said the rescue teams were performing "dangerous and perilous" work. "Every move is choreographed," she said. Man identifies his brother as one of those killed Jose Luis Caguana, 26, who was working at the construction site, died in the collapse, his brother told WNBC-TV. He was an immigrant from Ecuador who had been in the U.S. for about six years, Carlos Caguana said. He had a pregnant wife and a young child. "Her husband has passed away; he was the sole provider for the family. Now that he's gone, she is going through an immense amount of pain. She is in a very bad state right now — she's completely overwhelmed and can't even find the words to speak," Caguana said. The surrounding blocks are tightly packed with mostly older brick buildings and a few newly built apartment complexes. fcd926d4f419.text: By — River Zhang, Associated Press River Zhang, Associated Press By — Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/suspected-gunman-shoots-5-people-in-d-c-killing-1-before-dying-by-suicide Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Suspected gunman shoots 5 people in D.C., killing 1, before dying by suicide Nation Nov 12, 2026 11:26 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Five people were shot, one fatally, on Thursday in a Washington, D.C., neighborhood within walking distance of the White House, police said, and the suspected gunman later shot and killed himself as a swarm of officers responded to a nearby apartment building where he was barricaded. One victim died in the initial shooting, said Jeffery Carroll, interim chief with the Metropolitan Police Department. Carroll said the suspect then shot himself while barricaded inside an apartment. He added that the man apparently had a dispute with the building's homeowners association. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The suspect's death was confirmed by a law enforcement official, who was not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing investigation into what happened and spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity. The shootings were reported in Logan Circle, about a mile north of the White House. Much of the block on 15th Street was cordoned off as police urged people to avoid the area, which includes a VIDA fitness center, St. Luke's Episcopal Church, residences and a Whole Foods supermarket. Schools were on lockdown. Law enforcement SWAT teams and other officers had their guns drawn on the roof of an apartment building or on the ground below. Authorities believe the suspect shot at least one person inside the gym before going outside and firing again, according to another law enforcement official who was not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke to the AP on the condition of anonymity. Law enforcement agents believe the suspect shot another person in a parking garage elevator before barricading himself on the seventh floor of the building, the official said. Witness James Spellman, who was at the gym, said there were about 50 people there around 8 a.m. when the shooting began. "Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out," he said. "One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck." Spellman said he and others dashed out of the gym. He said he heard about two shots fired in the gym and about five or six fired outside. Another witness, Ryan Dubicki, said he was in his nearby apartment around the same time when he "heard about five bangs." "They were really spread out so I thought it was construction," he said. A short time later "there were cops everywhere." The federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives said it sent agents to the scene to help. And the FBI said its Washington field office was helping local police with the investigation. The neighborhood has seen violence before. In early August 2025, a onetime member of President Donald Trump's Department of Government Efficiency was assaulted early on a Sunday morning in the Logan Circle neighborhood by a group of teenagers attempting to carjack him and a woman, authorities said. Days later, Trump fulfilled his threat to bypass local authority and imposed direct federal control over the city, sending in hundreds of National Guard members to reduce crime. That deployment continues today. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 1344499a8b30.text: By — Stan Choe, Associated Press Stan Choe, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/sharp-swings-for-nvidia-and-oil-prices-weigh-on-wall-street Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Sharp swings for Nvidia and oil prices weigh on Wall Street Economy Nov 12, 2026 11:05 AM EST NEW YORK (AP) — Big swings for Nvidia's stock price and oil prices are weighing on Wall Street Thursday, but the U.S. market appears to be absorbing them. After falling nearly 1% at the start of trading, the S&P 500 quickly pared its drop to 0.4%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 50 points, or 0.1%, as of 10:15 a.m. Eastern time, while the Nasdaq composite was down 0.6% after trimming its early loss of 1.6%. READ MORE: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after his affair raises national security concerns At the center of the action was Nvidia's stock. It plunged as much as 14% at the start of trading following the resignation of Jensen Huang, its CEO, co-founder and face of the brand. The chip company's stock has been sinking since its board announced an investigation into Huang for a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese government agent. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News It's a stunning fall for Huang and for Nvidia, which had become Wall Street's most valuable and influential stock because of its central role in the artificial-intelligence boom. Its stock price set a record last month after soaring an astounding 1,722% in four years. That compares with the already healthy gain of nearly 109% for the overall S&P 500 over the same time. But Nvidia's price dropped 27% from then through Wednesday on worries about whether Huang would remain and how Nvidia would navigate a future without him. Nvidia's board answered the first question Thursday morning, when it said Huang resigned, and it named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as its interim CEO. READ MORE: How the Nvidia revelations could ripple through the AI industry and global economy The second question remains to be determined. And it looms over the entire market because Nvidia and the broader AI industry have been the main reasons the U.S. stock market has set so many records in recent years. Nvidia, to be sure, is still selling AI chips at a quick rate regardless of who stands on a stage and talks them up. Nvidia quickly halved its early loss from Thursday, and its stock was most recently down 6.1%. Outside of Nvidia, other stocks across the AI industry swung in the uncertainty. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, fell 9%. Micron Technology, which sells memory for computers that's been getting gobbled up in the AI frenzy, sank 4.9%. But Broadcom rose 5.3%, and Advanced Micro Devices added 1.8% on hopes for a competitive advantage. The rival chip companies to Nvidia were two of the strongest forces limiting the S&P 500's losses. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centers, flipped from a loss of 3% to a gain of 1%. Also swinging on Thursday were oil prices after President Donald Trump said he's no longer interested in a deal with Iran to end their war. Instead of that, Trump said he asked his vice president to focus on investigating U.S. cities and states run by Democrats. "We don't need a deal with Iran," Trump said on his social-media platform. "Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil suddenly went from about $92 to more than $94 following Trump's posting, before it later eased back. It was most recently at $93.79, up 1.1%. It's been veering sharply since the United States and Israel began the war with Iran in late February, bouncing between roughly $70 and $150. Higher oil prices push up worries about inflation, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 5.07% from 4.98% late Tuesday. Trading in the bond market had been closed Wednesday for Veterans Day. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following a weaker finish in Asia. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 1.3% for one of the world's biggest moves. AP Business Writer Yuri Kageyama contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Stan Choe, Associated Press Stan Choe, Associated Press

8e758e03e330.text: The White House is standing by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick despite a view within the administration that Lutnick delayed action to address concerns over chip smuggling to China. Why it matters: Congress smells blood in the water following bombshell reports that U.S. national security may have been jeopardized by former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Lawmakers want to know what the Trump administration did or did not do in response to that intelligence — and Lutnick, the official in charge of the department at the center of export control policy, is squarely in their field of view. President Trump, however, is not distancing himself from the secretary. "Secretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trump's America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments," a White House official tells Axios. "President Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history." Catch up quick: Lutnick was sent intelligence about Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and repeatedly did not take export control action — despite pressure from the broader administration and the president himself, Axios first reported. Lutnick's role is prompting scrutiny on the Hill from members on both sides of the aisle. "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military," Senate Banking Committee Chair Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a statement. "The obvious question is why did he choose to sell advanced chips?," Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told Politico. "Secretary Lutnick needs to answer that in front of God and country," Kennedy added. "I mean, there will be a congressional investigation. But I don't think he ought to wait on Congress." The Commerce Department has not confirmed for the record whether or not Lutnick has seen the memo. Yes, but: " It's impossible that Howard Lutnick didn't know about this memo," one senior administration official told Axios. "Of course Commerce got the memo. It had to get the memo. That's the point of the memo. It's about chips. Commerce deals with chips," a second official said. Meanwhile, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following reports of a second affair with a direct report. He previously admitted to an affair and apologized, but members on both sides of the aisle are also not letting him off the hook. "NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's decision to resign does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Warren said. Republican House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast (Fla.) and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford (Ark.) told reporters on Thursday that Huang's resignation doesn't change their plans to probe him and the company, Bloomberg Government reported. "Jensen Huang himself has been a pretty bold, some might even say arrogant promoter, sort of dismissing our concerns about China having access to these most advanced chips. And I do not take that lightly ... I would be happy to support a subpoena," Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer (N.D.) said on CNBC. The bottom line: Resignations and apologies aside, Washington is ready to hold someone accountable as the FBI, Congress and Nvidia's board all investigate in tandem.

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.
Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.
The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.
Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.
“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.
The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.
Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.
Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.
A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.
The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.
Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.
For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

71378d0ad1b2.text: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia after he reportedly had two affairs, including one with a purported Chinese spy. Why it matters: It's impossible to overstate how critical Huang is to Nvidia, to the AI buildout, to the stock market and economy. His departure could, per Wall Street sources, be the catalyst that endangers a ballooning AI bubble. It's also unlikely to ease congressional scrutiny of the company or Huang himself. Driving the news: Nvidia's board named longtime CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, while launching a search for a permanent replacement. Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, will continue serving as CFO while overseeing the company. Harvey C. Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair. The board said it expects Nvidia's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption. Zoom out: Huang's resignation follows revelations about two extramarital relationships. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, a senior Nvidia executive who reports to him. Nvidia's board had previously launched an independent investigation into Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia did not provide a reason for Huang's resignation in Thursday's announcement, which comes after reports that the board had an emergency meeting over whether to oust the CEO. By the numbers: Nvidia shares fell more than 10% after news of Huang's resignation. One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang. 🚨 Stunning stat: At these levels, Nvidia will have lost about $1.4 trillion in market capitalization in two weeks, since the initial Times report about linking Jensen Huang and Alice Huang. The big picture: This will likely go down as one of the biggest executive scandals in history. Nvidia is also one of the largest holdings in major index funds because of its size, meaning this move has massive implications for every American with a retirement account. The intrigue: Huang's resignation doesn't look like it'll ease congressional pressure over his behavior either. "NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's decision to resign does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a statement. The bottom line: The fallout is just starting. This is breaking news.

Hundreds of millions of dollars meant to help tackle Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo are not reaching the intended recipients, a medical charity has warned.
A report from MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF) said that while the outbreak remained "out of control", front-line workers were going unpaid, lacked proper training and were struggling with shortages of essential supplies.
It added that in some cases ambulances had run out of fuel.
More than 5,400 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
This makes it the second-most deadly outbreak of the disease ever recorded.
MSF has urged the Congolese government and UN agencies to "strengthen oversight and accountability" to ensure money already disbursed is effectively utilised.
This means "ensuring response personnel are properly trained, paid, equipped, and supported, and directing resources towards areas where needs are greatest", it said.
The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.
MSF's warning adds to concerns raised by Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) last month, when it said that $700m (Â£527m) out of $962m disbursed to organisations implementing Ebola response was unaccounted for.
At the time, Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya said it was too early to describe it as embezzlement, characterising the issue as a major transparency and financial reporting failure.
The Congolese health minister echoed these concerns, saying that aid agencies were required to provide details of their work so the ministry could provide oversight but that only 22% had done so.
"Our requirement is clear: transparency must be total. The response relies on a single plan, a single budget, and a single coordination," Health Minister Samuel-Roger Kamba said on X., external
In its report, external, the charity said: "Despite the vast amounts of money provided for the response, many frontline responders are left trying to contain the outbreak with empty hands and empty pockets."
It also mentioned Ebola monitoring "surveillance teams that exist on paper but are nowhere to be seen on the ground".
"Our teams are often left speechless by the dysfunctions they witness in many areas. Six months into the response, this situation is simply unacceptable," said MSF president Javid Abdelmoneim.
One important way of stopping Ebola from spreading is contact tracing - finding all those people who had come into contact with an infected person and putting them into isolation.
"Despite the resources officially allocated to this critical activity, surveillance remains deeply problematic," MSF said, adding that two-thirds of deaths were occurring in communities not treatment centres.
According to British epidemiologist Neil Ferguson, more than half of the cases are going undetected, meaning the outbreak is likely to last another year, reports the Reuters news agency.
MSF also raised concerns over "excessive concentration" of efforts in certain areas at the expense of other areas where needs were more urgent.
It said the response was "too slow" in North Kivu province while Haut-UÃ©lÃ© remained "dramatically overlooked".
In both provinces, MSF observed that teams were "inadequately resourced to respond effectively" with health facilities lacking essential items such as water, chlorine or triage systems.
"This has turned some facilities into new centres of transmission, rather than places of care that contribute to containing the disease," MSF said.
The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.
There are very few good roads in the area, making it very hard to travel around.
On Thursday, the UN and government warned that the areas worst affected by Ebola were also suffering from a severe food crisis, with almost 10 million in the region in dire need.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.
On Wednesday, the last person infected with Ebola in Kenya was discharged, marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation.
The Bundibugyo species is relatively rare and has no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Additional reporting by Emery Makumeno in Kinshasa
