- Published
Nvidia is now facing a scenario few would have considered until very recently - a future without Jensen Huang.
The influential co-founder of the AI chip-making giant resigned on Thursday over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Chief financial officer Colette Kress is in charge, for now, as the tech giant faces one of its biggest challenges - finding the right person to permanently lead the business that Huang helped create more than three decades ago and turned into one of the world's most valuable companies.
We take a look at which candidates have emerged as potential successors.
The finance chief
Colette Kress has been an industry veteran for more than 30 years, having previously held high positions at tech firms like Cisco and Microsoft.
Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's executive vice-president, has seen the firm's transformation from making chips for video games in the early 1990s to becoming an AI semiconductor powerhouse.
She has "fronted every earnings call" alongside Huang and is a "familiar and trusted voice for the market at a time when it badly needs one," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at investment firm eToro.
But doing the job permanently could be a different story, said Gilbert, as the firm, known for its edge in technology, could want an engineer in the chair.
The co-founder and the engineer
Another option is Chris Malachowsky, who founded Nvidia alongside Huang and Curtis Priem, and is the only executive that shares the same level of seniority.
Malachowsky has played a key part in developing the company's computing technology.
Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's high-performance computing business, has also emerged as a potential candidate if the company is keen to put an engineer in the top job.
Buck was among the early pioneers who helped popularise the use of graphic processors beyond gaming applications.
"He could protect Nvidia's technological edge, but his ability to manage the wider commercial relationships and geopolitical challenges would face scrutiny," said Charu Chanana, investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.
Today, Nvidia's leading processors are widely regarded as the gold standard for AI development.
Huang's children also work at Nvidia in executive positions but are relatively young and inexperienced.
Apple and Arm's top brass
Nvidia is likely to favour an internal appointment initially but could look externally for a more permanent replacement, said Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap.
Several names of tech entrepreneurs outside of Nvidia have been floated by experts.
Liu said Apple's former chief executive, Tim Cook, could be a possible choice as someone familiar with managing global supply chains, though she questioned whether he would be willing to leave the iPhone maker, where he is the chair.
Liu and Chanana also suggested Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm Holdings, the UK chipmaking giant.
Nvidia's processors are made with the help of chipmakers around the world, including Taiwan's TSMC and South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung.
Haas is familiar with leading a publicly-listed company and would bring semiconductor experience, though Nvidia's business model is considerably different from Arm's, said Chanana.
"The challenge is finding someone who can combine Jensen's technical understanding, strategic vision and relationships across the global technology industry," Liu said.
What now for Nvidia?
Ten Cap's Liu had believed it was just a matter of time before Huang would step down as Nvidia's chief executive.
"The issue is no longer simply about personal conduct," she said. "It is about corporate governance, national security concerns and maintaining confidence in the leadership of one of the world's most strategically important companies."
Several major investment firms have downgraded their forecasts for the chip giant - a rare shift given investors' longstanding optimism about the company.
An early indication came as markets opened in New York shortly after Huang's resignation was announced.
Nvidia shares opened down more than 13%, wiping more than half a trillion dollars off the firm's share market value.
Stacy Rasgon, senior analyst in US semiconductors at Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors that "our gut tells us we probably haven't fully probed the depths of what might be found here".
Rasgon halved Bernstein's share price target for Nvidia and said: "We've had enough and prefer to watch from the sidelines."
Ray Wang, chief executive of Constellation Research, said the crisis isn't so much an issue for the wider AI industry but rather one for Nvidia itself which has to consider if the person it appoints as its chief executive has the same appeal as Huang.
"That's really what the issue is, because a lot of these partnerships and investments have been made because of the trust with with Jensen," he said.
Additional reporting by Kali Hays

d25f2a6dcbf4.text:
The News
Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidiaâs CEO Thursday, a stunning fall for one of the worldâs most powerful figures. His downfall sparked fears of what his departure means for one of Americaâs chip champions and the unwind of the AI money machine he assembled.
Nvidiaâs CFO, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO while the board conducts a search for Huangâs replacement. Huang will also leave the board, which he chaired, and will be replaced by Harvey Jones, a board member since Nvidiaâs founding in 1993 who ran chip design company Synopsys in the 1980s and 1990s. Semafor had earlier reported that Kress was in the lead to run the company on a temporary basis.
The company said it will look at both internal and external permanent successors to Huang, whose departure leaves the giant chipmaker without a tested leader. Huang had nearly single-handedly turned Nvidia from a niche maker of graphics chips for video games into the centerpiece of the worldâs AI boom, and the company has never had another leader. It has no succession plan and few apparent internal successors.
One external candidate under consideration is Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who was among the executives considered for Intel CEO in 2019, Semafor reported Wednesday. Other names that have been floated are AMDâs Lisa Su, Huangâs first cousin once removed, as well as an offbeat suggestion by US President Trump on Thursday to tap former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the job.
Huangâs ouster came four days after he admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and followed a New York Times report that he had another affair with a subordinate. He is now wrapped up in a series of investigations by the board, Congressional leaders, and by the Department of Justice, Semafor reported on Thursday.
The ongoing saga has also shaved hundreds of billions of dollars off of what was once the worldâs most valuable companies â one crucial to the US remaining at the forefront of AI development around the world.
Shares fell as much as 7% Thursday, adding to Nvidiaâs losses since the first reports of Huangâs relationship with the suspected Beijing spy, who ran a Singaporean company that was a major buyer of Nvidiaâs advanced chips. Shares of neoclouds Nebius and CoreWeave, which rely on Nvidia to help AI startups rent space in their data centers, fell as much as 19% and 9%, respectively. Shares in Alphabet, whose TPU chips compete with Nvidiaâs GPUs, rose slightly.
Key-man risk
Huangâs ouster raises questions around Nvidiaâs ability to remain the de-facto central bank of the AI boom â and the fate of billions of dollars of chip financing from a slew of Wall Street firms that are tangled up with the company. Nvidia has provided tens of billions of dollars in financing to its customers, invested more than $50 billion in AI startups, and guaranteed huge data-center leases for firms including OpenAI.
Much of that spending rested on Huangâs singular credibility and power in the tech world, as well as his close ties to US President Donald Trump. His successor will likely have far less leeway from the chipmakerâs board, which is facing its own mountain of litigation, government investigations, and public scrutiny.
Still, Huang will remain one of Nvidiaâs largest shareholders, with a 3.6% stake in the company worth about $160 billion at todayâs price. While he doesnât have the same sort of control afforded to other former tech founders through super-voting stock, such as Alphabetâs Larry Page and Sergey Brin, heâll maintain a meaningful seat at the table. Itâs unclear what his exit package looks like and whether the board will claw back any additional share-based compensation from previous years.
Washington fallout
Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee whoâs been pushing for stricter export control laws, said Thursday that Huang agreed to come in for a closed-door briefing before lawmakers break again for Thanksgiving on Nov. 20. Other Congress members have sent letters asking Huang to come and testify in Washington.
Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under increasing pressure from members of Congress over how his office allowed Nvidia to to sell its advanced chips to what reports allege to be a front for banned Chinese buyers. The Trump administration is made more vulnerable by Huangâs close relationship with Trump and its deference to the Nvidia CEO on chip policy matters.
âThis incident raises significant concerns about the federal governmentâs ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,â Sens. Chris Coons, D-Del., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., wrote in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller on Thursday, asking them to preserve documents related to Nvidia.
Reports suggest government officials âwere aware of concerns about Nvidia, its relationship with Megaspeed, and the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips,â the senators said.
So far, Trump is standing by Lutnick. The president âmaintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position,â a White House official told Semafor.
Winners and losers
Jensenâs exit could scramble the AI chip market, elevate rivals that have been relegated to operating in Nvidiaâs shadow, and ensure more chips stay in the US rather than in China, which could explain hyperscalersâ share rises Thursday. While long chip design cycles mean it could take years for a competitor to eat into Nvidiaâs lead, a few companies stand out as beneficiaries.
AMD, whose stock is surging, competes most directly with Nvidia on data-center products. Broadcom and other custom silicon makers could gain as tech giants look to design more of their own chips, rather than relying on Nvidiaâs. Google may also get more momentum on its TPUs, which it began selling directly to out

2eb7ec89db85.text:
Some Silicon Valley executives are quietly celebrating Jensen Huangâs ouster from Nvidia and the national furor over chip exports to China. The good news for American companies is that tech exports that were going to China are now expected to be redirected to US firms, one person told me. That could accelerate the growth of the big AI labs and other Silicon Valley companies, and hobble Chinese rivals.
In the short term, theyâre probably right. Thereâs strong evidence that export controls have successfully slowed Chinaâs technological progress. The problem is that the US canât win the technological race with China in the long term by slowing its rival down. The bigger and more difficult part of that victory is speeding up American innovation.
And thatâs where Huangâs ouster is a counter-force to the gains made on China policy. Huang is one of Silicon Valleyâs great innovators. In the short term, his ouster wonât be terrible for Nvidia. Nvidia may actually become a more profitable company now, because any new CEO will optimize for profitability, as Apple did under Tim Cook. Innovators burn a lot of money thinking about the long term. And Nvidia will never be as innovative as it was under Huang.
Huang was Nvidiaâs one-man, long-term moat. Thatâs especially true now, in an era when AI allows pretty much any company to design a chip just like Nvidiaâs, as OpenAI did in a matter of months.
A less innovative Nvidia is not just a problem for Nvidia. Itâs a problem for the entire technology ecosystem. Big, powerful incumbents tend to be barriers to innovation. Cookâs Apple built the iPhone and then sat on that invention by defending its turf â a great business strategy but one that let the entire mobile ecosystem stagnate.
The key risk to the US tech industry isnât that Chinese spies will steal its cutting-edge technology. Itâs that Silicon Valley is at risk of seeing the magic formula that brought that technology into being in the first place weakened.

- Published
After winning a close race in Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom will become the state's first black US senator for more than 150 years, and the third in history.
It is a historic result in the deeply conservative southern state that last sent a Democrat to the US Senate in 1982, and had not seated a black senator since 1875.
Colom follows Hiram Revels, who became the first black person ever to serve in the chamber when he was seated from 1870 to 1871, and Blanche Bruce, whose term ran from 1875 to 1881. Revels and Bruce were both members of the Republican Party.
Revels was chosen as Mississippi's first senator after the Civil War, serving for just over a year and campaigning strongly for racial equality.
A few years later, Bruce, who was born into slavery, became the first black person to serve a full term in the US Senate. He remained in Washington after leaving the chamber and held a role in the Treasury.
Both terms came before the repressive Jim Crow laws began to enforce racial segregation across Mississippi and other southern US states.
A significant factor in Colom's victory was his success in mobilising young people and the state's large black population, who are expected to have turned out in high numbers.
In a victory speech, Colom referenced how Revels, who was a minister and served as a chaplain during the Civil War, gained support for his Senate campaign through his words.
"That's an example of the power of prayer, and through our history, there are so many people that lifted this state up through the power of prayer in very dark times," Colom said.
Prior to the result being called, the BBC spoke to students at Jackson State University, a historically black college in Mississippi. Many of them had voted for the first time and backed Colom.
"I really feel like a change is what we need," 18-year-old Jamyria Dunn said.
"I've had some amazing days in my life," she continued, "but seeing Mississippi, this state in particular, turn blue, would really bring a light to my heart that people just would not understand."

608cb0ecf4f8.text:
Lizâs view
Jensen Huang is out, and with him goes the âNvidia putâ that has underpinned the entire AI ecosystem.
Huang, who resigned from his post Thursday, was the AI worldâs central bank chairman and human security blanket, always there with a checkbook to backstop, acquire, hire, invest in, or otherwise underwrite the least underwritable corners of AI. That âputâ â finance speak for a guaranteed buyer on the other side of a trade â has kept the AI financing and fundraising markets lubricated, even as it invited criticism of their circularity. Itâs also helped prop up the stock market and padded 401(k)s for the last couple of years. Nvidia guarantees more than $100 billion of data-center leases, owns $51 billion worth of stock in privately held companies, and another $63 billion in listed ones. Its balance sheet was a sponge that absorbed the marketâs growing AI fears and put a floor under deal prices.
Whoever replaces him will face much higher stakes, akin to Tim Cook after Steve Jobs at Apple. Theyâll also be on a tighter leash from a board of directors I suspect will get a much-needed refresh by the time this saga is over. (Itâs hard to imagine the former president of Taco Bell or the former chief marketing officer of the NFL probing Huang too deeply on off-balance-sheet lease guarantees for next-generation data centers.) Not only will that change the fabric of one of the worldâs most valuable companies, but it will also push up the price of AI debt and equity â making the AI buildout more expensive for everyone â by taking a huge buyer off the table.
Notable
- Unlike with the 2008 financial crisis, âthis time we can see it on a blue-sky day: Nvidia is officially too big to fail,â I wrote in October. âWhat would be revealed by a stress test of Nvidia that contemplated a rise in the cost of AI-linked debt, a decline in venture-backed startup values, and a slowdown in data-center construction?â What happens under new leadership will determine the future of the company.

d71ab2107c7f.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-resigns-after-his-affair-raises-national-security-concerns Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after his affair raises national security concerns Economy Updated on Nov 12, 2026 9:29 AM EST — Published on Nov 12, 2026 9:10 AM EST HONG KONG (AP) — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after his extramarital affair raised national security concerns. The company named Colette Kress as interim CEO. She is the current executive vice president and chief financial officer. WATCH: Sen. Coons on Huang affair, Iran war and why Trump should fire Hegseth Huang faced growing calls to resign after his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Late Wednesday, media reports said Huang had another extramarital affair with an Nvidia employee who reports to him. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The board of directors said Thursday it also named its first-ever chairman, Harvey C. Jones, an entrepreneur and venture investor. READ MORE: How Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affair could cause collateral damage in Washington Shares of Nvidia, one of the largest companies in the world, plunged 10% in premarket trading Thursday. Nvidia's board had gathered to discuss Huang's future after revelations that he was having an affair with a former Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese government agent. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. The Associated Press could not independently confirm those reports. In its first statement since the scandal broke, Singapore-headquartered Megaspeed International said Thursday that it takes its obligation to comply with U.S. export control laws "extremely seriously." Details about Huang's affair with the former Megaspeed executive are unclear. "Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government," said the statement signed by its chairman and CEO, Tan Yong Pong, who also goes by James Tan. WATCH: What China stands to gain from Nvidia's CEO's alleged affair with spy Nvidia has said it had "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. The New York Times reported that the woman with whom Huang had an affair was Alice Huang, who also goes by the name Huang Le, and was a top executive at Megaspeed. The company prominently touts a partnership with Nvidia on its website. The two are not related. Last month, the Times reported that U.S. intelligence agencies discovered Nvidia's Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang — and determined she was feeding information directly to Beijing. On Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump announced that the FBI was investigating. WATCH: How the Nvidia revelations could ripple through the AI industry and global economy Megaspeed faced claims last year that it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was "no evidence" of such exports. Singapore has also said it is investigating such allegations. China has denied that it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, who heads one of the world's most valuable companies. Nvidia has become a leader in making chips that power AI and Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. In January, he won Trump's approval for selling to China its H200 chips. Megaspeed said Thursday that it has cooperated with the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which handles enforcement of national security restrictions on exports of technology, and was ready to "cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority." It said it has hired a U.S. law firm to handle a "comprehensive census" of its computer chips and to verify its export controls. "Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws," it said. Apart from questions over national security, Megaspeed's finances also have drawn attention. Its total assets soared roughly 90-fold from late 2023 to 2024, to almost US$3 billion, according to Singapore corporate records. Revenue surged to over US$294 million in 2024 from none in 2023. AP Business Writer Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. The Scoop
New York-based AI startup millionways on Thursday launched its new AI model that claims to offer insight into human intent and motivations.
The company also told Semafor it has raised $6 million in US funding, with investors including football stars Jason Kelce and DK Metcalf.
The Thorsten-4 model was born out of a research project in Germany in which dozens of psychologists interviewed more than 7,000 people about their personal lives and aspirations. That data â which the psychologists labeled by hand to capture what peopleâs words revealed about their motives and thinking â was used to train the model.
Millionways cofounders Martin Cordsmeier and Max Weidemann argue that understanding is missing from regular AI models, which are trained on internet text. They see the model as particularly useful in sales and executive hiring, where a search firm could prompt it to evaluate an interview transcript to gauge how a candidate will behave under pressure.
âWe can add a level of human understanding that the language models cannot get to by themselves,â Weidemann said, adding that the model should be âa decision-making support tool rather than the ultimate decision-maker.â
J.D.âs view
Enterprises are increasingly injecting task- and industry-specific models into their tech stacks, rather than defaulting to the frontier models for every task. Just this week, leading voice AI company ElevenLabs, for example, announced a healthcare-focused version of its new transcription model.
This gives CIOs more choice and customization, but it also adds the burden of testing whether specialized models actually beat fast-improving frontier ones.
Cordsmeier and Weidemann ran our conversation for this story through Thorsten-4, which deduced that I was most focused on relationship-building and being conscientious: âYou move between logic and intuition, and tough questions energized you.â (Iâll take the compliment!)
I ran a transcript of the same call through Anthropicâs new Claude Fable 5.2 model and asked for a psychology analysis: Claude also gave a solid assessment, though it was less sure of itself, focusing more on the job I was doing than on me as a person. It (correctly) noted that my âunstated goal was source cultivation.â

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.
On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.
Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.
Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.
The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.
That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.
“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”
DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)
Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.
Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.
Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.
Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.
Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.
“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.
Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.
For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.
Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.
Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

Data center developers had a rough election, losing 40 of 41 ballot measures nationwide.
The volunteers behind one of those measures celebrated this week at Big Walnut Grill in Sunbury, Ohio, a suburb of Columbus. These were the 20 or so people who gathered signatures, delivered yard signs and knocked on doors to support a referendum to ban large data centers within city limits. They won 79 percent to 21 percent.
The campaign taught them about the power of community organizing, said Alicia Doty, one of the leaders. She lives near the proposed Amazon Web Services data center that inspired the ballot measure.
“We are much stronger together,” she said, in an interview later that evening.
Doty and her neighbors won partly because they were a movement that emerged from genuine community concerns, and if I were a data center developer, I’d be chomping on antacids right now. It is difficult to see how the data center industry—including some of the largest companies in the world—can shake off rejection in so many of the best locations for construction.
Data center opponents are apprehensive about the scale of these projects, their potential emissions and their demands for electricity and water, which could drive up costs and strain supplies for other users. Fears of artificial intelligence also play a role, since the largest data centers provide the computing power for AI systems.
It helped, Doty said, that the people campaigning for data centers hurt their own cause. The most visible local campaign against the referendum was from NetChoice, a trade group whose members include Amazon. NetChoice canvassers and printed materials sought to discredit the ballot measure as funded by “extreme California special interests,” according to a door-hanger distributed in Sunbury. That message didn’t connect with voters.
Pataskala, which is 23 miles from Sunbury, also had a data center referendum. Pataskala voters rejected data centers with a 74 percent to 26 percent vote.
In at least one case, the people handing out materials opposing the ballot measure appear to have gotten their cities mixed up. One piece distributed in Sunbury said, “PATASKALA BEWARE” and then showed a cartoon wolf holding a clipboard. “There is a California wolf at our door.”
The warning about funding from California refers to a $10,000 donation to Conserve Ohio, a statewide organization opposing data centers, from PowerSwitch Action, an Oakland, Calif.-based nonprofit that supports progressive causes. The donation was the largest of $16,356 listed in Conserve Ohio’s most recent report filed with the Ohio Secretary of State.
Conserve Ohio’s average donation was $103. Excluding PowerSwitch’s contribution, the average was $40.
Conserve Ohio provides free legal advice to groups such as the one in Sunbury. I wrote about Conserve Ohio last month, including how it began with a few volunteers in rural Adams and Brown counties.
Austin Baurichter, one of several Conserve Ohio leaders, said it’s ironic that data center developers, largely based on the West Coast, such as Amazon, would criticize his group for accepting a donation from a California organization.
“We are and will continue to be grateful for any donation help we can get from anyone,” he said.
It’s a stretch to say PowerSwitch Action was funding the Sunbury campaign. Doty’s group spent about $5,000 and raised that money largely from group members, she said.
NetChoice didn’t respond to messages seeking comment.
“We appreciate the opportunity to engage with communities on the benefits that our data center investments bring,” said an Amazon spokesperson in an email. “We remain committed to setting a high bar for responsible data center development [and] continuing to engage communities early in our development process.”
Amazon also explained its approach to data centers and responses to common objections in an Oct. 2 blog post.
The Data Center Coalition, a trade group for data center companies, had this statement:
“The data center industry is committed to engaging with residents and local leaders to understand community priorities, towards ensuring that the growth of digital infrastructure meets local standards and delivers clear benefits that communities are seeking,” said Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition.
Diorio said communities that indicate they are “closed for business and investment” may lose opportunities, costing them high-wage jobs and tax revenue.
The election was a big win for Conserve Ohio. With a tiny budget, the group has worked with data center opposition campaigns across the state, advising residents how to get measures on their local ballots.
“I was amazed,” said Nikki Gerber, a leader of Conserve Ohio, about the election results. Voters “acted like they want democracy back, and that gave me hope.”
Gerber owns Moondoggie Liveree, an outdoor tourism business. She joined the push against data centers this year after Amazon Web Services proposed building a data center in her county.
Voters in Sprigg Township, which includes the project site, passed a referendum last week to establish zoning regulations that would limit data centers. But Gerber is concerned the referendum, with text revised by township officials, isn’t strong enough.
Gerber is also wary of the potential for state or local officials to find ways to push the project through, despite local opposition. I asked if she’s pleased to see Democrat Amy Acton, former director of the Ohio Department of Health, win the election for governor. Acton has said she supports a “conditional moratorium” on data center development.
“I still don’t have any faith in the government until I see the government do something for us,” Gerber said.
Nationwide, data center opponents won in 40 of the 41 local races where development was on the ballot last week, according to Ballotpedia. Ohio was the epicenter of voting on the issue, with 21 measures, followed by Illinoi

A senior leader of Colombia's largest criminal gang, the Gulf Clan, is among eight people killed in an air strike carried out by the country's armed forces, according to President Abelardo de la Espriella.
De la Espriella said he had personally authorised the bombing targeting the Gulf Clan in the province of Antioquia, in north-west Colombia.
He added that Haminton Mosquera, whom he described as a senior member of the crime gang and one of 10 "priority targets" for Colombia's security forces, had been "brought down".
De la Espriella was elected in June after campaigning on a promise to crack down on Colombia's powerful criminal gangs, including by launching air strikes.
In a post on X, external, he said that Mosquera was suspected of having ordered attacks against the security forces, including the murder of a police officer in the municipality of TarazÃ¡ last year.
The Gulf Clan has been engaging in criminal activities for decades, mainly trafficking cocaine from Colombia to destinations in the US and Europe but also illegal mining and people smuggling.
The US added it to its list of Foreign Terrorist Organisations (FTOs) last year.
In his post, President de la Espriella said that "the offensive won't stop" and vowed to regain control of areas currently controlled by criminal organisations such as the Gulf Clan.
While his offensive against criminal gangs has been welcomed by many living in areas where extortion and gang violence are rampant, de la Espriella has faced criticism for the way he has made some of his announcements on security.
Less than a month after taking office, he published a video showing him walking among 23 body bags containing the remains of 23 people killed in an air strike on a suspected guerrilla camp.
On Wednesday, he shared a photo, external in which he can be seen writing his campaign slogan, "Welcome to the miracle homeland" on a bomb.
He has also defended his decision to wear an army uniform at a recent event in CÃºcuta at which he confronted a detainee suspected of being a Farc rebel.
"What did you make of the bomb I sent you, signed by me?," the president can be heard asking the man.
He later told journalists that he wore the uniform because "I am a soldier of the homeland. That's why I dress like a soldier, because I came to serve Colombia. Because I honour the heroes, police officers and military."
Additional reporting by BBC Monitoring's Luis Fajardo.

a4a1fa09b4d7.text: President Trump directed Vice President JD Vance on Thursday to turn his "complete and total attention" toward alleged corruption in Democrat-run cities and states, contending that "[w]e don't need a deal with Iran." The big picture: After Vance concluded that the Iran war drove Republicans' stunning midterm walloping, Trump is reorienting his No. 2's focus — and directing him to go after Democrats the president labeled as "CORRUPT AND EVIL." Oil prices surged, and stocks sank after Trump's post reinjected a note of uncertainty into a market that was acting like the Iran war was all but over. Driving the news: "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Also on Truth Social Thursday, he threatened new tariffs on Mexico and criticized GOP senators for failing to pass the Save America ACT — adding that failure to do so was "devastating" for Republicans during the midterms. He said that he had asked Vance to "focus his complete and total attention" on so-called "Corruption and Crime" in Democrat-run cities and states, naming Minnesota, California and Illinois. Vance has chaired Trump's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud since the president created it via executive order earlier this year. Throughout the first half of his administration and federal crackdown on U.S. cities, Trump has repeatedly framed blue areas as hotbeds of crime and corruption, even when the stats haven't necessarily backed up those arguments. Catch up quick: Vance was recently heavily involved in a push to reach a new ceasefire with Iran and resume nuclear negotiations, Axios' Barak Ravid reported. Vance was a skeptical voice in Trump's inner circle about the war, Ravid reported, and led U.S. negotiating delegations after it began. Vance's office and the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Between the lines: Vance offered a surprisingly candid assessment of the midterm shellacking, writing in an X post last week that "[t]he reason we lost is the war." He continued: "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest." "But everyone knows why we lost." What we're watching: Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with his G7 counterparts in Paris on Tuesday, where he said Trump had considered resuming the war or cutting a deal but instead settled on strangling the Iranian regime, Axios previously reported . Rubio has signaled skepticism of a diplomatic breakthrough — and Trump's post indicates that door is closed, for now. Go deeper: Trump: New Iran attacks "quite unlikely"

43ff1f42a9c9.text: By — Ali Swenson, Associated Press Ali Swenson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/senators-probe-rfk-jr-s-reason-for-samoa-trip-after-letter-refuting-his-testimony-published Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Senators probe RFK Jr.'s reason for Samoa trip after letter refuting his testimony published Politics Nov 12, 2026 7:50 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — Two Democratic senators are launching an investigation into whether Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. lied to Congress about his reason for a 2019 trip to Samoa after The Associated Press and The Guardian published documents in August refuting his testimony. READ MORE: AP report: RFK Jr. said a Samoa trip had nothing to do with vaccines. New documents refute that AP and Guardian reporting in August showed that while Kennedy repeatedly told senators who held the key to his confirmation last year that his visit to Samoa before a deadly measles outbreak had "nothing to do with vaccines," a letter he sent to the Samoan prime minister ahead of the trip showed otherwise. In the letter, Kennedy used the words vaccine or vaccination eight times. The new inquiry is one of a vast array of investigations planned into the Trump administration after Democrats regained control of the House and Senate from Republicans in the midterm elections. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., said in a letter Wednesday to Children's Health Defense, a nonprofit group known for anti-vaccine activism that was formerly chaired by Kennedy, that they were starting an investigation. The lawmakers asked the group for a broad range of documents related to Kennedy's Samoa travel, his 2024 presidential campaign and his Senate confirmation process. The letter also requested all communications between the group and federal government officials since President Donald Trump's second term began in January 2025. The senators gave the group a deadline of Dec. 4 to comply. "We intend to hold Secretary Kennedy accountable for the grave harm he has caused to vulnerable children," Wyden and Alsobrooks wrote in their letter. "We also intend to hold him accountable for any false statements made to Congress, a crime that undermines the Senate's ability to fulfill its constitutional duties." The Department of Health and Human Services has maintained that the Samoa visit "was unrelated to vaccines." In response to an AP inquiry in August, it said "any claim or insinuation based on these letters that Secretary Kennedy lied under oath or to Congress is not only false but outright defamatory." Kennedy was not under oath during his confirmation hearing. Knowingly giving material false testimony to Congress is a crime that carries a possible prison sentence regardless of whether a person is under oath, though it is rarely prosecuted. Spokespeople for Children's Health Defense and HHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday. Kennedy's Samoa visit has become one of the most contentious events in his career. At the time, he was leading Children's Health Defense. Critics said the visit fueled anti-vaccine sentiment in Samoa, which later experienced the measles outbreak that killed 83 people, mostly children under 5. In the letter reported by the AP and Guardian, dated Jan. 20, 2019, Kennedy addressed then-Prime Minister Tuilaepa Sailele Malielegaoi and described his desire to study Samoa's use of the MMR vaccine. Kennedy speculated that the deaths in Samoa may have been caused by issues with different vaccine lots. Writing on CHD letterhead, he said his team wanted to evaluate whether that was the case through a "detailed health informatics assessment." He expressed his belief that it was difficult and time-consuming in most of the world to investigate "adverse health events associated with vaccines" and said health information systems are rarely designed to quickly study links "between diagnoses and specific vaccination events." The letter did not specifically discuss anti-vaccine activism. While in Samoa, Kennedy met with anti-vaccine activists, including one who helped arrange the trip with a U.S. Embassy employee, the AP and the Guardian previously reported. Months later, with vaccination rates still dangerously low, measles broke out, sickening thousands. Public health experts have said their efforts to address the outbreak were hampered by anti-vaccine activists, some of whom they claim were emboldened by Kennedy's visit. Wyden is expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee, which has oversight of Kennedy's health department, when Democrats retake Congress in January. Alsobrooks serves on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, which also oversees the department. The same senators on Wednesday announced a separate investigation into hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of gifts reportedly given last year to Kennedy by a donor and former employee. e0e13ddf37c6.text: A week that was supposed to see House Democrats transition seamlessly from a landslide midterm victory to a leadership coronation has instead been pocked by surprise Republican victories on the House floor. Why it matters: Skeptics of Democratic leadership have seized on these strategic fumbles to cast doubt on their much-heralded managerial abilities in the lead-up to the party's leadership elections next week. "It's really unfortunate that this happened this week when, obviously, that is a narrative we hear leadership portray," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) told Axios. Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said this week has "certainly not given me confidence," and that the election was an "indictment on how our party has been operating thus far, and this is a big part of why." "We do know that the Democratic caucus has blundered before on things, like whipping the votes to protect NPR last spring," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "We botched that one." What happened: The House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday to quash an effort by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, with support from all House Democrats present. The outcome quickly sparked backlash because nearly a dozen House Democrats were absent, many of whom got caught in a traffic jam returning from an Elect Democratic Women event. That was followed by an incident on Wednesday in which House Republicans passed a veterans bill by voice vote despite Democratic opposition. The incidents follow a procedural blowup in September in which a pair of centrist House Democrats repeatedly broke with leadership and helped the GOP advance key bills. What they're saying: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), asked about these incidents by Axios, touted a different veterans bill Democrats forced to a successful floor vote on Thursday via a discharge petition. "House Democrats once again successfully forced a vote on a piece of legislation designed to make life better for the American people," he said. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) did not respond to Axios' question and walked off the House floor into her office. The intrigue: Even some current and incoming House Democrats who are voting for Jeffries as speaker acknowledged the vote was a black eye. "I think everyone's frustrated with how that all went down, I'm not going to lie to you about that," said Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.). "People are pissed," a senior House Democrat told Axios. The other side: Other Democrats told Axios the absences were an inevitable reality of Congress, noting that several who missed votes have said they were attending to emergencies. "I think everyone's explained what the situations were — somebody was recovering from surgery. There are certain things that are unavoidable," said Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.). Others said the upshot is that House Democrats need to do a better job of getting to votes on time: "The general consensus among the new members is on Jan. 3, it's time to lock in," Rep.-elect Matt Little (D-Minn.) told Axios. Others said the speakership election offers a window into how Jeffries' approach to the speakership might play out over the coming year. Jeffries has always taken a more hands-off approach than his predecessor, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), preferring to let issues and fights among members resolve themselves.

84bd7d934351.text: Senate Democrats could find some of their most surprising allies next Congress from the right wing of the Republican Party . Why it matters: Senate Democrats are on track to need only four GOP votes to break filibusters next Congress. They could find those votes from a bloc of GOP senators with a shared appetite for taking on corporate power. Enter Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), Jim Banks (R-Ind.), Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.). Each has already worked with Democrats, and their votes could put legislation over the top. Who we're watching: Hawley has co-led multiple pieces of legislation with progressive star Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) this Congress. Hawley is often viewed as a loner in the GOP, pairing populist economics with hardcore culture war issues from abortion to transgender care to religious freedom. He's been scathing in his postelection critiques. "This Congress did not come and work for the people. This Congress came and worked for AI companies, and it worked for data centers, and it worked for big tech companies," he told reporters on Tuesday. He's scoping out areas for potential bipartisan deals: "You want to raise the minimum wage? I'm for that. You want to work to get gas prices down? I'm for that. I am open to anything to bring down the cost of health care," he said. Zoom in: Watch the health care space, specifically undoing cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and drug price controls. President Trump has specifically asked Congress to codify his most favored nations drug pricing deals, which could give Republicans an opening to work with Democrats. Hawley and moderate Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) were among the loudest GOP voices opposing the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act credits last year. Zoom out: Social Security and tech safety issues could also be huge areas of unexpected bipartisan work. Over the summer, Warren and Moreno released a sweeping plan to "save Social Security." Warren and Banks have tag-teamed on numerous tech and AI safety bills, including a joint statement on Nvidia this week. Hawley is also a major critic of AI. Schmitt worked with Warren in 2024 and 2025 to challenge Big Tech's dominance of Pentagon AI contracts, and with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) in July to crack down on search engine monopolies. What to watch: While there will be fewer this Congress, Democrats will also have a club of more moderate Republicans they can try to pick up too. Murkowski, along with Sens. John Curtis (R-Utah) and Todd Young (R-Ind.), will be top targets.

7728abcee02f.text: By — Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/what-to-know-about-dengue-fever-as-florida-reports-more-than-500-cases-this-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about dengue fever as Florida reports more than 500 cases this year Health Updated on Nov 12, 2026 7:57 PM EST — Published on Nov 12, 2026 7:31 PM EST This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. On Nov. 5, low flying helicopters blanketed areas of Florida's Pinellas and Hillsborough counties with a fine mist. It's one of the ways Florida health officials hope to slow the country's largest dengue fever outbreak in more than a decade. READ MORE: Florida's dengue outbreak is largest in continental U.S. in decades Dengue starts with a mosquito bite, so killing the insects is key. The helicopters spray water mixed with Bti, a natural bacteria found in soil that kills black fly and mosquito larvae. Most people become infected when traveling in high dengue risk areas, and Florida had recorded 382 international travel-associated cases as of Oct. 31. But the state has also counted a recent record high number of people infected on Florida's turf: 524. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Florida has had domestic dengue outbreaks before. In 2010, it counted 58 locally acquired cases, after nearly eight decades of reprieve. Since then, the largest outbreak was in 2023, when the state reported 189 dengue cases contracted in Florida. As Florida navigates its largest dengue outbreak in more than 15 years, it might help to understand how this virus spreads and how to recognize symptoms and protect yourself. We sought answers to some pressing dengue fever questions. What is dengue fever? Dengue fever can develop after a person is infected with any of the four dengue viruses. The virus is not transmitted person-to-person, and there is no widely available vaccine to prevent infection. About 3 in 4 people do not get sick, but if symptoms develop, they typically set in about four to 10 days after an infected mosquito's bite. The most common symptoms of mild dengue fever include high fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, rash, pain behind the eyes and muscle, joint and bone pain. About 1 in 20 people infected with a dengue virus develops a more severe form of dengue fever sometimes called dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. Severe dengue is a life-threatening medical emergency that can cause shock, internal bleeding and death. Warning signs of a severe infection include serious stomach pain or tenderness, vomiting at least three times in 24 hours, bleeding from the gums or nose, rapid breathing, blood in stool or vomit, restlessness, feeling extremely tired and bleeding under the skin that might appear as purplish spots or patches. Those symptoms typically happen 24 to 48 hours after the fever, and they often come on quickly. Anyone experiencing them should seek immediate medical care. What is the treatment for dengue fever? There is no specific cure or treatment. Most people recover in about one week, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said. The CDC recommends people rest, hydrate, and take acetaminophen to reduce fever and pain. Avoid other pain relievers such as aspirin and ibuprofen because they can raise the risk of bleeding. For severe dengue fever, medical professionals might monitor a patient's blood pressure and platelet count and provide blood transfusions or intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement. Can someone develop immunity to dengue? After being infected with a dengue virus, a person's immune system learns to fight that type of virus, which helps protect them from reinfection with that same virus. But he or she could remain susceptible to the other three dengue viruses. A person might be asymptomatic or have mild symptoms during an initial dengue infection, and then develop more severe symptoms — or, in rare cases, dengue hemorrhagic fever — after being infected with a second type of dengue virus, said Kristi Miley, a University of Florida public health professor. "Dengue is a doozy, mainly because the second infection can be more dangerous than the first," Katelyn Jetelina, an epidemiologist and public health expert, said in social media posts. Florida has documented all four dengue viruses since 2009. The type of dengue virus that's predominantly circulating now "has been noted to cause more severe symptoms than the other three serotypes," Miley said. Why are there so many cases in Florida this year? Florida's climate and environment provides ideal conditions for the Aedes species mosquitoes that spread dengue to thrive. If someone travels to a dengue endemic country and becomes infected even asymptomatically, dengue can enter a community. When a mosquito bites a person infected with the dengue virus, it can introduce the virus to the local mosquito population. An infected female mosquito will remain infected for her life — and she can pass the virus to her eggs, which can result in more than 500 infected offspring, said Miley. WATCH: Florida has a dengue problem. The solution may be more mosquitoes "When you consider the multiplication equation here and add that to the amount of excessive rainfall that the state has been experiencing this late in the year, one can quickly see how an outbreak of this magnitude can happen," she said. All told, the previous 16 years saw only 606 total locally acquired cases. "Studies are ongoing to better understand the factors contributing to the dengue activity being seen in Florida in 2026," said Isabella White, a Florida Department of Health spokesperson. Does the risk extend beyond Florida? Yes. Not every state has the climate to support Aedes mosquito pop

The News
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has kept his job through scrutiny over his ties to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein; his cryptocurrency firm, Tether; and his former financial services firm, Cantor Fitzgerald.
The Nvidia fallout may be the toughest test yet of his staying power.
A growing GOP contingent is pointing the finger at Lutnick for not cracking down hard enough on Megaspeed, the AI chip firm with ties to an alleged Chinese spy with whom former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair, and for what they see as the Commerce Departmentâs broader failure to restrict AI chip exports to China. In the wake of reporting that other administration officials had urged the Commerce secretary to move faster, Republicans on and off Capitol Hill are accusing Lutnick of defying President Donald Trump by not imposing curbs on the firm â and even positing his job could be at risk.
âWeâre hearing â¦ Trump has directed three times that [Megaspeed be blacklisted],â Rep. John Moolenaar, the top Republican on the House Select Committee on China, told Semafor. âIf thatâs true â¦ then clearly, it seems that those questions need to be answered.â
But so far the balance of GOP officials are coming to Lutnickâs defense, suggesting the commerce secretary wonât be going anywhere soon.
The president himself is so far standing by Lutnick despite the bipartisan backlash, reinforcing his willingness to go easier on China as he pursues a trade detente with Beijing.
âWhat I would say to everybody: Just settle down,â Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., told Semafor. âWe donât need to shoot Howard today.â
âThereâs lots and lots and lots of stuff here thatâs going to come out. Should it come out? Absolutely,â Justice continued. âShould we get on some witch hunt running through the wilderness? â¦ I donât do that.â
Congress will get more answers soon: Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Thursday that Lutnick will testify before the chamberâs Commerce Committee. And House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., said that Huang, who resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following revelations of another affair with a colleague, will appear before his panel.
Even Lutnickâs critics think heâll eventually pull himself out of trouble, even as longstanding interagency tension threatens to boil over.
âWhen you saw [Treasury] Secretary [Scott] Bessent blowing up at Lutnick in the Situation Room, you can rest assured the working level at Treasury was all over Commerce about chip sales for over a year,â Steve Bannon, the MAGA commentator and Bessent ally, told Semafor. âNow the issue becomes: Does Lutnick start inventing excuses to save himself?â
A Commerce Department spokesperson said that âTreasury and Commerce have a great working relationship,â adding that both âare committed to advancing President Trumpâs agenda.â
The Nvidia news landed just in time for Democrats, who are finalizing their oversight plans for the next Congress. Already, lawmakers have laid the groundwork to investigate Lutnickâs involvement with Cantor Fitzgerald, Tether, and Epstein.
The detractors
No GOP lawmaker has called explicitly for Lutnickâs firing. But they havenât hesitated to blame him for many of the recent revelations about Nvidia â including the fact that Huang accompanied Trump to China earlier this year despite the since-revealed existence of a State Department memo outlining his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy.
âHow on Earth do you put somebody on Air Force One [when you have] been informed there was a suspected improper relationship beforehand? How is that protecting the president?â Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said. âShame on Lutnick for allowing that exposure to happen for the president; to me, thatâs a disqualifying moment for Lutnick.â
Compared to Epstein, âthis, to me, is next-level,â he added.
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., rebuked Commerce for not shedding more light on the circumstances, particularly when it comes to the sale of AI chips to Megaspeed.
âIf I were the secretary, Iâd call a press conference and explain what happened,â Kennedy said. âThis is as serious as an aneurysm.â
Even some of the Trump administrationâs staunchest allies have weighed in, accusing Lutnick of defying the president by failing to rein in Megaspeed.
âLutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen,â China hawk Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Fox News. He urged Lutnick to testify before the Senate Banking Committee.
The defenders
Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Semafor that âyouâve got to get the factsâ before drawing any conclusions, adding that Lutnick has âalways responded to my questions, so thatâs all I can ask.â Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., also cast doubt on whether Lutnick really was at fault.
âIn a lot of cases, where they simply blame someone, I want to know what the rules are that heâs trying to comply with,â Rounds told Semafor. âIs there something that weâve done, in terms of policy, that might have either delayed his ability or something else? I donât know, and Iâd rather get the facts before I make a decision as to guilt.â
The AI industry sees little problem with Lutnickâs conduct either way.
âCommerceâs job is to expand the economy, domestic and foreign, pretty much at all costs,â National Artificial Intelligence Association CEO Caleb Max said. âSo if you zoom out, I donât think it looks nefarious; I think it looks natural.â
The View From the white house
Far more crucially, the White Houseâs public posture on the debacle indicates that Trump is not particularly concerned about the fallout, let alone Lutnickâs role in it.
âSecretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trumpâs America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments,â a White House official said. âPresident Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary

Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment.
"People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC.
After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter.
"Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion.
Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next."
Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.
But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force.
Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements.
Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority.
Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat.
"The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage."
Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says.
Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost.
Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC.
He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy."
The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability.
It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored.
Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes.
Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days.
"We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active.
Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents.
The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives.
As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds.
Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded.
Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC.
Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations.
However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael.
Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. Jensen Huang has abruptly quit as chief executive of AI chipmaking giant Nvidia after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves from Silicon Valley to Capitol Hill.
Nvidia is now under scrutiny from US lawmakers in Washington DC demanding Huang answer questions over whether one of his alleged relationships was with a Chinese spy.
One of the world's most valuable companies as a result of the AI boom, Nvidia has lost $550bn (Â£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.
Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, called an emergency meeting of her executive team to discuss the company's future.
His alleged conduct not only potentially crossed professional boundaries, but has made Nvidia the target of questions from US politicians who have expressed concern about national security risks.
Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.
Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear.
And US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing.
Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons, along with other Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, publicly demanded that Huang brief Congress on the matter.
If he refuses to appear voluntarily before any committee that calls him, he could be subpoenaed, one Senate staff member told the BBC.
Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday.
According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company.
Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close.
Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.
It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said.
Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public.
Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared.
Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information.
The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures.
Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming.
But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data.
Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.
Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires.
He is far from the first tech titan to become embroiled in revelations of infidelity.
Bill Gates of Microsoft and Jeff Bezos of Amazon had affairs exposed in the last decade. Both men are now divorced from their wives.
Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia.
Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago.
Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector.
Because of Nvidia's size and success in recent years, such a drop can have a direct impact on the savings accounts of ordinary Americans.
Nvidia's value makes up about 7% of the S&P 500 index. That index is offered as a popular index fund in US retirement savings accounts.
Those account balances rise and fall with the changes of the stock market.

588ea8faec4c.text: By — John Hanna, Associated Press John Hanna, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/cindy-holscher-wins-election-for-kansas-governor-extending-democrats-wave-of-victories Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Cindy Holscher wins election for Kansas governor, extending Democrats' wave of victories Politics Nov 12, 2026 6:15 PM EST TOPEKA, Kan. (AP) — Democrat Cindy Holscher has been elected Kansas' next governor, fending off Republican Ty Masterson to keep the office in her party's hands and extend a massive wave of Democratic victories across the country. WATCH: Sen.-elect Hamilton reflects on why Kansas voters chose a Democrat for U.S. Senate Democrats had already secured a majority of governorships in the U.S. for the first time in two decades, even prior to the narrow win in Kansas, where Holscher had already declared victory following Tuesday's midterm elections. The Associated Press did not call the race until Thursday. Holscher, a state senator, promised to halt new data centers and overcame a flood of money that Republicans poured behind Masterson, the president of the GOP-controlled state Senate. She will succeed outgoing Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat who was term-limited. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Kansans have sent a clear message that they want to keep our state moving forward," Holscher said in a video posted online Tuesday, two days before the race was called. "The work of preparing to lead has already begun." Masterson remains the Kansas Senate's top Republican leader. Before the race was called, he promised to keep fighting to cut property taxes — his biggest campaign promise — and for safer communities and better schools. The political tailwinds helping Holscher also pushed U.S. Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, pastor of the nation's largest United Methodist church, to Democrats' first victory in a Senate race in Kansas since 1932. In another big victory for Kansas Democrats, Chris Mann ousted state Attorney General Kris Kobach, a champion of strict voter ID laws who served as vice chair of President Donald Trump's commission on election fraud in 2017. Masterson had reasons for optimism after emerging from a contentious primary in August with Trump's endorsement. For 60 years, when a Kansas governor has retired or been term-limited, the other party's nominee has won the next election. The Republican Governors Association poured $19 million into television and digital advertising, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, and attacked Holscher as an extreme liberal. The two candidates' fall fundraising was comparable, but Republicans outspent Democrats more than 3-to-1 overall. Holscher also faced early resistance to her bid from Kelly, who had earlier backed another Democratic state senator and once suggested that Holscher could be too liberal to win in November. Kelly later endorsed Holscher and produced a video for her — though not until after she did a spot for Iowa's new governor-elect, Rob Sand. Holscher made a state moratorium on building new data centers for artificial intelligence a cornerstone of her campaign. She said people want limits on their energy and water use and want to make sure the centers create local jobs. "It cuts across party lines," she told reporters in Topeka late in the race. "The people are asking for reasonable things." A former manager for Sprint Corp., Holscher lives in the Kansas City, Kansas, suburbs in Johnson County that boomed after World War II. It's the state's most populous county, home to 23% of the state's 2 million voters. Johnson County has become increasingly Democratic since Trump's first run for president in 2016. Holscher won a Kansas House seat that year and was elected to the Senate in 2020. She captured more than 60% of Johnson County's vote, offsetting Masterson's big margins in solidly GOP rural areas. Hamilton, who also lives in Johnson County, took the same path to victory. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
