d458fdcc5ba7.text: Data: Photos: Getty Images, Nvidia, Apple; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Nvidia has begun searching for a permanent replacement for longtime CEO Jensen Huang , who resigned Thursday amid scrutiny over reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Why it matters: Nvidia's next leader will inherit one of the world's most valuable companies — and the daunting task of succeeding the pioneer who transformed it into an AI powerhouse. The job will require as much political savvy as technological expertise, Axios' Nathan Bomey says. The next CEO must navigate regulatory scrutiny, geopolitical tensions and the economic upheaval unleashed by the AI boom. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Thursday that CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO following Huang's departure. The board said it would consider both internal and external candidates. Longtime director Harvey Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair following Huang's departure. Reality check: Huang never publicly named a successor , leaving investors and analysts to speculate about who could take the helm. In an October Bloomberg interview released Thursday, Huang said he hoped Nvidia's next CEO was already working at the company. Here are 11 names that have surfaced in reporting and speculation — from leading contenders to long shots. Colette Kress Colette Kress, the new interim CEO of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia bio page Kress could stay on permanently, with analysts and investors viewing her as a leading contender because of her financial expertise, per Reuters . Nvidia's new board chair, Harvey Jones, praised Kress for her deep understanding of the company's business and customers. Kress has represented Nvidia on investor calls for more than a decade, making her one of the company's most recognizable executives. She's also the only person, aside from Huang, who had much visibility across the company, according to Axios' Ina Fried. Huang had several dozen direct reports, many of whom oversaw relatively narrow parts of the business. Yes, but: Her finance background could raise doubts about whether she could match Huang's technological prowess. Ian Buck Ian Buck of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia media assets Buck is among the potential successors drawing attention from analysts and investors, Reuters reported, given his engineering expertise and prominent position inside Nvidia. He currently serves as Nvidia's vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing. He also helped develop CUDA, Nvidia's computing platform that made its graphics processors essential to modern AI development. Chris Malachowsky Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia media assets Malachowsky co-founded Nvidia with Huang in 1993 and helped shape the company's technology over the next three decades, according to his Nvidia bio page . "Malachowsky has been instrumental in managing, defining and driving the company's core technologies as it has grown from a startup to the global leader in accelerated computing," the page reads. Much of his background is in engineering and technical leadership. Yes, but: His role today is less focused on day-to-day company management, raising questions about whether he would want to assume the CEO position. René Haas Arm CEO Rene Haas at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on Sept. 14, 2023. Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images Haas, the CEO of British chip designer Arm Holdings, has emerged as an outside contender because of his chip industry experience and previous work at Nvidia, per multiple reports . He's a former Nvidia executive who has the public-facing skills that may be required as Nvidia faces heavy scrutiny from investors and government probes . Nvidia uses Arm's processor technology in some products. Flashback: Nvidia previously tried to acquire Arm in a $40 billion deal, but the companies abandoned the transaction in 2022 amid significant regulatory opposition. Tim Cook President Trump and Apple CEO Tim Cook shake hands in the Oval Office at the White House. Photo: Win McNamee/Getty Images Former Apple CEO Tim Cook's name entered the succession conversation Thursday after President Trump publicly suggested he take over Nvidia. Cook's high profile and experience running one of the world's largest technology companies have fueled speculation that he could be a dark horse. Cook has also been mentioned in prediction market speculation. Yes, but: It's unclear whether Cook would want the job after recently stepping down as Apple's CEO. Johny Srouji Johny Srouji appears on a laptop screen during Apple's 2020 virtual Worldwide Developers Conference, viewed in Arlington, Va. Photo: Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Bloomberg has identified Srouji , Apple's chief hardware officer, as another potential successor. Before that, he led the development of Apple's custom chips for the iPhone, Mac and other Apple devices. Nikesh Arora Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora attends the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, India in Feb. 2026. Photo: Prakash Singh/Bloomberg via Getty Images Arora, the CEO of Palo Alto Networks , has emerged as a potential successor, with The Economic Times reporting investors have floated his name. Arora has led Palo Alto Networks since 2018 and overseen the company's expansion into AI-powered cybersecurity. He previously served as president and chief operating officer of SoftBank and worked for a decade at Google, per his official biography . Yes, but: His experience is largely in cybersecurity and other areas of tech, rather than chip development. Lisa Su AMD CEO Lisa Su speaks onstage during the company's Gamers Day 2026 event in Seoul, South Korea. Photo: SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images Su has led AMD, one of Nvidia's biggest rivals, for more than a decade. Bloomberg identified her as a potential successor given her deep experience in the chip industry. Yes, but: Su already runs one of Nvidia's biggest

When neighbours hammered on Jean Powell's door and evacuated her to safety because the nearby river had burst its banks and swamped her town, little did she know she would never return home.
Jean sought a 10-month refuge at her local Wetherspoons but kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow hit 18-times its normal level in south Wales last November.
But the 95-year-old never got to go back home and died in September - one of those who suffered a personal toll from the effects of being flooded.
"Jean used to say, when am I going home?" said friend and neighbour Wyn Smith. "All she wanted to do was come back home and we couldn't fulfil that."
Jean was forced out of her home when the river hit record levels in the early hours of November 15 last year as a major incident was declared after almost a month's worth of rain fell in 24 hours.
It has been officially described as a one-in-75-year event when the river flooded more than 400 properties in Monmouth during Storm Claudia - and overwhelmed the defences that were built 35 years ago to protect the centre of town.
Jean, like many in the small town near the Wales and England border, was rescued and after sleeping the night on her neighbour's chair sought temporary sanctuary in Monmouth's Wetherspoons as she had no close family to look after her.
"She was happy in the beginning because she was in town where she wanted to be," recalled Wyn, who visited her friend staying in one of The Kings Head's hotel rooms most days.
"The Wetherspoons staff were brilliant with Jean, they'd take her food and really looked after her."
"We never thought she'd be there that long," said Wyn. "It's nobody's fault, it took a long time to dry her home out. It had to be done properly."
Residents have been with family, some are in rented accommodation, some have been in an Airbnb while another is in a care home.
Their story is typical of many in Monmouth who have been out of their home since Claudia struck - and that trauma and anxiety from the devastation of 12 months ago is never far from the surface.
"Some had been through the war and they said it upset them more than that. It was just awful," said Wyn.
"But unfortunately it could happen again. There's that fear. If they see water coming, it'll freak them out. They need to feel at home and not worry about the weather."
The Met Office estimates that with current levels of global warming, record-breaking wet winters have gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events.
Wales' environmental body has warned long-range forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of wetter, windier weather than usual this winter with Natural Resources Wales (NRW) saying people should prepare for "the unthinkable".
Apart from three nights at the local Premier Inn over Christmas when Wetherspoons was shut - where Jean had sandwiches from the nearby petrol station for Christmas dinner because she wanted to "remain independent" - she stayed above the pub in the town's main square for almost 10 months.
"As time went on, living in one room was awful for her," recalled Wyn, 70.
"When Jean got ill, it wasn't a place for her to live. Her health deteriorated and she didn't come back home, which is sad."
Jean's death will be acutely felt when the first displaced residents return to the Chippenham Court retirement complex she called home following its Â£1m refurbishment in the next few weeks.
One in seven properties in Wales are at risk of flooding, including the Frost household on the other side of Monmouth where Emily says she and her young family will never recover from being evacuated on a lifeboat last year.
The mum-of-two breaks down as she recalls being woken by the coastguard telling her she's got five minutes to evacuate her family as the floodwaters surge towards her end-of-terrace cottage.
"Opening the door, I completely freaked out to the lifeguard," Emily told the BBC.
"They were waist deep in water and said our house was at risk. I just needed to get our boys, who were then aged three and five, and they'd be back with a raft. We didn't have time to think about it."
What was supposed to be a night of celebration for her and husband Jake's 10th wedding anniversary, turned into a nightmare.
Emily and Jake didn't take their boys when they returned home the following day where more than a foot of water had penetrated their home.
"There was sludge and mud everywhere," she recalled.
"We didn't bring the boys home for a good while because we didn't want them seeing everything that they'd treasured had been destroyed.
"It was the toll it would take on them that worried us the most."
The Frosts lived in rental accommodation nearby for six months as they ripped out the downstairs of their home and started again.
Emily and Jake, who had also been flooded in 2020, have seen their boys "playing floods" so know their children have been "trying to process" their ordeal.
"They couldn't really understand why we weren't able to go home or have their things" said Emily.
"Because it's the time of year, even now when it rains they'll ask "are we staying home, is it okay? Luckily they're resilient as kids, but you still worry. People don't recover, it's something you'll just live with."
Environmental bodies estimate about 275,000 properties in Wales are at risk of flooding with another 400,000 in Scotland, while in England about 6.3 million properties - around 11.3m people - live in flood risk areas.
An official report said the River Monnow swelled to more than six-and-a-half metres after significant rainfall locally and upstream over the Black Mountains during a week where more than half-a-dozen Met Office rain warnings were issued.
Jennifer and Alan Morgan's 18th Century cottage near the banks of the Monnow had two more doors to hang after a five-year renovation when Claudia struck and they had to start it all again.
"I've not slept well for a year as it's been an absolutely living nightm

More than 76,000 sewage spills were recorded after new monitoring equipment was installed at waste overflow sites in Scotland, BBC analysis suggests.
The addition of 1,009 sewer monitors in 2024 increased the proportion of the Scottish Water network being monitored from 6% to 30%.
Now the latest figures have revealed tens of thousands of spills which would previously have been unrecorded, including hundreds at beauty spots like Loch Lomond.
Scottish Water said the vast majority of the spills were not harmful to the environment, and that increased monitoring had improved understanding of the sewer network.
BBC Scotland News has used the latest data to create an interactive map which you can use to find out how many spills were recorded in your area, and how long they lasted.
Map of every sewage spill in Scotland
Sewage spills happen automatically at overflow sites, which are permitted to release excess water into natural waterways.
They usually consist of a pipe - set much higher than the usual water level - which provides an escape route when the system is deluged.
These overflows act as relief valves to prevent the sewer system from becoming overwhelmed during heavy rainfall and flooding into homes, businesses and streets.
The spills can last anywhere from a few minutes to hours.
Scottish Water currently has over 4,200 overflows across its network. The number of overflows with monitoring rose from 273 to 1,275 in 2024.
More than 100,000 spills totalling to almost 277,000 hours were recorded last year â an average of about 274 a day.
It is difficult to assess how the numbers compare to the previous year's figures, when 24,000 spills were recorded because of lower coverage.
The sites are all licensed to release untreated or partially-treated waste but just under 12% of overflows are legally required to report their data to the regulator, the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).
Sepa said it has a "risk-based approach" which prioritises areas for monitoring based on population and environmental need.
However, none of the new monitors were required to be reported to Sepa.
Scottish Water figures, external show that Glasgow's River Clyde was one of the most impacted waterways in Scotland last year, receiving almost 6,150 spills - or the equivalent of 17 a day.
When adding in the Clyde Estuary, Firth of Clyde and other unnamed tributaries that run into the Clyde's waterways, this almost doubles to nearly 14,200, or 39 a day.
The Clyde Estuary also recorded the longest duration of spills - more than 25,000 hours - followed by the River Clyde with more than 15,000 hours.
Barcloy Mill Burn in Dumfries and Galloway, which is one of the newly-monitored sites, received the most spills last year, with a total of almost 3,500.
The data suggests that 225 sites recorded no spills and 525 recorded fewer than 10. There may also be errors which suggest a monitor is active when it is not.
'It's what's not visible'
There were 1,270 spills, totalling almost 1,500 hours, last year into West Lothian's River Almond, which is nearly 28 miles in length.
Local campaigner Ruth Plevin said swimming in the river was part of her childhood and that she now wants to protect it for her own grandchildren.
She said any investment in improving the infrastructure of the water system was welcome.
"It's what's not visible that is our concern - the microplastics, the pharmaceuticals, the agrichemicals, stuff that you can't see," she said.
Plevin, a member of the River Almond Action Group, said she wants the group's legacy to be clean, safe water.
"It's precious and I think we need to regard it as precious. Value it, look after it and make it safe.
"I want it to be clean - it's not a lot to ask for, really," she said.
Are spills affecting water quality?
Further along the east coast at Belhaven in East Lothian, surfer Brian Allen has been testing the local water for pollution.
Each week he sends samples to an accredited laboratory to be tested for E.coli and intestinal enterococci.
He says this is the same sampling as done by Sepa, except he tests all year round and not just during the bathing season.
Sepa monitors bathing water quality at about 80 sites across Scotland between May and September. It also looks out for algae, seaweed and waste.
Allen, the regional representative for Surfers Against Sewage, said the results had been providing "really good news" for Belhaven.
He said 86% of the samples were rated as excellent, good or sufficient water quality, which was fine for recreational water users.
"In fact 77% of the results are coming back as excellent. What we don't know is whether that picture is being replicated across the rest of Scotland," he said.
Allen welcomed Scottish Water's increase in data publishing and said working collaboratively would help build up a bigger picture of water quality.
He said the figures had showed there were almost daily discharges from the two overflows in the area â but it was not known if there was a link between discharges and water quality.
One of them, at West Barns at Dunbar, recorded 3,300 spills last year - the second highest number in Scotland last year and a newly-monitored site.
What are the new monitors showing?
Simon Parsons, director for wastewater at Scottish Water, said most of the time overflows were doing the job they were designed for - draining rainwater out of the sewer system.
"The vast majority of those spills aren't harmful to the environment because they're nearly always about rainwater," he explained.
Scottish Water said 99% of spills were rainwater, surface water, road run-off, "grey" water from households (not human waste), infiltration of groundwater, and trade effluent.
Parsons said the increase in monitoring had improved understanding of the sewer network and helped identify locations requiring improvement.
"We didn't necessarily know how and when our overflows were operating so we've got a much better picture now than we've ever had before.

Enforcement actions and penalties levied by the US Securities and Exchange Commission have fallen to multi-decade lows, reflecting a dramatic pullback by Wall Streetâs top watchdog.
The agency, which has seen budget and staff reductions under the Trump administration, doled out $1.1 billion in penalties last year, the lowest in two decades.
The decline drew a rebuke from Democrats who vowed increased scrutiny of its enforcement program in the next Congress, though an SEC official cautioned that âactivity and effectiveness are not the same.â
While some suggested the figures were consistent with the agencyâs stated aim of promoting more IPOs, âthe obvious risk is, with less enforcement, you have a greater risk of fraud,â a law professor told the Financial Times.

9e99e3683a3c.text: By — Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/what-we-know-after-jensen-huangs-resignation-as-nvidias-ceo Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What we know after Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO Nation Nov 12, 2026 5:37 PM EST Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned from his top post at the chipmaker he co-founded, after reports of the tech titan's extramarital affairs came into the spotlight this week. One of those relationships has raised national security concerns. The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with a businesswoman U.S. intelligence suspects to be a Chinese spy, which Beijing denies. Separately, the outlet and later others reported that Nvidia employees said Huang had another affair with an executive who reported to him directly — compounding calls for him to step down. Nvidia announced Huang's resignation on Thursday, effective immediately. The California-based company said that Colette Kress — who has been Nvidia's chief financial officer and executive vice president since 2013 — will step into the role of interim CEO. The scandal marks the most tumultuous chapter yet for Nvidia, whose high-end chips have emerged as the leading building blocks for artificial intelligence. Huang himself has become a key face in the AI race, both across the industry and often on U.S. President Donald Trump's side in Washington. Here's what we know. Nvidia's new leadership Nvidia said Kress is now interim CEO. Prior to joining Nvidia over 13 years ago, Kress worked at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments. In a statement about her new post on Thursday, Kress said Nvidia's "strength has always come from its people" and that she's "committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years." Huang co-founded Nvidia, alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, back in 1993 — and until Thursday had led the company ever since, with no clear successor in sight. Huang's ouster has led to a scramble for a new permanent CEO, and Nvidia said it's considering both "internal and external candidates." The company's board of directors also said Thursday that it has named its first-ever chairman, Harvey C. Jones. Affairs in the spotlight Over the weekend, following news reports of Huang's relationship with a woman identified as former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, Nvidia's then-CEO apologized for being "unfaithful to my wife." "My actions hurt her and our children," Huang wrote in a Sunday email to employees, adding that his colleagues also "deserve better" from him. Neither Huang nor Nvidia identified who he had been intimate with by name, but the apology arrived shortly after Nvidia said it was investigating whether Huang had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort." Last month, the Times reported that U.S. intelligence agencies discovered Nvidia's Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, who also goes by the name Huang Le — and determined she was feeding information directly to Beijing. (Huang is a common surname and the two are not related). Nvidia initially maintained Huang would stay on as CEO as the company conducted its investigation. But scrutiny grew late Wednesday after reports emerged that Huang had a separate affair with an Nvidia executive. Huang's resignation arrived shortly after. The company didn't address either relationship in its Thursday announcement. Later on Thursday, Reuters reported Huang had an intimate relationship with a second employee, citing unidentified sources. Where investigations stand Nvidia hasn't provided any notable new updates in its internal review announced Sunday. At the time, the company said it had "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. Trump was reportedly briefed about intelligence findings involving Huang well before the scandal erupted publicly. But when asked over the weekend whether he wished he had acted sooner on that information, the president said "I don't think so" and maintained that Nvidia's CEO was an "honorable guy." Trump later said the FBI is looking into Huang's affair with Alice Huang, although where exactly that probe stands is unclear. Meanwhile, lawmakers from both sides of the aisle on Capitol Hill are calling for further investigations. Many eyes have been on Nvidia's ties to Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which prominently touts the companies' partnership on its website. Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was "no evidence" of such exports. On Thursday, Megaspeed maintained it takes its obligation to comply with American export control laws "extremely seriously" — and that it was committed to working "constructively and transparently" with the U.S. government. Singaporean authorities said they questioned Alice Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed. They concluded there wasn't enough evidence that she had committed a crime, but suspected she provided "inaccurate information" to downplay her role at Megaspeed and barred her from returning to the country. China, meanwhile, has denied that it attempted to ensnare Jensen Huang. Its Foreign Ministry earlier this week called the spying allegations "unsubstantiated" and said they amount to a smear campaign against Beijing. Trump continues his praise for Huang Huang has maintained a close relationship to Trump throughout the Republican president's second term in office. He's successfully lobbied for looser AI regulation overall — including less strict limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. And he's among tech CEOs who have dined at the White House, and even traveled on Air Force One. Trump has called Huang "smart"

f509f5983545.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press By — Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press By — Astrid Suárez, Associated Press Astrid Suárez, Associated Press By — Franklin Briceno, Associated Press Franklin Briceno, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/after-emotional-return-pope-leo-denounces-machismo-in-peru-and-demands-respect-for-women Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter After emotional return, Pope Leo denounces 'machismo' in Peru and demands respect for women World Nov 12, 2026 5:06 PM EST LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Thursday denounced widespread "machismo" and violence against women in Peru, demanding that women be protected and respected as he set out marching orders for his beloved Peruvian church and people. After his emotional homecoming Wednesday, the Peruvian pope got down to business and turned to the challenges facing a church and country he knows well. READ MORE: Pope visits care home in Argentina for people with disabilities, renewing call to protect the vulnerable He called on the influential Catholic hierarchy to be models of unity and communion, and instructed Peruvian bishops to accompany their flocks and respond to victims of clergy sexual abuse with truth and justice. But the 71-year-old pope also showed himself to be positively overjoyed to be home and as relaxed as he has been in public since his 2025 election. Leo sang along enthusiastically as 40,000 people in Lima's Plaza Mayor serenaded him with "Contigo Perú," a famous song from Peru's Pacific coast that celebrates national unity. He drew huge applause when he recited the lyrics of another famous Creole hymn, "Mi Perú." "It's a blessing not only for us Chiclayans but for all of Peru," said Ángel Esquives, a craftsman originally from Leo's former diocese in Chiclayo who now lives in Lima. He said he left his home at 3 a.m. to go to the historic center and stand in line to get as close as possible to the pope. As he showed in the first two legs of his South American trip, Leo was in fine form despite having undergone lung cancer surgery last month. He bounded up a steep flight of stairs Thursday morning without any apparent problems and joked with the bishops that some "doubting Thomases" had predicted he wouldn't be able to come. "But God is great and his grace is bigger than all of us and I'm very happy to be here with you," he said to applause. An appeal to protect and respect women In a speech to Peruvians in the plaza, Leo denounced the culture of "machismo" and violence against women that is prevalent in Peru, saying it went against the Christian teaching that proclaims men and women share equal dignity. "It pains us to see that violence against women — who could be our grandmothers, mothers, sisters or daughters — continues to be a reality that wounds all of humanity," he said. He noted that poor, Indigenous and Afro-Peruvian women are doubly penalized, and called for all women to be valued, protected and respected. Gender-based violence is an urgent social issue in Peru, which recorded 1,261 femicide victims between 2016 and 2024, according to the National Institute of Statistics and Informatics. During that period, the number of women killed because of their gender rose by 44%, suggesting the problem is only getting worse. "While we've made progress with women's suffrage and in being heard more, femicides are still on the rise — or at least they're receiving more attention," said Nicole Cruz, who was in the Plaza Mayor for the pope's speech Thursday. Cruz said she hopes the pope's words will help unite women and help "men understand that we're not complaining, but that we want help and to be loved and heard." A massive welcome home for 'Padre Robert' The former Robert Prevost spent two decades as a missionary priest and bishop in Peru and credits the place with teaching him how to be a shepherd. He in many ways has modeled his vocation as a bishop on the 16th century St. Turibius de Mogrovejo, the first archbishop of Lima. Mogrovejo is revered for having traveled long distances to be with his flock and for having defended the rights of Indigenous and enslaved peoples. He studied Quechua and Aymara and oversaw the printing of the Catechism of the Catholic Church in these Indigenous languages, because he believed the faith had to be transmitted in a language people could understand. Leo urged bishops on Thursday to model their vocation on his example. Being a bishop, he said, means "entering people's homes, accompanying the sick, meeting young people and reaching out to communities which, due to their geographical remoteness or social vulnerability, are rarely able to make their voices heard." While the clergy sexual abuse scandal hasn't exploded publicly in Peru as it has in other Latin American countries, Leo identified it as a "reality that has caused us so much pain." "We must respond as Jesus would, with truth, justice, forgiveness, making amends and an ever more resolute commitment to fostering a culture of prevention and protection for the weakest in light of such crimes," Leo said. The online database BishopAccountability has identified 77 priests, brothers, seminarians and lay consecrated in Peru who have been publicly accused of sexually abusing minors. But based on trends in other countries, the organization said that number is a "small fraction" of the total, arguing victims simply haven't come forward yet in the overwhelmingly Catholic country where the church wields significant influence. Leo, who was the Peruvian bishops' point-person to welcome victims while he was Chiclayo bishop, was expected to meet with survivors during his stay in Peru. A protest by a victims group was also planned later Thursday. Leo's friends say he is particularly attuned to Peru's needs Peruvian Cardinal Pedro Barreto, the president of the Amazonian bishops conference,

c6ce34a76a67.text: By — Matthew Perrone, Associated Press Matthew Perrone, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-trump-administration-officials-announce-ptsd-research-funding-for-psychedelic-drug-ibogaine Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Trump administration officials announce PTSD research funding for psychedelic drug ibogaine Politics Nov 12, 2026 4:58 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump. Watch the news conference in the video player above. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said his department is awarding up to $4.9 million to prepare for the first U.S. studies of ibogaine for post-traumatic stress disorder, a hard-to-treat condition linked to higher suicide and substance abuse rates among veterans. READ MORE: Trump signs order to hasten review of psychedelics The money will not go directly to patient research, Kennedy said, but to lay the groundwork needed to manufacture, dose and design studies of the drug. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Ibogaine is made from a shrub native to West Africa. It can cause intense hallucinations, nausea, vomiting, tremors and sometimes deadly irregular heart rhythms. Ibogaine is currently illegal, in the same ultra-restrictive class as LSD, ecstasy and most other psychedelic drugs. Veterans organizations and psychedelic advocates contend that ibogaine has great promise for intractable conditions such as PTSD, severe depression and opioid addiction. U.S. research on the drug has essentially been frozen for decades due to ibogaine's restricted status. READ MORE: RFK Jr. suggests psychedelic therapy for depression and trauma has Trump administration's support Kennedy said the government will receive data and treatment guidance from Beond Inc., a Texas-based company that has treated more than 3,000 patients with ibogaine in Mexico, where the drug is not illegal. "That is going to allow us to dramatically accelerate the clinical trial process," Kennedy said. "We're going to have, I think, a record drug approval process." Additional funding awards may explore ibogaine's use for addiction, he said. Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins, who joined Kennedy for the announcement, said the collaborative effort would focus first on safety and "best-in-class research." "For veterans living with PTSD, we owe them both urgency and the best science we can produce," Collins said. Kennedy and Collins have previously voiced support for the potential of psychedelics, citing the experiences of veterans who have traveled abroad for therapy with ibogaine and other mind-altering substances. Thursday's announcement was previewed in April, when Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to speed up review and research of psychedelics that could help with mental health conditions. Three applications for psychedelics are pending review at the Food and Drug Administration. They include the first potential medicines made from psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, and MDMA, also called ecstasy. Decisions on those drugs could come within weeks or months. Because of its safety risks, ibogaine research has moved more slowly. The little data currently available mostly comes from patients who have traveled to Mexico or other countries where ibogaine is not heavily regulated. Ibogaine clinics typically charge $10,000 to $20,000 for one course of treatment, which often involves monitoring of a patient's heart readings while emergency medical workers are on standby. Trump's order on psychedelics came after podcaster Joe Rogan said he texted Trump about ibogaine, which he repeatedly has discussed on his show. According to Rogan, the president quickly responded: "Sounds great. Do you want FDA approval? Let's do it." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The News
Republican and Democratic leaders are coalescing behind a new crackdown on advanced chip exports to China following the Nvidia scandal that could become law by the end of the year.
In the House, both Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries favor strengthening chip export controls following revelations that Nvidiaâs now former CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Thatâs raised national security concerns about the gargantuan chip manufacturer, which sold $4 billion in chips to Singapore company Megaspeed, which is suspected of diverting that technology to China and under investigation by the Justice Department.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune told Semafor that thereâs a âhigh probabilityâ that Congress imposes more restrictions on chip exports to China. Three measures were included in the Senateâs version of must-pass defense policy legislation, known as the NDAA, however both Thune and Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., acknowledged there is no deal yet to include them in the final version of the bill currently under negotiation between both chambers.
âI give it a better than even chance,â Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told Semafor of the possibility of strengthening export controls, which are handled by the Commerce Department. âI understand people have affairs but if youâre going to do it, try not to have an affair with a Chinese spy.â
Whatâs on the table
There are three main bills that could be included in the NDAA and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer wants Congress to pass all three of them âto cut off Chinaâs access to advanced American technology before itâs too late.â
The Chip Security Act aims to prevent illicit smuggling of advanced AI chips to foreign adversaries, partly by verifying their location once theyâve been shipped out. The MATCH Act closes loopholes around chipmaking equipment and export rules in allied countries. And the AI Overwatch Act would make it so chip sales are treated more like foreign arms sales and give Congress oversight of how Commerce approves or disapproves a license to sell chips to a âcountry of concern,â including China.
Johnson told reporters Thursday that thereâs âa developing consensus in Congressâ around more chip restrictions, calling it âan important position to take, especially in light of recent developments.â And Democrats like Jeffries have signaled their support for putting the AI-related provisions into the NDAA, as have some Republicans.
âI think the NDAA does provide us an opportunity to put guardrails around AIâ or export restrictions, said Rep. Mike Levin, D-Calif., who said heâd otherwise defer to Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the incoming House Armed Services chair.
Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., argued the Nvidia debacle âreinforcesâ the need for Congress to include more export controls in the defense bill, adding that thereâs âstrong demandâ to do so even as thereâs no final agreement on what it will entail.
âWhich plan takes priority in the final product, I donât know yet. I think thereâs several different strategies to be vetted yet,â Rounds said.
Why this year is different
During last yearâs NDAA fight, the GAIN AI Act from Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., an earlier version of the AI Overwatch Act, made it into the Senate version of the NDAA but got dropped from the House version after pressure from Nvidia, the broader semiconductor industry, and the White House (including then-AI adviser David Sacks). Congress did include some investment controls, but senators in both parties wanted to do more.
This year, the bills are much further through the process, buoyed unexpectedly by the Nvidia scandal and gaining momentum among GOP leaders, one Senate Democratic aide told Semafor. Anthropic has publicly supported all three bills, and OpenAI has been warming up to them as well after initially being reticent to support the proposals.
Nvidia hasnât stood alone in its opposition to the bills â the broader tech industry has also lobbied against them, with the Information Technology Industry Council arguing they would âundermine the American tech stack.â But Congress will feel more emboldened to act than ever giving the security risks exposed by the controversy.
Still, the defense bill, one of the few pieces of legislation that passes on an annual basis, could be imperiled by Democratic efforts to add provisions to sunset the war in Iran. Many in the party are pushing to use the must-pass legislation or a December government funding deadline as leverage over President Donald Trump, which could poison Republican support for the bills.
âWe have leverage. Take when the appropriations bills run out. I want the war in Iran stopped. I think we should put provisions into that bill, into the NDAA for that matter to stop it,â said Smith, the incoming House Armed Services Committee chair.
Democrats face tough decisions about how hard to push for those provisions now and risking a government shutdown or the failure of the defense bill, especially when they could put the legislation together on their own terms next year when they take control of the House and Senate.
Room for Disagreement
Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said Congress has already done âa lot before more than people probably realizeâ on restricting chip exports to China and that they need to think before they do more.
Thereâs also worry about going too far and inducing more Chinese manufacturing of chips by denying China technology.
âThis is a balance. Until someone comes up with a better construct, we need to put very strong export controls on the most powerful computer chips. That seems like a no-brainer to me,â said Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind. âThen the question is, how robust in terms of processing power can those chips be that we sent to them? â¦ I donât think itâs formulaic.â

A natural-gas project off Alaska may be a Russian ploy
Surveys for the plant were funded by a UAE company steered by a Russian natural-gas giant under U.S. sanction.
This story was originally published by ProPublica.
To an outsider, the research boats bobbing in the frigid and stormy Beaufort Sea off Alaska would seem little cause for alarm. Oil and gas companies have regularly explored the area for decades.
For this project, businessmen from the United Arab Emirates were touting a plan to tap the vast natural gas reserves that lay beneath the tundra of Alaska’s North Slope. They promised the operation would eventually be American-owned. No one could dispute Alaska’s dire energy needs — not to mention the potential for lucrative exports.
The surveyors last year used specialized equipment to map the depth and shape of the seabed, collect samples of shallow marine sediments and conduct sonar scans to check for obstructions such as shipwrecks. Documents show that their work was not far, as the crow flies, from the start of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System — a cornerstone of U.S. energy production. An Air Force long-range radar station sat just to the west. More than 100 miles off the coast, the Navy’s fast-attack nuclear submarines sometimes practiced surfacing through the thick Arctic ice.
But this project was far from routine. While the contractors performing the work were American, the UAE company paying for the surveys was actually being steered by Russia’s liquefied natural gas giant, Novatek — a company under partial U.S. sanctions, documents and interviews show.
The proposal to create an LNG processing plant on Alaska’s coast has already put reams of scientific data about the strategically critical region within reach of Novatek’s leader, an oligarch who is close to President Vladimir Putin, a ProPublica investigation found.
The Financial Times and The New York Times reported on the Russian ties to the venture last month. But the extent to which the company gathered detailed information about sensitive areas of Alaska has not been previously disclosed.
Such information is highly valuable in the ever-changing and unpredictable Arctic, with its potential routes for both naval ships and missiles. Norwegian security services and U.S. lawmakers have expressed concerns this year about the danger of increased spy and sabotage operations by Russia in the Arctic.
Russia-backed information gathering so close to the U.S. shoreline can be seen as “a direct challenge to sovereignty and security,” said Heather Conley, a former State Department official who is now a senior fellow with the American Enterprise Institute.
“It’s super, super sensitive,” she said, adding, “Any scientific data, it immediately is dual use,” meaning it can serve both military and civilian ends.
Information on changing sea ice and other conditions off the North Slope could help Russia plan activities that undermine U.S. security, said Troy Bouffard, director of the Center for Arctic Security and Resilience at the University of Alaska, Fairbanks. The fact that the surveys were given permits and done without interference could be seen as an intelligence failure, he said.
Bouffard added that it’s “highly unlikely” that intelligence personnel didn’t learn of the effort because any work in the austere, remote and militarily sensitive North Slope area stands out.
“All this is really surprising,” Bouffard said. “Should not have happened.”
The surveys were conducted in the second half of 2025, paused during harsh weather, then restarted in mid-2026, documents and sources say. By late August 2026, dozens of contractors were stationed on three large vessels — the Annika Marie, the Ukpik and the Uŋalaq — loaded with equipment for tasks such as monitoring waves, testing currents, and tides, and drilling core samples in the mud, according to a person familiar with the situation.
Then, in September, the CEO of the project’s U.S. arm, Polar Train LNG, resigned, questioned the operation’s legality and asserted it was a Russian ploy to gain control of a strategic U.S. asset, Alaska’s natural gas reserves.
In 2025, the survey work was focused on an area just west of Prudhoe Bay, which is near where the pipeline originates, documents and sources say. The next year, as the area thawed, Polar Train’s CEO, Joel Riddle, and his team told his financiers that location was not ideal for an LNG operation because of the high cost of dredging that would be needed and the potential to interfere with whaling by local residents. They urged the company’s UAE parent to focus on a site more than 250 miles to the west.
But the UAE company asserted its control over the purportedly American outfit Riddle led in late August and ordered the contractors offshore to head back to a site closer to Prudhoe Bay. Riddle resigned the next month, on Sept. 19, warning that Polar Train’s “investments” were “very likely sooner or later to trigger” a federal inquiry.
Polar Train had applied to the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control the month before, seeking a waiver of U.S. sanctions to allow it to purchase a partially built LNG plant sitting in a Murmansk, Russia, shipyard and transport it to Alaska.
“Deploying this technology in Alaska serves not only to unlock U.S. LNG resources in the Pacific basin closer to key export markets in Asia,” said the application, which ProPublica obtained, “but also to ensure this cutting-edge equipment is deployed primarily to the benefit of the United States rather than Russia.”
The six-page application did not make clear who was behind the effort, steering the financing and decision-making needed to get the venture off the ground. The document’s digital properties held a clue: Many computer applications include what is known as metadata in a document that can reveal who has previously worked on it. GOP tries to speed-walk search for GAO's next chief
Given 24 hours to name candidates, Democrats decry efforts to "ram through another Trump crony."
A lame-duck Congress is suddenly hastening the process to find a new long-term leader of a governmentwide watchdog agency that has drawn the ire of the Trump administration.
House and Senate Republicans faced calls over the past two years to start the bipartisan process of interviewing candidates to lead the Government Accountability Office.
Under the current process, the selection of the GAO comptroller general begins with a commission of 10 senior House and Senate lawmakers from both parties that recommends individuals for the position to the president.
Whoever the president selects is subject to Senate confirmation for one nonrenewable 15-year term. The last time lawmakers vetted candidates for GAO’s top job in 2010, the congressional commission spent more than a year on its search.
This time around, members of the commission are being given a single day to come up with candidate recommendations, after receiving notice on Veterans Day. The commission is meant to recommend at least three candidates for the job.
Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., requested commission members on Wednesday to submit candidates to serve as GAO’s next comptroller general within a 24-hour deadline, according to top congressional Democrats who criticized the expedited timeline as a “sham" process.
Paul is responsible for convening the commission. Congressional Democrats said the commission “has not interviewed a single candidate for this critical role, despite repeated requests to begin the process over the last two years.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Senate Homeland Security Governmental Affairs Committee Ranking Member Gary Peters, D-Mich., and House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Ranking Member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., called the fast-tracked nomination process a “transparent effort to ram through another Trump crony at the 11th hour, and undercut Congress’ ability to conduct effective oversight of the Trump Administration.”
“This is clearly a sham to enable President Trump to appoint a handpicked nominee to lead Congress’ watchdog. We cannot allow President Trump to install a fox in the henhouse at an agency Congress relies on to provide independent, nonpartisan oversight, and expose waste, fraud, and abuse across the Trump Administration,” they said.
The committee is currently slated to have a currently unnamed “nominee to be Comptroller General” slated to appear at a confirmation hearing next Thursday, along with nine other nominees.
“This is a 15-year nomination,” a HSGAC aide told Government Executive. “Really, they're just rushing through this entire process.”
The Washington Sun reported last month that the Trump administration is floating the idea of having Office of Management and Budget Deputy Director Eric Ueland serve as the next GAO comptroller general. The HSGAC aide said the committee is aware that Ueland’s name has been floated for the job.
Ueland said Monday at an industry conference that the Trump administration’s reshaping of the federal government has been “long overdue.”
“We have a high degree of confidence that the sorts of changes and improvements that we are making throughout the federal government – how it works, how it's able to cooperate and interact with itself, and ultimately how it delivers key services to the public – aren't partisan. They just make sense. And so we'll be able to both persevere and then compound that over time,” Ueland said at a conference hosted by the National Academy of Public Administration.
The Senate in May 2025 voted 52-45 along party lines to confirm Ueland as OMB's second-in-command. A potential vote to confirm him as GAO comptroller could come down to a few outgoing Republican senators who have challenged some of the Trump administration's decisionmaking.
The comptroller general position opened up in December 2025 when Gene Dodaro retired. Orice Williams Brown, the agency’s chief operating officer, is currently leading GAO in an acting capacity.
The Trump administration has criticized GAO, particularly over instances when the agency found that officials violated rules around impoundments, which is when the executive branch delays or withholds congressionally approved spending. Lawmakers also have accused agencies of not cooperating with and being slow to respond to GAO audits under the current president.
Sarah Kaczmarek, managing director of GAO’s Office of Public Affairs, said in a statement that "GAO has been preparing for a leadership transition and remains focused on its mission of providing Congress with independent, fact-based, and nonpartisan information to support its oversight and decision-making."
Daniel Schuman, executive director of the American Governance Institute, said that after failing to convene the statutorily-required commission for almost a year, “HSGAC Chairman Rand Paul should work to protect Congress's independent watchdog, not engage in an end run that undermines its credibility.”
“The position of Comptroller General is too important to rush through a lame-duck session of Congress, especially when doing so requires bypassing the law's requirement that a bipartisan congressional commission recommend well-vetted candidates,” Schuman said.
The bipartisan Commission is made up of the speaker of the House, the president pro tempore of the Senate, the majority and minority leaders of the House and Senate, HSGAC's chairman and ranking member, and the chairman and ranking member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

4e9f7436acea.text: Mississippi, a state with the largest share of Black residents in the country, has elected its first Black U.S. senator in nearly 150 years. Why it matters: For generations, Black Mississippians left the state to escape Jim Crow and pursue economic and political opportunities elsewhere. Now, Mississippi faces a new question: Was Scott Colom's victory a once-in-a-generation breakthrough, or the beginning of an era of Black political power? Driving the news: Colom's defeat of incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith broke a barrier that had stood since Reconstruction. Mississippi was the first state to send Black senators to Congress, before violence and disenfranchisement stripped Black residents of their political power. In Colom's race, Democrats gained ground in 75 of the state's 82 counties, Marvin King, an associate professor of political science and African American studies at the University of Mississippi, told Axios. "It wasn't just a fluke of super high turnout in one particular region," he said. "Scott Colom's victory can signal that maybe Mississippi is ready to govern differently." The big picture: During the Great Migration , roughly 6 million Black Americans left the South to escape discrimination and seek better opportunities. Many Black Mississippians built political power in Northern cities such as Chicago, said Keneshia Grant, a Great Migration expert at Howard University. For many, the question became, "should we go and try for a better life in these other places ... or should we stay and fight where we are?" Grant said. "It was about economic opportunity, but I also think it was about terrorism too," Cassandra Overton Welchlin, executive director of the Mississippi Black Women's Roundtable, told Axios, pointing to the lynchings that drove families away. Welchlin left Mississippi for graduate school and considered staying away. "I did not want to come back to Mississippi because it is hard here," she told Axios. Mentors encouraged her to return. She did, eventually becoming a voting rights organizer. Zoom in: "What Colom did is he really jazzed up his base. He didn't run from them," King said. "His campaign style and that strategy can certainly serve as a model" for future campaigns. Welchlin pointed to years of "nickeling and diming, doing organizing work to make sure that people had what they need to turn out the vote." Between the lines: Colom rode a Democratic wave and discontent with the Trump administration's economic policies, but those conditions may be difficult to recreate, said Andra Gillespie, who studies Black voter behavior at Emory University. Black residents make up roughly 37% of Mississippi's population, while most white voters favor Republicans. Unlike Georgia, Mississippi lacks the same diverse potential Democratic coalition. "[T]he conditions that we see this year are probably not going to be the new normal," Gillespie says. "It'd be way too early to diagnose that there's a realignment happening." Welchlin also cautioned that one historic victory doesn't mean Mississippi's racial barriers have disappeared. "We understand here in Mississippi that racism ain't over, ... Racism is still very much embedded in everything from our policies to our elections." What we're watching: Mississippi holds elections for governor, other statewide offices and state legislators in November 2027, testing whether Colom's coalition can hold. "For the first time in forever, Mississippi Democrats will go into an election with momentum," King said. The bottom line: Welchlin hopes Colom's victory changes how Black Mississippians view their futures: "I believe ... this election has given people hope that maybe I can stay here and be that change." Go deeper: The Mississippi Delta helped carry Scott Colom to Senate history

6c8eb9d29495.text: By — Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/alaska-judge-rules-a-request-by-peltola-campaign-for-ballot-data-in-senate-race-is-not-reasonable Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Alaska judge rules a request by Peltola campaign for ballot data in Senate race is 'not reasonable' Politics Nov 12, 2026 3:24 PM EST JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — An Alaska judge ruled Wednesday that a request by Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign for a list of absentee voters whose ballots have been rejected is "not reasonable," particularly given the time crunch election officials face as they continue counting ballots from last week's election. READ MORE: Judge weighs lawsuit brought by Peltola campaign over absentee ballots in Alaska's Senate race Ballots are still being tallied in the ranked vote election, in which Peltola and two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan are the main contenders. Alaska's is the only Senate race in the country that remained too early to call. The state accepts ballots up to 15 days after general elections from overseas voters, making Nov. 18 the final day to receive them. That date is also the Division of Elections' target for conducting ranked vote tabulations if no candidate wins more than 50% of the first-choice votes. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Attorneys for Peltola's campaign last Friday sued state elections officials, seeking a list of voters whose absentee ballots have been rejected and the reasons for the rejections. They said their intent was to ensure that all qualified voters have their ballots counted. But attorneys for the state said the information requested would violate voter privacy. They also said producing such a list from a voter database would constitute an "electronic service or product" that under state law may not take priority over an agency's main responsibilities. Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews, in a written ruling, said that "in theory" records from the voter database could be redacted and produced in a way that would allow their release. But he said the division is not required to disclose the records requested by the campaign because they "cannot reasonably be produced at this juncture, nor redacted of confidential information." The division has deadlines to meet and says its staff is working long hours to accomplish the agency's "fundamental responsibility" of administering elections, he wrote. "The timing of the Campaign's request could simply not be worse," Matthews wrote. An email seeking comment from one of the law firms representing Peltola's campaign was not immediately returned Wednesday, which was a holiday. The state Department of Law, which represented the Division of Elections, in a statement said it was pleased with Matthews' decision. Abha Khanna, an attorney for Peltola's campaign, said during arguments Tuesday before Matthews the campaign wasn't seeking to disrupt the ballot counting process. She said the absentee ballot review process was going "incredibly smoothly." But Khanna argued the information sought is a matter of public record and in line with what campaign observers have access to in locations where absentee review boards are meeting. The campaign wanted access to that information in a more centralized way, she said. Attorneys for the state have argued that reports generated by the division with lists of ballots to be reviewed during the absentee ballot review process are not public records because they contain confidential information and are "ephemeral working documents that are not meant for preservation." Michaela Thompson, who oversees the absentee ballot review boards for the division, said in an affidavit that the version of the report received by observers of the review process — including those affiliated with the campaigns — does not include as much confidential information but does include home addresses that many voters seek to keep private. The observers sign confidentiality agreements and cannot keep, copy or record information in the report, she said. The division's "old, inflexible" database cannot produce a report that excludes confidential addresses, meaning the agency would have to work with a vendor to create a more tailored report, Thompson said. Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.
Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.
The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.
Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.
Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.
The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.
Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.
Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.
Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."
The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.
"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.
Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.
Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.
Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.
He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.
Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.
Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

91b0f5bf6332.text: Jensen Huang's self-destruction has left a trail of collateral damage that threatens to ensnare the board of Nvidia and the AI boom itself . Why it matters: Huang was a singular leader in the global economy, capable of exciting or calming markets with a single sentence and viewed as a virtually indestructible force behind Nvidia's rise. The big picture: His sudden exit after reports of multiple affairs — one with a suspected Chinese spy and the other with a direct report — has wiped out more than $600 billion in value from Nvidia's market cap. "His visionary leadership is going to be missed — it's not going to be replaced," Joel Shulman, CEO of ERShares, which has owned Nvidia shares since 2005, tells Axios. Zoom in: With the uncertainty over Huang's tenure at Nvidia now resolved, the attention will quickly pivot to a slew of unanswered questions, including: What will the investigations uncover? Just because he's gone doesn't mean this is over. If the FBI probe or the independent investigation ordered by the board show that Huang gave favorable treatment to Megaspeed — the company led by the suspected spy Alice Huang — he and Nvidia could face serious consequences. Huang is also expected to testify behind closed doors next week before a Congressional committee. Critics say the Nvidia board wasn't fulfilling its duty to provide proper oversight of Huang — particularly if it had any reason to be aware of his reported affairs before they become public. Peter Jaworski, business ethics professor at Georgetown University, said the situation raises questions about what the board knew and when they knew it. Nvidia reps haven't responded to Axios requests for comment on the board's handling of the matter. Who takes the permanent role as CEO? CFO Colette Kress was named to the interim role, but the board is conducting a global search that will consider outside and internal candidates for a permanant successor. She "has built enormous credibility internally and externally and we are big fans of her strategically," tech bull Dan Ives wrote Thursday in a research note. Prediction markets point to Nvidia hyperscaling tech exec Ian Buck as the the leading candidate, but the political ramifications of Nvidia's position in the global economy may demand someone with more experience with geopolitics. President Trump suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook, whom Ives also floated, but Kalshi traders rate that as a 1 in 25 shot. Threat level: Could this be the catalyst that pops the AI bubble? Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy, with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars — and Huang is at the center of that vast flywheel, Axios' Zachary Basu writes . Next week becomes a "critical" moment with Tuesday's Nvidia earnings report and Thursday's likely Anthropic IPO, Shulman says. "This Nvidia story is going to take a little air out of the balloon for the Anthropic IPO," he says. The other side: Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at consultancy West Monroe, argued that Huang's departure won't change the demand for chips: "The company was never the source of AI demand. It has been supplying the capacity to meet that demand," which remains "enormous," he wrote today. Follow the money: Will Huang's exit fundamentally reshape the long-term competitive landscape of the chip industry? Competitors like AMD, Alphabet and Intel could benefit if chips customers are soured on working with Nvidia. "When a star leaves a Wall Street firm, the first question is always the same: did the clients sign with the banker — or with the bank? Nvidia is about to answer that question on the biggest stage in the market," writes Mark Malek, CIO at Siebert Financial. What's the floor for Nvidia's stock? Nvidia shares were down another 5.7% just before 3pm Thursday and are now down 27% over the last month, having lost about $1 trillion in value. "With this kind of leadership uncertainty, it's very difficult to predict where shares go over the next several trading sessions," writes Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management. "Sometimes huge news catalysts like this take all technicals out of the equation." The intrigue: Will someone take a risk on hiring Huang? Elon Musk has already hinted he could hire the former Nvidia chief as he moves toward a possible merger of SpaceX and Tesla . But it'll be hard for anyone to hire Huang unless and until the FBI probe in particular is resolved. The bottom line: The fallout is just beginning.

'We just ran' - One killed, four injured in shooting near Washington DC gym
One person has been killed and four others injured after a gunman opened fire in Washington DC.
The shooting began on Thursday morning local time inside a gym in an apartment building in the Logan Circle neighbourhood, which is about a mile (1.6km) north of the White House.
Police said the male suspect was "contained" after barricading himself in one of the apartments. They later confirmed he had died.
Of those injured, one is in a critical condition and the others have non-life-threatening injuries.
Authorities are still working to understand the exact timeline, suspect's motivation, and other details of the incident.

- Published
Eight people have died and 18 more were injured after a three-storey building collapsed in the Flatbush neighbourhood of Brooklyn, New York.
Witnesses described hearing a loud boom and seeing dust in the air as the building came down and fell into an adjacent construction pit where people were working on Wednesday.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, described a harrowing scene, saying workers "who had only barely survived themselves turned back and dug victims out of the rubble".
The city's fire commissioner, Lillian Bonsignore, said firefighters were on the scene within minutes and called their actions "incredibly heroic".
Speaking on Thursday, she said fire crews "are still in a recovery phase".
Despite the hard rain and falling temperatures at the site, she said, their efforts would continue until every victim was located.
Where is the collapsed building?
The building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn was constructed in the 1930s. It contained apartments and a store.
At the construction site next door, plans have been approved for a new building that will include 64 residential units and a grocery store on the bottom floor.
Active work was happening on the site, and it appears part of the building fell into the construction pit, trapping and killing some workers.
Why did the building collapse?
It is too early to say what caused the building to collapse at around 16:00 local time (21:00 GMT) on Wednesday, but officials say they are looking into the possibility of filing criminal charges.
The structure was fully occupied by residents, and construction workers were performing excavation work on a neighbouring site at the time, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
It's not clear if the construction had anything to do with the collapse, and the city's buildings department says it is still investigating.
Investigators have said developers have active permits for excavation and foundation work associated with the new building project. The developer has been identified as Robert Fischman.
In a post on X, Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said: "We are working closely with the Department of Buildings and our law enforcement partners to determine whether any criminal conduct contributed to this tragedy."
Mayor Mamdani later emphasised this message in a news conference, saying that every entity involved in the building and the construction site will be investigated, and held accountable.
Who was hurt?
Eight people - six adults and two children - were killed, authorities said. Two were construction workers.
A further 18 people were injured.
Mamdani said that six people were pronounced dead at the scene, while another two died in hospital.
Four of the injured are firefighters. One person still in hospital is in a critical condition.
None of the victims have yet been identified by city officials.
Mamdani said they were "our friends and our neighbours. Our parents and our children.
"Young families building their lives in our city, and immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Trinidad and beyond."
The consul general of Ecuador visited the site and confirmed that two victims are Ecuadorian nationals, the New York Times reported.
Gicela Andrade told newspaper that one victim, Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, will be flown back to Ecuador for burial. She identified the other victim as Gabriel Ariolfo Siguencia.
What are the conditions at the site?
More than 250 firefighters responded to the collapse, working through the night to locate trapped victims.
Reporters at the scene described the chaos, which occurred on a normally busy avenue of Brooklyn.
The head of the NY Department of Buildings, Ahmed Tigani, said in a news conference on Thursday that there were no violations of building codes reported at the building before the collapse.
He said the property developer has ties to at least 100 other sites around the city, which are also now being checked.
What are the weather concerns?
Forecasters predict scattered showers throughout Thursday, and then heavy rain across the New York region from 17:00 local time (22:00 GMT).
The CBS meteorologist for New York, Tony Sadiku, warns there is a possibility of severe storms later in the evening, which could hamper search and recovery efforts.
What did witnesses describe?
One man told the BBC that he had just delivered an Amazon package to an apartment just a few minutes before the building crumbled.
The man, who didn't want to share his name, described hearing a loud "boom" sound.
He was shocked to see the building he had just been in reduced to rubble, he said. Within a minute or two the fire department was on the scene with several trucks, and they quickly closed the street.
"I live literally right behind the building", Emmanuella Carilus told the New York Times. "It sounded like a big boom and you just heard a bunch of screaming."
The husband of one woman who was filmed being rescued spoke of his relief to CBS News New York.
"She is alive... I'm very happy. I'm very happy. I'm very happy. I thank all of you guys. She's pregnant, six months," he said.
With additional reporting by Nada Tawfik and Madeline Halpert in New York

A 370-acre (150-hectare) area of land on the edge of Cambridge has been returned to the care of the National Trust - for the first time in 60 years.
The area - known as Northfield - runs alongside the opposite side of Quy Road towards Bottisham, seven miles (11km) from the city and close to Anglesey Abbey.
The National Trust hopes to restore the natural site to create new wildlife habitats and improve community access to green space.
Emma Ormond-Bones, general manager of the National Trust's North Cambridgeshire Portfolio, said: "We want Northfield to become a place where nature can thrive, helping wildlife recover and building resilience to a changing climate."
The project comes at a time when Cambridgeshire remains one of the most nature-depleted counties in the UK, where demand for accessible green space is increasing as the county's population rapidly grows.
Northfield has been acquired by the trust for the first time since the 1960s, following an agreement with the owners.
The site has a rich natural and cultural heritage as well as a chalk stream, with the trust describing the area as "a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge".
There is evidence of human activity on the site stretching back thousands of years including the Roman period.
The National Trust said it hoped that, over time, species such as harvest mice, water voles and turtle doves would benefit.
Northfield is the first project within the trust's new masterplan for the area, which forms part of a wider Wicken Fen Vision and long-term initiative to "create a more connected and resilient landscape for wildlife and people stretching from Wicken Fen to the edge of Cambridge".
Ormond-Bones added: "Northfield has the potential to deliver meaningful benefit to both people and wildlife and we want local people to play a vital role in helping shape what that future will look like."
The charity said it was keen to understand what mattered most to local people and how the site would become a place people felt connected to, valued and enjoyed for generations to come.
Community drop-in sessions about the vision, external will be held between Saturday 21 November and Friday 27 November.
Feedback will be used to help inform the next stage of planning before proposals are developed during 2027.

d5ff0d0bfca7.text: Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday that he'll challenge Chuck Schumer for majority leader. Why it matters: Van Hollen's bid gives grassroots activists nearly three weeks to pressure Senate Democrats before they cast secret ballots in the Dec. 1 leadership election. The attempt to oust Schumer (D-N.Y.) underscores that deep divisions are plaguing the Democratic Party despite its overwhelming midterm success . Van Hollen (D-Md.) has served in the Senate since 2017 and has been in Congress since 2003. Schumer has been the Senate Democratic leader since 2017 and has served in the Senate since 1999. Driving the news: "In this election, the American people called for change," Van Hollen said in a statement on Thursday. "They called for a change from Donald Trump's disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn't working for working people." "It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader." In a statement of his own, Schumer said: "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader." Zoom in: Van Hollen acknowledged he's the "underdog" in the race but claimed Thursday on MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side. "[T]he time is now for change," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Tuesday. He appeared with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who demanded a plan for change from party leadership. Progressives have accused Schumer of not fighting hard enough against President Trump and the MAGA agenda. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) is a vocal backer of Van Hollen for majority leader. The other side: Schumer has far more public backers at this stage than Van Hollen. That includes Sen. Angus King (I-Maine), Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (Ohio) and Democratic Sens. John Fetterman (Pa.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Kirsten Gillibrand (N.Y.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii) and Sheldon Whitehouse (Rhode Island). Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and has been updated.
