Four top Australian Football League (AFL) players who were investigated in relation to an alleged sexual assault at a hotel in Melbourne earlier this year will not be charged, police have said.
After a "thorough investigation and based on legal advice" police would not proceed with criminal charges due to "insufficient evidence", police said in a statement.
Four Sydney Swans players - Isaac Heeney, James Jordon, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey, who now plays for North Melbourne - had been suspended for the rest of the season over the incident in August.
The men previously denied wrongdoing but apologised for breaching club standards by inviting women back to the hotel after a game and drinking.
Australian media reported that three women, understood to be adult entertainers, had alleged inappropriate touching during the incident at the Pullman Hotel and are looking into civil action.
"Due to the ongoing civil matter, Victoria Police is unable to make further comment," police said in a statement on Friday.
A fifth player, Riley Bice, who was also suspended by the club, had already been cleared by police.
A lawyer for one of the women said she was "devastated" by the police decision.
Jackson Pannam, of Slater and Gordon law firm, added that the move "does not amount to a finding that the incident our client reported did not occur, nor does it diminish the seriousness of what she says happened or its profound impact on her".
John Karantzis from Carbone Lawyers, acting for the other two women, told the ABC his clients were "very disappointed and distressed".
They would "vigorously pursue" a civil action, he said.
"My clients' civil claim is based on a different burden of proof, it is based on the balance of probabilities," he said.
Heeney welcomed the police announcement, saying the past three months had been "incredibly difficult for my family, [my fiancee] Steffie and those close to me".
"To my family and friends, your love and loyalty has meant more than words can do justice," he continued.
The Swans said in a statement that it had been "clear from the outset" that its decision to suspend the players was "separate from the police investigation, and it stands by that decision".
"The Club has commenced a comprehensive examination of its AFL program and is committed to acting on the findings and implementing meaningful change to build an environment that players, staff, members, supporters and corporate partners can be proud of," it said.
Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich told reporters it was "not a day for anyone to really celebrate" and "we're still looking very hard at the programme and understanding where we need to get better".
He said the club would be doing everything to "restore the standards that this club has held for a long period of time".
In a separate statement the AFL acknowledged the police decision and said it reserved the right to investigate should any further relevant information come to light.

State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say.
More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau.
"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.
This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) from the company.
US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim.
Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.
According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.
Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call â except that the audio would appear to malfunction.
A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims.
Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities.
The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user".
"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday.
"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough."

Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.
European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.
Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.
The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.
But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given.
Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."
He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table".
"He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.
Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".
Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.
Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) MicheÃ¡l Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war.
"Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.
Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common.
Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.
Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

For the last few weeks, in addition to its usual payload of passengers, medicine, and supplies, Alaska Seaplanes has carried some unique cargo: midterm election ballots.
The regional airline is a piece of a complex logistical puzzle that sees Alaskans' ballots cast by mail and in person carried across the vast expanse of America's largest state, which is primarily connected by water and air rather than roads.
This considerable task explains why, a week after most US states knew their results in the midterms - in which the Democrats won back both chambers of Congress from the Republicans - Alaskans are still waiting for the Senate race to be called.
The victor in this close contest between the incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan and his Democratic challenger, former congresswoman Mary Peltola, could remain unknown until 18 November, when officials expect to have counted all eligible ballots.
"We do feel a sense of pride of making sure we do the job right - the really complicated job of getting all these ballots across thousands of miles in Alaska," Andy Kline, the marketing director of Alaska Seaplanes, which serves the south-eastern part of the state, told the BBC.
"We feel like we're part of the last leg of that journey of those ballots."
Some precincts in Alaska are able to communicate their initial results to centralised election offices on election night, allowing state officials and news outlets to report some preliminary vote tallies.
But it takes some time for the full picture of how people have voted to emerge.
As well as having the logistical challenge of counting votes from across a state more than six times the size of the UK, there is a delay waiting for mail ballots to arrive, says Charles Stewart, an election expert at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
These ballots can arrive up to 10 days later, or 15 days for overseas voters, if postmarked by election day.
Stewart said that election officials had "chosen to err on the side of getting it right rather than a rush to report the second and third tranches of ballots that get counted".
Regardless of whether ballots were cast in person or by mail, all of them eventually wind up in the state capital of Juneau â which is only reachable by plane or boat â for scanning and counting.
While more urban districts can get their materials on a plane late on election night, it takes longer for smaller or more remote parts of Alaska.
In some places, "you get someone who's basically running the election for their family and their neighbours because it's such a small village", says Scott Kendall, an election lawyer who previously worked on two campaigns for Alaska's other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski.
In these smaller areas, ballots are sealed up in special envelopes or containers and sent it through the mail - which is where companies like Alaska Seaplanes comes in.
Ballots are put on the planes and sent to Juneau, where they then get dropped at the post office and delivered.
"It's part of our daily routine, just another couple of boxes," Kline said.
Once all the in-person and absentee mail ballots reach Juneau, election officials will complete their review.
If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote in the first round, officials will quickly use ranked-choice voting to re-allocate votes from the lowest-scoring candidates to their voters' second choices.
Then Alaska will finally declare a winner for its Senate race, as well as contests for governor and US House of Representatives.
Adding to the suspense of who will win the Senate race is the question of whether another Republican candidate called Dan Sullivan, who was allegedly recruited by Democratic operatives, would affect the outcome. Results released so far suggest a low probability.
This week, President Donald Trump alleged Alaska's Senate election had been "rigged" due to the second Dan's involvement. His administration is appealing its rejected lawsuit to halt certification of the election over the issue, which a lower court dismissed.
Meanwhile, a judge has denied an attempt by Peltola's campaign to get information about how many absentee ballots election officials rejected, as well as information about those voters.
The state argued it had no obligation to share this data, and doing so would violate voter privacy.
While the result of the election is of the greatest importance to many, for people like Kline the process is also key.
"We're all citizens," he said of himself and his colleagues.
"We all feel like we have skin in the game to make sure that our elections are accurate and timely."

ca1994eb9eea.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/high-airfares-may-become-new-norm-as-jet-fuel-costs-soar-says-asia-pacific-airline-industry-chief Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter High airfares may become new norm as jet fuel costs soar, says Asia-Pacific airline industry chief World Nov 13, 2026 11:06 AM EST KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia (AP) — High airfares could become the new norm as airlines contend with soaring jet fuel prices and mounting operating costs, the Association of Asia Pacific Airlines' chief said Friday. Wong Hong, director-general of the association grouping 18 airlines in the region, said carriers were trying to contain ticket prices while protecting their finances and avoiding fare increases that could drive passengers away. But the industry is operating in a substantially different cost environment from a year ago when jet fuel was about $80 a barrel, compared with around $180 currently, he said. Fuel accounts for a third of airline operating costs, making further price increases a threat to carriers' financial performance, he said. READ MORE: What to know if your flight is canceled as jet fuel costs rise "I believe so," Wong said after an AAPA conference when asked whether high airfares would become a lasting feature rather than a temporary adjustment. "We are living in completely different market conditions and a completely different cost environment ... and it looks like these high prices will continue to prevail." On whether airlines could implement another round of fare increases if fuel prices remain high, Wong said there was no clear answer as passenger price sensitivity varies across markets. Major airlines across the Asia-Pacific, Europe and North America have raised base fares, hiked fuel surcharges or added extra fees since the Iran war began in late February. The AAPA's data showed that passenger traffic across Asia-Pacific slumped for five consecutive months from April to August, before rebounding marginally in September. For the first nine months this year, overall passenger traffic in the region still grew by 1.9%. WATCH: U.S. inflation report highlights strain of rising food, energy and housing costs "Airlines will try their best to hold on to the fares that they can charge without trying to lose passengers, but it is a tricky dilemma," Wong said. Airlines face a mismatch between ticket sales and fuel purchases, complicating their ability to manage rising costs, he said. Passengers often book flights months in advance, locking in fares before airlines purchase the fuel needed to operate those flights. Beyond fuel costs, Wong said airlines continued to face supply side challenges including aircraft delivery delays and the high cost of maintaining older aircraft. But he said carriers had shown resilience and travel demand remained strong. Airlines are doing their best to find the right levels in different markets to strike a balance between absorbing higher costs and pricing passengers out of the market, he added. 579523ff4775.text: It took just minutes for a gunman to shoot six people and upend one of D.C.'s busiest neighborhoods. The big picture: Thursday morning's violence left one person dead in a Logan Circle gym and five others injured nearby. The gunman later shot himself, police said. The massive police response shut down streets, sent nearly a dozen schools into lockdown and forced residents to shelter in place. By evening, the streets around VIDA Fitness, where the shooting began, were quiet. Several nearby businesses remained closed, with police tape blocking off storefronts and officers standing watch. Councilmember Brooke Pinto held a vigil . People left flowers and notes outside of the VIDA . "Logan Circle is still a place for love," read one. "VIDA, you are and will continue to be a safe haven for many," read another. But life also carried on: A delivery van unloaded Christmas trees at Whole Foods, and 14th Street bars put out signs advertising happy hour. Flowers and handwritten notes line the outside of VIDA Fitness. Photo: Mimi Montgomery/Axios One note reads: "VIDA, you are and will continue to be a safe haven for many." Photo: Mimi Montgomery/Axios What we know: At an afternoon press conference, interim MPD chief Jeffery W. Carroll identified the suspect as 55-year-old Matt Wade Lambert, who lived in the apartment building connected to VIDA Fitness. The man killed was 46-year-old James Stuart, the building's manager and a Northwest D.C. resident, Carroll said. Police believe the shooting was linked to an ongoing dispute between Lambert and his condominium association over maintenance issues, including mold. The timeline: Police responded to a shooting inside VIDA Fitness, at 15th and P streets NW, just before 8am. Additional reports of shootings nearby followed. Carroll said the shootings themselves likely unfolded in less than five minutes, though investigators are still reconstructing the timeline. Police announced a sixth shooting victim — a woman with nonfatal injuries — on Friday morning, per the Washington Post . The victims: Stuart was pronounced dead inside VIDA. Police say the gunman then returned to his apartment, where he fired at people below from an upper-level private balcony. Two men and two women were hospitalized, one of whom suffered serious injuries. The standoff: Lambert barricaded himself in his apartment, where he broke a gas line connected to his fireplace and started a fire inside the apartment, per police. Flames were visible outside the building, but sprinklers helped contain the blaze. Police recovered gasoline and other flammable materials. Police negotiators heard a gunshot while speaking with Lambert by phone, after which he stopped responding. Officers forced entry and found him suffering from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The weapons: Investigators recovered a handgun, shotgun and rifle from Lambert's apartment. Carroll said the suspect used all three firearms, none of which were registered in D.C. People stand behind police tape in Logan Circle early Thursday. Photo: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images A U.S. Park Police helicopter flies above the scene. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images U.S. Marshal officers move position at the scene of the Logan Circle shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Residents cross a street as law enforcement responds to the shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Behind the scenes: Lambert had been fighting his condo association over alleged leaks and mold, per court records. He filed a lawsuit against the group in March 2025. Months later, he told now- Washington Sun reporter Michael Brice-Saddler that he'd spent nearly $200,000 on legal and engineering fees. In those interviews, Lambert said he knew Stuart's daily gym routine. What we don't know: Police have not determined whether Lambert knew the five surviving victims or deliberately targeted them. The precise timeline and extent of the suspected planning also remain under investigation. Context: The shooting prompted a massive response from local and federal authorities, including MPD, D.C. Fire and EMS, U.S. Park Police, Metro Transit Police and other federal law enforcement agencies. Asked whether the show of force was due to the shooting's proximity to the White House, roughly a mile away, Carroll said it was because police were responding to an active shooter. "The expectation is folks will go there to try to stop the loss of life," he said. Mayor Bowser confirmed the White House had been briefed. President Trump has surged federal law enforcement in D.C. through his Safe and Beautiful Task Force . In a speech before the midterms last week, Trump declared D.C. "one of the safest cities in the country." Asked about Trump's role in reducing crime during Thursday's morning briefing, Bowser pushed back: "I praise MPD for bringing down crime in the city, and I praise our prosecutors." Editors note: This story has been updated to add details about a sixth shooting victim.

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.
It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.
In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.
The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.
Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.
When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.
This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.
These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”
Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.
“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed the Commerce Department, run by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec Nvidia chips, as the fallout from the scandal widens.
Jensen Huang left Nvidia after revelations he had an affair with a former Megaspeed executive who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. The firm had been buying advanced chips from Nvidia.
Megaspeed had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it had been smuggling chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms that US companies are prevented from working with.
Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.
There is growing pressure on Lutnick from both sides of politics to explain his department's actions.
He has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to keep all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.
Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.
"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.
There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.
However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.
"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme, external.
"The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?
"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."
Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The Commerce Secretary has been summoned to appear before the committee in December.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.
Democrats on key congressional committees have also asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E. Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations over the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.
According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection.
A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security.
"Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

Now, sweeping Democratic gains in Congress have shifted the balance of power in Washington, teeing up an onslaught of expected investigations into those actions and others as well as scrutiny from the majority party that the current Justice Department had until now managed to skirt. Political pressure from the White House is unlikely to wane given the promotion of Stephen Miller, a devoted Trump loyalist, to chief of staff. The divisions will have temporary leaders but are unlikely to get Senate-confirmed ones in light of the Democratic majority. "What that means for DOJ, potentially, is just a lot of inaction, with tough decisions not being made because typically those tough decisions are made by confirmed people at the top of the components," said Greg Brower, a former U.S. attorney in Nevada during President George W. b5bdf3ffe612.text: The director of the Israeli spy agency Mossad is in Washington Friday for talks with senior Trump administration officials about the war in Iran , according to three sources with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters : The visit by Roman Gofman, one of Benjamin Netanyahu's closest confidants, comes as the Israeli prime minister is pressing President Trump to resume the war against Iran. Driving the news: Gofman is meeting with CIA Director John Ratcliffe, the sources said. He is also expected to travel to Miami to meet White House envoy Steve Witkoff, one of the sources said. Mossad, the CIA and the White House declined to comment. State of play: Trump has so far rejected pressure from Netanyahu to return to combat. The two discussed the Iran war during a Nov. 5 call, per a U.S. official. Instead, the president has sided with Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE to continue the naval blockade and economic pressure campaign against Iran, while seeing if a deal is possible. "I could end it immediately. At the request of the nations that I'm looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a little bit more civilly," Trump said on Thursday. "Saudi Arabia has asked me to please just let it be the way it is now for a while, because [Iran is] disintegrating. Qatar, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain, all of them would much prefer the waiting period." The intrigue: Netanyahu has lost his majority in parliament after the Oct. 27 election in Israel. His opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, has received a mandate to form a new government. It is unclear whether he'll be able to do so. In the meantime, leaders of the Israeli opposition are concerned Netanyahu will try to launch an attack on Iran — or provoke Iran to attack Israel — in order to undermine Eisenkot's efforts, sources say. Netanyahu would be removed from power if Eisenkot succeeds. On Thursday, Netanyahu met with Eisenkot for two hours and briefed him on the situation with Iran. A source close to Eisenkot said he doesn't think the current situation demands immediate military action against Iran.

School children are taking part in an event aimed at inspiring climate action, to coincide with the COP31 international climate conference in Turkey.
Hosted at the Kingston Maurwood campus, the first Dorset-wide Youth COP has brought children from 14 schools together to discuss issues including future careers.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said young people should be "given a voice" over dealing with climate change.
A Dorset COP 2026 event is also being held on Saturday as world leaders and delegates gather at Antalya in Turkey for the COP31 climate summit.
The Dorset Youth COP event includes discussions about how young people feel about climate change as well as a panel session introducing them to the range of jobs and careers in the climate and energy sectors.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said: "Young people are inheriting the climate and ecological emergencies that previous generations have created and need to be given a voice in jointly developing and implementing the solutions to these issues."
"The Youth COP aims to raise awareness, inspire and support them to take action now and into the future."
The main Dorset COP 2026 event takes place on Saturday also at the Kingston Maurward Campus near Dorchester.
The fourth annual event brings together community groups, environmental organisations, experts and political leaders.
The programme will explore how Dorset can respond to climate change, nature loss, food resilience, pollution and other environmental challenges.
The programme will also feature an exhibition of over 30 local organisations and a Question Time-style panel bringing together Dorset MPs, council leaders and independent climate experts.
Giles Watts, chair of Dorset CAN said the event's focus was on making "a lasting positive impact" on climate and nature local areas.
"We want to bring people together, listen to different perspectives and energise local communities and politicians to act more quickly on the pressing challenges we face," he added.

Alexisâs view
Jensen Huangâs shock exit from Nvidia could prove to be a turning point in the rollout of AI in Africa. The technology offers the potential to turbocharge economies across the continent, but chips form the backbone of this revolution. And, as our San Francisco Bureau Chief Reed Albergotti put it, âHuang was Nvidiaâs one-man, long-term moat.â Without Huangâs singular vision, thereâs uncertainty. The questions swirling in the wake of his departure are a reminder that the development of African compute still relies on hardware and software supplied by US companies.
Huangâs resignation raises questions, for example, about the US chipmakerâs relationship with Cassava Technologies: Nvidia last year became an investor in the pan-African digital infrastructure company, which it supplies with chips. The partnership is central to Cassavaâs push to expand services in the more than 30 African countries in which it operates. Nvidiaâs financial commitment and supply of hardware offered an opportunity for African companies to access the compute needed to train and run their own AI models.
If Huangâs successor takes a different approach, the Cassava partnership may not be replicated elsewhere on the continent, limiting the access African firms have to cutting-edge technology.
The implications extend to the public sector, too. Only last month, the World Bank named Nvidia and Cassava as partners in an initiative aimed at expanding digital access in Africa to improve services and create jobs.
Any change in Nvidiaâs strategy would, in the long term, have the biggest implications for South Africa. The continentâs largest economy is home to about 40% of its roughly 160 data centers. So next weekâs visit by South African President Cyril Ramaphosa to the US is well-timed.
Ramaphosa, who will speak at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World event, will be accompanied by a delegation that includes his ministers for finance, trade, and energy. He plans to meet tech executives, researchers, and investors during his trip, which will focus on AI infrastructure. Ramaphosaâs team has described it as an attempt to position South Africa as a âcompetitive AI hubâ on the continent â but itâs shaping up to be a first peek at Silicon Valley after the departure of one of its central figures.

- Published
A major global Microsoft outage has caused problems with emails and artificial intelligence products, affecting systems used by schools, healthcare, courts and governments.
Efforts to completely resume services remain ongoing after problems were first reported on Thursday.
Microsoft said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident.
Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.
What happened?
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".
Customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.
Some users have been able to use Teams and are using messaging and online meeting functions without issues.
Will emails sent during the outage ever arrive?
Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery".
In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away.
Earlier, Microsoft said it was extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up".
The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email.
When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent.
How many people have been affected?
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website.
The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening.
The real figure affected is likely much higher because Downdetector relies primarily on users self-reporting.
Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems as a result of the outage.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected.
From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas warned that communications might be delayed.
In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.
The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.
Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.
What has Microsoft said?
Microsoft has ruled out a cyber-attack and attributed the ongoing outage to "elevated load" on its infrastructure.
The term refers to when servers are handling a much higher volume of stress than they usually do.
In the case of the Microsoft outage, a large number of servers became "unexpectedly unavailable", the company said, which sent added traffic to remaining servers, straining these.
On Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.
The company added it is focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" and warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue".
In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".
Why has it taken so long to fix?
Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming for some, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.
Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues.
"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.
"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.
"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.
"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."
The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.
Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".
He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.
Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.
"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.
"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.

DR Congoâs president has signed a law allowing the constitution to be changed or replaced through a referendum, a move opponents warn could pave the way for him to seek a third term in the mineral-rich country. FÃ©lix Tshisekedi, in power since 2019, is due to complete his second and final term under the current constitution in just over two years. He said in May he was not seeking constitutional changes to stay in power, but would accept a third term if the Congolese people wanted it.
The country was ruled by dictator Mobutu Sese Seko for three decades until his overthrow in 1997. After years of war, its 2006 constitution introduced safeguards against a return to dictatorship, including presidential term limits. But Tshisekediâs predecessor, Joseph Kabila, still stayed in office for two years after his final term expired.
Opposition leaders have joined forces to resist any attempt to extend Tshisekediâs rule, organizing protests at home and seeking support from European governments. They argue that a referendum cannot override the constitutionâs ban on changing presidential term limits.

Nvidia got caught without a succession plan for CEO Jensen Huang, but it wasnât for lack of trying, according to people briefed on the effort to hire a replacement. The next Nvidia CEO doesnât just have to keep its own products shipping on time. The person who takes the top job also has to keep the entire industry alive. Thereâs really no replacing him.

423b01f0850d.text: Oil markets are heading into an unusual period as the Iran conflict remains in dangerous limbo: The supply crunch is easing, but prices could stay stubbornly high. Why it matters: While gasoline prices have dropped lately, don't expect pre-war levels anytime soon even as Middle East exports fitfully recover. Getting oil out of the region is expensive, which filters down to consumers. The threat of new attacks can keep oil costs higher, too, thanks to the risk premium embedded in prices. The big picture: Traders are watching the state of potential diplomacy — and the possibility of a prolonged stalemate. Oil prices jumped yesterday after President Trump said on his Truth Social that "we don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed." Driving the news: Crude oil export levels bounce around, but have recently returned to pre-war levels at times, barrel-tracking firms and analysts say. Yet shipping threats will "persist in 2027," and attacks spiked last month ( see the chart above ), per political risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft. A new agreement on navigating the Strait of Hormuz would just be a piece of the puzzle — if it ever happens. "The threat of a renewed wave of shipping attacks will remain high as long as the underlying confrontation over Iran's nuclear and missile programmes remains unresolved," the firm's analysis states. Catch up quick: Tracking how much supply is returning is a moving target, and higher production from countries outside the Middle East — including the U.S. — matters too. The oil market is "showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the International Energy Agency said this morning . Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf region rose to 82% of pre-war levels last month, though recovery of refined product shipments is weaker, its monthly analysis states. With supply rising and oil demand lowered by the conflict, IEA predicts the global market will return to a surplus this quarter. Yes, but: Insurance and shipping costs are elevated, and that puts upward pressure on prices. "Both Iran and the Houthis have demonstrated that they can severely restrict oil flows from the region using a range of attacks and tactics. This is something that will have to be priced in," Torbjorn Soltvedt, a senior Verisk analyst, tells me via email. And there's no guarantee that higher tanker transit and increased shipments through pipelines that avoid the Strait of Hormuz won't be curtailed by fresh attacks. Zoom in: Goldman Sachs estimates that the tanker market's "adaptation to Mideast shipping risks" accounts for most of the $20-per-barrel year-over-year increase in average costs for shipping oil. These freight rates reflect vessel availability, insurance, fuel cost, logistics, travel distances and more. What we're watching: It's unclear how much more oil can keep leaving the region in the near term, as intermittent attacks keep happening. "The current recovery may be close to the limit of what the existing logistics system can sustain," HSBC's Kim Fustier said in a recent note. The bottom line: "We would not equate [oil] exports with normality," Fustier writes. She cited substantial volumes of well production that remain curtailed, lower refined product shipments, and "and the cost of sustaining exports." Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

The Scoop
The FTC is flexing its regulatory muscle again.
The antitrust regulator is planning to file suit to block a $3.5 billion veterinary deal later today, according to people familiar with the matter, seeking to prevent a private equity-owned company from acquiring a smaller rival.
The regulator plans to cite increased costs for pet owners and veterinary clinics as part of the suit to block CD&R and TPG-owned Covetrus from acquiring MWI Veterinary Supply, the people said. Covetrus and MWI are both national suppliers of medical supplies and products. The Commission believes that the combination would result in a highly concentrated market, the people said.
Neither Covetrus nor MWI returned a request for comment.
Rohanâs view
Under Andrew Ferguson, the FTC, unlike the Justice Department, has managed to focus on its regulatory mission â even if it has allowed many mergers to pass uncontested.
It has used its enforcement tools to execute President Donald Trumpâs agenda, which has recently centered on affordability. It is that focus, Washington insiders say, that has now given Ferguson a degree of latitude to pursue cases and merger enforcement that he desires.
The FTC is also planning to block a $5 billion merger of two uniform and office equipment suppliers, Semafor reported. The FTC plans to set a last-rites meeting â a precursor to that formal suit â in the coming days, other people familiar with the matter said.

The News
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa is due to land in California this weekend for a week-long push to court billions in American AI infrastructure investment.
The roadshow will throw him into the backyard of Elon Musk, the worldâs richest man, whose regulatory clash with Pretoria is at the center of a widening diplomatic rift with Washington. Ramaphosa is likely to face questions about domestic ownership rules which Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has slammed as âopenly racistâ and cited as the reason his Starlink satellite-internet venture does not operate in Africaâs biggest economy.
The working visit, which kicks off on Monday at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & the World summit, unfolds against a deepening diplomatic row as Washington steps up pressure against Pretoria over everything from race policies to its foreign policy choices. South Africa was recently also removed from the African Growth and Opportunity Act preferential trade program.
US Ambassador L. Brent Bozell III warned in recent weeks that South Africaâs mandatory local equity ownership transfers under Black Economic Empowerment laws, a policy designed to address dispossessions caused by South Africaâs racist past, are holding back âbillions with a Bâ in American capital.
Ramaphosa, whose itinerary includes meetings with Google, Cisco, Palo Alto Networks, and Microsoft, is bringing eight cabinet ministers, including his finance, trade, energy, and communications chiefs â in a bid to capture a slice of Americaâs $650 billion AI capital expenditure this year.
Speaking to the press ahead of the trip, Ramaphosaâs spokesman Vincent Magwenya said South Africa aims to court American capital while firmly âsafeguarding digital sovereignty, policy autonomy, data protection, and responsible AI governance.â
The BEE controversy
Under South Africaâs BEE rules, companies in regulated sectors like telecoms and mining must hand at least 30% of their local ownership to Black people to secure operating licenses â a redress policy that prompted Bozell to say that âtime for dialogue has endedâ after South Africa failed to meet US demands for regulatory reforms, and executive condemnation of inflammatory political rhetoric.
The stand-off has triggered US visa restrictions on unspecified South African officials deemed responsible for âgovernment sponsored discrimination,â led Washington to pull PEPFAR funding to the country, which poured $8 billion into treating the worldâs largest HIV/AIDS caseload over two decades, as well as the AGOA ejection.
Tiisetsoâs view
Ramaphosaâs flight to California deliberately skips a potentially frosty reception in Washington. The itinerary, which starts off at Semaforâs inaugural Silicon Valley & The World summit, tells you everything you need to know about Pretroiaâs game plan. It is a bold geopolitical arbitrage, an attempt by Pretoria to wall off diplomatic tensions to chase a slice of billions of dollars in AI spending.
Pretoria has reasons to believe US boardrooms can look past Washingtonâs hostility. To start with, boardrooms seem to have a high tolerance for political noise when the economics make sense, if what has been happening in the background is anything to go by. The value of trade between these two countries rose in 2025, industrial giants such aluminum producer Alcoa and transportation behemoth Wabtec keep writing checks despite tariffs, visa curbs, and Bozellâs warning that billions in investment are frozen over South African domestic policies.
Next week, we will find out if commerce can keep outrunning politics.
Room for Disagreement
Sakeliga, a pro-business lobby group, took South Africaâs telecoms regulator to court, arguing that forcing companies to hand over 30% of their local equity to obtain a license acts as a hard barrier to entry that shuts out global players like Starlink.
Notable
- SpaceX has floated a $110 million local infrastructure commitment alongside hundreds of millions rand in free satellite broadband for rural schools as an alternative to handing over its local equity to Black South Africans.

- Published
The UN's nuclear watchdog has said it is "increasingly concerned" about a nuclear facility in Iran which it has not been allowed to inspect.
Iran informed the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of plans to set up the uranium enrichment plant in the city of Isfahan a day before Israel began attacking its nuclear sites last June. The US joined the strikes later that month.
In a report seen by news agencies, the IAEA said it does not know the exact location or whether it contains nuclear material.
Since the start of the latest war, Iran has restricted IAEA inspectors' access to its nuclear sites, preventing the agency from verifying its enriched uranium stockpile.
Under a 2015 nuclear deal, Iran agreed to limit its enriched uranium stockpile to 300kg and enrichment to 3.67% purity. It subsequently exceeded both.
Before the June 2025 strikes, it had accumulated an estimated 441kg enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade.
The nuclear complex at Isfahan suffered extensive damage in US and Israeli strikes, particularly the parts above the ground. The condition of its underground facilities is not clear.
The IAEA believes much of Iran's highly enriched uranium was stored there.
"The Agency's lack of information about [Iran's] nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern... and needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency," it said in the latest report.
Iran announced plans for the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP) on 12 June 2025, shortly after an IAEA resolution which declared Iran had failed to meet its nuclear safeguards obligations.
Iran initially agreed to allow inspectors to visit the facility, but the inspection was cancelled after Israel launched attacks the following day.
The IAEA's latest calls come almost a year after it made a similar appeal to Iran. At the time it said it had only inspected some of the 13 nuclear facilities that were "unaffected" by the attacks and none of the seven that were.
The US and Israel said they attacked Iran's nuclear sites to prevent it developing nuclear weapons - something Iran has consistently denied seeking. It says its nuclear programme is for peaceful civilian purposes only.

cff244ad535c.text:
The Scene
When Massachusetts-based Commonwealth Fusion Systems looked for companies that could produce large metal components and complex machinery for its prototype, it landed on the oil and gas industry. CEO Bob Mumgaard said the hydrocarbons industry shares many of the same skills and tools that fusion developers need to achieve a breakthrough and eventually take a share of the energy mix.
The UAE is well positioned to use its expertise in oil and gas to adopt fusion technology, Mumgaard said, especially after it has developed a track record of building nuclear power plants and its embrace of AI. âThey understand what energy leadership and first mover advantage, advanced technologies can bring to their society, their place in the world,â he said.
Abu Dhabiâs government-owned fusion fund, Plynth Energy, acquired a minority stake worth more than $100 million in Commonwealth this year, according to Axios. The US company raised $1 billion in July, bringing its total funding to $4 billion, which Mumgaard said would be enough to build the prototype and prepare for a larger, utility-scale plant in the early 2030s.
Next decade
Scientists have long predicted that the fusion breakthrough is a decade away. The prospect of unlimited, clean, and safe power is tantalizing, and it now appears that mastery of the reaction that essentially powers the stars is within reach.
Commonwealthâs Massachusetts prototype uses powerful magnets and hydrogen isotopes (deuterium and tritium) to produce a reaction thatâs hotter than the sunâs core. The machine is about 80% complete, Mumgaard said, and is due to start up in 2027. Its goal is to show that it can release more energy than it takes in.
The company then plans to build a 400-megawatt plant in Virginia and has secured Google and Italian energy company Eni as buyers, Mumgaard said.
Global adoption at scale is still decades away, but Mumgaard said the US-Iran conflict is also making the case for accelerating research and deployment. âFusion is one of the most secure, resilient energy systems because it doesnât need pipelines or ships, and it doesnât have emissions,â he said.
Notable
- Former Abu Dhabi government official Tareq Alotaiba explains why the country is betting on fusion, in a Semafor column.
- The International Atomic Energy Agency lays out the science behind nuclear fusion in this explainer.

How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?
The answer is very.
The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.
Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.
Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.
But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.
Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.
But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.
The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.
US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?
That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.
On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.
A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny.
Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.
There were also questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.
This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.
Now the political pressure is building.
Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.
And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.
Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.
Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.
The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.
It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".
That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.
There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?
The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.
The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.
This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.

Some bin collections were missed over the summer in a county partly because the heatwave became so serious it posed a risk to the lives of workers, a council worker has said.
Flintshire County Council's Chris Goddard said crews faced a "perfect storm" of challenges during the UK's record-breaking hot weather, causing a spate of widespread missed collections.
During the summer, drought was declared in all of Wales and wildfires caused devastation in parts of the country.
Goddard said: "We do have to make some difficult decisions but ultimately if there is a fatality in the workplace because of a decision I've made, that's something that I would have to live with â and probably defend."
Despite the missed collections the council remained on target to hit the Welsh government's national 70% waste recycling target this year, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.
Goddard, the council's streetscene service manager, said: "We had maybe five or six operational challenges that all came at the same time in a perfect storm this summer.
"Unfortunately, the heatwave was one of them and it was a contributing factor. We do have to prioritise staff safety above all else.
"My number one job every day is to make sure that everybody goes home safely and we take that really seriously within streetscene. That was only one of several contributing factors.
"That level of change is naturally going to cause a few bumps in the road, particularly with staff being asked to do a little bit more. There were some staffing issues during that period too."
Councillors praised Flintshire residents for largely embracing three-weekly residual waste collections and ensuring that the authority remained on-target to hit its statutory recycling rate.
"Three-weekly was very controversial at the time it came in," said Saltney councillor Richard Lloyd.
"It's quite clear to see now that the three-weekly black bin collection has been a good new factor. Recycling has improved at the kerbside."
Councillors said in the authority's meeting the change to three-weekly bin collections meant the council should still hit target despite the disruption.
The council also cut the amount of waste it sent to landfill or Parc Adfer by 6,467.49 tonnes between 2024 and 2026, and that improvement continued this year despite problems this summer.

Four Nigerian students have died after attending a party in the south-eastern town of Nsukka to celebrate the end of their final exams.
The cause of death has not been confirmed but police spokesman Daniel Ndukwe said the two men and two women had reportedly fallen ill after consuming alcoholic drinks at the party.
The University of Nigeria Nsukka has declared three days of mourning, during which academic and social activities will be suspended.
The tragedy comes amid a wider crackdown on fake and adulterated alcoholic drinks in Nigeria, where the food and drug regulator has been raiding suspected producers of unsafe food and beverages.
The university's Vice-Chancellor, Professor Simon Ortuanya, said the university had received a distress call at 22:00 on Wednesday, and sent security personnel to a house party at Praise Lodge, outside the campus in Nsukka's Hilltop area.
"The preliminary investigation and interim report point to alleged alcohol abuse or drug paraphernalia and things like that. But we are not conclusive on those matters," he said.
He described the deaths as "tragic and painful".
"As a community, we mourn, not just alone, we mourn with the families, the parents that have suffered these years to train the men and women in their studies," he said.
Ortuanya also announced a ban on signing-out celebrations, which are commonly held by final-year students to mark the completion of their studies.
The celebrations often involve parties, dancing, photographs and friends signing one another's shirts. He urged students to use graduation as a time to reflect on their university experience and prepare for life beyond campus.
The university said it was working with security agencies to establish what had caused the deaths.
The police have also launched an investigation. They said alcoholic drinks had been recovered from the scene and the bodies taken to a mortuary for autopsies.
The investigation comes amid wider concerns about unsafe alcoholic drinks in Nigeria.
In September, dozens of people fell ill after consuming locally made alcoholic drinks and herbal mixtures in communities across Ondo State, south-west Nigeria.
More than 11 people died in the Araromi-Obu area, while more than 50 others were hospitalised.
Investigations found that some of the drinks had been contaminated with methanol, a highly toxic form of alcohol that can cause blindness and death.
Nigeria's food and drug regulator, Nafdac, reported more than 150 cases, including 48 confirmed deaths. More than 80 people were hospitalised, and five lost their sight.
The regulator has been carrying out raids across the country, targeting facilities suspected of producing fake or adulterated alcoholic drinks, food and beverages.
Nigeria has long struggled with the sale of unsafe and adulterated products, which campaigners warn pose a serious threat to public health.

The News
Nigeriaâs electoral commission will obey any court ruling on whether the main challenger to President Bola Tinubu is eligible to contest Januaryâs presidential election, its chairman said, potentially handing the judiciary a key role in Africaâs biggest poll.
Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar is set to appeal last weekâs high court ruling that invalidated his candidacy. The chair of the Independent National Electoral Commission, Joash Amupitan, speaking at the Chatham House think tank in London, said the body would be constitutionally âobligatedâ to âobey every court orderâ if the appeal fails.
INECâs position adds to uncertainty around the vote in Africaâs top crude oil producer with less than 10 weeks until polls open.The commission is currently embroiled in more than 300 legal cases related to local elections, Amupitan said, adding that unresolved disputes could complicate its preparations for the forthcoming polls.
Credibility test
Bukola Idowa, executive director of civil society group Kimpact Development Initiative, warned any impression that the electoral process was opaque would undermine the validity of the vote. âWeâre looking at an election that will put the credibility of all our constitutional institutions to the test,â he told the Chatham House event, adding that this was particularly true of the judiciary.
Tinubu won the 2023 election with 36% of the vote with Atiku coming second with a 29% share. But voter turnout stood at just 27% â the lowest since the return to civilian rule in 1999.
Atiku has vowed to restore a fuel subsidy the removal of which by Tinubu has been blamed for driving up the cost of living. The price of fuel has increased five-fold since the president announced the scrapping of the subsidy at his inauguration.
The View From London
Nigeriaâs net direct investment inflows have improved significantly since Tinubu took office in 2023 and, in recent years, the nation has received credit rating upgrades. The president has campaigned on a strengthened economy that is projected to grow 4.2% this year. In a tacit acknowledgment of the criticism aimed at him over the higher cost of living, last month Tinubu said the country would shift its economic policy goal from administering âemergency treatmentâ to delivering shared prosperity.
Meanwhile, the oil industry is booming. Africaâs top crude oil exporter has benefited from higher prices sparked by the Iran war and in the past year the regulator has approved 145 new well operations.
âThe macroeconomic backdrop for these elections are probably the strongest that weâve seen in a very long time,â said Yewande Sadiku, senior investment banker, international, at Standard Bank. But she stressed that investors care most about consistency around policies. âElections matter, but the identity of the winner is not as important as the commitment to policy continuity,â she said.
Notable
- Nigerians have limited confidence in the credibility of the upcoming elections, according to polling firm Afrobarometer which found fewer than four in 10 people it surveyed believe the poll will be free and fair.

Defense Business Brief: This Ukraine-founded drone maker is now worth $6 billion. What now?
Build more, faster—and then integrate it all together. That was the gist of my conversation with Oleg Rogynskyy, CEO of Ukraine-founded drone company UFORCE, that’s now valued at more than $6 billion after landing a $700 million series A funding round this week.
“Our m.o. is to go to exercises and actually do stuff,” Rogynskyy said via video conference while at a defense conference in Oslo, Norway. “The unmanned surface vessels have had a massive impact on the Black Sea fleet. That has been public and recorded. Our Nemesis UAV platform has destroyed over 10,000 Russian vehicles. We know we shine the best when we are in real operations.”
And now with “a very deliberately designed funding round” complete, the next move is to become ubiquitous.
It “supports our mission to help Ukraine defend itself, but also bring out these platforms…that have been so effective in making defense operations so much cheaper and so much more effective in Ukraine to help the rest of the democratic world defend itself and prevent a future war,” he said.
Valor Equity Partners and the U.K.’s National Wealth Fund led the funding round. The U.S.–Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund, URIF, which was first funded by the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, also participated and its investment will go towards UFORCE’s Ukraine operations and research and development. Other notable investors include Menlo Ventures and Shield Capital.
“This round is helping us scale manufacturing, R&D both in Ukraine and outside Ukraine—where it’s [needed] to support Ukraine—as well as our presence in key markets and partnerships,” he said.
Scaling manufacturing is expensive and requires a different approach for a country at war, but the lessons could be applied elsewhere.
“In Ukraine, for example, you have to approach manufacturing very differently because of the threat of airstrikes,” Rogynskyy said. “You cannot build large factories with big logos on the roof in Ukraine. You have to be very discreet, and you have to be very flexible, while not impacting your economics.”
That means distribution centers, a flexible supply chain, and malleable assembly lines that can adjust for volume, while remaining secure.
Rogynskyy declined to specify production numbers, timelines, or hiring goals. Instead, he said, the company has doubled revenue and tripled its staff to more than 1,000 people in the past year.
Now that the funding round has closed, UFORCE is putting together next year’s operating plan.
“You're gonna see more USVs, more effectors on the USVs. You're gonna see more integration of our other products”—includng with unmanned ground vehicles and aerial drones—and “you're gonna see new energy-based capabilities coming out. So, energy effectors,” Rogynskyy said.
There will also be more software integration, autonomy, and AI to help manage large numbers of drones. And new products will crop up as mergers and acquisitions get underway.
And the main challenges that lie ahead are “people and politics,” he said.
“The products are there. The capital is there. The know-how is there. The IP is there. The demand, unfortunately, is there. So it’s all about execution now.”
Welcome
You’ve reached this week’s Defense Business Brief with Lauren C. Williams and Jennifer Hlad, where we dig into what the Pentagon buys, who they’re buying from, and why. Send along your tips, feedback, and song recommendations to lwilliams@defenseone.com. Check out the Defense Business Brief archive here, and tell your friends to subscribe!
A battery-powered Pacific. Two companies have teamed up to deliver “expeditionary power systems” to the military in the Indo-Pacific, which could help keep bases and installations operating for months in case of power grid failure.
