4ec49f82bf19.text: The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence in hospitals and clinics is leading the nation's biggest physicians group to lobby for new legal protections if AI harms patients. Why it matters: The use of increasingly sophisticated AI tools and recommendations is blurring the lines around negligence in health care, raising questions about whether doctors should be held responsible for decisions that rely on software. There's added urgency as autonomous AI takes on more and more important medical tasks with less direct oversight. The question is who's responsible when something goes wrong. Driving the news: The American Medical Association this week called for federal and state legislation to protect physicians from liability when AI products injure patients, despite physicians using the tools as intended. The group also is pressing for new laws mandating that AI companies carry adequate liability insurance and disclose product limitations and performance data. Hospitals, health systems, insurers and health tech vendors should be responsible if the required use of specific AI products results in harmful errors, the AMA policy states. Between the lines: The group's push comes as AI clinical tools are flooding the health system, unlocking new efficiencies but giving algorithms increasing power to make decisions like whether to order a diagnostic test or prescribe an expensive drug. Legal and medical experts point to the possibility of triage errors, in which AI systems that process clinical histories, vital signs and imaging can misjudge the severity of a case without the attending doctor's knowledge. The AMA also raises the possibility of an AI system making a plausible recommendation for treatment, but with incomplete laboratory results or an outdated diagnoses. In such cases, a physician may be unable to verify the inputs. In cases where a patient is harmed, responsibility should fall on AI manufacturers and vendors — and possibly on health systems that require the AI systems' use — instead of through a medical malpractice claim against the physician, the AMA argues. Context: There already have been lawsuits around algorithm-driven medical decisions, including a wrongful death case in Alabama involving a screening tool for heart abnormalities. The software developer wasn't held liable because its licensing agreement left final medical decisions to doctors. The big picture: Courts around the country are concluding that companies that design, train and deploy AI systems bear responsibility for what the systems do, said University of California, Davis professor Martin Hilbert, who studies the role of digital information and algorithms in society. Accountability hinges on factors including who shares responsibility when multiple parties build an AI system, how to prove fault inside an opaque model, and what to do when damages surface only after the system is deployed. "Different parties are responsible for different cases, and you can't just hold the end user responsible," he told Axios. The AMA wants to address situations when use of an AI system is mandatory. What we're watching: The Food and Drug Administration is weighing whether a new framework is needed for regulating AI-enabled medical devices. But the agency oversees software that meets the definition of a medical device, not all of the AI in health care. Hospitals generally support putting the onus on developers and vendors for monitoring the systems' performance, saying the "black box" nature of many systems can make it hard to identify flaws. AdvaMed, the trade group representing device makers, is urging the FDA to continue using its current approaches for evaluating generative AI-enabled medical devices. It also wants the agency to avoid post-market monitoring that imposes added burdens regardless of a product's actual risk.

88d6ec4aa598.text: Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries are both cautious, calm, compromise-minded leaders fantasizing about a serious, sensible Democratic-run Congress. But social media is a temptress no party leader has tamed. The seduction of attention, likes and followers invariably proves too strong for the savviest, most self-promotional politicians to resist. Why it matters: That's the lesson of the Internet Era of American Politics — the algorithms always win. A few provocative members of Congress and online activists dominate the national conversation because they master the biggest social media platforms. That creates the impression that their views reflect a party, or a nation, when in reality they don't. And it shapes the party's image and agenda. Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), vice chair of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus , told us: "Governing isn't about getting the most followers on X — it's about delivering actual results ... It's easy to scream and yell, and say no — it's much harder to figure out a way forward." By the numbers: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed had 1.6 million Instagram followers as of Sept. 13. Today: 7.6 million and rising. One clip of him pulled an estimated 50 million-plus views across X, Instagram and TikTok. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, sits at 466,000 Instagram followers . A man who hasn't been sworn in has roughly 15x the leader's audience. El-Sayed telegraphed this in July: "If you're Chuck Schumer, I'm pretty damn dangerous!" True. Jeffries has nearly 1 million followers on Instagram. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has 9.8 million on her personal account alone. Yes, President Trump remade the GOP. But social media sucked in countless others to try to copy him, pushing rhetoric or ideas few politicians would've touched in the past. You see this in the rise of celebrity politicians who do little legislating but lots of instigating. You see this in the explosion of not just Instagram, X and YouTube followers by politicians, but also in the many starting their own shows — unthinkable a decade ago. Several see themselves as content producers: California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas host podcasts while doing pretty important day jobs for big states. Trump started his own social media platform, Truth Social . You see this in the daily media feeding frenzy when someone, somewhere goes viral because they lit up social media with a meme or menacing post. The trap is springing before Democrats have even been sworn in: Several incoming senators have publicly said they won't support Schumer as leader, calling for new blood and more fight. James Talarico of Texas has sidestepped the question for months. Petitions to replace Schumer passed 100,000 signatures a day after launch. At Crooked Con, the post-election summit hosted in Washington last weekend by the parent company of "Pod Save America," the crowd booed and jeered his name all day. The pressure worked: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who's thinking about a 2028 presidential run, announced Thursday night on MS NOW he'll challenge Schumer for majority leader. Doug Sosnik , a top official in Bill Clinton's White House and closely followed analyst of Democratic politics, told us: "You would never know it from the internet or press coverage, but the fact is there are only 130,000 members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)." "It has taken a while, but I think that Democrats have finally figured out that X/Twitter is not the real world," Sosnik added. "The best proof point of Democrats' 'getting this' was our success across the entire country." What we're watching: The biggest siren song of the algorithm this next year will be impeaching Trump. Schumer and Jeffries have tried to set a disciplined path focused on affordability, not impeachment. Trump is prone to taking provocative actions that would juice talk of impeachment. A crowded presidential primary field will make the topic even more tempting — a massive distraction for the new Democratic majorities. Reality check: Schumer only needs about 29 of his members to vote for him in a secret caucus vote. He'll likely win the room. But he's losing the feed, and the feed sets the narrative. Among the senators-elect who say they won't vote for Schumer are Adam Hamilton of Kansas and Troy Jackson of Maine. Running against your own leader is now a red state play, too. Accountability creep: In December, Jeffries waved off a Hegseth impeachment push. On Sunday, he said he was a " hard yes ." (House Republicans tanked the effort on Tuesday.) Bernie Sanders, the incoming HELP chair, says Democrats may go after RFK Jr. next, alongside aggressive investigations into Trump's staff and family. To be fair: Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky forced the vote, and Jeffries tied it to an Iran war he says has driven up prices. But removal would take two-thirds of the Senate, which Democrats don't have. It was a Week 1 fight they couldn't finish. The bitter truth is there's little market for moderation or sanity or heads-down, excruciating policymaking. This wasn't always true: Pre-internet, politics wasn't minute-by-minute combat and most media played by similar rules and stuck to daily rhythms. So how can Schumer and Jeffries overcome this? You could argue no party is better positioned than Democrats to resist, or at least tame, the social media temptation. The scale of the win gives them cover: at least 54 Senate seats to 44 and 255 House seats to 168, with some races still uncalled . That's Democrats' largest House majority since 2008, with a lead of nearly 14 points in the total House vote. Democrats clearly won because voters are tired of Trump's ideas, rhetoric and tactics. They clearly won because they fielded very moderate candidates in very red states: flips in Kansas (which hadn't elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century ), Iowa, Texas, Ohio, North Carolina and South Carolina. House Democrats are looking askance at Rep. Jim Jordanâs election as minority leader, given the Ohio Republican has few relationships across the aisle â but next year, they might not have to work with him much.
Democrats are likely to put up bills at the beginning of next Congress that could draw some bipartisan support like a stock trading ban, but their cushy House majority is likely to eliminate the need for Republican support on key funding and rule votes. And the narrower House Republican minority will reduce the effectiveness of discharge petitions, which Democrats and a small bloc of Republicans used successfully this Congress to force votes.
Republicansâ procedural hijinks on a veterans benefits bill this week wonât help cross-party ties: House Minority Whip Katherine Clark registered her objections with Republicans but was rebuffed about reversing course, though that courtesy has typically been extended to the House minority, according to a person familiar with the situation.

Democrats are facing heavy pressure from AI safety groups to ramp up oversight of the Trump administrationâs AI policy when they take power next year, according to two letters shared first with Semafor.
The AI safety group Guardrails Action and nine other groups wrote to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, arguing that voters were clear in the midterms that they want AI and government accountability.
The groups seized on the recent Nvidia controversy, demanding hearings with now-former CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Department officials.
âThe concentration of power and wealth from AI, and the risks that come with it, are historic. Countering that power is the most important fight of our lifetime,â the letter reads.
A second letter from the Alliance for Secure AI and the Tech Oversight Project addresses Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick directly, demanding he support strengthened export controls.

Senate Republicans are considering a defense-only party-line spending bill after getting the green light from President Donald Trump and paring down their lame-duck ambitions.
âIn my mind itâs crystal-clear â the narrower, the more likely,â Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., told Semafor. âEven the most mean-spirited ogres among us can rationalize no pay-fors for defense if thatâs what it comes to.â
Still, no one is guaranteeing success on the reconciliation effort, which can evade a Senate filibuster.
And Republicans will have to pass a budget resolution setting up the process soon â their margins are set to get narrower when Democrat Sherrod Brown replaces defeated Sen. Jon Husted on Dec. 15.
Trump wants a $350 billion bill, a sum meant to replenish the military after nine months of war with Iran. At this time, the proposal under discussion doesnât include a debt ceiling increase.

91a96cc36bd5.text:
HILLSBORO, N.D. — The Kritzberger family has farmed in the Red River Valley for more than a century. They once had livestock. Now they grow sugar beets, soybeans, and grains.
Like many farmers, they labor to balance the books. “We’re in an incredible amount of debt,” Ang Kritzberger said as she walked the farm on a recent fall morning.
For the past 10 years, the Kritzbergers have had another worry. Their daughter Nina has Type 1 diabetes. That’s landed the family in a national debate about how to protect patients from high insulin costs.
Nina was diagnosed when she was 7.
“I slept by her bedside for the first 60 days,” Ang Kritzberger said. “And I had to stick her finger every two hours, 24 hours a day, to make sure that she was OK.”
The Kritzbergers also pay a lot out-of-pocket every year for medical care, despite having insurance — at least $8,000 for drugs, supplies, and medical appointments.
That’s not uncommon. Soaring insulin prices for years forced people with diabetes to pay hundreds, even thousands, of dollars. Many rationed insulin, with sometimes deadly consequences.
But today, there’s a growing movement across the country to cap what people with diabetes pay for insulin. That’s brought together Democrats and Republicans, tapping an emerging consensus that the government should protect people from high drug prices.
“Typically, Republicans are more on the free-market side of things, Democrats are more supportive of intervening,” said North Dakota state Sen. Sean Cleary, a Republican. “But in this case, I think there was broad-enough agreement that this market just wasn’t functioning for folks.”
Cleary co-sponsored legislation last year to cap patients’ insulin bills at $25 a month. North Dakota is one of 29 states that have enacted such measures.
The cap limits what patients have to pay out-of-pocket every month for insulin — even if they have a high deductible that might force them to pay thousands of dollars before coverage kicks in for other healthcare, such as physician visits, hospitalizations, or other prescriptions.
Patient advocates, including the American Diabetes Association, began pushing for out-of-pocket caps and other protections amid spiking insulin prices and stories of patients who had died because they couldn’t afford their medicine.
About a fifth of the estimated 40 million Americans with diabetes depend on insulin. The drug has been in use for a century. But steep price hikes boosted patients’ out-of-pocket costs, which hit an average $470 a year in 2018 for people with private health insurance, according to federal data.
Prices have since moderated as drug companies faced a public backlash. Average yearly out-of-pocket costs for people with private insurance declined to $220 in 2025.
But for many families like the Kritzbergers, the prospect of a government cap offered protection from future price hikes and some relief from the anxiety of a serious disease.
Nina Kritzberger, now 17, said she already has a lot to worry about.
“I have to make sure I have insulin, a spare pump, a spare Dexcom,” she said, ticking off the equipment that patients with diabetes rely on. “Oh, what if my pump doesn’t work, or my Dexcom? Then I have to bring a testing kit. What if I go low? I need Gatorade, glucose.”
A missed dose of insulin could land her in the hospital. “My body would start attacking itself and start shutting down,” she said. “And then I would die.”
The price cap strategy initially caught on with Democrats. In 2019, Colorado became the first state to enact what was called an insulin copay cap. State-regulated health plans there cannot charge patients more than $100 for a 30-day supply of the drug.
In 2022, President Joe Biden signed legislation that capped insulin prices for Medicare enrollees at $35 a month. Biden and congressional Democrats wanted to extend the cap to people with private health insurance, including Americans with employer-provided coverage. But Republican opposition sank that proposal.
In North Dakota, state Sen. Tim Mathern led the effort to enact an insulin copay cap for health plans regulated by the state. For a long time, Mathern struggled to find supporters. He’s one of only five Democrats in the Senate. There are 42 Republicans.
“One is very lonely being a Democrat,” Mathern said, “especially if you espouse the more progressive end of public policy.”
Health insurers and the state chamber of commerce said price relief for people with diabetes would mean higher insurance premiums for everyone else. “We do not make health insurance more affordable by passing coverage mandates,” Blue Cross Blue Shield of North Dakota lobbyist Megan Hruby told lawmakers.
The industry tapped into many lawmakers’ skepticism about regulation, said Janelle Moos, a state lobbyist for AARP. The nonprofit advocacy group for older Americans supported the insulin bill.
“It wasn’t the role of government,” Moos said she was told by many GOP lawmakers. “In a state like ours, we hear that all the time.”
Ang and Nina Kritzberger joined other families driving hours across the state to testify at the Capitol in Bismarck.
It was intimidating at first, Ang Kritzberger said. “It was me and six other lobbyists that were going to be giving their testimony against me,” she recalled.
But supporters of the insulin bill showed that a similar measure that limited out-of-pocket costs for state employees with diabetes had little impact on insurance premiums.
It also became clear that many lawmakers, including Republicans, had grown very frustrated with drugmakers, health insurers, and others in the healthcare industry.
“Why are folks paying hundreds of dollars a month for a drug that’s been commercially available for decades?” asked Cleary, the state senator. “I just kept coming back to the fact that this market seems so broken and these families are having to make impossible decisions about rationing medication or skipping treatment.”

Medicaid Work Rules Don’t Apply to Native Americans. They Could Still Lose Coverage.
CHEROKEE, N.C. — Two months before the deadline to implement new Medicaid work requirements, states had yet to receive detailed guidance from federal health officials on how to exclude Native Americans from those rules, leading to a patchwork of eligibility checks that pose challenges for qualified enrollees trying to keep their health insurance.
President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act excluded Native Americans from having to meet the work requirements to keep their Medicaid eligibility. But the rules issued by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services didn’t provide a standardized system to help states identify Native Americans who should be excluded, leaving states to figure it out for themselves.
Native leaders fear the limited guidance will mean a repeat of the Medicaid “unwinding” in 2023, when states resumed checking qualifications for eligibility after a covid-era pause. An estimated 850,000 Native Americans lost coverage by May 2024, often for paperwork reasons.
The latest carve-out for American Indians and Alaska Natives also left out some Indigenous people, such as Native Hawaiians.
“I’m nervous. I’m extremely nervous,” said James Burns, who oversees the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians’ Medicaid managed-care program in the Qualla Boundary, the tribe’s sovereign land in western North Carolina. “When you look at any state that’s rolled out Medicaid work requirements, the unintended consequences have been vast, and that’s what we don’t want to happen.”
CMS published its guidance on work requirements in June, instructing states to use data they already have before potentially asking Native enrollees for additional records. But the rule didn’t set a standard process for states to prove Native American status, allowing states to raise the threshold for proof higher than federal requirements.
The rule also didn’t require states to share data with tribes, coordinate with Native health providers, or advise on managed-care plans like the one Burns oversees. Managed-care programs contract with the state to provide Medicaid benefits and connect patients to providers when they need care.
In July, a tribal advisory group for CMS recommended that the agency require states to allow Native Americans to self-attest to their eligibility as the standard proof. The group also wanted CMS to require states to share their Medicaid eligibility data with tribal health programs to catch when tribal citizens are mistakenly kicked off Medicaid. The National Council of Urban Indian Health pushed for similar guidance.
Native leaders expect additional guidance to come, said A.C. Locklear, CEO of the National Indian Health Board, which advocates for federally recognized tribes. But Locklear said that if CMS waits until December to issue more specific guidance on the exemption, states will have already determined their own processes. CMS did not respond to KFF Health News’ questions about whether it planned to provide more guidance.
“There’s 30-plus states who are independently repurposing their administrative processes for this, and they really all happen in a vacuum,” Locklear said. “That’s why it’s really important for CMS to provide guidance.”
Falling Through the Cracks
KFF Health News asked 14 states how they would apply the exemption and found that they plan to ask tribal citizens to prove their status in different ways.
Arizona, Colorado, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, and Washington plan to let enrollees identify their tribal status on their Medicaid application forms. The Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System, the state’s Medicaid agency, will continue to allow tribal members to self-identify, then will confirm their status through the state’s data on services received through the Indian Health Service or tribally run health centers.
South Dakota linked its claims system to identify people served by IHS, according to the state Department of Social Services. Oklahoma relies on a data-sharing agreement with tribes dating to 2022, according to Cherokee Nation Health Services. North Carolina requires a tribal enrollment card, a tribal census record, or confirmation from the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians’ Tribal Option managed-care program.
“There’s still going to be folks that fall through the cracks,” said Locklear, a citizen of the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina.
In North Carolina, 3,400 Native Medicaid enrollees are verified as eligible for the exemption from the work requirement, health department spokesperson Summer Tonizzo said, and those enrollees will be automatically exempted. But the state doesn’t know how many more people might be eligible for an exemption through tribal citizenship.
And Native Americans who don’t live in states where their tribes are based may face challenges in affirming their status. About 87% of Native people live outside of what the U.S. Census Bureau calls tribal statistical areas, such as reservations, according to 2020 data.
A Navajo Nation citizen living in Connecticut, for example, may have a difficult time being identified by the state because it doesn’t have a close working relationship with the tribe based in the southwestern U.S., said Liz Malerba, director of policy and legislative affairs for the United South and Eastern Tribes. She’s a citizen of the Mohegan Tribe in Connecticut.
Most states didn’t say how many Native enrollees they had verified as exempt from the work requirement. Several said they don’t track tribal affiliation, noting that ethnicity questions that would show Native status on applications are optional. In a comment on CMS’ work requirements guidance, the National Council of Urban Indian Health warned CMS that “not all states collect data on their American Indian and Alaska Native residents.”

Last week, Pennsylvania Democrats won competitive state legislative races, taking control of the State Senate for the first time in more than three decades. One key issue at the core of their campaigns: opposition to data centers.
“I’ve never in my career seen anything as unpopular as data centers,” said Molly Parzen, executive director of Conservation Voters of Pennsylvania.
Newly elected state senators and representatives who flipped their seats from red to blue say data centers played an important role in their wins. Now they are preparing to act on that mandate.
In the next legislative session, they say they want to address Pennsylvanians’ concerns about the lack of transparency around the AI buildout, study environmental impacts, ensure costs don’t land on electric ratepayers, push for moratoriums, codify data center regulations, empower local governments to reject proposals and repeal tax breaks for data center developers.
A number of bills related to data centers that fell short during split control of the legislature could be re-introduced in the state House and Senate in the next session. In the last year, Sen. Katie Muth introduced a three-year statewide moratorium, Rep. Paul Friel introduced a bill that would allow municipalities to set 180-day local moratoriums on all data center applications and Rep. Greg Vitali introduced legislation that would repeal the data center tax exemption.
Notably, Gov. Josh Shapiro pivoted on his data center stance in the last year—from fast-tracking developments to signing an executive order that established stricter guardrails. Advocates say the order is a step in the right direction but are calling for stronger protections that only legislation could provide. The order still allows room for developers to press on without complying with some standards, such as using clean energy.
People in the Poconos want to preserve their natural land, said Democrat Brian Wrightson, who won a key senatorial race in the 40th District and flipped a Republican seat, with data center resistance fueling his campaign.
The region has seen roughly 24 data center proposals, according to the Data Center Tracker. Wrightson wants a complete halt in Northeastern Pennsylvania. Come January, he would support a moratorium, whether it’s 180 days for municipalities or three years statewide. He’d love a retroactive one pausing projects already underway so municipalities can get answers they need before development moves forward.
“I’m never gonna close my mouth about it,” Wrightson said in an interview with Inside Climate News.
“Is [180 days] enough? No. Is it something to get it started, to continue the conversation? If that’s what it takes to get the conversation started and slow down and give a six-month breathing room to people, then that’s where we need to go.”
Along with a pause, he wants to modify the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code. Right now, it essentially says municipalities must allow for every type of development.
David Masur, executive director of PennEnvironment, is just one of the environmental advocates pushing for changes to the code. He said it’s essential to stopping data centers in Pennsylvania at the local level. While Shapiro’s order requires developers to gain approval from local authorities before they can receive state permits, Masur argues that local officials need more tools at their disposal.
Wrightson plans to find out if there’s a way a municipality can reject a proposal on the basis that it changes the town’s character.
“ Ultimately, I’d love to never see one of these built in Pennsylvania, period,” Wrightson said.
Democrat Jeff Warren, who flipped Pennsylvania’s 137th House District in Northampton County, also wants to change the planning code, so local governments have the “autonomy to make decisions for their own community in the way that they want to.”
Warren supports the tighter data center regulations within Shapiro’s executive order and wants them to become law.
He said data center developers should take care of their infrastructure responsibilities so costs don’t land on residents. “They need to pay for their own power, they need to generate their own power, distribute their own power,” Warren said. “ We cannot let them tap into the grid and let utility costs continue to increase for consumers in our communities. It’s unacceptable to me.”
Despite energy costs rising in the state, Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, has denied data centers are the cause. In a statement to Inside Climate News, Diorio said the industry is “committed to advancing Pennsylvania’s digital infrastructure, supporting energy reliability and affordability, and promoting long-term, responsible economic development.”
He added that the trade group “looks forward to working with federal, state, and local policymakers, communities, and other stakeholders to earn trust, support responsible data center growth, and help build a stronger economic future for every Pennsylvanian.”
Shapiro’s order only asks data centers to comply with the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development standards, which tasks them with providing 100 percent of their own electrical energy (and use 32 percent renewables by 2035). But developers could still move forward without consenting, though that path would be more difficult. Wrightson worries this could lead to companies relying on gas power rather than renewables.
“ The ‘bring your own power’ scares me,” Wrightson said. When Shapiro’s GRID plans were circulating, he said, developers added natural gas plants to their data center proposals.
He already lives near a 1.4 megawatt natural gas plant in Jessup. “I hear it start up, I can smell it and I can see it,” Wrightson said. Now developers are proposing more on the other side of the valley. “So what air do we breathe? That’s unacceptable.”

9a73df5bc71e.text: The AI boom without Jensen Huang will test a hard truth: Even if the tech world has grown somewhat less reliant on Nvidia's chips, it remains highly dependent on its checkbook. Why it matters : With rival chips maturing and recent software breakthroughs, the tech ecosystem has achieved what would've seemed impossible a year ago: a viable path around Nvidia. But replacing a CEO willing to bankroll startups, backstop billions in cloud debt and aggressively fund rivals to the AI giants will be much harder. The big picture : The next chapter without Huang will be more cautious, but the industry is capable of absorbing the change, for two key reasons: 1. New chips - Semiconductor competition has become harder to contain. At OpenAI and other startups, a longstanding joke was that the best way to get a discount on Nvidia chips was to openly talk to Google or others about alternatives. Huang would often swoop in enthusiastically, eager to lock in a customer. The progress of custom chips from Google, Amazon, Microsoft and OpenAI , as well as new deals with Broadcom and Nvidia rival AMD, gives those conversations more substance. Customers have options, and far more leverage than ever. AI itself has also made those offerings easier to use. Anthropic says its Mythos model helped run certain workloads on AMD chips in about three days , compared with six to 12 months in the past. 2. Washington - In DC, China hawks are ascendant. Huang's departure strengthens calls from administration forces, some lawmakers, and companies such as Anthropic that have pushed for tighter controls on chip sales. Legislation is rapidly advancing to cut off loopholes and strengthen export restrictions for advanced chip sales to China, and the Commerce Department is reportedly preparing additional ways to limit such access. Cutting off those routes could help protect America's lead and offer a major pre-IPO boost to Anthropic and OpenAI. Reality check : Alternative chips and leaps forward in software won't solve the near-term computing crunch that all the big players in AI are facing. Nvidia's chips remain the most sought-after because they are the most widely supported, making them critical for the industry's smaller players and important for the big companies who need maximum efficiency out of each data center they build. There are two reasons a strong Nvidia still remains essential: 1. Finance - The company's checkbook will be far more difficult to replicate than its computing power. Nvidia has made $530 billion of off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantees , including to buy memory and backstops for data centers and certain companies building them, according to data firm SemiAnalysis. Smaller cloud providers, often called neoclouds, as well as a vast array of startups all over the world, have lost perhaps their most enthusiastic champion . Nvidia will remain a formidable competitor, but it will almost certainly become less aggressive about startup funding, acquisitions and backstops, tempering its efforts to spread exposure among institutional investors in ways that some critics said resembled the mortgage bubble. 2. Open models - Nvidia has been the most enthusiastic funder and champion of the Western open-model ecosystem—giving developers cheaper alternatives to the expensive offerings from frontier AI companies. Its pending acquisition of Hugging Face , licensing agreement with model-developer Poolside, backing of Reflection and development of the Nemotron family of open models extend well beyond chip sales. Without Nvidia, it's not clear whether the U.S. will be able to develop open-weight alternatives to China, since many don't have a clear or easy path to financial returns given that such systems are often free to download. What we're watching : Whether the industry's growing freedom to choose its chips can compensate for an Nvidia that is suddenly much less willing to finance its ambitions. Bottom line: Huang's departure won't derail America's AI ambitions. But it leaves a hole in the ecosystem that will be harder to fill than any shortage of Nvidia chips.

d1d7d5533ab5.text:
The Signal Insight
Jennifer Morgan, who became the first female leader of a DAX-listed company when Germanyâs SAP named her co-CEO in 2019, now leads a US business processing $1 trillion of payroll data each year. UKG, formed in 2020 from the merger of Ultimate Software and Kronos, provides HR services and workforce management technology to organizations employing 65 million hourly and frontline workers in industries including retail, healthcare, and manufacturing.
Since arriving in 2024 from Blackstone, one of UKGâs private equity owners, Morgan says she has not seen those jobs become much more vulnerable to AI disruption. But she has struck partnerships with the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI, seeing opportunities to âgive the worker agencyâ with AI-powered tools that let them plan schedules around their childcare, or volunteer for overtime when they need to earn extra money.
Morganâs pitch to employers is that pairing these tools with data-driven insights into wages, absenteeism, and inefficiencies in schedules can cut billions of dollars from corporate Americaâs $1 trillion-a-year attrition bill. Replacing just one hourly worker costs the average employer about $5,000, she notes.
Morganâs strategy is to reposition UKG from a provider of administrative support tools to a âworkforce intelligence hubâ that uses shift data to inform operational decisions in real time. She has overhauled the companyâs leadership, replacing about 80% of her direct reports and 40% of the tier below them, to bring in more people with experience of operating at the scale and speed this moment demands.
But she has also tried to stay on her own front line, spending a quarter of her time with customers, which include Marriott, the Mayo Clinic, PepsiCo, and the Transportation Security Administration. And she says that sharing their positive and critical feedback with her staff has been equally important.
Hereâs how she sees AI bridging the gap between companies and the workers who are often furthest from their headquarters, yet closest to their customers.
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson: What will AI mean for frontline workers?
Jennifer Morgan: Think about a world where that frontline worker on their app can say, âI need to make $500 extra between now and the end of the month. What are the shifts that are available for me to do this? Oh, and by the way, hereâs my school schedule; schedule around this.â Or workers who need access to their pay before [their] paycheck arrives; one of our customers [who offered early âearned wage accessâ saw] the retention for people who took advantage of that was 14% higher.
AI gives the worker agency because AI can be a better advocate for what they need. Thatâs whatâs been missing. If you think about the person whoâs trying to put the schedule together, they donât have all that texture, and they definitely donât have it in real time. So thatâs where the expectation gap gets bigger and bigger, because what the worker needs and what the operation needs are different.
Do you think you have better insight into whatâs happening in companiesâ workforces than they do?
Yes. Whether weâre talking to Pepsi or T-Mobile, we can show them what we see happening. We can talk to them about their overtime, their wages, absenteeism, and the attrition thatâs happening because people donât get the hours that they want. If they get too many [hours], or they donât get enough, they leave. That information is ready in real time, [but] companies look at that after the fact.
What does private capital bring to this very expensive and uncertain AI transition?
I remember when I read my first investment memo at Blackstone for a company we were looking at, my first reaction was, âI wish somebody had given this to me when I was the co-CEO of SAP.â Having somebody who can unemotionally look at your business and tell you all the opportunities, all the great things, and all the things that you can address to make it even better, as a leader, thatâs what youâre looking for: Just take out the filter and give it to me. I love having a board with both investors and operators, because operators understand all the nuance and all of the intended and unintended consequences of what could happen if I do X or if I do Y. Investors tend to look at things very unemotionally, factually. And it helps bring a level of focus.
Do you ever see tension between that left-brain and right-brain way of looking at the business?
Absolutely. I remember, again, my first investment committee meeting at Blackstone. We were talking about [investing in] this one company and all of a sudden there was this strong intellectual debate. Iâm thinking to myself, âOh my goodness, they donât like this company.â But it was really about just getting to the right answer. There were no corporate politics. It was just that intellectual honesty about what this was, what we could do, what you needed to believe in order to get to where everybody wanted to go. So that is really positive when youâre able to have those discussions, and make change at a pace that I donât have to constantly worry about the [next quarterly earnings]. Because the amount of change that weâre making to the organization is a lot, and the longer you wait to react, the more you have to catch up, and the change is twice as much and twice as hard.
UKG was put together from two different companies. To what extent has your job been about defining a single culture?
[I was asked] as a new CEO, âJen, are we going to be a product-led culture? Are we going to be a sales-led culture? How are we going to define it?â I said weâve got to be customer-led. To be a winning culture, youâve got to understand whatâs going on outside the four walls. And so I spend a lot of my time sharing what Iâm hearing. Iâm used to being in bigger companies, and when youâre talking to tens of thousands of employees, you donât tend to just go out there unscripted, off-the-cuff.

- Published
As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.
Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.
But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.
"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."
A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.
Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.
His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.
Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."
"I'm a bit bored of it," another spectator at the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.
Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.
There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.
And there's a sense of injustice that Australia can't seem to escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.
"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.
"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."
Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.
In it, he said he had wanted the team to take collective responsibility for the tampering after batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught with the sandpaper on field.
"I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team'."
However Khawaja has since said he didn't want to start a "witch hunt" and has refused to answer questions on exactly who he claims knew of the scheme, and what they knew.
David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja had written the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".
Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.
But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.
And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.
Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".
"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.
"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."
He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.
He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.
"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.
Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.
Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.
But he was also frank - using strong words to reject what he said were "vague" claims by Khawaja and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."
As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioned Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.
"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."
Few people think he'll get his wish.

Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.
Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory.
"We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.
Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.
Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas.
"Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.
Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026.
The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.
In a statement, the Miss Universe organization in Zambia said Mubanga's situation was a consequence of the travel restrictions rather than individual circumstances.
"Unlike situations where a contestant's visa is denied due to personal circumstances, documentation or organisational challenges, Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction affecting Zambia and other African countries," the statement read.
Mubanga, 25, a registered nurse, was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October and was due to represent the country at the international pageant.
The statement said five other African countries faced similar difficulties, although it did not name them.
Hall said she shared their concerns, adding that she had spent the past few weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa.
"I am not alone in this predicament. Some of my African sisters are facing the same predicament, and I know exactly what they are going through," she said.
Miss Universe South Sudan also expressed uncertainty about her participation, commenting on Hall's video: "It is 50/50 whether we will make it, Miss Universe."
In another video posted three days earlier, Hall said she was still hoping to make it to Puerto Rico.
She captioned the video: "The fight to get Zimbabwe to Puerto Rico continues,"
The pageant's final is scheduled to take place at the JosÃ© Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan.

Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?
If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.
A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.
Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?
Someone, somewhere, knows something.
The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.
Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.
"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.
"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."
His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.
They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.
"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.
"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."
Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.
The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.
Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.
What happened next, though, was not part of the script.
While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.
The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.
Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.
Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.
Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.
In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.
Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.
It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.
"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.
He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.
"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.
"That hour and a half waiting for the race toâ¯finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."
By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.
But there were plenty of theories.
Theory: it was not a real diamond
Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.
"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.
"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.
"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."
Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.
"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.
"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.
"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake,â¯but I don't think so."
Theory: someone pocketed it
"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.
"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].
"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.
"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. Bu

The big picture: With approximately 180 people on the ship, the rescue of all aboard is "truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a press conference. Catch up quick: The American Heritage, a vessel operated by American Cruise Lines, had docked for passengers to disembark at the port Friday afternoon about two hours before it was hit, according to a press release from the Port of New Orleans. A city spokesman confirmed to Axios that the riverboat had rolled onto its side in the water, which social media videos appear to corroborate. Zoom out: The Atlantic Asphalt tanker is registered in the Marshall Islands, and had arrived at the Port of New Orleans on Nov. 11. Per data from myshiptracking.com, the tanker began its current journey in Paulsboro, New Jersey, in late October. Zoom in: The tanker was immobilized on the river Friday at about 2pm CT, with two tugs positioned on either side. The US Air Force said it responded to "suspected unauthorised drone activity" over RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk on Friday evening.
No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, a spokesperson for the US Air Force said.
It comes after unconfirmed reports that sirens were sounded at the base, which residents reported hearing from a nearby village.
A Ministry of Defence spokesperson told the BBC it was "coordinating with all relevant parties", adding that US Air Force security personnel responded to the reports and the situation was resolved.
"We are working closely with them to establish the facts," they added.
West Suffolk MP Nick Timothy said he had been in touch with authorities at the base, and was told "there is no threat to the public, and the incident is now resolved".
"Given the raised threat level, I continue to encourage everyone to report anything suspicious or out of the ordinary to the authorities," he added in a social media post.
Earlier this week, at least 12 US Air Force aircraft departed the nearby RAF Mildenhall base.
They included two Boeing Stratotanker KC-135 refuelling aircraft, with one apparently headed towards Germany and another seen landing at Prestwick Airport near Glasgow.
There has been heightened security activity at US bases in the UK following an incident at RAF Fairford in September that Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran played a part in.
Police said petrol but no explosives were found during searches of vans near the base.
Two men have been charged by the Crown Prosecution Service over their alleged involvement in the incident.
While Iran denied any responsibility, the US removed all of its bombers from the base in October.
The Wall Street Journal reported the departure of the US aircraft from RAF Mildenhall this week was in response to a further threat from Iran but the BBC has not independently verified the claim.
Earlier this week, Downing Street insisted British airbases were safe and that their security is a "top priority".
RAF Lakenheath hosts the US Air Force's 48th Fighter Wing, or the Liberty Wing as it is also known, which has nearly 7,000 active-duty personnel, some of whom are stationed at the base.
The Liberty Wing is the largest US fighter operation in Europe, its website says, employing four combat ready fighter squadrons.

When U.S. Sen. Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma started work this year on legislation to speed approval for infrastructure projects, he hired the chief lawyer at one of the nation’s largest gas pipeline developers to lead his Senate office.
Armstrong had previously led the Williams Companies, stepping down before entering public office. But his new chief of staff, T. Lane Wilson, maintained his position at the company even while serving in the Senate.
During his nearly three-month stint in the Senate, Wilson kept the title of senior vice president and general counsel at Williams, a company spokesperson said. That means Wilson’s colleagues at Williams were lobbying his new colleagues in the Senate on pipeline permitting reform.
A chief of staff is typically second-in-command in a Senate office, supervising staff and advising on policy. While a Williams spokesperson said Wilson did not take his corporate salary while serving on the Senate staff, he maintained a significant financial stake in the company.
Delaney Marsco, director of ethics at the nonpartisan Campaign Legal Center, said it is highly unusual for such a high-level staffer to maintain outside employment. She said the fact that Armstrong was working on legislation that would affect Wilson’s company raised “serious questions.”
Wilson’s 89-day tenure may have allowed him to avoid restrictions that generally prohibit Senate staffers who serve 90 days or more from serving as an officer at, or affiliating with, corporations.
Craig Holman, the government affairs lobbyist for watchdog group Public Citizen, called the arrangement “an obvious conflict of interest,” even if Senate ethics rules did not prohibit it.
Armstrong, a Republican, was appointed in March by Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt to finish the Senate term of Markwayne Mullin, who was tapped to lead the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. At the time, Armstrong was serving as executive chairman of Williams and had previously served as the company’s chief executive. Oklahoma law barred Armstrong from running for a full term and he is now slated to serve until Nov. 30, when the newly elected Republican Kevin Hern will be sworn in.
As soon as he took office, Armstrong touted his experience leading Williams as an asset in advancing permitting legislation through the Senate.
“I am retired from the industry,” Armstrong said in his first Senate speech. “I am here because I have seen how this system strangles our great country.”
Armstrong introduced a bill in June with provisions that would have restricted the ability of states, tribes and others to challenge pipelines. While the legislation never came to a vote, it drew 20 cosponsors. Armstrong celebrated the inclusion of similar provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the permitting bill that cleared an initial Senate vote on Monday.
The bill includes a range of measures to accelerate permitting, including provisions that would limit states’ authority to reject or impose conditions on planned interstate gas pipelines and transmission lines. Williams stands to benefit from those provisions.
Wilson was Armstrong’s chief of staff from April 13 to July 10, according to Blake Jackson, a Williams spokesperson. Jackson said Wilson did not receive a salary from the company during this period. Wilson also shifted his responsibilities and communications to avoid potential conflicts of interest, Jackson said, including separating himself from the company’s government affairs team and recusing himself from any meetings between that team and Armstrong or his staff.
A spokesperson in Armstrong’s Senate office declined to comment.
Upon entering the Senate, he held more than $20 million in company stock, according to a securities filing. Wilson also continued making regularly scheduled stock sales under a pre-arranged broker agreement, selling nearly $450,000 worth of stock from May through July. Since leaving the Senate, Wilson has sold an additional $1.5 million in Williams shares, including nearly $1 million in two transactions made outside the pre-arranged agreement, according to a securities filing.
Experts said it is unclear whether Wilson’s dual employment violated Senate ethics rules. One provision prohibits outside “employment for compensation which is inconsistent or in conflict with the conscientious performance of official duties.” Wilson may have complied with this rule by not taking a salary from Williams while working in the Senate.
Wilson did not file a financial disclosure report. A Williams spokesperson said he was not obligated to do so. Senate rules say all staff with annualized salaries of at least $151,661 must file reports. Williams did not disclose Wilson’s salary there, and staff salaries for the period have not yet been published. But a Congressional Research Service report said the minimum salary for a Senate chief of staff last year was just over $163,000.
Experts say another key question is whether the Senate Select Committee on Ethics approved the terms of Wilson’s employment. Jackson, the Williams spokesperson, said the committee had signed off, but he declined to provide a copy of any advisory letter. Such letters generally remain confidential unless a recipient makes them public.
Neither the Ethics Committee nor the office of Republican Sen. James Lankford, the committee chairman and Oklahoma’s senior senator, replied to questions for this article. The office of the committee’s vice chairman, Sen. Christopher Coons (D-Delaware), also did not reply to inquiries.
“Everything might be, by the letter of the law and the Senate rules, totally above board, but it doesn’t solve the problem of looking really bad,” said Marsco, with the Campaign Legal Center. “And in the ethics world, that’s just as bad.”
The Ethics Committee website says it has long interpreted its rule on outside employment “as applying to both actual conflicts of interest and the appearance of a conflict of interest.”

âWe have plan Aâs all the way to plan Zâs, from our best-case scenarios to our worst-case scenarios,â Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak says, when asked how the culture, tourism, and property groups he leads are preparing for what might happen next in the conflict that has shaken the Middle East.
Many of those plans are contingent on the US-Israeli conflict with Iran ending, but âif this conflict gets worse, we also have a very clear route,â says the chairman of the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi.Â
The manga-loving 44-year-old member of Abu Dhabiâs Executive Council, whose other interests include sneakers, rap music, and basketball, has spent more than a decade at the heart of the cityâs strategy to diversify its economy using museums, UFC fights, and theme parks. Last year alone, the city opened five museums and welcomed a record 26.6 million visitors.
Culture and tourism are âthe building blocks of our future,â he says. But the conflict has forced him to craft a response that combines a strategic pivot, reassurance to local staff and foreign partners, and continued commitment to his cityâs long-term aims.
When the Iran war started in February, flights and events were canceled and the number of Western tourists to the Gulf plunged, emptying local hotels. âWe had to basically rethink how weâreâ¦promoting ourselves,â Al Mubarak says. But, he adds, âWe always understood that, no matter what happensâ¦ the machine doesnât stop.â
A pivot to new growth markets
Before the conflict, Abu Dhabi was working toward a goal of attracting 39.3 million visitors a year by 2030, up from 24 million in 2023. It projected that those tourists would contribute AED 90 billion a year to the cityâs economy.
Al Mubarak is still sticking to his 2030 goals, but he says the assumptions underlying them have changed. He now expects a 10-15% drop in visitors from the US and Europe compared to its original estimates, for example, with growth from other parts of the globe making up the difference.
So he has changed the focus of Abu Dhabiâs marketing, looking to pull in far more visitors from its own region, and from Eastern Europe, India and the rest of Southeast Asia, and Africa. The city is already seeing 5-8% growth in visitors from âsome of our Eastern geographies,â he says, and much larger numbers from around the Gulf.
On Yas Island this summer, he says, âSome days I felt I was in Saudi, some days I felt I was in Qatar, some days I felt I was in Moscow.â He recalls talking to two tourists as they watched the smoke from a drone attack on a French navy base in the first week of the conflict: when he asked if they were alright, they replied: âWeâre Russians, so this is nothing.â
Abu Dhabi has been a magnet for wealthy Westerners, with its Formula 1 track and outpost of the Louvre. But Al Mubarak wants to use the current crisis to broaden its appeal to other parts of the world whose populationsâ economic power is growing.
Under his worst-case scenarios for the warâs outcome, his plans would focus Abu Dhabiâs culture and tourism strategy much more on its immediate region and the Global South. That grouping of poorer countries comprises more than 70% of the worldâs population, he notes, and its people want âto experience a lot more than they have.â
Westerners have been more put off by news coverage that he says exaggerates the security threat, but he has not stopped marketing to them, too.
âWe havenât stopped acknowledging that they are a traveler and they are a future potential traveler,â he says. âWeâve kept [at the] front of their mind that the UAE is here and Abu Dhabi is here, and itâs going to continue to develop, itâs going to continue to grow. So when the time is right for you as a traveler, our doors are wide open.â
Three-quarters of Abu Dhabiâs hotel rooms were full again by August, Al Mubarak notes. At Aldar Properties, the commercial real estate developer he also chairs, new sales dropped 34% in the first nine months of this year, but at AED 18.9 billion were still higher than for the same period in 2024. Overseas buyers â from China, the UK, Russia, and elsewhere â made up 28% of the total. After the first day of Iranian attacks, he maintains, âbusiness has really been as usual.â
Projecting normality, and an alluring vision
Informed by its experience during the pandemic, Abu Dhabi kept cultural institutions open throughout the conflict to give residents places to connect and âa sense of comfort,â Al Mubarak says.
To reassure his own teams, he set up daily management group meetings, and a stream of video conferences, emails, and helplines for employees. What mattered most was to show that leaders were listening rather than just talking, he says.
âSmall things like that make a difference,â he notes, adding that his strategy starts with Abu Dhabiâs own residents. The city wants to be a âhome away from homeâ for the worldâs culture-lovers, he says, but âwe did not develop our cultural strategy and our cultural infrastructure for people to come [to Abu Dhabi]. We developed it for people that are here.â
But Al Mubarak is equally keen to project a sense of normality for potential visitors who are contemplating Abu Dhabi from afar.
âImagine yourself in Abu Dhabi today,â he says. The weatherâs good this time of year, so âyouâd wake up in the morning and youâd sink your feet in beautiful white sand,â then maybe go for a swim, he suggests. Then a tourist could go for an AI-personalized museum tour, a round of golf, some shopping, a concert at the Sphere (a $1.7 billion entertainment venue opening in 2029), or a comedy show.
Itâs âan imaginary story,â he says, but one âthat could be a realityâ for a visitor. The next step in realizing that vision will come on Dec. 11, when a branch of New Yorkâs Guggenheim Museum opens on Saadiyat Island. c0a59917a6f6.text: By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/faa-grounds-all-flights-at-u-s-airports-due-to-air-traffic-control-communications-problems Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter FAA grounds all flights at U.S. airports due to air traffic control communications problems Nation Updated on Nov 13, 2026 5:19 PM EST — Published on Nov 13, 2026 4:41 PM EST The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon because of communications problems at regional air traffic control centers. The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." WATCH: What it will take to update the aging U.S. air traffic control system Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said there is a communications issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers that direct planes en route between airports nationwide. He said FAA technicians are investigating. This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication yet that "this was a nefarious attack against us. It's just a telecommunications outage." "Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying," Mullin said. There is no timeline for restarting flights. Mullin said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But that system operates out of one location near Washington, D.C., and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centers. The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country. But much work remains. Duffy has said that another $30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it. The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers. "If you don't have that ability, whether it's because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you've got to stop airplanes on the ground," said Arroyo, who is a former United Airlines pilot. "And not put them in the air where you're going to risk not being able to communicate with them." Friday's ground stop was different than the one after Sept. 11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said. AP writer Mead Gruver contributed to this report from Fort Collins, Colorado. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. House Democrats are all but certain to elect House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries as their speaker designate next week.
There could still be some turbulence, though, with progressive activists calling for Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., to launch a bid against Jeffries.
Ricardo Sanchez, a Pressley spokesperson, said she was in âactive conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment, and deliver for the people. She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership.â
Most Democrats donât believe Pressley will actually launch a bid ahead of next weekâs leadership elections. Sheâs privately denied interest in running to other lawmakers, according to people familiar with her comments, and she hasnât laid the groundwork for a bid by sounding out support from other lawmakers.
House Democrats are staring down brewing fights as younger lawmakers jostle for power and influence ahead of the party assuming its largest majority in decades. Once their leadership slate is set, the caucus will weigh major changes like implementing term limits, shaking up panel leaders, and standing up select committees on controversial policy issues.
âWe can have the fight about how many terms should be the limit, but I think the time is right â with all these new members coming into the caucus â to set some limits,â said Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt. At the âWhatâs Nextâ conference on Friday, Jeffries said discussion about term limits was the âright conversation to have.â And Rep. Janelle Bynum, D-Ore., launched an effort this morning to change the seniority system for subcommittee leadership positions.
Jeffries and Democratic leaders could face an influx of new members who arenât as beholden to caucus traditions when it comes to picking leaders based on seniority. âI think itâs going to be important for the Democratic Caucus to make sure that the voices of this large, energetic, new class of members are included at the table, and in general, I think we, as a party and as a Congress, are healthier when we allow for new perspectives and more renewal,â said Rep.-elect Luke Bronin, whoâs coming to office after unseating a longtime Democratic incumbent.
Democrats are also weighing the future of the select panel on China and whether to stand up a select committee on AI. Some Democrats have argued for changing the China committee, keeping it as is, or sunsetting it altogether. Top House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., who is close to Jeffries, has advocated for folding the China committee into his panel, and for standing up a separate Foreign Affairs subpanel on AI and chips. Doing so could set off a turf war with other powerful committee leaders.

A critical Microsoft outage lasting more than 22 hours has raised questions about how heavily vital services rely on a handful of major tech firms.
The disruption, which affected Microsoft 365 services such as Outlook, was caused by routine automated checks that took some servers offline, overloading the remaining ones with traffic.
The recovery took nearly a full day while engineers gradually restored services, highlighting how embedded the tech giant's services are in modern society.
Flora Hamilton, executive director of the Small Business Charter, said the outage was a "stark reminder" of how much firms "rely on digital systems" - like Microsoft Outlook - "to keep their operations running".
"For many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), access to email is fundamental to everything from communicating with customers and suppliers to generating income," she said.
The disruption was not just confined to businesses, but also affected organisations and public institutions around the world.
Around 430 million people globally use Microsoft 365, and issues were reported across more than 70 countries.
The fallout from the outage had a wide-ranging effect, knocking out email systems for the US House of Representatives and Australian intelligence agencies, as well as disrupting court systems in Singapore and airline support desks in India.
Microsoft has since apologised for the issue, which it said was due to a technical failure rather than a cyber-attack.
There was no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered, Microsoft added in a statement late on Friday (GMT).
Walter Pasquarelli, an AI strategist, told the BBC that for governments, businesses and critical infrastructure, the outage had "put their vulnerabilities and dependence in plain sight".
"Looking ahead, as AI assistants are plugged into our email, calendars and files, a failure like this may spread even further," he said.
Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies, said while these kinds of outages weren't unheard of, what was unusual was the time it took for Microsoft to recover from it.
A spokesperson for the US tech company said "given the scale of demand" it restored services gradually.
"While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration," a spokesperson said.
Orosz said the resulting upset showed "our reliance on a few large US corporations".
He said a solution for the future could be to split services per region to reduce the impact, something which already happens with Amazon's cloud computing service, AWS.
For now, Microsoft said it was reviewing what went wrong, with the findings expected to inform steps to prevent a similar disruption from happening again.
