- Published
Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.
Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover.
The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.
Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.
Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.
Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.
By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.
In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected, as were some schools and police forces.
UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.
In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.
In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.
Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.
In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.
The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.
Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business was basically brought to a "standstill".
His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" was been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".
Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she was due to complete her first house purchase today after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that.
"The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies.
"We're not the only one completing today, there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible," Georgia said.
'Encouraging recovery signals'
Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.
While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.
By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.
Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remain stable once they are up and running again.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said.
"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."
Microsoft said it has no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered.
A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.
Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.
"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.
Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.
"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said.
"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

6ced7944d598.text: By — Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press By — Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press By — Russ Bynum, Associated Press Russ Bynum, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/watch-brooklyn-community-leaders-residents-hold-meeting-on-building-collapse Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Brooklyn community leaders, residents hold meeting on building collapse Nation Nov 13, 2026 3:44 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — One man's pregnant wife was pulled alive from the rubble, while two of his roommates perished. A woman living next door woke from a nap to bright daylight flooding her bedroom because her apartment wall was suddenly gone. Watch the news conference in the video player above. Survivors of the Brooklyn apartment building collapse that killed eight people wept as they recounted their terror and grief during a news conference Friday. WATCH: New York building collapse kills 8, including 2 children New York officials, from building inspectors to prosecutors, say they're investigating what caused the three-story building to come crashing down as workers were digging at an adjacent construction site. Those who lost family, neighbors and their homes demanded answers. "As they're taking me, evacuating me from the building, I could see my neighbors coming out on stretchers," said Ciahola Lawrence, whose apartment building next to the one that collapsed had a shared wall ripped away, exposing an abyss of dust and debris below. "We didn't deserve this," said Lawrence, who sobbed in her husband's arms as she spoke with reporters. Among the dead were two children, ages 9 and 10, according to city officials. Another 18 people were injured, including four firefighters. Members of the New York City Department of Buildings and New York City Fire Department stand on the roofs of buildings next to the site of a deadly building collapse, in the Brooklyn borough of New York City, Nov. 12, 2026. Photo by Brendan McDermid/Reuters 'I no longer knew where I am' Mamadou Mouctar Balde stepped out to buy groceries Wednesday, leaving his pregnant wife and two roommates, 31-year-old Mamadou N'Diaye and 23-year-old Mamadou Barry, at home. Barry was cooking and N'Diaye was sleeping on the couch, he said. He returned to find firefighters, police and neighbors gathering outside and assumed there had been a traffic accident. Then a woman told him a building had collapsed. "I didn't see my wife. I didn't see my friends," Balde recalled, a tear streaking his cheek. "I no longer knew where I am." First responders found the bodies of N'Diaye and Barry while combing the wreckage. Balde's wife, Fatoumata Bah, was pulled alive from the rubble. He said she and their unborn child were doing OK. N'Diaye and Barry were Guinean nationals who came to the U.S. about five years ago from Conakry, the capital of the West African nation. Their uncle said their family is heartbroken. "We ask the city and the Guinean community to stand for us, to have a justice for this tragedy," he said. Other victims came from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador and Trinidad, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. New York police identified the others who died as Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, 9; Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, 31; Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, 10; Gabriel Siguencia, 22; Edgar Sapon, 26; and Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 26. Mayor says authorities will pursue 'any evidence of criminality' Ahmed Tigani, commissioner of New York's Department of Buildings, said Friday that his office is conducting "an exhaustive investigation" of the Brooklyn collapse. The city has ordered inspections at more than 160 sites in New York that are associated with six entities linked to the construction and demolition site next to the fallen building, Mamdani said, significantly raising an earlier count of sites subject to renewed scrutiny. "I think it is always an outrage when eight New Yorkers lose their lives, when 18 New Yorkers are hospitalized, and when families are shattered as a result of all of this," Mamdani said. If investigators uncover "any evidence of criminality," Mamdani said, "it is one that we follow through to the fullest extent of the law." One witness who works across the street said he watched bricks fall minutes before the disaster. A woman in a neighboring building said she and fellow residents blamed vibrations from the construction for cracks that appeared in their apartment walls. Video shows survivor descending stairs suspended over wreckage Lawrence said the construction work had been a source of constant disruption, producing noises so loud that "you would hear that thumping and movement in your soul." A security camera above Lawrence's door recorded video of her apartment's shared wall and the building next door collapsing in a clattering rumble and a thick cloud of dust. Inside her apartment, a closet filled with hanging clothes and bags was exposed to the outside. The security video shows Lawrence leaving her damaged home with a firefighter, who held her hand as they descended a stairway overlooking mounds of wreckage below. "This feeling is indescribable," Lawrence said. "I was right there." Zariah Coleman, who lived in the building next to the one that collapsed, was concerned about her cat. She said Friday that she too had felt the building shake because of the construction. "I just really hope they come and get our cat," Coleman said in tears. "He's hiding from them, and I think he's scared." Rescue operations ended Thursday after crews spent more than a day searching for victims beneath debris removed with power saws, pickaxes and an excavator. Building records show there were four apartments on the upper two floors and a commercial unit on the ground floor of the collapsed building. The Scoop
In January, the general counsel for what was then the worldâs most valuable company delivered a blunt directive on chip export controls to more than a dozen government officials: What Donald Trump and his friend Jensen Huang want, goes.
âI was with the president when he and Jensen discussed this so I want to let you know what the president wanted,â said Nvidiaâs Tim Teter, according to people with access to a detailed account of the call. âHe wants this to go fast.âÂ
People on the call fell silent.
At issue were proposed conditions on licenses to export Nvidiaâs H200 chips to China, which included requirements that chipsellers know who their cloud customers were before shipping and conduct know-your-customer checks on any buyers purchasing more than a few thousand chips.
Nvidia objected, with Teter calling the cloud-customer requirement a âpoison pillâ for the company, the people said. Nvidia also wanted the threshold for the know-your-customer checks to be in the tens of thousands (the equivalent of billions of dollars of chips) and pushed for end-of-life conditions to only apply to chips that were facing export controls. While itâs not unusual for big corporations to work with US government agencies and Congressional staffers on legislation or agency rulemaking, or even to see draft regulation in advance, people familiar with Nvidia and its former CEOâs Washington connections say the chipmaker wielded an unprecedented level of influence in shaping guidelines with far-reaching global security and business implications for the entire industry. The previously unreported discussions have only taken on greater significance since Huang stepped down from the company he co-founded decades ago after media reports of extramarital affairs with two subordinates and one with a customer and suspected Chinese spy.
Nvidia declined to comment. Spokespeople for the White House didnât immediately respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security, which is housed within the Department of Commerce, said it was âcompletely routineâ for the department and other agencies to work with individual companies in this manner and that âoften the conditions change in response to legitimate commercial considerationsâ raised by corporations. The final version of all license conditions are reviewed by the state, defense, energy, and commerce departments.âNvidia would have gone through the same process for license conditions as any other license applicant. Nvidia consulting with non-political experts at multiple US government agencies regarding its proposed changes to the conditions is consistent with standard practice,â the spokesperson said.
Invoking the president
If Trump was Huangâs friend in the White House, Teter was his muscle in Washington. After more than two decades at law firm Cooley LLP, Teter joined Nvidia in 2017, soon after the chipmaker announced the beginning of the âAI computing era.â Nvidiaâs GPUs had sparked the âbig bangâ of modern AI, Huang wrote at the time, years before Nvidia would turn into the worldâs most valuable company.
But as Nvidia became a bigger geopolitical force â and Huang became a fixture alongside Trump at meetings, dinners and the Oval Office â Huang and Teter developed a âscorched earth, adversarial attitude,â according to a former government official familiar with their Washington presence. âThey make things more personal, going after think tankers, government officials, and the like,â the former official said, referring to reports of Nvidia targeting critics of the company and proponents of export controls.
As he bulldozed through Washington, Teter regularly invoked President Trumpâs name to push Nvidiaâs agenda. In one exchange viewed by Semafor, Teter accused government officials who were developing export restrictions of misrepresenting Nvidiaâs products and President Trumpâs policies, chiding them for not carrying out Trumpâs agenda and insisting that Trump deserved their support. Teter and the team of Nvidia lobbyists would often capitalize on their implicit White House backing and on the fact that most Hill staffers didnât have the technical expertise to fight back on the companyâs claims that certain restrictions werenât technically feasible, even if later they were proven wrong, current and former congressional staffers told Semafor. Staffers âwere kind of just believing whatever they were told,â and Nvidia would get all sorts of bills watered down, one staffer said.
Nvidiaâs âMO has largely been gaslighting,â creating an âintense trust deficit between the government and the Hill and Nvidia,â a former staffer said. And âobviously, the canonical example at this point is Nvidia denyingâ improper chip sales to China, this person said.
Huang has said thereâs no evidence chips were getting diverted to China, but Bloomberg has reported that Nvidia undercounted the Megaspeed sales it reported to the US government by 50,000 chips, worth billions of dollars. Companies tied to Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, have purchased at least $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips since 2023, The Information reported.
But well before Nvidia came under fire for its relationship with Megaspeed, Nvidia told staffers that a provision in the 2025 Chip Security Act, which would require chipmakers to be able to locate their chips, was a nonstarter. âThey basically said it was not technically feasibleâ the former staffer said, âthey were like, âwe would need completely new technology to do this, and even if we did it would be very easily spoofable.ââ
In meetings with committee staff, Nvidia lobbyists argued location verification would create security holes. They âran this line of bullsh-t on how the Chip Security Act was going to create all these cyber vulnerabilities,â a second former staffer said. âWe spent six months going behind them and having to unpack all of the bullsh-t that [they were] telling to other offices.â

The Birmingham darter, though only recently discovered by science, is a survivor.
The roughly two-inch long fish, adorned with red spots and stripes along translucent fins, has survived 100 years of coal mining, steel-making, quarrying and suburban development along the rolling Appalachian foothills running southwest from Birmingham to Tuscaloosa.
But the fish might not survive the new 4.5-million square foot hyperscale data center planned just upstream from one of the six known locations where it still survives.
“Clearly they’re endangered in fact, if not by law, because their populations are so small,” Charles Miller, policy director for the Alabama Rivers Alliance, said in an interview. “They’re only found in Jefferson County, and so the loss of even one of those populations can be devastating for the species as a whole.”
The Rivers Alliance, along with the Center for Biological Diversity and Black Warrior Riverkeeper, petitioned the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service nearly a year ago to consider whether the species should be listed under the Endangered Species Act, a move that would likely force developers of the Project Marvel data center to make accommodations to save the fish.
Now, after nearly a year with no action and crews already clearing land for the data center, they are threatening to take the matter into court.
On Thursday, the groups sent a notice of intent to sue the Fish and Wildlife Service and the Department of the Interior, saying they will file suit if the FWS does not respond within 60 days. The groups are required to give 60 days notice before filing a lawsuit under the Endangered Species Act.
Laurel Jobe, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, said the FWS missed a legally required 90-day deadline to issue an interim decision on the darter’s status, and that time is of the essence.
“Birmingham darters don’t have time for the Fish and Wildlife Service to slow-walk this decision,” Jobe said in a news release. “Every day these darters spend waiting for protections brings them that much closer to extinction.”
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and data center developer QTS did not immediately respond to requests for comment for this story.
The data center, called Project Marvel, was announced in 2025 as having 18 warehouse-style data center buildings spanning 4.5 million square feet on 700 undeveloped acres in the city of Bessemer, just west of Birmingham.
Since then, developers purchased an additional 900 acres of property surrounding the original site plan. Virginia-based data center developer QTS purchased the project for $432 million in June, according to local media reports.
Clearing Continues for Project Marvel
Recent municipal elections in Bessemer installed a new mayor and city councilors, after strong public backlash against the data center. The previous mayor and other officials signed non-disclosure agreements with the original developer that even required them to destroy records that the developers deemed confidential.
In October, new Bessemer Mayor Louise Alexander asked QTS to pause development operations until a scheduled meeting with city officials. According to AL.com, the company responded saying it would continue clearing the site, which had already been permitted by the city.
QTS has offered to buy homes surrounding the site from residents, and subcontractors have sent letters to residents informing them they are within a half mile of a potential blasting site, seeking to conduct “pre-blast inspections” on structures in that radius.
When completed, Project Marvel will be one of the largest users of electricity in the state, needing an estimated 1,200 megawatts of power. That’s almost half the total capacity of Alabama Power’s James H. Miller Jr. Electric Generating Plant, a coal-fired power plant located about 20 miles away.
Birmingham Darter’s Habitat Dwindles
The darter is surviving, but definitely not thriving. The species has already been extirpated from parts of its range, in a number of streams feeding into Valley Creek, a Black Warrior River tributary. The clear, spring-fed streams that it needs to survive have been impacted by urban runoff and industrial pollution.
According to the groups’ notice, there were populations of the Birmingham darter in Fivemile Creek, just east of the data center site, that have seemingly been wiped out due to quarrying operations in the area. The groups say darters haven’t been seen there since 2006.
“Birmingham was the center of a coal and an iron and steel industry that really messed with these streams,” Miller said. “The darters that we have left are so precious because they represent individuals and species that were really put through the wringer.”
Now, the darter is facing threats from the development of the new data center, as well as the controversial Birmingham Northern Beltline highway project, which is planned to run directly through the area. The highway is being built not to alleviate traffic problems, but in an attempt to spur economic development through sparsely populated areas north and west of Birmingham.
The route will take it directly through many forested and undeveloped areas, clearing hundreds of acres of wetlands, critics say, imperiling the Birmingham darter and numerous threatened and endangered species in the area. The project’s estimated total cost is more than $6 billion in 2026 dollars, though the road is not expected to be completed for several decades.
These two massive new developments on top of the existing pressures on the darter threaten its survival as a species.
“We’re seeing this new form of industry come in that is posing threats to our natural environment in similar ways as mining did back in the day,” Miller said. “And we’ve got to make sure that these species can survive this next revolution in terms of AI and data centers.”
Darters Are Key Part of Alabama’s Celebrated Biodiversity
Alabama is a well-recognized hotbed of biodiversity, boasting more freshwater

- Published
SpaceX will attempt to catch both parts of its huge Starship rocket after it launches on its next test flight on Friday.
Elon Musk's company will use the mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower to grab the rocket parts mid-air as they return to Earth.
If successful, this will be the first full recovery of a rocket that's been to space, paving the way for making Starship reusable so it can fly repeatedly.
Nasa will be closely watching the flight: the SpaceX rocket is set to play a vital part in its Artemis programme, which will see astronauts land on the Moon.
The 124m-tall rocket is scheduled to blast off from the Starbase launchpad in Texas at 1645 local time (2245 GMT) with a 75-minute-long launch window.
After six and a half minutes, the first planned catch will be attempted when the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - returns to the launch tower.
The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, will continue its journey to space and deploy 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high speed internet from space.
The Ship is then due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning for the second catch attempt about 22 and a half hours after taking off.
Until now, SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.
But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead it's splashed down in the ocean.
SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it's in space.
If any problems are detected there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.
Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX.
In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster.
Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than a hundred times a year, and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch.
But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, President of Royal Aeronautical Society.
"A successful double catch would be visually spectacular, but full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said.
"One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate."
After SpaceX went public earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will the US Space Agency.
The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.
SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.
But it's not the only company working with the US Space Agency. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touch down.
Both companies will also play a key role in Artemis III, which is currently planned for summer 2027- another challenging schedule.
This mission will see four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers.
Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.
But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.
Blue Origin had said they would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.
Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said America is in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

9321f6ec53e0.text: Sen. Chris Van Hollen is picking up endorsements in his challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader. Why it matters: The leadership fight exposes divisions within the Democratic Party days after its sweeping midterm victory , with some demanding a new direction and others crediting Schumer for the historic blue wave. Driving the news: Van Hollen (D-Md.), a senator since 2017, announced Thursday he's challenging Schumer because "we need new leadership." "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people." The other side: Schumer has far more public endorsements than Van Hollen. "Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?" Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said in a statement of support for Schumer. Van Hollen has disputed Schumer's claim to credit for the party's midterm performance, arguing that the wave was powered by voters rather than leaders in Washington. By the numbers: Schumer has public support from 14 senators, including himself, compared with five for Van Hollen. A candidate will need 28 or 29 votes to win, depending on the outcome of Alaska's Senate race, where votes are still being counted. Senators backing Van Hollen State of play: Van Hollen told MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side, though only four have publicly endorsed him. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) endorsed Van Hollen on Thursday night, saying he will fight for working families. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) threw his support behind Van Hollen when he announced his challenge Thursday. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) issued an endorsement for Van Hollen Friday afternoon. Incoming Sen. Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) endorsed Van Hollen Friday morning after previously calling for new leadership. Who wants new leadership? Some sitting senators have called for a leadership change without endorsing Van Hollen. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) has called for change but hasn't endorsed either candidate. Before Van Hollen announced his candidacy, Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) told NBC 5 Democrats "absolutely are committed to change," but didn't rule out supporting Schumer. Several Democratic senators-elect have also called for new leadership, including: Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.). Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Ill.). Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine). Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.). Sen.-elect Chris Pappas (D-N.H.). Context: Progressive critics say Schumer hasn't fought hard enough against President Trump and his agenda. Schumer's decision to help advance a Republican-backed government funding bill in March 2025 fueled the progressive backlash against his leadership. The progressive Working Families Party urged Schumer "not to seek another term as Senate Democratic Leader" in a letter, as first reported by Axios . Another labor group has also opposed Schumer and endorsed Van Hollen. Who's backing Schumer? Schumer entered the leadership fight with broad support among Senate Democrats. "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader," Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement this week. Schumer's public supporters include Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and King , along with Schumer himself. Also backing Schumer: Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Tammy Baldwin (Wis.) and Jack Reed (R.I.). Schumer also received pre-election endorsements from Sens. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), though neither has publicly reaffirmed that support since Van Hollen entered the race. Senators who haven't picked a side Several sitting senators have yet to publicly back either candidate. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) and Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) have not publicly committed to either candidate. Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) have called for a caucus debate over leadership. Sens. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) have expressed openness to a leadership change without endorsing either candidate. Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) hasn't committed to Schumer and wants to hear his vision for the Senate. The 2028 factor Several potential 2028 presidential contenders face a choice over who should lead Senate Democrats. Ossoff and Booker , both possible 2028 presidential contenders, have yet to pick sides — leaving them to choose between the party's longtime leader and a changing of the guard. Meanwhile, Gallego and Kelly , also seen as possible 2028 contenders, have backed Schumer. Zoom out: Schumer himself is up for reelection in 2028 and could face a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who has also been mentioned as a potential presidential contender. Schumer could also retire rather than seek reelection . What's next: Senate Democrats will hold a secret-ballot leadership election Dec. 1. Incoming senators will participate, and members can cast their ballots differently from their public endorsements.

60c9f17eae11.text: As House Democrats barrel toward a speakership coronation , Senate Dems are getting their first contested race for leader in over 30 years. Why it matters: Democrats have spent years tearing themselves apart over the party's direction — without forcing their leaders to win a head-to-head vote. Senate Democrats will get that fight this year for the first time since Tom Daschle vs. Chris Dodd in 1994 — courtesy of Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) challenging Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.). But no one's challenging Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) for speaker. The last contested Democratic House leader race was in 2016, when Tim Ryan failed to beat Nancy Pelosi for minority leader. Between the lines: House Democrats are being bombarded with calls and emails urging them to oppose Jeffries, but the two most frequently floated alternatives — Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) — don't appear to want the job. Raskin told Axios that chairing the Judiciary Committee is his "dream job" and that he's "absolutely ... not a candidate for speaker in any way." "I am supporting Hakeem and voting for Hakeem," Raskin added. Pressley has privately told colleagues she isn't interested, multiple House Democrats told Axios. "Congresswoman Pressley is in active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment and deliver for the people," spokesperson Ricardo Sanchez said in a statement to Axios. "She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership." The big picture: Since the last contested Democratic leadership election, Republicans have endured the rise of MAGA, former Senate GOP leader Mitch McConnell's fall from power and a revolving door of House GOP leaders. In 2018, Kevin McCarthy drubbed Jim Jordan 159–43 to become House minority leader. In 2022, McConnell had to beat Rick Scott after the Florida Republican challenged him for Senate GOP leader. In 2023, McCarthy needed 15 ballots to become speaker and was ousted later that year. Republicans burned through nominations on Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan before settling on Mike Johnson . In 2024, John Thune had to beat two challengers — Rick Scott and John Cornyn — to succeed McConnell as Senate GOP leader. In 2026, Jim Jordan ... well, you know what happened. It was Tuesday. The intrigue: Van Hollen told reporters in Denver on Friday he's stopped "pursuing" a 2028 presidential bid because the "size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call with the American people." Van Hollen is up to five public votes (himself included) ahead of the Dec. 1 secret ballot. Schumer's at 14. The winner will need 29. Over in the House, the real question at this point feels like whether any House Democrats will oppose Jeffries on the House floor on Jan. 3. Jeffries has enjoyed unanimous support from his caucus since becoming leader in 2022 and is "confident that we're on a positive trajectory" but takes "nothing for granted," he told reporters yesterday. The bottom line: For once it's the Senate, not the House, providing all the drama on Capitol Hill.

3f2f79064cdd.text: Courts and governments worldwide felt the impact of this week's Microsoft outage, which sidelined work and stymied communication. Why it matters: When Microsoft's popular workplace software went offline Thursday, it meant an extended lunch break for some offices — but for the courts and governments, it raised questions about the vulnerabilities of the technology underpinning justice and governance. Case in point: The state of Maine's judicial branch warned in a Thursday alert that requests for protection orders filed by email — urgent requests to keep parties safe from harm — may not have been received. Multiple court documents reviewed by Axios show lawyers requesting deadline extensions or alerting judges to the outage impacting their work. That includes DOJ lawyers: Government attorneys asked for an extension in the case brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over President Trump 's Kennedy Center takeover , saying the outage prevented them from "completing the necessary coordination." In a separate filing, Beatty's team acknowledged they were impacted as well. Zoom out: The impacts were also felt in courtrooms and offices internationally. The AP reported that a U.K. criminal trial was delayed as a result, with a Manchester judge saying, per BBC's reporting , "We are learning of the dangers of relying on computers and data systems." U.K.-based police forces also urged the public Friday to call first responders for aid, rather than using online forms. The Supreme Court of the Philippines said it, too, was affected by the outage. What they're saying: "We obviously need backup methods to keep the wheels of justice turning," says Gissou Nia, the founder and director of the Atlantic Council's Strategic Litigation Project. She pointed to a prior incident that previewed international reliance on U.S. tech: Though not exposed by an outage, the Trump administration's sanctions on the International Criminal Court prompted the Netherlands-based court to move off of Microsoft software to avoid its work being paralyzed. While court deadlines can be pushed back, service disruption for individuals seeking urgent injunctive relief is more critical, she notes. "If the only way to communicate ... is through these servers, and the request wasn't reached, it can result in somebody having left the country or having moved money out of an account," Nia says. Reality check: Shay Cleary, a National Center for State Courts consultant who specializes in tech and cybersecurity, emphasizes that courts typically have manual back-up plans in place. "Many of the people who work in courts are dedicated public servants, and they can figure out how to do things right," he adds. With Congress back in session, Hill communications were also left in a holding pattern Thursday — with one staffer writing on X, "Hope nobody needs Congress for a little while, your Legislative Branch is currently paralyzed by the Outlook outage." Municipal governments in Austin , Texas, and Jacksonville , Florida, among several others , warned that their emails — and in some cases, phone systems — were impacted. What we're watching: A page providing updates on the suite of Microsoft tech tools said in a Friday morning post that it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress." That statement came some 22 hours after the page first said the company was investigating reports of issues with email access. The bottom line: The very tools that connect us digitally can also divide us when things go wrong — underscoring the importance of preparing old-school backup plans to fill the gaps. Go deeper: The internet's hidden security nightmare — and how AI exposed it

New voluntary water conservation programs in the Upper Colorado River Basin appear on track after the 320th meeting of the Upper Colorado River Commission concluded this week. But Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming and the federal government have yet to agree on how any conserved water would be credited and stored.
These questions, experts say, may not come with easy answers.
This June, the federal Bureau of Reclamation put $100 million on the table for the four states in the Upper Basin to fund their own voluntary water conservation programs, which usually entails paying ranchers and farmers to use less water. Overuse and drought-diminished flows on the Colorado River threaten the water supply of roughly 40 million people, 30 tribes, seven states and Mexico.
Most Upper Basin states are planning to implement programs in 2027 (Utah already has one running), and their success could be crucial to the states’ assertion that they should only have to ease the pressure on the Colorado River through voluntary measures. This fall, the federal government implemented new mandatory reductions on the Lower Basin, and Nevada, later joined by Arizona, sued over the potential for even deeper cuts.
“It’s … important to recognize, and I say this in a positive way, a complimentary way, the audacious ambition of attempting to put this together in the time frame that we have,” Wayne Pullan, the Bureau of Reclamation’s Upper Colorado Basin regional director, told negotiators from the Upper Basin states at the virtual meeting.
Colorado made it clear that its program can only move forward with an agreement from Reclamation that conserved water would remain under the state’s jurisdiction.
“We really need to get some credit for the upper division states through a program like this,” said Amy Ostdiek of the Colorado Water Conservation Board, who presented the state’s conservation program. “What that means in Colorado is seeing that that water is treated as operationally neutral, and not simply passed downstream.”
“Operationally neutral” water is conserved by one state and stored in federal reservoirs for future use by that state. Arizona, California and Nevada, the Lower Basin states, have banked water in Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States, with the option to withdraw it for future use. But the Interior secretary is the legal water master in the Lower Basin and has the ability to allocate surplus water there. The secretary does not play the same role in the Upper Basin.
Pullan said that Reclamation is “able and willing” to keep working on how the government would credit and handle water conserved by the Upper Basin. Some observers wondered how the Upper Basin’s condition would sit with the federal government, which built and financed the dams that store the water.
“They don’t like to turn over the keys of the car to the states,” said James Eklund, a partner at Taft Law and Colorado’s Colorado River negotiator from 2013 to 2019.
The Lower Basin would also need to agree that water conserved in the Upper Basin could be stored for the upstream states’ use, something Kathryn Sorensen, director of research for Arizona State University’s Kyl Center for Water Policy, had a hard time envisioning.
The Lower Basin states “would expect some sort of quid pro quo for that type of arrangement,” she said.
The Upper and Lower basin negotiators from each of the seven Colorado River states had years to agree on new guidelines for the federal government to implement. After they missed several deadlines, Reclamation implemented its own new operating plan this year, and the states appear no closer to an agreement.
The possibility of one of the seven basin states suing another before the Supreme Court looms over the basin.
Various conservation programs in the Upper Basin are in different phases of development. Utah’s program saved about 5,500 acre feet of water in 2025, Amy Haas, executive director of the Colorado River Authority in Utah, announced at the meeting.
One acre foot of water can supply anywhere from three to six homes for a year, depending on the region’s climate and urban density.

New Mexico and Wyoming made their programs compatible with other funding sources, like state appropriations or grants from nonprofits, should they become available, state representatives said.
The Upper Basin uses less water than the Lower Basin, which recently reined in its consumption after years of drawing more water than it was allocated, though it has plans to divert yet more water from the river. In its operating guidelines released this summer, Reclamation modeled up to 200,000 acre feet of voluntary conservation annually in the Upper Basin—if hydrology allows.
Eklund, who attended the virtual meeting, said it’s disappointing the seven basin states still can’t agree on a solution to the problems plaguing the Colorado River. “If this system collapses, it doesn’t really matter what we’re legally entitled to,” he said.
“If Phoenix sneezes, the Upper Basin catches a cold,” he added. “We’re very, very connected economically to each other, and if we don’t start governing the system like we’re all part of one country and not seven different sovereign countries, then we’re A: only going to have ourselves to blame, and B: we’re not going to like the results.”

Two horses briefly board public bus in Detroit
CCTV footage shows the moment a bus approaches a stop with two riders waiting with their horses. After a discussion with the driver, the riders walk the horses onto the bus briefly before de-boarding.
The City of Detroit said its Department of Transportation allows service animals on buses in accordance with the Americans with Disabilities Act. But officials say that in this event, the horses appeared to have been brought on board for unrelated reasons, creating safety concerns for other passengers and for the horses themselves.
The city said it would now provide additional training for bus drivers.
One of the riders later told local media that he brought the horses on board to raise awareness of black cowboys and urban equestrian culture.

2b58e314e90a.text: By — Suzan Fraser, Associated Press Suzan Fraser, Associated Press By — Tammy Webber, Associated Press Tammy Webber, Associated Press By — Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Seth Borenstein, Associated Press By — Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/un-chief-says-immediate-and-drastic-emissions-cuts-needed-to-avert-climate-change-catastrophe Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter UN chief says 'immediate and drastic' emissions cuts needed to avert climate change catastrophe World Nov 13, 2026 2:45 PM EST ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — The world must immediately and drastically cut fossil fuel emissions to avert the most catastrophic effects of climate change, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said Friday at his final climate summit, urging the world to "follow the science" and face hard facts. "You cannot build peace on a burning planet," Guterres told reporters, stressing that climate change is central to the U.N.'s work because it contributes to geopolitical instability by driving hunger and displacement, pushing countries into debt and fueling competition for land and water. READ MORE: At UN climate talks, 5 nations back plan to double rooftop solar panels by 2030 "You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it," he added. "You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause this crisis suffer first and worst." World leaders meeting in Turkey for the annual U.N. climate talks are trying to reach consensus on concrete actions to address climate change — which is fueling more intense and deadly heat waves, droughts, floods and other disasters — and help countries at greatest risk, including island nations that also are losing land to rising seas. Electrification goals emerge as point of contention Achieving reductions in emissions is setting up a point of contention at the climate talks, especially around electrification. A goal introduced this year would increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% to 35% by 2035, preferably from renewable energy such as solar and wind. But it does not require that electricity be generated by renewable sources — something Guterres said is essential — meaning coal and other fossil fuels could be used, at least initially. Climate TRACE, which tracks global emissions via satellites, found that prioritizing clean energy would cut global emissions 14% compared to 7% if fossil fuels also are used for electrification. READ MORE: Democrats plan to challenge Trump's fossil fuel agenda and push clean energy to lower bills International Energy Agency Executive Director Fatih Birol said it's more important that as many countries as possible sign on to the pledge, which works best without a clean energy requirement. But environmental groups say that electrification will only have a real impact if fossil fuels are omitted. "Electrification must end fossil fuel dependence, not be an end in itself," said Jasmin Duregger, from Greenpeace's Global Gas Campaign. Vulnerable nations seek more compensation as warming takes a toll Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable countries that contributed little to the problem — also are calling for more money to deal with climate disasters and adapt to a warming world. Leaders of small island nations, who say climate change is a life-or-death matter for their people because rising seas are engulfing their lands, have been the most vocal at this year's summit, COP31, saying a U.N. fund created for compensating vulnerable nations must be urgently strengthened. Guterres said wealthier countries that have contributed most to climate change "must deliver the finance they have promised" at past summits — but also contribute much more. "Let us be clear about the scale of the gap," he said. "Even tripling adaptation finance would meet less than 30 percent of what is needed." Progress stalls, top-emitting countries skip summit Progress is difficult without the cooperation of all nations, "particularly the biggest emitters," Guterres said. A report released Thursday by the independent Climate Action Tracker found that progress in slowing global warming has essentially stalled for the past five years. That means the world is sure to overshoot the goal set in the 2015 Paris Agreement of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures. Climate change is caused primarily by greenhouse gases emitted by burning gas, oil and coal, and countries have established plans to reduce those emissions. But even if they fulfill all their promises — a big if — the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than pre-industrial times, the report said. "Our responsibility is to keep it as small as possible, for as short a time as possible and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees as quickly as we can," by cutting emissions about 6% per year for several years, Guterres said, calling the overshoot "a recipe for catastrophe." READ MORE: COP31 climate summit begins after disastrous year of extreme weather But some of the top-polluting countries stayed away from this year's summit, most notably the United States — the world's second-largest polluter after China and the largest historical polluter. It's the second year in a row the U.S. skipped the summit, after President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from climate negotiations. "Facts are facts," Guterres said. "No country can protect itself from climate change alone. We share one planet, and whether we like it or not, we share one fate." Webber reported from Fenton, Michigan; Borenstein from Kensington, Maryland; and Delgado from Bangkok. Th

567504dd51c4.text: By — Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/supreme-court-will-consider-trumps-executive-order-suspending-asylum-access-at-the-southern-border Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Supreme Court will consider Trump's executive order suspending asylum access at the southern border Politics Updated on Nov 13, 2026 3:59 PM EST — Published on Nov 13, 2026 2:16 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed Friday to consider President Donald Trump's ban on asylum at the southern border, a pillar of the Republican president's far-reaching crackdown on immigration. WATCH: Supreme Court allows border wall in Big Bend The Trump administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court decisions that found it was illegal to block asylum applications following an executive order that called the situation at the southern border an "invasion." The suit is the latest in a series of immigration cases before the high court. Federal law allows people to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the U.S. At the same time, it also lets the executive branch decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Federal attorneys say yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision. "Since the proclamation took effect, border encounters have fallen by 93 percent, dropping to the lowest levels since the 1960s," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote, calling the asylum restrictions "critical" to the effort. But attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union and several immigration rights groups counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office. They say his executive order is an unlawful attempt to unilaterally "eviscerate" legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries. The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the U.S. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn't allow the president to unilaterally stop people from even applying, immigration attorneys argue. "The plaintiffs in this case fled persecution and torture, including political imprisonment and threats from the Taliban," said Keren Zwick, executive director of the National Immigrant Justice Center. "Yet, the Trump administration refused to honor its obligation to consider them for asylum." The ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation. The justices are expected to hear the case in the spring and hand down a decision by the end of June. It's the third major immigration case the high court will hear this term. The justices will also decide whether people can be swiftly deported to countries other than their homelands and if immigrants can be detained indefinitely during deportation proceedings. The justices decided another asylum case in favor of the administration earlier this year, clearing the way for the Trump administration to potentially revive a "metering" policy that has been used to turn back immigrants at the border in years past. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett is expected to depart his role at the White House in the coming weeks, three people familiar with his plans told Semafor.
Hassett has been inquiring about roles outside the administration since well before this monthâs midterm elections, some of the people said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who could hold both jobs, and his counselor, David Zervos, are among those being eyed to replace him.
Hassettâs plans havenât been officially announced and, like much in the Trump administration, thereâs always the chance they could change. The Treasury Department did not comment for this story.
A White House official told Semafor that âthere is no factual basis for this reporting,â adding that âKevin Hassett is a key member of President [Donald] Trumpâs economic team and will continue working to advance President Trumpâs economic policies.â
âUnder President Trump, Americans have received more than $82 billion in individual tax relief, over 70 million children have been enrolled for a Trump Account, nearly 20 fair trade deals have been secured, poverty is at an all-time low and real wages for hardworking Americans have increased,â the official continued. âThe Trump administration will continue delivering results for hardworking families.â
Hassett later denied he planned to leave in a text message to CNBC.
Trump tapped Hassett, who served in the first Trump administration, to return as his top economic adviser nearly two years ago. Since then, Hassettâs served as the face of everything from the economic fallout from the Iran war to the presidentâs campaign against former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell.
Hassett, who was in the running to replace Powell, saw one of his top priorities advance in February, when the president signed an executive order that sought to expand access to retirement plans for workers whose employers donât provide one. The order, first reported by Semafor, followed Hassettâs longtime advocacy for recreating the governmentâs Thrift Savings Plan for private-sector workers â but ultimately took a less ambitious approach, creating a website where workers can shop existing plans.
Hassettâs expected departure, while not tied to Republicansâ lackluster midterm results, would be the latest in a series of staffing changes hitting the Trump administration in recent weeks. Hassettâs deputy, Ryan Baasch, left the White House at the end of September.
More recently, Trump replaced his then-chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, the architect of the administrationâs strict immigration policies. Roles under Miller have been shifting in recent weeks, as Semafor reported.
Multiple people inside and close to the administration say they expect further staffing changes and departures as the year comes to a close. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is currently in the crosshairs amid scrutiny over his handling of export controls on AI chips.
This story has been updated to reflect comment from the White House provided after publication.

bd1a3b179ecb.text: By — Brian Melley, Associated Press Brian Melley, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/uk-police-launch-sex-offense-investigation-into-childrens-author-and-tv-personality-david-walliams Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter UK police launch sex offense investigation into children's author and TV personality David Walliams World Nov 13, 2026 2:05 PM EST LONDON (AP) — British children's author and TV personality David Walliams is under investigation for serious sex offense allegations made after news outlets reported that he used his fame to groom girls and young women for sex, London police said Friday. The Metropolitan Police said it had received a number of allegations of past abuse following the joint investigation this week by ITV News and the Guardian newspaper. One woman said in the reports that she was sexually assaulted by Walliams at his London home when she was 15, while others accused him of grooming them when they were teens. READ MORE: British comedian and children's author David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct Police said the allegations made in recent days are different from those reported by the news outlets. Investigators, however, will look into the news stories for evidence of other crimes. Walliams, 55, has denied the allegations, saying he had not broken any laws and was not a sexual predator. "I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me," Walliams said in a letter to ITV and the Guardian. "Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did." Film producers distance themselves from best-selling author Walliams is best known as the co-creator and co-star in "Little Britain," a hugely popular TV comedy sketch show in the 2000s, but he's also a celebrated children's book author with some 40 published titles that sold more than 60 million copies worldwide, according to his website. Several books, including "Gangsta Granny," have been adapted into BBC comedy dramas and stage productions. Producers of "Fing!" — an upcoming film based on another book by Walliams — said in a statement Tuesday that they had removed his cameo appearance and he "will have no involvement in the film's release or promotion." He is credited as a co-writer. READ MORE: Russell Brand is sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault U.K. distributor Sky told Variety it was dropping the movie. Angel Studios, the U.S. distributor, did not answer The Associated Press' emailed query about its plans for the film. Walliams was dropped last year by publisher HarperCollins after allegations were made of inappropriate behavior. Few details were published at the time, but the Guardian reported that there were concerns about his behavior for years, including an allegation he had an inappropriate sexual relationship with a junior female employee. Police offer little detail of new allegations He was also a judge for a decade on "Britain's Got Talent," though he stepped down in 2022 after apologizing for making "disrespectful comments" about auditioning contestants. Police did not name Walliams, as is customary when someone hasn't been charged, but said the allegations involved a man in his 50s and were related to the ITV and Guardian report. The Met did not indicate how many complaints it received or describe the nature of the allegations or where and when they were said to take place. READ MORE: AP report: Thomas Markle Sr. arrested on charges related to child sexual abuse material The reports into Walliams' alleged behavior were published a day after British actor-comedian Russell Brand was sentenced to 10½ years in prison for rape and sexual assault. The two stories together drew comparisons and caused wider soul-searching over celebrities getting away with sexual misconduct in the U.K. Brand's accusers in court had come forward after a joint investigation by The Times and Channel 4. Since his sentencing, more women have come forward to make claims against him, The Times reported. Police are also investigating two other cases against him. The Guardian and ITV said they spoke to more than 100 people during a three-year investigation into Walliams. Failed effort to keep his name out of the headlines Walliams had sought a court injunction to prevent the news outlets from identifying him, but a judge rejected the application, saying such a legal measure would be "an exceptionally serious interference" with the media's rights. Walliams had claimed that publication of sexual misconduct allegations would lead him to take his own life, but Justice Matthew Nicklin said it was the responsibility of mental health services to look after his safety. Walliams has not spoken publicly since the story was first reported Tuesday afternoon. Police, meanwhile, encouraged any sex offense victim to come forward. "We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process," Det. Supt. Mike Cagney said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Brian Melley, Associated Press Brian Melley, Associated Press

Senator Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge to his position as US Senate majority leader from his fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, as the party prepares to take control of Congress after sweeping the midterm elections.
Van Hollen, 67, said in a post on X on Thursday that Americans voted for change earlier this month and "to deliver, we need new leadership".
Schumer, 75, has led Democrats in the chamber since 2017, serving as both majority and minority leader. He was first elected to the Senate in 1999.
Following the midterms earlier this month, his position has come under pressure by some left-wing Democrats who see him as too moderate and part of the party establishment.
Responding to the challenge, Schumer, who represents New York, said he welcomed "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead".
He added that he was "proud of what we've accomplished together" in the midterms, and he had "the votes to continue as Democratic leader".
The vote on Senate leader will be held behind closed doors in early December and the winner will assume the role on 4 January, when Democrats take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives after their midterms successes.
The move by Van Hollen, who represents Maryland, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership following last week's midterms victory.
Announcing his plans to run in a post on X, he wrote that Americans had called on the party to "unrig an economy rigged against working people".
"We should not be preserving our institutions if they are not delivering for the American people," he said at a summit in Colorado hosted by majority Democrats. "And we should be making delivering for the American people the single mission of our government, even when that means shaking things up."
He added: "This country does not belong to the people who can afford to buy influence. It belongs to all of us. And it's time we govern like that."
In recent years, Van Hollen has taken positions popular with those on the left of his party.
In 2024, he supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticised the Biden administration over its role in the war in Gaza.
In an interview with MS NOW, Van Hollen - who has served in the Senate for nearly a decade - acknowledged that he was an "underdog" but added that he believed the race was "very much in flux".
Independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed have both publicly come out in support of Van Hollen - while others have also called for new leadership.
In a post on X, Sanders said he believed Van Hollen "will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families".
El-Sayed said the challenger would bring "bold leadership" and lead with both "courage and experience".
Others Democrats have publicly backed Schumer.
Senator Jacky Rosen of Nevada said: "He has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment".
Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said: "You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position."

5eefb7321fbf.text:
As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.
The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.
Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.
Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Indian Ocean.
The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.
“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.
The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.
The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.
Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.
Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.
Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill. 
“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.
From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.
I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.
“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”
That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.
In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.
But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”
Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.
“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croft Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.
As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

The developing El NiÃ±o - already the strongest on record by some measures - continues to grow and could have profound effects on the weather across North America this autumn and winter.
The naturally-occurring climate phenomenon sees trade winds over the Pacific Ocean, which usually blow from east to west, weakening or reversing with warm water instead spreading eastwards.
This releases heat into the atmosphere which can drive major shifts in global weather patterns.
Impacts in the US and Canada are varied, with a greater chance of a warm and dry winter in northern areas and more risk of flooding rain further south.
There is also some evidence that El NiÃ±o can increase the likelihood of disruption to the stratospheric polar vortex which can, in turn, bring snowfall later in winter.
No two El NiÃ±os are the same and the impacts are not guaranteed - the odds are just shifted in favour of certain outcomes.
Wet in the south
The eastward shift of warm ocean waters associated with El NiÃ±o can cause the Pacific jet stream to move south and extend eastwards, directing rain-bearing weather systems across the southern USA.
This typically leads to wetter winters during El NiÃ±o years.
The latest three month forecast, external from the US National Weather Service (NWS) suggests this is a likely outcome for the winter of 2026-2027.
South-eastern states, including Florida, Georgia and the Carolinas, have the greatest chance of seeing above-average rainfall.
The El NiÃ±o winter of 1997-1998 brought significant flooding in the south-east and spun up tornadoes for Florida.
Risk of west coast floods
California could well find itself in the firing line with forecasts suggesting a wet winter is likely.
Governor Gavin Newsom has already declared a state of emergency, external ahead of anticipated floods and mudslides.
Areas scarred by recent wildfires are particularly susceptible, with the effects of climate change exacerbating the risks.
Many past El NiÃ±os have been wet here, with winter 2023-2024 bringing relief from drought. However this is not always the case. In the strong El NiÃ±o of 2015-2016, California actually had below-average rainfall.
Coastal erosion and large waves could be worsened by a rise in the overall sea level driven by so-called Kelvin waves.
This is where ocean water which sloshes eastwards across the Pacific due to El NiÃ±o reaches the west coast of the Americas, where it can travel no further.
It causes a large-scale wave which then spreads along the coast over a period of weeks and months, raising sea levels by 15cm (6in) or more.
Dry and warm further north
The shift of the Pacific jet stream generally leads to warmer and milder winters in the north-west USA, Northern Plains and Ohio Valley - as well as western and central Canada.
This lessens the risk of flooding, but reduced rainfall can leave groundwater and river levels low, fuelling drought and wildfires in spring and summer.
Ski resorts can also suffer from a lack of snow.
Long-range predictions suggest a dry, warm winter is more likely than usual this year.
However, El NiÃ±o does not guarantee this. For instance, the winters of 1982-1983 and 2015-2016 were wetter than normal in the north-west USA.
Mixed news for snow lovers
In much of the northern USA, and large swathes of Canada, a greater chance of dry and warm weather makes snow less likely.
Further south, however, above-average precipitation typically leads to big snowfalls in the Californian mountains and southern Rockies - good news for water stocks.
It can also increase the probability of snow at lower levels in the southern and eastern USA - but only if enough cold air is in the mix.
The area around Washington DC often receives more snowfall than usual in an El NiÃ±o winter - but not always.
The winter of 2009-2010 delivered record-breaking snowfall that brought the city to a standstill, while widespread blizzards affected much of the US east coast in 2016.
However, some of Washington DC's least snowy winters have also occurred during El NiÃ±o events, including 1972-1973 and 1997-1998 which brought just 0.1in (0.25cm) of snow.
Higher winter temperatures in eastern Canada and the north-east USA can mean precipitation that might normally fall as snow gives rain instead.
This can increase the chance of freezing rain events, with the so-called Great Ice Storm of 1998, external being blamed partly on the effects of El NiÃ±o.
It is worth saying that snowfall amounts are decreasing overall in most places due to human-induced climate change, meaning predicting the impact of El NiÃ±o is even more complex.
What about the polar vortex?
An added complication is the possible impact of El NiÃ±o on the polar vortex, a ring of strong winds that circles the North Pole in winter, around 10-30 miles (16-48km) up in the stratosphere.
It holds cold, dense air in place above the Arctic but sometimes it can weaken and disrupt, and there is some evidence that the energy released into the atmosphere by El NiÃ±o makes this more likely.
Disruptions to the polar vortex sometimes ripple down through the atmosphere, weakening the polar jet stream and opening the door for cold air to spill across Canada and the USA.
However this does not always occur and the links are far from clear.

Trump himself has said he doesn't want to spend the final two years of his presidency simply vetoing bills from the Democrats in control of Congress. It was only a few short years ago, during his first term, that Trump stunned Republicans by cutting deals with the Democratic leaders he called "Chuck and Nancy" — Senate Leader Chuck Schumer and then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi.
