The costs of expanding Medicare to cover more people would depend on the scope, and Democrats have considered plans that include dropping the eligibility age to below 65 or including children and young people. The Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2022 that various so-called single-payer options could increase federal subsidies for healthcare from $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion by 2030, while the total out-of-pocket costs for patients would decline. Trump's willingness to slog through extended negotiations with Democrats is an open question, and his past promises of dealmaking have been hit and miss. He reiterated Thursday he is willing to work with Democrats. "I'm going to be vetoing a lot of things that they're going to send me initially that are bad for the country, and I think eventually they're going to call in, they're going to say, 'Let's make a deal,' and we'll be able to make deals on healthcare, on drug prices," the president told commentator Stephen A. Smith in an interview. Trump's choice of Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff may foreclose some of those opportunities, however. Jeffries described Miller as a "stone-cold racist" and said he has "zero interest" in working with him. The pitches from Democrats keep coming The pitches from some of Democrats' most high-profile new arrivals in Washington will help shape the party's approach for the rest of Trump's presidency. Talarico, the Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas, described the ways that Johnson is memorialized on Capitol Hill and remembered for shaping civil rights and social services as a senator and president. "If President Trump wants the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality," Talarico said Thursday at the What's Next conference in Denver, where many Democrats gathered to plot their way forward. Talarico made his pitch to Democrats as much as to Trump. After getting the fulsome repudiation of Trump they've been seeking for a decade, the party's base voters may not be eager to see their newly elected leaders standing with him for a bipartisan signing ceremony at the White House Rose Garden that he paved over to create a patio resembling his Mar-a-Lago resort. However, Talarico said Americans are counting on bold changes before the next president takes office after Trump's second term ends. ANTALYA, Turkey—Despite the lack of progress toward the goal of curbing global warming, outgoing U.N. Secretary General António Guterres urged climate activists and environmental justice advocates at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference here not to give up hope.
“You pushed governments to face up to the role of fossil fuels,” he said during his speech Friday to about 800 representatives of civil society groups from around the world. “You fought for finance for communities facing the worst impacts of a crisis they did little to cause. But let’s be clear. We face powerful lobbies that are pressuring governments. So civil society must put the needed counter-pressure against that.”
Guterres, former prime minister of Portugal, said a big part of the effort is to protect future generations who can’t influence today’s decisions. He said it’s essential to “do everything to make sure that those responsible for essential decisions create the conditions for a rapid, drastic reduction of emissions.”
While cutting carbon dioxide emissions is the only proven way to stop warming, this year’s Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, once again is far from addressing the issue of fossil fuels.
A voluntary global pledge to increase electrification holds the most promise for reducing emissions, but even that has become contentious, as some countries are resisting using the term “clean electrification,” which means producing electricity from renewables, rather than fossil fuels. Converting systems to run on electricity doesn’t reduce emissions if the electricity is produced by burning coal, oil or gas.
And there is a danger the U.N. process could backslide. Observers at some of the closed-door sessions this week said several countries, mainly Russia and Saudi Arabia, may be trying to block adoption of a final conference decision document—an outcome that could lead to the summit being widely perceived as a failure, even if such a text is not procedurally required.
All decisions and documents at the conference must be adopted by consensus, and Saudi Arabia’s 30-year history of obstructing efforts to address fossil fuels is well documented.
Guterres’s 10-year term as U.N. secretary-general ends Dec. 31. He has been outspoken about global warming and environmental justice. Even though international cooperation on climate and other issues has deteriorated recently, he has an abiding faith that collective action can overcome seemingly intractable social and political circumstances.
That belief, he has said, is rooted in part from his experiences during Portugal’s 1974 Carnation Revolution, when citizens arose against the country’s military dictatorship to establish what has become one of Europe’s most stable democracies.

“We are losing ground to climate change because we are not doing enough,” Guterres said. “We must turn the promise to transition away from fossil fuels into clear commitments … with clear timelines and real support for the workers and impacted communities.”
Shamini Selvaratnam, director of international climate and clean energy at the Ocean Conservancy, applauded Guterres’ leadership on climate change.
“Secretary-General Guterres has been a tireless champion for climate action and a powerful voice for protecting our ocean and the communities that depend on it,” she said. “His unwavering belief that cooperation is possible, even in a deeply divided world, was the message many of us needed to hear.”
Selvaratnam said his promise to keep up the fight after leaving office affirms that ”none of us can give up on protecting our oceans and our planet.”

Pope Leo XIV has celebrated Mass near the Peruvian city where he made his name as a compassionate bishop who worked closely with poor and migrant communities.
The ceremony was held on Friday at a park in Pimentel, about 10km (six miles) from Chiclayo in northern Peru as part of his tour of Latin America.
The Vatican estimates more than 1.5 million people gathered to welcome the pontiff.
"Thank you for your affection, support and prayers," the Pope told followers.
"Especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," he added, referencing the surgery he had for lung cancer which took place just weeks ago.
Some of the crowd arrived 12 hours in advance to wait in vigil before the Mass began.
"We spent the night praying, alongside family, excited to welcome the Pope from Chiclayo," said Isa Orderique.
Many came from across Peru and even neighbouring countries to attend.
Merli Cruz Guerrero, from an area near the Ecuadorean border, travelled several hours by bus to attend. She also spent the entire night waiting.
Of all the events the Pope has attended so far during his visit to Peru, this felt particularly emotional.
The crowd fell into a hushed silence as the pontiff's motorcade approached.
They waited eagerly for his arrival despite spending long hours out in the open with the temperature pushing past 30C.
For many living here, the fact that the Pope worked extensively in this region before becoming the head of the Catholic Church has put them in the spotlight.
"The Pope has come home and Chiclayo is celebrating," said Lisbeth DÃaz, a teacher who worked with Pope Leo when he served as the city's bishop between 2015 and 2023.
Peru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the pontiff, who was elected in May 2025.
The trip has also taken in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in this country carries particular significance.
The Pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.
Around Chiclayo, it is hard to meet anyone who doesn't claim to be a friend of the Pope or have a special anecdote about him.
Some recall how he would enjoy sampling Peruvian delicacies at El TrÃ©bol, a restaurant next to the city's cathedral. Others remember his love of tennis.
But for many it's the more serious moments of his time here, such as helping launch soup kitchens during the Covid-19 pandemic, or wading through deep waters on horseback when floods hit the area.
Several of these images are on display in a small museum dedicated to him at the entrance to the bishop's residence.
But for the city, and for a country that calls him the "Peruvian Pope", his return home means much more than a collection of photographs and anecdotes.
"It is the return of the man who brought Peruvians closer to the Church," said Samuel David Miranda Atoche, a local parish priest from Chiclayo who was ordained by the Pope back when he was still the bishop and known under his birth name of Robert Prevost.
And it is not just local people he connected with, according to DÃaz, who came to Chiclayo from Venezuela.
"It was difficult for him to see so many migrants living on the streets," she added, recalling the time when large numbers of Venezuelans came through Chiclayo escaping the political and economic crisis in their home country.
"So, he got in touch with the migration authorities and coordinated with other organisations to speed up the paperwork needed for many of us to obtain legal residency and work permits."
Robert Prevost's time here as bishop also involved difficult decisions, such as having to deal with the controversy and scandal surrounding the dissolution of Sodalitium of Christian Life, a Peruvian Catholic organisation that had faced decades of sexual abuse allegations.
Santiago Roncagliolo, a Peruvian writer and journalist who has studied the Pope's life, believes his handling of that crisis earned him the favour of his predecessor, Pope Francis, and helped set him on the path to the papacy.
Father Miranda also stressed the role the now-pontiff played in bringing people together.
"If there is one thing Bishop Prevost worked for here," he added, referring to the Pope by his previous title, "it was unity".
That unity has been on display in the run up to the Mass, with the square in front of Chiclayo Cathedral filled with joyous celebrations for days.
Normally, 800,000 people live in the city and its surrounding area, but estimates say the Pope's visit has caused that to double.
Local businesses have been capitalising on the Pope's popularity to boost sales and hotels have sharply increased their nightly room rates.
But that didn't seem to put off the faithful who gathered for the Mass.
Shouts of: "The Pope is from Chiclayo!" echoed across the field during the event.
Their affection was clearly reflected by the pontiff.
"As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart," he said from the stage, "for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."

In 1935, a group of Hawaiian school boys embarked on a secret military operation to colonize remote Pacific islands for the United States.
Inhabiting one of America’s most distant outposts in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, they built the runway Amelia Earhart never arrived at, endured fatal Japanese bombing and forged a Native Hawaiian cultural presence more than 6,600 miles from Washington. Decades later, and with bipartisan support, the legacy of the Hui Panalā‘au was enshrined with one of the largest marine protected areas in the world to safeguard the vibrant waters surrounding several of the islands.
This week, the Trump administration proposed reintroducing commercial fishing to parts of the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument.
Following the public comment period, if the National Marine Fisheries Service enacts the proposal, longline fishing boats and purse seiners that encircle dense schools of fish with vertical walls of netting would be allowed to return to more than 400,000 square miles of pristine, ecologically rich and culturally-valued waters.
“You take people and their lives, and now you want to come back and take the resources,” said Sol Kahoʻohalahala, a Native Hawaiian elder and knowledge holder, questioning the administration’s move. “We need to stop this idea of extraction and taking for profit and not being concerned with the children yet unborn,” said Kahoʻohalahala, whose uncle from the island of Lānaʻi died during Japanese raids on one of the island settlements.
“This is one of the last wild, healthy ocean ecosystems on the planet. It’s truly a gem,” said Sheila Sarhangi, founder and executive director of the Pacific Islands Heritage and Papahānaumokuākea Coalitions. “It’s completely reckless and shortsighted to allow industrial fishing, with its heavy amount of bycatch, to come back into the area.”
It’s not the administration’s first time pushing to fish these waters.
In April 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order dismantling Obama-era protections around Johnston Atoll, Jarvis Island and Wake Island, temporarily allowing commercial fishing to return between 50 and 200 miles offshore. Three days later, the National Marine Fisheries Service notified permit holders that they could fish the waters.
Following a lawsuit filed by Earthjustice, the federal district court in Honolulu halted commercial fishing operations in the area in August 2025, citing the fisheries service’s failure to adhere to due process and incorrect invoking of the Antiquities Act, a legal precedent which allows the president to establish marine protected areas but not shrink boundaries or strip protections.
A historically bipartisan conservation issue—President George W. Bush originally established the monument in 2009—the latest proposal reverses course.
With a 5,000-year-old coral system and at least 165 seamounts, the monument functions as a biodiversity hotspot for blue whales, leatherback sea turtles and seabirds. Conservationists consider it to be one of the most important habitats for threatened and endangered wildlife in the world.
The administration has suggested the potential ecological harm would be “negligible” because the proposed fishing gear would “not come into contact with the ocean floor.” Yet the harmful impact of industrial fishing in the area, whose ecological health has beneficial spill-over effects for the wider Pacific Ocean, is evident from historic data.
In 2013, the last year industrial fishing was allowed within the expanded range, the Hawaiian longline fleet ensnared over 2,300 sharks. Keeping just 10, the vast majority were discarded dead or injured, including the threatened silky shark and the globally critically endangered oceanic whitetip shark.
“The proposed rule threatens to reverse decades of progress in protecting one of the planet’s last wild, healthy ocean ecosystems,” said the Pacific Islands Heritage Coalition in a press release. “[It’s] a place of profound cultural significance for Indigenous Pacific Islanders.”
Framed as part of President Trump’s efforts to “unleash American commercial fishing” in the region, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration contends re-opening the area would mean American boats “do not have to compete with foreign fleets” nor pay other nations to fish in their waters.

Donate Now
However, the economic benefit would likely be limited. The fisheries service concedes the change would only offer a “minor, beneficial impact” by “reducing transit times” and fuel use.
This June, Trump signed a proclamation seeking to undo protections in three other Pacific areas: the Islands Unit of the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument in the Northern Mariana Islands, the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument in Hawaiʻi and the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument in American Samoa.
“This is driven by politics. It’s more show than go,” said David Henkin, an Earthjustice attorney who helped defeat the administration the first time around. “Sending the bull into the china shop messes up important scientific research, affects pristine ecosystems and for what?”
Indeed, even when fleets were briefly granted access to the area in 2025, activity was limited. Just over 1,700 fish were caught—a testament to the geographic impracticality of fishing in the monument’s remote protected waters.
“They know that ‘unleashing American fishing’ in the monument will not result in any more fish being caught because these fisheries operate under international quotas. They can’t catch any more fish,” Henkin added. “The whole thing is a charade.”

078d1d6de157.text: By — Jill Lawless, Associated Press Jill Lawless, Associated Press By — Sam McNeil, Associated Press Sam McNeil, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/europe-to-send-a-diplomat-team-to-ukraine-talks-as-leaders-push-for-a-voice Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Europe to send a diplomat team to Ukraine talks as leaders push for a voice World Updated on Nov 13, 2026 2:26 PM EST — Published on Nov 13, 2026 1:22 PM EST DUBLIN (AP) — Europe will send a team of diplomats from the European Union and five individual countries to the next round of Ukraine talks, a top EU official said Friday after a summit focused on how to avoid being shut out of U.S.-led negotiations on ending the nearly five-year war. European Council President Antonio Costa said the continent will be represented by officials from the 27-nation EU bloc and five members of the "Coalition of the Willing" that backs Ukraine: the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Poland. READ MORE: Ukraine fires nearly 1,200 drones at Russia as U.S.-led talks consider wider European security "We need to integrate all of us. And for this it's essential to have a team and to speak with only one voice," Costa said. European leaders have been concerned that a U.S.-backed process will leave them sidelined and Kyiv vulnerable as Moscow and Washington decide the fate of a conflict that has roiled the continent. Ukraine is eager for support from its European allies. It's reluctant to leave the talks solely in the hands of a U.S. administration that has often seemed to lean toward Moscow's views. Russia does not want European countries involved in direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine's military effort. European leaders also distrust U.S. President Donald Trump to negotiate on their behalf after a series of tense standoffs over trade, Greenland and conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. "Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine," French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin. "There is no more U.S. support." "At the end of the day, we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans," he said. Europe is broadly aligned but not unified European leaders fear Russian President Vladimir Putin will press Trump to back a peace settlement that weakens not just Ukraine but broader European security. Putin has demanded NATO troops be pulled back from Russia's borders and that no European forces be deployed in Ukraine. As envoys from Washington, Moscow and Kyiv met this week in Abu Dhabi, several European countries, including the U.K., France and Germany, attended discussions nearby, but not the main talks. U.S. envoy Jared Kushner and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after they met in Dublin late Thursday that Europe would be part of the next round of talks. Zelenskyy said Europe would send a negotiating team, adding, "They will have a voice." "We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table," Kushner said. He said Putin "is willing to give it a try." An old question with no clear answer European leaders are united in wanting a place at the table. But they have tussled over whether Europe should be represented by one person — as Russia has demanded and the U.S. suggested it would prefer — or a team. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that "the Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar" and they should name a representative. Supporters of a single envoy, such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, argued that the absence of a united European voice has allowed individual countries or small groups to engage in freelance diplomacy. "There are too many different groupings discussing the issue," she said. READ MORE: U.S. envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then head for Dublin to see Zelenskyy The question of who represents Europe is an old one. Europe itself is loosely defined. Is it the 27-nation EU, the 32-nation NATO military alliance made up mostly of European countries, the 29-nation Schengen zone, or the 47-nation European Political Community? That has long frustrated Washington. After this week's U.S.-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia in the United Arab Emirates, Kushner said that "if Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation." That echoes the famous question often misattributed to former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger: "Who do I call if I want to call Europe?" A job-share team of envoys from the EU and beyond The decision to send a team, rather than an individual, allows for participation by members of the "coalition of the willing," a group of nations that have pledged to underpin a future ceasefire with military support. That includes the U.K., which left the EU in 2020. Poland is a voice for nations on the EU's eastern flank that face constant hybrid threats from Russia, including influence campaigns and disruptive drones. It was not immediately clear who would represent the EU's institutions. Speculation had centered on Costa and the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas. Earlier this year, Costa faced criticism within the EU after his office set up a hush-hush back-channel with Moscow. Kallas, a former prime minister of Estonia, laid claim to the envoy role Friday, saying, "I'm the one who is representing Europe in the foreign and security policy." "We can't send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending." Some leaders deeply distrust the U.S.-brokered talks. 866319e998c2.text: The movement to prevent House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) from becoming speaker is struggling to get off the ground due to a fatal flaw: Nobody else wants the job. Why it matters: Despite the phone calls and online petitions, the demands from progressive holdouts, Jeffries' ascent has become a self-fulfilling prophecy. The House Democrats most often floated as potential challengers don't appear to be interested: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) told Axios on Thursday his "dream job" is to chair the House Judiciary Committee. "I am not a candidate for speaker in any way. ... I am supporting Hakeem and voting for Hakeem," said Raskin. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) has privately told colleagues she doesn't want the role despite an online movement seeking to draft her, according to multiple House Democrats who have spoken directly with her. "Congresswoman Pressley is in active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment, and deliver for the people," spokesperson Ricardo Sanchez said in a statement to Axios. "She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership." "He's the only one running," Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.) told Axios on Thursday when asked if she plans to vote for Jeffries as speaker. Said Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.): "I am really encouraging our leadership to make it easy for me to vote for the one person that's running. But as of right now, there's ... no one else that has put their name forward." "As far as I've heard, Jeffries is the only person running," said Rep.-elect Randy Villegas (D-Calif.). Jeffries said in a NY1 interview : "Someone could always emerge in the next week or so, but right now there are no declared challengers, no indication that anyone may put themselves forward." The intrigue: For once it's the Senate, not the House, providing all the drama on Capitol Hill. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) launched his bid to replace Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Thursday night. Yes, but: The progressive grassroots have continued this week to swamp sitting and incoming House Democrats with calls and emails urging them to oppose Jeffries, according to lawmakers and aides. Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) told Axios he has gotten an "avalanche of messages." Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said she is getting "hundreds" of calls "every day" urging her to oppose Jeffries. A senior House Democrat who is supporting Jeffries told Axios the callers into their office have suggested "like 10" different members as possible alternatives. Jeffries has pushed back on Axios' reporting that members are being flooded with calls, saying in his NY1 interview: "There's no indication that members of Congress have been overwhelmed by any calls." State of play: Jeffries has begun meeting with skeptics ahead of House Democrats' Nov. 18 leadership elections. He is expected to easily win the nomination for speaker, determined by a simple majority vote of the caucus. The real question is whether any House Democrats will oppose him on the House floor on Jan. 3 and deny him the unanimous support he has enjoyed from his caucus since becoming leader in 2022. "We're going to continue to talk to every single member of the House Democratic caucus, both current members and incoming members, about what we all can do together for the American people," Jeffries told reporters at a press conference on Thursday. The Democratic leader said he is "confident that we're on a positive trajectory" but takes "nothing for granted." Between the lines: Several Democratic House members and members-elect predicted that, given the grassroots pressure bearing down on progressives right now, at least a handful are likely to openly oppose him. What they're saying: Leonard told Axios he sat down with Jeffries on Wednesday and shared what he has heard from callers, including "that the Democratic establishment brand is in the toilet and that the leader's name is synonymous with the Democratic establishment." Ramirez said she has "begun conversations" with Jeffries and intends to "have more next week." Asked if Jeffries has met with the Jeffries-skeptic "Bloc" of incoming progressives, she said: "It is my understanding that that they're scheduling time to meet with them." Reps.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) and LaKesha Womack (D-N.C.) said Jeffries met Wednesday with members of the North Carolina delegation, many of whom are holdouts in the speaker election. "We're still having conversations, we're still listening ... at the end of the day, we're going to all sit together, we're going to listen to everything and we're going to move forward like that," said Ojeda. The bottom line: "I mean, right now, I don't even know if there's anybody that's stepping up against him," Ojeda added.

756b9546ce7e.text: By — Lauren Neergaard, Associated Press Lauren Neergaard, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/what-men-need-to-know-after-a-major-update-to-prostate-cancer-guidelines Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What men need to know after a major update to prostate cancer guidelines Health Nov 13, 2026 12:58 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Middle-aged men should undergo regular screening for prostate cancer, the American Cancer Society said Thursday in a major change to its guidelines. The screening involves a simple blood test, and men at average risk of getting prostate cancer should receive that PSA test every two years between the ages of 50 and 69, the cancer society advised. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Men at high risk, including Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer, should get yearly PSA checks and start earlier, at age 45. Thursday's guideline update marks a shift in thinking about routine blood tests for PSA, or prostate-specific antigen. WATCH: What to know about screening, diagnosis and treatment for prostate cancer Since 2010, the cancer society has recommended that men at average risk talk with their doctors about whether and how often to get PSA tests. That's a protein produced by both normal and cancerous prostate cells, meaning a high level might signal a tumor but also could be from a benign enlarged prostate or be a temporary spike from vigorous exercise. Catching prostate cancer early without overtreating Prostate cancer is highly survivable if caught early, but widespread PSA testing in the past was blamed for overtreatment of slow-growing tumors and unnecessary follow-up testing in men who turned out to not have cancer. The updated advice comes after advances in understanding how regular PSA testing can help catch prostate cancer before it spreads and becomes harder to treat, as well as how to reduce potential harms from screening, according to the cancer society. That includes steps such as repeating a PSA test to be sure it's really high or adding an MRI scan to help identify who needs a biopsy, as well as monitoring rather than aggressively treating low-risk tumors. A prostate cancer specialist not involved with the guideline said the change will be especially helpful for primary care doctors who introduce cancer screenings to patients but may be less familiar with the complexities. READ MORE: Joe Biden's prostate cancer has spread and is causing him pain, Hunter Biden says "This has taken ambiguity out of it. They are basically saying, 'Do it,'" said Dr. Ash Tewari, who leads the urology department at Mount Sinai's Icahn School of Medicine in New York. "This guideline will only make things easier for men and hopefully it will have more grandfathers eating dinner with their family 10 years from now." Still talk with your doctor about your prostate cancer risk There still needs to be a doctor-patient conversation about the pros and cons, the cancer society guideline stresses. "We want to find the right balance," Tewari agreed. "Patients need to understand that their risk of prostate cancer differs," which explains why the recommendations aren't one-size-fits-all. What is a strong family history? The cancer society says that means having one close relative — a father, brother or son — diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or multiple close relatives diagnosed at any age. That puts them in the high-risk category for yearly PSA checks starting at 45. But if men have just one close relative with prostate cancer diagnosed after 65, they should still start screening at 45 but can go two years between testing. READ MORE: Why are Americans paying more for health insurance? Experts give 3 reasons How long should screening continue? It's not for men of any age whose health is so poor that they aren't expected to live another 10 years. For everyone else, the guideline advises talking with a doctor at age 70 about the choice, saying benefits are less clear. The cancer society no longer recommends screening at 75 — while acknowledging that particularly healthy 75- to 79-year-olds may choose to continue — and discourages it once men turn 80. Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men. The cancer society estimates more than 333,000 men in the U.S. will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2026, and about 36,000 will die of it. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The U.S. Department of the Interior could transfer swaths of public lands to state, local and tribal governments through sales or land swaps, according to the agency’s new strategic plan.
Critics are concerned that many states, cities and counties can’t afford to maintain the lands, and would sell them to private interests—the first step toward a wholesale privatization of lands that have belonged to Americans for more than 150 years.
“This is the biggest attack we’ve ever seen on public lands,” said Kate Groetzinger, communications director for the nonprofit Center for Western Priorities.
The Interior Department did not respond to requests for comment.
The agency manages more than 500 million acres of land in addition to 3.2 billion acres of offshore resources and 700 million acres of underground minerals. All told, the department manages 20 percent of the country’s lands, from national parks to wildlife refuges.
Data center developers, mining firms and energy companies—all favored industries of the Trump administration—could seize the opportunity to acquire vast tracts for their environmentally harmful operations, critics say.
The plan says Interior “will work to decrease the size of the federal estate” through the sales. That will allow the department to “focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands,” according to the plan, with some of the sales proceeds going back to “the purchasing entities to use for conservation purposes.”
The plan also says the agency will “consolidate its workforce to advance operational efficiencies.” Interior has already lost more than 17 percent of its workforce under the second Trump administration.
In the plan’s introduction, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote that the agency will streamline environmental reviews and expedite leasing and permitting for energy companies. Nowhere in the plan does the agency mention wind or solar power. The first goal outlined in the plan is “Increase American Prosperity,” and the opening pages feature pictures of an oil rig and an offshore oil operation.
“Together, we can simplify processes and remove red tape that creates drudgery for our team members and impedes progress,” Burgum wrote. “We can bring forward new ideas and better ways of working. For the first time in human history, we can turn electricity into intelligence.”
Burgum has made millions of dollars off investments in artificial intelligence, powered by data centers, ProPublica reported Nov. 6.
The plan doesn’t specifically identify data centers as potential customers to purchase federal property, but the White House previously asked Bureau of Land Management state offices to identify lands that would be appropriate for these uses.
Last June, BLM approved an AI data center on 81 acres of public land near Boulder City, Nevada. The builder had received federal approval in 2023 to construct a solar farm, but amended its application to include a data center.
A federal judge has halted the project because BLM did not conduct a new environmental analysis but rather used the previous one for the solar project, a likely violation of the National Environmental Policy Act.
Energy and mining interests have long sought—and received—access to the oil, gas and minerals beneath public lands via leases. The new Interior plan would allow BLM to sell or transfer those properties outright to agencies that could then resell them.
The plan runs from fiscal year 2026 to 2030. However, the Trump administration has already begun planning to offload some public lands in particular.
This September, the Forest Service, which is under the U.S. Department of Agriculture, issued a permit to Pitkin County in Colorado to manage a section of the White River National Forest that contains the Maroon Bells Scenic Area, the gateway to stunning burgundy peaks where hundreds of thousands of recreators visit annually. Critics see this move as a trial run for public land transfers.
In Alaska, the federal government is expected to soon open 28 million acres to new development and land ownership, according to the Juneau Independent.
Last March the Forest Service officially transferred a sacred indigenous site to Resolution Copper, a mining company.
BLM needs congressional approval to sell public parcels over 2,500 acres. However, federal law contains loopholes, Groetzinger said. The sales, for example, must serve the national interest, which can be broadly interpreted. The plan lays the foundation for that claim by repeatedly justifying future sales on national security grounds.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
Not only does the Interior Department propose shrinking its current inventory of public lands, but the plan also forecloses the possibility of buying more. Instead of using the Land and Water Conservation Fund to purchase additional acreage, the agency says it will “shift its investment focus” to buying recreational and conservation easements on privately owned lands.
The Land and Water Conservation Fund protects thousands of parks, natural areas, historic sites and other projects nationwide from private development. “That’s an important function of the fund,” Groetzinger said. “For them to not use any of those funds to buy new land is just unprecedented.”
Jayson O’Neill is a spokesman for Save Our Parks and lives in Montana, where recreation and tourism driven by access to public lands and waters is critical for the local economy. “We need somebody that actually understands how important this is to the economic viability of our communities and also our way of life,” O’Neill said. “Instead they’re literally calling to give away federal public lands and public resources to industry.”
Inside Climate News reporter Jake Bolster contributed

cde7c9c96588.text: By — Andrew Gillis, Associated Press Andrew Gillis, Associated Press By — Mallika Sen, Associated Press Mallika Sen, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/meet-the-new-bachelor-a-quarterback-for-the-washington-commanders Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Meet the new 'Bachelor,' a quarterback for the Washington Commanders Nation Nov 13, 2026 12:44 PM EST After a troubled year for "The Bachelor" franchise, the ABC reality dating show is going back to a familiar well: the NFL. The network announced Friday that Sam Hartman, a quarterback for the Washington Commanders, will be handing out roses on the 30th season of the show. Season 30 will premiere March 21, the network said in a statement. Hartman, 27, is a member of the Commanders' practice squad and has yet to play a regular-season game. He appeared Friday on "Good Morning America," shortly after the Commanders' win over the New York Giants on Thursday night. "I have a tough time holding conversation with one girl; 30 is going to be pretty tough," he joked to the hosts. He said his first reaction to the overture was "no way" — but a conversation with the show's host, Jesse Palmer, changed his mind. Palmer himself is a former lead on "The Bachelor" — and was a quarterback for the Giants when he appeared on the show's fifth season. Colton Underwood and Clayton Echard — both contestants on "The Bachelorette" who later became leads of "The Bachelor" — also had brief NFL careers. Underwood was on practice squads while Echard went to a training camp. Mel Owens, the titular "Golden Bachelor" for Season 2 of the spinoff, was a linebacker for the Los Angeles Rams. Hartman's selection again breaks with the typical formula of casting past contestants on "The Bachelorette" and "The Bachelor" as leads. The network tried that last year when it selected "Secret Lives of Mormon Wives" star Taylor Frankie Paul for "The Bachelorette," but the experiment ended with that season being scrubbed entirely in March amid domestic abuse allegations. READ MORE: Utah court rules Taylor Frankie Paul can't have unsupervised visits with her 2-year-old son No show in the "Bachelor" universe has aired since summer 2025's "Bachelor in Paradise," a remarkable hiatus for a franchise that's been a near-constant in the world of reality TV since 2002. Hartman, a Charlotte, North Carolina, native who played college football at Wake Forest and Notre Dame, said he was nervous. He told the "Good Morning America" hosts his criteria for his would-be fiancee included someone he could chase — "chase in the way they have a drive for something that motivates me to wake up every day and chase them" — and "compassion and some type of caregiving," citing his family history in the medical field. Gen Z is often cast as souring on AI, but theyâre no more negative about the technology than their parents and grandparents.
A new survey from Milltown Partners, shared first with Semafor, found that 73% of Gen Z adults havenât made up their minds on AI, while half said they expect AI to harm society. That matches baby boomers (50%) and Gen Xers (48%), while millennials were the most upbeat, with 39% expecting harm.
Companies and politicians are all eager to understand the generationâs stance on AI, given how much they drive tech trends and how AI and data centers played an outsize role in the US midterm election.
The report also pointed to a paradox that seems to define young peopleâs relationship with AI: Many say it makes them worse at thinking for themselves and harder to find a job â but 46% said they use it every day, the second-highest rate behind millennials.
Young people are also less worried than older generations about the existential risk that dominates much of the AI safety discourse. And they are more conflicted about their own use: 30% of Gen Zers said they sometimes feel guilty using AI, more than double the rate among respondents over 30.

The scene was 145 years in the making.
Dozens of people filled a tiny room inside the historic Masonic Lodge Hall in Jackson, Mississippi, on Wednesday, waiting to hear whether Scott Colom would become the state's next US Senator.
The 70-year-old building is the permanent residence of the NAACP's state headquarters, where civil rights leaders, many of them there that night, worked for decades to create this moment.
When a large speaker blared the news of Colom's win, it ended a long, anxious wait for results that came over a week after election day. The room exploded with emotion.
"Yes sir," one man yelled, dropping to the ground and moving his arms and legs as if to make a snow angel on the carpet floor.
Colom's victory is the first win for Democrats in the seat in more than 40 years. And that candidate, who was elected for the final time in 1982, supported segregation.
It is also the first time a black politician has held the seat since 1881. Mississippi's population is almost 40% black, which is a larger share of the electorate than any other state.
Republicans have, following a ruling by the US Supreme Court overturning parts of the Voting Rights Act, made moves to reduce the number of majority-black districts, which many experts say weakens black voting power. It is partly due to this backdrop that Colom's victory resonated with many.
"All the stories that my father used to tell me about him growing up here in Jackson, and all the hardships and unjust treatment that he faced. And having experienced some of that myself, it's hard to put it into words what this moment means for us," Cedric Haynes said.
"Whoever thought this day would have come."
People cheered, hugged, kissed and cried, celebrating the achievement.
"I think it is special. It is holy, and it something different," Charles Taylor, executive director of the NAACP's Mississippi branch, said.
Taylor now sits in the same office that was once occupied by Medgar Evers, a black WWII veteran and civil rights activist who was killed by an assassin's bullet in Mississippi, in 1963, in part for his effort to register black Americans to vote.
To win in the Magnolia State, Colom has not only had to overcome the state's racial history, but defy its political gravity. Mississippi has long been a Republican stronghold. Donald Trump won re-election to the presidency here by over 22 points, just two years go.
In the early days of the midterm election season, which ultimately ended in Democrats flipping a record number of seats in Congress, not even the party's wildest ambitions included a Mississippi victory.
Two days after election day, with a lead of only a few hundred votes, Colom said the national party had long given up on the state.
"I've been in Mississippi for 15 years," Colom told NBC News on 5 November. "Most of the time Democrats have conceded the state."
He continued: "What you're saying is, I don't care enough about those voters."
But Colom won anyways, despite having a roughly $2m campaign donation deficit compared to the Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to the most recent FEC records.
The tide turned for Colom and Democrats, with help from massive grassroots campaigning and organising.
The NAACP said it knocked on more than 150,000 doors across the state and made stops at over 2,500 churches in the lead-up to the election - compared to 70,000 doors and 500 churches in the last election. The NAACP is non-partisan and did not favour a candidate - but exit polls showed 91% of black voters in Mississippi backed Colom.
About 300,000 more voters showed up to Mississippi's polls in 2026, compared to the last mid-term's in 2022.
His victory against nearly impossible odds was also bolstered by a strong showing from young voters, corralled by organisations like Mississippi Votes who showed up on college campuses across the state to encourage voter registration.
Arekia Bennett-Scott, executive director of Mississippi Votes, said over 600 students from Jackson State University, a local historically black college, voted this midterm election â trumping the figure of roughly 100 Jackson State students who voted during the last midterm.
The night of Colom's win, a group of drum majors from Jackson State's historic marching band, the Sonic Boom of the South, were heading into the locker room after practice, relishing their part in making history.
"I'm absolutely ecstatic. I'm overly excited that (Colom) won," drum major Jared Thompson said. "This is one of the first elections that I voted on as a young adult."
"And, you know, we hear a lot of this rhetoric that, 'oh my vote doesn't matter,'" he continued. "Tonight was proof, without a shadow of a doubt, that your vote matters."
Another major factor that contributed to Colom's success was a national backlash against the Republican party, driven by a rise in the cost of living linked to Trump policies, which caused several other Republican fortresses to fall on election night, including Texas, Kansas, and Iowa.
Hyde-Smith was also criticised for running a lackluster campaign, where she made very few public appearances. Meanwhile, Colom visited each of Mississippi's 82 counties, including a five-day campaign called the Where's Cindy Tour.
After the Republican recommended people pick another protein if the cost of beef was too high, Colom released an attack ad that went viral, encouraging voters to "pick another senator".
At his victory speech, on the grounds of the historically black university Tougaloo College on Wednesday evening, hundreds of supporters gathered, many holding signs that said: "Picked another Senator."
A member of the Tougaloo Concert Choir sang the US National Anthem. Colom's two daughters, Gwendolyn and Brooklyn, aged 9 and 8, respectively, then led a recital of the Pledge of Allegiance, as hands were held over hearts.

Microsoft reported progress, but not a full recovery, following an outage Thursday that affected Outlook, Teams, and Copilot across more than 70 countries.
The consequences have been wide-reaching: Several police departments in the UK said Friday that the public shouldnât report crimes via online submission forms, and should call them in instead. Schools and agencies in Australia and Japan had to go analog. At least one company delayed its earnings call.
Itâs the kind of issue that reminds the world how much of our digital infrastructure is reliant on just a few companies, each a potential single point of failure. Microsoft ruled out a cyberattack, a relief given the recent wave of AI-powered hacks. The other silver lining for the company: Jensen Huang has been taking up all the oxygen in the tech world.

0a74c7ff8fd9.text:
Reedâs view
Jensen Huang made a lot of mistakes, but the one that really brought him down was getting too involved in DC.
The skillset of a great technologist is the opposite of someone whoâs great at politics. Technologists have to think years, sometimes decades in advance. When they figure out a winning formula, they bet everything on it.
Thatâs a really bad way to operate in Washington, where things move on two-year election cycles and commitment to any one idea, faction, or ideology is a liability if and when the political winds change.
When Donald Trump was elected president for a second term, it seemed like the world was suddenly a fundamentally different place. The White House was open for business in a way never seen in history. It was irresistible for a lot of tech people (Elon Musk and Marc Andreessen also fell into this trap).
For a while, it seemed like Huang was one of the few technologists to find success in DC. His friendship with the president helped advance his worldview â that America should export its technology around the world, even to China. But it was all a mirage. Political people understood this would never last, and it would end in hearings, investigations, and prosecutions. This has all come as a shocking surprise to many in the tech industry.
Nvidia was aggressive in its policy positions in part because it had the backing of the president. It should have used that influence sparingly, and not just to get what it wanted but to make more allies on both sides of the political aisle.
So far, the underlying allegations against Huang are unproven. The alleged spy who led to this mess may not even be a spy. And many in the tech industry are angry and want to fight back. Thatâs the wrong instinct. In the tech industry, the relentless will to win is perhaps the most redeeming quality of every operator. In DC, you canât ever really win. You can only lose.
The Nvidia scandal and the post-midterm tech industry peril are exactly the reason we came up with the idea for our convening, Silicon Valley & The World, which takes place next week in the heart of the industry. Weâre bringing leaders in from around the globe to burst Silicon Valleyâs bubble and make it a more worldly place. We have what I think is the best lineup of speakers ever assembled at a media industry convening and I hope Jensen Huang, who was supposed to speak, will reconsider. If youâd like to tune in, register for a virtual broadcast pass, or watch live on YouTube and at Semafor.com.

07c168b29768.text: By — Martha Bellisle, Associated Press Martha Bellisle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/bigger-and-more-frequent-wildfires-threaten-water-supplies-across-the-u-s Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Bigger and more-frequent wildfires threaten water supplies across the U.S. Nation Nov 13, 2026 12:21 PM EST Wildfires leave behind charred trees and scorched vegetation that impact the streams and rivers providing drinking water to much of the country, and new studies show that contamination could remain for more than a decade. These findings about the longevity of contamination in the nation's drinking water supplies are especially concerning as climate change and increasingly strong El Niño weather events, which intensify drought conditions, have led to bigger and more frequent wildfires in the U.S. So far in 2026, there have been 68,179 blazes burning more than 14,062 square miles (36,420 square kilometers). Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. After a wildfire sweeps through hillsides and forests, rains carry ash and organic matter into the streams that feed water treatment plants for towns and cities alike. Communities are working to adapt, but it can take years and require stopgap solutions. People in the City of Las Vegas, New Mexico, went without water for months after the Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon wildfire contaminated the Gallinas River in 2022. In the four years since, they've had to give residents bottled water and ship tanks in from nearby towns as they collected funds to build a new treatment plant. WATCH: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns Karen Pettine, who has owned the Hillcrest Restaurant for 50 years, said the water crisis forced them to close, sometimes for a week at a time. "It's hard to run a restaurant without good water," she said. "We used some paper plates at times. They brought in semi-truckloads of bottled water. You could pick up four cases at a time. The water situation is ongoing because when it rains, it floods and it brings dirty water down the stream." Las Vegas Mayor David Romero said climate change has made the things that used to be reliable less predictable. "It's a scary situation that we're all going to encounter," he said. Sediment from burned landscapes a headache for water-treatment plants Wildfires are a natural part of forest ecosystems, but an increase in their severity has made areas that capture, filter and regulate the flow of water, known as watersheds, vulnerable, said Amanda Hohner, an assistant professor at Montana State University who specializes in wildfires and water quality. Forested watersheds provide water to nearly two-thirds of municipalities in the U.S., according to Carli Brucker, lead author of a University of Colorado Boulder study that assessed wildfire-affected water quality in hundreds of burned basins and compared them to unburned areas. Their study found that the impacts can last up to eight years. Garrett McKay, an associate professor of civil and environmental engineering at Texas A&M, said utilities are extremely concerned about the impacts wildfires have on water. They're reaching out to experts like him for help finding different water sources or to learn how to treat the organic matter coming into their plants. Water treatment facilities that rely on streams and rivers typically treat high quality water, aided by trees and soil that act as a natural filtration system, Brucker said. But wildfires cause spikes in heavy metals or dissolved organic matter, which the plants aren't built to handle, she said. READ MORE: Is El Niño making storms and flash floods in the Southwest worse? This can force treatment facilities to shut off the incoming water and resort to other sources, which may not be immediately available, Brucker said. Some have groundwater or reservoir backups, but even those can be impacted. But sediments from burned vegetation are rich in nutrients, like nitrogen and phosphorus, and as they sit in still water, algal blooms can grow, he said. The algae can make people sick and kill the fish. Chlorine, routinely used to treat water, also is impacted by wildfires, said McKay at Texas A&M. When facilities add disinfectants, like chlorine, to water, they react with the dissolved organic matter left behind by the fires to form "disinfection byproducts," which are regulated by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency because they can cause illnesses, including cancer. Since plants can't remove the disinfection byproducts, they must get rid of the organic matter before disinfecting the water, which can cause delays in the water supply. 5c55308a1c02.text: A defining story of this decade has been a series of global economic shocks: pandemic, war and geopolitical shifts. New research quantifies a rising set of vulnerabilities for the global trade system . The big picture: Many crucial global goods are built on supply chains that have one or more Achilles' heels, a report from the consulting firm McKinsey finds — a critical input, concentrated suppliers and geopolitical strain. That manifests partly in physical chokepoints. The Strait of Hormuz is the one most in the news, but the McKinsey researchers identify a couple dozen others globally, through which 80% of maritime trade passes (although with varying levels of difficulty for shippers to route around). In effect, as the global economy has become more integrated over the last few decades, these vulnerabilities have become more pronounced — which in turn helps explain why the 2020s have brought an ongoing series of disruptive supply shocks. By the numbers: They find that the share of global imports that face at least two of three major vulnerabilities has risen to 23% in 2024 from 15% in 2000. The list of items with overlapping vulnerabilities includes basic materials like iron ore and more advanced items like lithium-ion batteries, smartphones and memory chips. What they're saying: "It's not necessarily that trade has gotten less reliable," Tiago Devesa, a co-author of the report, tells Axios. "I think it's more that we have the realization that we actually want to understand what are the potential points of failure, so we can anticipate them." "I think you could make a case that throughout all of these shocks, trade has continued to increase, and trade was actually a very important balancing mechanism," he adds. "It's been increasing precisely in part because we've integrated the fabric of the global economy much more, and in particular, we've led a specialization effort that led to more concentration around the world," says Devesa, a senior fellow at the McKinsey Global Institute. Reality check: Reducing vulnerabilities and building economic resilience isn't necessarily as simple as relocating a factory. "Some companies just change their suppliers or factory from a geopolitically distant country to a geopolitically closer country, and they think that they achieved resilience," said Jeongmin Seong, a co-author and McKinsey partner. "Even though you change the location of the final assembly, unless you eliminate the risk at this upstream level, you are still exposed." Between the lines: The steady march of globalization paid major dividends in recent decades in making goods more affordable and powering global growth. Now companies — and governments — are seeking to mitigate the vulnerabilities that system has created and that the last several years made plain to see.

Two Democratic lawmakers said Thursday that the Navy failed to inform Congress that it fired the entire leadership team of a nuclear-powered attack submarine last month after an underwater collision. Separately, the sea service in September fired the commander of a destroyer deployed to the Middle East, according to a defense official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe sensitive personnel matters. Please check your inbox to confirm. Dr. Brian Monahan, a Navy rear admiral and attending physician for Congress and the Supreme Court, also departed his post during a Navy investigation — with no public announcement or confirmation. All three are a break from the Navy's longstanding policy to announce major removals of commanders and other highly visible officials. They also follow an increasing level of secrecy over military operations, especially in the Middle East. "As a result of the Navy's failure to communicate, what should have been a standard exercise in information sharing has instead raised questions about the Navy's commitment to transparency and its commitment to a productive working relationship with Congress," Reps. Joe Courtney of Connecticut and Adam Smith of Washington wrote in a letter to Navy leaders. The developments could set up a contentious confirmation hearing next week for acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao as he seeks to permanently take over as the top civilian official. In a letter to Cao and the Navy's top uniformed officer, Adm. Daryl Caudle, Courtney and Smith said they had "deep frustration" over the Navy's failure to notify the House Armed Services Committee about the firing of the commander, second in command and top enlisted sailor of the USS South Dakota submarine. The letter says they were fired after the submarine ran into something on the seabed, but the Navy would not offer public comment. READ MORE: Hegseth fires the Pentagon's top military planner even as Trump considers new Iran strikes The Navy also on Sept. 27 relieved Cmdr. Caitlin Cunningham, commander of the USS Michael Murphy destroyer, which has been deployed to support operations against Iran, due to a loss of confidence, the defense official said. She had been in the job less than a year. Typically, the firing of someone like Cunningham would be announced by the Navy within days, but the service did not offer public comment even when asked about it. On Thursday, Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California also confirmed the departure of Monahan, the attending physician for Congress and the Supreme Court, but provided few other details. The Navy has opened an investigation, according to a person familiar with the situation who was not authorized to discuss the matter and spoke on the condition of anonymity. For nearly 18 years, Monahan held the top job in the Office of the Attending Physician, which is responsible for providing emergency medical assistance to members of Congress and the Supreme Court as well as congressional staff and visitors. Monahan was sometimes in the news for discussing matters such as Sen. Mitch McConnell's health and for administering a COVID-19 vaccine to then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. Restrictions on the military sharing information go beyond the Navy. U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, has released few details on recent limited strikes on Iran and refused to comment on or specify damage to bases or equipment, usually citing the need for operational security. Major satellite imagery providers with U.S. contracts have blocked or delayed public release of images in the region at the request of American officials. As a result, it took months to determine that Iranian drone and missile strikes damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment in the region, according to an Associated Press analysis. The spiralling winds of the polar vortex high above the Arctic have reversed direction marking the earliest 'major sudden stratospheric warming' on record.
These polar winds usually blow in a westerly direction keeping cold air locked high above the North Pole.
However in recent weeks the polar vortex has weakened and shifted position. Observations have now shown a switch to easterly winds, which experts say defines a 'major sudden stratospheric warming' or SSW.
Similar disruptions can occur during winter and are often linked with colder weather in the UK. But this event happening so early in autumn is unprecedented in modern observations.
What is sudden stratospheric warming?
The polar vortex is a normal feature of our climate in the months around winter. As the North Pole tilts away from the sun, temperatures above the Arctic drop and strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere.
Sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) is when a rapid and dramatic rise in temperature occurs high in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles (15-50km) above Earth's surface.
It can happen due to atmospheric disturbences causing a shift in the position or shape of the polar vortex which can make its winds weaken.
This sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) can eventually lead to the strong westerlies reversing into easterly winds.
In the following days and weeks these changes can slowly filter lower down in the atmosphere altering the position of the jet stream which drives what type of weather we experience on the ground.
A snowy winter for the UK?
Major SSW events have often historically increased the chance of drier and colder weather in the UK with northerly or easterly winds bringing in Arctic air.
It can also boost the possibility of snow, especially across eastern parts of the UK.
The 2018 Beast from the East followed a major SSW that occurred a few weeks earlier.
However, an SSW does not automatically lead to cold or snowy weather and any influence would take time to develop.
There are very few historical examples of early season major SSWs to compare with and so it is unclear exactly what, if any, impacts may happen a few weeks from now.
The previous earliest SSW on record happened on 28 November in both 1969 and 2025.
We do know that it is definitely not connected to the cold spell right now.
Will it bring snow to the US and Canada?
Because the stratospheric polar vortex operates at a global scale, disruptions and reversals can have impacts right around the world - increasing the possibility of cold weather, ice and snow in many regions, including North America.
However the possible impacts of this major SSW on the USA and Canada are, as in the UK, very uncertain.
There are historical examples of cold, snowy spells that can be linked - at least in part - to polar vortex disruptions.
The deadly winter storm that swept as far south as Texas in February 2021 followed a major SSW event that took place the previous month.
Widespread snowfall in February 2018, external was also linked to shifts in the polar vortex, and the same goes for the record 'snowmageddon' event that brought record-breaking snow to Washington DC in February 2010 - a winter when the vortex was unusually weak.
What these examples have in common is that they occurred in late winter - when polar vortex disruptions are most likely.
The difference this time is that the SSW has taken place unprecedentedly early - in the autumn - so its expected impacts are even less certain than normal.
Even if widespread northerly winds were to develop, the Arctic has not yet become as bitterly cold as it will be by late winter, so any chill spells may well be somewhat muted.
How will El NiÃ±o impact winter?
We are currently heading towards the expected peak of the strongest El NiÃ±o on record.
El NiÃ±o is a natural weather pattern that develops in the Pacific Ocean and the atmosphere above it.
When the winds that typically blow east-to-west weaken or reverse, warmer water can spread across the central and eastern tropical Pacific leading to changes in atmospheric conditions.
It is no surprise that the regions that see the most obvious weather impacts are the areas bordering this part of the Pacific, such as Peru and Ecuador in the east and Australia and Indonesia to the west.
However, El NiÃ±o can also affect weather patterns much further away.
In the UK, it means we tend to see a higher chance of wetter and stormier conditions in autumn and early winter.
There is also a higher chance of colder wintry weather developing late in the winter.
In the US and Canada there can be a greater chance of a warm and dry winter in northern areas and more risk of flooding rain further south.
There is also some evidence that El NiÃ±o can increase the likelihood of disruption to the stratospheric polar vortex which can, in turn, bring snowfall later in winter.
Lots of uncertianty
Any link between a strong El NiÃ±o and early onset of a SSW event, external is unclear and will need further research.
No two El NiÃ±os are the same. While it may increase the chance of certain types of weather occurring, this is not guaranteed.
Longer-range forecasting can give an idea of probabilities of certain weather patterns but there are always lots of different things going on and interactions between the atmosphere and oceans are complex.
These complexities are further compounded when happening against a backdrop of human-induced climate change.

Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.
That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.
And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?
The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."
Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.
What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.
The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 â the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.
What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".
That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.
But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.
"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.
"Our proposals were almost laughed at.
"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".
"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."
Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.
Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.
This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.
After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.
But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.
"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
And what of Putin?
At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.
You can see why.
The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.
And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.
And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.
The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.
Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.
But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

The US Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the longest nationwide ground stop of flights since the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks.
The FAA said Friday's stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, was "due to extraordinary circumstances" from a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centres.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of an attack and that everybody was safe.
Here's what we know.
How many flights were affected?
The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.
The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.
The Federal Aviation Administration opened skies again at until 20:15 EST.
What about international flights?
All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended "on request of the FAA due to technical issues", according to Eurocontrol's website.
There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK, Ukraine, and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.
Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, grounded all US-bound flights until further notice.
Air Canada cancelled flights between the US and Canada.
When will normal service resume?
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a news conference on Friday night that the outage would cause a ripple effect for a few days.
"It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.
Tens of thousands of people were stranded in airports around the country, many of them "without any knowledge of where they're going to sleep tonight", Duffy said.
JetBlue cancelled all remaining domestic flights on Friday evening. But Delta Air Lines said it was resuming operations. There was no statement yet from United or American Airlines.
What caused the ground stop?
Duffy said a legacy air traffic control communications system became overloaded.
"So this is analogue telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down," Duffy said.
He said this had affected communications and radar. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said, estimating a $50 billion price tag.
"It's going to continue to fail," he said.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the news conference said they had seen "zero evidence" it was a cyber-attack.
He also ruled out any link to the global Microsoft outage that began on Thursday.
Mullin said the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system had overwhelmed it.
Both cabinet secretaries insisted the public was never in danger during the stoppage.
When was the last ground stop?
It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001.
"This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.
Dr Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system.
"That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.
The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published, and flights were grounded until that system was restored.
But Friday's incident lasted longer than the 2023 event.

729635c933e3.text: The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop Friday night after hours of chaos and thousands of delays and cancellations. Why it matters: The effects of the rare and extreme move will likely ripple through the weekend, with travelers stranded and airlines' planes and crews out of position. Driving the news: In a Friday evening press conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was issued after outdated air traffic control communications equipment suffered from "overloaded data, and they went down." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin added that officials are looking into incompatibilities between that older equipment and newer technology currently being installed. Mullin added that there's no evidence that the problems were tied to a cyberattack. Yes, but: Duffy and Mullin didn't specify the exact initial cause of the problems. "We're still working on the details of what went wrong today," Duffy said. Duffy spent much of the press conference pushing Congress for more funding for air traffic control upgrades. "I can't build things if I don't have money," he told reporters at the White House briefing room. He later added that similar problems could occur again without more funding. Catch up quick: The FAA initially issued the stop due to "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety." "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," the agency said in an earlier statement after the ground stop was issued. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates." Air Route Traffic Control Centers, often simply called "centers," mostly handle high-altitude en route airspace between airports. Between the lines: The FAA has been rolling out a new AI tool designed to help manage airspace congestion, but it's unclear if that system has any connection to Friday's communication issues. The developer of that tool denied any connection. By the numbers: As of 9 p.m. ET, FlightAware reported more than 6,000 cancellations over the course of the day Friday. Many travelers are stuck at the airport or on their planes on the tarmac Friday evening. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.
