Destroyer returns from 11-month-deployment
The Michael Murphy left Hawaii last December. Navy officials say this will be the norm for some time.
PEARL HARBOR, Hawaii—After a 346-day deployment that included operations in the South China Sea, 12 contested transits of the Strait of Hormuz, 43 replenishments at sea and the removal of its commander 10 months in, the guided-missile-destroyer Michael Murphy returned home Thursday, welcomed by hula dancers and a rainbow stretching over the channel.
The ship was attached to the Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group for much of its deployment, though the aircraft carrier returned to its home in San Diego on Oct. 8. But any deployment-length records it may have broken were short lived. The Spruance, another Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, returned home today after a 12-month deployment, and the Japan-based John Finn crew has been told to expect a 13- to 14-month deployment.
As Defense One reported on Oct. 22, Navy officials have told families to expect 10- to 10-month deployments for the foreseeable future—a stark contrast from the typical 7-month deployments of recent decades. The Navy’s top enlisted sailor, Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy John Perryman, confirmed that a week later, saying 10-11 months will be the norm for at least a few years.
The Micheal Murphy left Hawaii on Dec. 1, 2025, and sailed through the South China Sea and Strait of Malacca before reaching the North Arabian Sea, where it spent the bulk of the deployment, said Cmdr. David Nicolas, who took command of the destroyer a month ago.
The Michael Murphy launched Tomahawk missile strikes during Operation Epic Fury and took part in the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, Nicolas said.
“I’m incredibly proud to be part of this team,” he said. “This is the most resilient crew that I’ve had the pleasure to serve with.”
Nicolas previously commanded the Oscar Austin, another guided-missile destroyer. When he handed over the helm to his successor on Sept. 10, he was slated to become an instructor at Surface Warfare Schools in Rhode Island, according to a Navy press release. But a Navy official confirmed to Defense One that his plans were changed when the Michael Murphy’s previous boss, Cmdr. Caitlin Cunningham, was relieved on Sept. 27 due to a “loss of confidence” after roughly 11 months in charge.
At Thursday’s homecoming, Petty Officer 3rd Class Jesse Bryson was first off the ship, as the winner of the “first kiss” raffle. Standing with his wife, Arianna Rios, he joked that the deployment involved “a lot of water.”
“Join the Navy, see the world—but the world is 70-percent water,” he said with a laugh. But, he added, the crew was great.
“I think you could put anyone from this ship on any other ship and they’d stand out,” Bryson said.

READ MORE: SpaceX's supersized Starship launches into orbit for the first time but flight ends early Elon Musk's company had to lower its expectations when the first part of the double catch flopped. Instead of returning to its Texas pad following liftoff, the first-stage booster ended up in the Gulf of Mexico after an automatic abort. Despite the setback, the bullet-shaped spacecraft continued toward orbit. It will steer toward the pad Saturday for a similar grab, barring further trouble. The Super Heavy v3 Booster 22 explodes upon being diverted to the water while retuning from the launch of a Starship 42 during the 15th test flight from the SpaceX launch complex in Starbase, Texas, Nov. 13, 2026. Photo by Joe Skipper/Reuters It's the first time that the spacecraft will try to return to the pad from orbit, to be plucked in midair by mechanical arms secured to the launch tower. If all goes well, the flight will last 22 hours. The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars. Please check your inbox to confirm. Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship prepared to deliver 26 of the company's most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday's grand finale. SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company's sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) — the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world's biggest and most powerful rocket — an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height. The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight's end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket's self-destruct system was activated. The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages. SpaceX plans to start launching Starships from Florida within a few months and from Louisiana in a few years. Scaled-up infrastructure, combined with full rocket reusability, is "how you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000," SpaceX's Kiko Dontchev, vice president of launch, said at a NASA tech summit last week at Florida's Kennedy Space Center. SpaceX's smaller Falcon rockets will continue to fly from Cape Canaveral, carrying astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA and from California carrying Starlinks. Satellites also will keep hitching Falcon rides for now. Musk wants Starships to eventually replace Falcons. Falcon rockets "are still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship, we're going to catch both the first stage and second stage," Dontchev said. NASA is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to land Artemis astronauts on the moon with Starships. Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin is the other major player. NASA expects to decide a year before the Artemis IV lunar landing — the first by astronauts in more than half a century — whether to get the moonwalkers to the surface with Musk's Starship or Bezos' Blue Moon. During next summer's Artemis III mission, astronauts will practice docking their capsule with a Blue Moon and then a Starship in orbit around Earth. The first case of Bluetongue in Northern Ireland this season has been confirmed on a farm in Kilkeel, County Down.
Officials from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs said the virus had been detected in three sheep.
There will be no additional movement restrictions or disease control zones, because the virus has been present in Northern Ireland since November 2025.
It presents no risk to public health.
The minister Andrew Muir said the discovery of the virus was "disappointing but not unexpected", given the spread of the disease in Great Britain and Ireland.
The Chief Veterinary Officer Brian Dooher urged local farmers to be alert to any symptoms in their livestock.
The confirmation of the virus in Kilkeel comes after more than a hundred cases across the Republic of Ireland in recent months.
Cases in England have been increasing, with 2,950 now confirmed.
There have been 512 cases in Wales and 57 in Scotland.
The mild winter means more of the biting midge that spreads the disease are likely to have survived and become infectious this season.
'Active surveillance'
Muir said awareness was key, adding: "Continued vigilance and strict biosecurity measures remain of paramount importance and I would once again urge all farmers to report any suspicion of disease to DAERA.
"It is important that I reiterate that Bluetongue poses no threat to public health nor to food safety â milk and meat are safe to consume."
Dooher said any suspected cases on farms should be reported to Daera.
"Active surveillance is ongoing at abattoirs alongside post-import testing of susceptible animals imported from mainland EU countries.
"I also want to stress the importance of safe and responsible sourcing of animals."
The disease was first detected here near Bangor in County Down in November 2025.
A number of other herds along the eastern coast of Northern Ireland have also been affected.
Farmers have been urged to vaccinate their animals.
The disease affects ruminants such as cattle, sheep, goats and deer.
It poses no risk to human health.

Atlantic fisheries managers this week agreed to lower the cap on industrial menhaden fishing in Chesapeake Bay but stopped well short of imposing deeper coastwide cuts.
At its annual meeting, held from Nov. 9–12 in Newport, Rhode Island, the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission’s Menhaden Management Board reduced the coastwide catch limit by about 9 percent in 2027 and another 9 percent in 2028. The Chesapeake Bay cap was also reduced by 27 percent in 2027 and 34 percent by 2028.
Menhaden are small, oily fish that filter plankton and in turn feed predators along the coast, from ospreys to striped bass and bluefish. The Chesapeake Bay is a critical nursery for the species.
The multibillion dollar aquaculture industry has made the omega-3 and fatty acid-filled menhaden a prime commodity for producing fishmeal to feed farmed fish, fish oil and other products, a process known as reduction fishing.
Industrial fleets, aided by spotter planes and small aluminium chase boats, are deployed to encircle dense schools of menhaden with a vertical wall of netting, including in the lower Chesapeake Bay. Though researchers have not proven these industrial fleets are the cause of predators’ food depletion, some conservationists point to them as an important factor.
Ospreys’ declining population have become the most obvious warning sign.
As Inside Climate News previously reported, researchers have documented acute food stress and poor breeding performance in the Bay. The 2026 survey by the Center for Conservation Biology at William & Mary found that 81 percent of monitored nesting pairs in the Bay’s saltier waters failed to raise a chick this year. Ospreys in fresher parts of the Bay, where other fish are available, have fared better, according to Bryan Watts, the center’s director.
Under the new limits, the coastwide total allowable catch, covering the commercial fishery from Maine to Florida, including the Bay, will drop from 186,840 metric tons this year to 170,000 metric tons in 2027 and to 155,000 metric tons in 2028. That follows a 20 percent reduction in 2026.
The commission said it measured the ecological benefits of leaving more menhaden in the water against economic harm to harvesters and fisheries that rely on menhaden for bait.
But the commission’s projections paint a different picture. Its technical committee found that a 39 percent cut, to 114,200 metric tons in 2027, would give managers a 50 percent chance of meeting the ecological fishing target. That target is designed to leave enough menhaden to keep striped bass at healthy levels but does not account for ospreys or measure how many menhaden are available in the Bay.
The commission acknowledged that the new limits will very likely allow more fishing than the target. But it said they carry no risk of overfishing, which it measures against a looser limit that allows heavier fishing than the ecological target.
Actual catches are another point of contention. The commission’s fishery review puts last year’s commercial catch at just under 147,000 metric tons, below both of the new adopted limits. That means the 2027 limit leaves room for about 50 million pounds more than the industry caught last year.
In the Chesapeake Bay, the board tied the reduction fishery’s cap to 21.8 percent of the coastwide limit. That lowers the cap from 51,000 metric tons to 37,123 metric tons in 2027 and 33,847 metric tons in 2028. The cap cannot exceed 51,000 metric tons even if the coastwide limit rises, and the board decided to revisit it at least every three years. The Bay cap applies to reduction fishing, not the bait fishery, which catches menhaden to be used as bait for recreational and commercial fishing.
The new coastwide limit will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027, while the Bay cap takes effect May 1.

The board did not adopt seasonal quota periods, which supporters said would spread the Bay harvest across the fishing season and ease pressure on menhaden while ospreys feed their chicks. Debate over whether to redistribute the coastwide quota among states was put off until January.
Virginia holds about 75 percent of the coastwide quota and is home to the Atlantic coast’s only active menhaden processing plant. Maryland, North Carolina, Florida, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and New York backed deeper coastwide cuts, according to the nonprofit Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership, but they were outvoted.
In the Bay, the majority of the menhaden fishing is done by Ocean Harvesters, which supplies Omega Protein’s processing plant in Reedville.
In emailed comments, a spokesperson from Ocean Harvesters said the company was disappointed with the cuts.
“[T]he consequences will be felt by the fishermen, processing workers and families who depend on the fishery, as well as businesses,” he said. “The commission should have allowed the newly funded research to proceed before imposing additional restrictions.”
The representative disagreed that the commission’s decisions to impose new catch limits struck the right balance, and questioned “whether additional restrictions will produce the benefits being claimed.” The company said it supports ongoing research and will keep working with scientists to better understand menhaden in the Bay, adding that its future depends on a healthy bay and a sustainable fishery.
The commission’s latest assessment, based on data through 2023, found menhaden are not overfished along the coast. But it acknowledged it lacks the data to say how many menhaden are in the Bay or how fishing affects the population.
The Chesapeake Bay Foundation has pointed to falling catches in Maryland, Potomac River and Virginia waters as examples of low menhaden availability. Chris Moore, CBF’s Virgin

In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.
Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.
More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary â but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.
Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla â that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.
"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.
Jojo was less than a year old â an infant clinging to his mother â when he was captured and sold.
Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.
Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".
"He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat â to interact with us," he says.
Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Ãric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary.
"He definitely feels lonely," he says.
Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says., external
Experts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised.
"If they're old enough to understand what happened to them, to understand their family was killed, they just lose the will to live," explains conservationist Tony King, from UK charity the Aspinall Foundation. "You see it in their eyes â the light goes out. I never knew where that expression came from, but I've seen it in gorillas."
King â who specialises in rehabilitating rescued great apes â remembers rescuing two infant sister gorillas who were brought to a sanctuary in the Congo Basin.
"They were clinging to each other," he says. "They stayed together in a little tight ball for about three days before they sort of unravelled. I think that's what kept them alive."
African charity the Gorilla Rehabilitation and Conservation Education (Grace) Center uses what it calls "gorilla-led" rehabilitation. When the team rescues a young gorilla from the pet trade, they put it with a group as soon as possible so they can socialise and essentially learn to be a gorilla.
But Jojo's case is unusual. He is fully mature and showing signs of harmful, chronic stress, according to Forrester.
In a game-changing approach to studying anxiety and trauma in apes, she has used a thermal camera to film Jojo's face. This allows her to monitor blood flow, revealing what appears to be a chronically cold nose.
It's a sign of a malfunctioning stress response. When any primate â a human, chimp or gorilla - is stressed, blood flow to the eyes and ears increases. It puts them on high alert for danger, but leaves their nose, temporarily, colder. For Jojo, this "nasal dip" as it is known, does not seem to recover.
"Being connected to others is incredibly important to our psychology as great apes," Forrester says. "Having another individual to share his life with would be so healing for him.
"I would assume other gorillas would help him process this grief and trauma."
Dr Katie Fawcett, from the Grace Center, says it's also "essential" for an animal to form social relationships to be considered for release into the wild - which is the ultimate goal for Jojo's keepers.
The bonds between gorillas â what we would call friendship - is key to their society, adds Dr Robin Morrison from the University of Zurich, who studies the social lives of mountain gorillas. In one recent study, she discovered that female mountain gorillas would seek out females they knew, even if they hadn't seen them for many years, when joining a group.
And she says a big part of a gorilla's normal social life is "just sitting together quietly sharing space".
But Jojo has never been given the opportunity to sit quietly with another gorilla.
No one knows how Jojo will react to a companion. Moving an animal from an accredited zoo would be a decision for an international committee and based on genetics, health and the animals' personalities and compatibility.
Any introduction to another animal would be done very carefully â perhaps giving them an object that smells of the other before they see each other.
These slow, cautious ape introductions do happen â when an animal moves from one zoo group to another, for example. Forrester has contacted a number of accredited zoos to explore the possibility of doing this for Jojo. But those discussions have fizzled out with no sign of progress.
The problem, she says, is "there aren't clear processes in place to do these kinds of trans-locations".
The international rules and processes for moving captive gorillas across international borders - from one zoo or safari park to another - are designed for breeding programmes.
"They're not designed for reintroductions into the wild, or to find companions for animals that might need them," says Forrester.
And because Jojo, who is probably in his 20s, has reached maturity, King thinks it might be too late for him to bond with other gorillas.

In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.
Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.
The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.
Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.
This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.
The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".
This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.
Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.
At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.
A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency.
Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal.
Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.
In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".
He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".
Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project".
"Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC.
He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question.
Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness.
The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu, has brought the crackdown into sharper focus.
The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region.
His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted.
"The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X.
He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested.
The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post.
The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations.
Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper.
They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations.
Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption.
He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him.
Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor.
His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him.
Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications.
The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces.
Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge.
He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive.
"Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done."
But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted.
"The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says.

d7b35189e016.text: Air travel across the country came to a standstill on Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop citing “extraordinary circumstances” and “reasons of safety.” Aviation correspondent Miles O’Brien reports. Amna Nawaz: Air travel across the country is at a standstill tonight after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop, citing extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety. Runways across the country were emptied tonight, and hundreds of flights have been impacted so far. A short time ago, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters he did not believe this was tied to a specific attack. Markwayne Mullin: I want to make sure we say this again. There's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones. This isn't another 9/11. I just can't repeat that enough. People are making that assumption because that's the last time we had a nationwide ground stoppage. This is a telecommunication outage. This is much different. Amna Nawaz: It's just the third time in recent decades that there's been a nationwide grounding. The last time was in January of 2023 after the failure of a pilot communications system. Information is still very limited, but let's try to answer what we can. Our aviation correspondent, Miles O'Brien, is here for just that. Miles, welcome back, and thanks for joining us. These kinds of nationwide ground stops are extremely rare. I know you have been talking to your contacts. Do we know what's behind this moment? Miles O'Brien: Well, there's a lot of speculation right now, Amna. We should characterize that, that no one really knows for sure, or at least is not saying so. But what you have is a systemwide problem in a system that is built on redundancy, and so you have to wonder what the single-point failures could be and why those exist. There are 22 regional en route centers that manage aircraft at cruise altitude passing across the country. They are connected to each other by simple landlines, kind of old-fashioned landlines, and there's some speculation that that system of connecting those en route centers has failed. Now, what caused that? Could that have been some sort of hacking event potentially? Or could it have something to do with the modernization of the system, which we all know relies on floppy disks and paper strips and spinning radars which go back to the 1940s? So, what the FAA is trying to do is attach a rocket booster to a horse and buggy. And that's where you start realizing the vulnerabilities in a system that should have layer upon layer redundancy on them. Amna Nawaz: I mean, Miles, just to give people a sense of the scope of this ground stop, take a look at this flight tracker graphic. This is showing all the flights across the U.S. and in the region there halted. Those are yellow. Those are not moving. And so, Miles, tell us about this communications outage as the secretary alluded to there. Obviously, some folks are asking, could this have something to do with the massive Microsoft outage that we have been talking about? And does it potentially give way to other vulnerabilities here? Miles O'Brien: Well, that's just it. It shouldn't be that vulnerable. And if it is possible to take down one layer, there should be at least another layer. This is a function once again, Amna, of kicking the can down the road, as Congress and Washington has done for years and years, on infrastructure in the air. This is a system that is bursting at the seams. Travel is at an all-time record, in spite of the cost of it. You know what it's like getting on these planes, and we're still using systems that date back many decades. This -- it is high time that we got serious about investing in this system and creating something that is more resilient, more redundant, and God forbid we end up with a situation where we have a mishap. Fortunately, everybody's safe, extremely inconvenienced, but at least everybody is safe through all this. And that is a testament to the heroic air traffic controllers who work in this system, antiquated as it is, heroically every day to make it work. Amna Nawaz: That is our aviation correspondent, Miles O'Brien, with the very latest. Miles, thank you so much. Appreciate your time. Miles O'Brien: You're welcome, Amna.

9ccc85598ca2.text: In our news wrap Friday, a ship collided with a river cruise boat in New Orleans, causing it to sink in the Mississippi River, some Microsoft users were offline for a second day as the company scrambled to restore its widely used suite of workplace software and the White House is tightening rules on how staffers interact with lobbyists. Amna Nawaz: We start the day's other headlines in New Orleans, where a tanker collided with a river cruise boat this afternoon. Eyewitness video shows the larger ship slamming directly into the American Heritage paddle boat, and then another angle captures the ship as it starts tilting on its side. Officials say there were nearly 130 people on board at the time, and multiple individuals were rescued from the water. The city's mayor says more than 30 people are being treated at local hospitals, and that all passengers are accounted for. Following the collision, the cruise ship could be seen on its side in the water. It was just finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations. Some Microsoft users were offline for a second day as the company scrambled to restore its widely used suite of workplace software. Services like Outlook and Teams, as well as the AI tool Copilot, went down worldwide yesterday, disrupting operations for millions of businesses and institutions. Today, Microsoft said it is deeply sorry for the disruption and blamed the outage on -- quote -- "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change." The company added it was not related to cyber or AI agents. Russian authorities say they shot down nearly 1,200 Ukrainian drones overnight and into today. It was one of Kyiv's largest aerial attacks since the war began. In the meantime, Russia kept up attacks of its own. A barrage of more than 100 drones damaged a hospital in Kyiv and tore into an apartment block in Zaporizhzhia, injuring dozens. The attacks come after a week of diplomacy and, in particular, a push to include Europe in future talks. In Dublin, today, European leaders agreed to send officials from five countries and the E.U. itself to the next round of negotiations. Antonio Costa, President, European Council: The weeks ahead will be a decisive test of Russia's readiness to bring this war to an end. Its record so far, with escalation and strikes on the Ukrainian civilians, suggests otherwise. Russia must change course. Amna Nawaz: European leaders have expressed concerns about President Trump's trip next week to China, where he will meet with both President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin. They're worried that the U.S. president could agree to concessions that favor Russia without Europe or Ukraine having a chance to weigh in. In Washington, D.C., the White House is tightening rules on how staffers interact with lobbyists. A memo from the new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, says employees must first get permission before discussing government business with lobbyists on the building's grounds. A White House official tells the "News Hour" that, according to the memo -- quote -- "Staff are expected to dedicate their time unwaveringly to the working people of the nation." The official called this -- quote -- "a much stricter process than before." Miller took over the role from Susie Wiles, who had come under criticism over her ties to lobbying groups. In Colorado, Congresswoman Lauren Boebert has lost her reelection bid in a close race against Democrat Eileen Laubacher. The Associated Press called the race for Laubacher this afternoon. The retired Navy rear admiral and Afghanistan war veteran is just the latest Democrat to flip a House seat. Democrats will hold at least 256 seats when the new Congress begins in January. Boebert was a hard-line Republican and MAGA favorite known for her controversies and clashes with fellow lawmakers. She had moved to a more conservative district after a narrow win in 2022, but even that wasn't enough to secure victory. In Peru, Pope Leo made an emotional return today to the Diocese of Chiclayo, the city that helped to shape him. The Vatican estimates that one million people lined the streets to greet the pontiff, known affectionately there as Padre Roberto. Leo served as bishop of Chiclayo for nearly a decade, and he rejoiced in today's homecoming. Pope Leo XIV (through interpreter): What a joy to return to Chiclayo. It is a blessing for me to be with you again. Amna Nawaz: Leo presided over mass in the nearby desert venue of Pampas de Pimentel and gave thanks for the support during his recent hospitalization for lung cancer. The pope is set to conclude his South American visit with a final mass in Lima on Monday. The head coach of the U.S. men's soccer team, Mauricio Pochettino, is heading to the U.K. to take over at Manchester United. Mauricio Pochettino, Outgoing U.S. Men's Soccer Head Coach: One of the most difficult in our career. Thank you, guys. Thank you so much. Amna Nawaz: The 54-year-old got emotional at a press conference announcing the news. He helped lead the American team to the Round of 16 at this year's World Cup. Just a few months ago, he signed a deal to stay on through the 2030 tournament. Pochettino takes over a Manchester United squad that is far from its past glories. The club has won 20 English titles, but is off to its worst start of the season in four decades. On Wall Street, today, stocks ended mixed to close out a turbulent week. The Dow Jones industrial average managed a gain of about 50 points, but the Nasdaq fell nearly 1 percent. The S&P 500 also ended lower.

c10b42a67e95.text: The fallout of Jensen Huang’s downfall expanded into a public fight between two of President Trump’s top advisers. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia’s most advanced chips. Nick Schifrin looks at the finger-pointing and the ongoing efforts to control advanced technology exports to China. Amna Nawaz: Today, the fallout of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's downfall expanded into a public fight between two of President Trump's top advisers. The treasury secretary accused the commerce secretary of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia's most advanced chips. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang played an outsized role in President Trump's technology policy. Nick Schifrin looks at today's finger-pointing and the ongoing efforts to control advanced technology exports to China. Jensen Huang: Here it is, our brand-new GeForce RTX 50 Series Blackwell architecture. Nick Schifrin: They're the American chips powering the AI revolution. And, for years, Jensen Huang wanted them sold to China. Woman: Jensen, how do you like China? Jensen Huang: I love China. Nick Schifrin: And Huang had an administration ally. Jensen Huang: Howard is the person I talked to most in the administration. Nick Schifrin: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose agency controls the entity list of countries and companies banned from buying U.S. technology. Howard Lutnick: We want to keep having the Chinese use the American technology stack. Nick Schifrin: Last year, Commerce and the Trump administration decided to let China buy some less advanced Nvidia chips. But international companies believed to collaborate with Beijing, including the Singapore-based Megaspeed, the company whose leader Huang had an affair with, reportedly gave China access to the most advanced chips. And, today, Lutnick was accused of looking the other way. Scott Bessent: Treasury, War, USTR, and State, they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months. But Commerce has the pen. Nick Schifrin: Today, on CNBC, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the Commerce Department for not implementing the U.S.' export blocks on Nvidia's most advanced chips. Scott Bessent: I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s. And so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts the -- our -- hurts our great companies in the AI race, gives the Chinese an advantage. Chris McGuire, Council on Foreign Relations: If we did prevent them from getting these chips, they actually would be, instead of months behind us in AI, they would be years behind us in AI. Nick Schifrin: Chris McGuire is a senior fellow on the council of foreign relations and was the director of technology on President Biden's National Security Council staff. He says the effort to restrict Chinese access to chips began when the first Trump administration blocked the Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei from buying semiconductors with U.S. technology. The U.S. realized the export restrictions were some of the best ways to constrain Chinese military and AI advancements, so they continued into the Biden administration. And, in early 2025, the Biden team pushed through new regulations that required most foreign companies to get Commerce Department permission to buy advanced chips. Chris McGuire: It was slated to go into effect in May 2025, but two days before it went into effect, the Commerce Department said they're not enforcing it. If the Commerce Department had enforced this, Megaspeed would not have been able to get chips unless the U.S. government green-lighted it. But because they didn't enforce it, Megaspeed could just buy whatever they wanted completely uninterrupted. Nick Schifrin: Today, Bessent also blamed Nvidia for selling to Megaspeed. Scott Bessent: Did Nvidia know their client? And was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? Nick Schifrin: But it was Huang, who is a celebrity in China, who helped push President Trump to allow the sale of U.S. chips to China in the first place. Jensen Huang: Why is it that we don't come up with a regulation that's more balanced so that Nvidia can win around the world, instead of giving up the world? We want United States to win at every single layer, including the chip layer. And conceding the entire market is not going to allow the United States to win the technology race long term. Chris McGuire: Well, Jensen certainly wins if they if they sell chips to China, but I would argue America does not win. Nick Schifrin: In fact, independent researchers this week discovered that China's AI models were all developed thanks to smuggled Nvidia advanced chips. Chris McGuire: While I think the poor implementation on export controls has probably cost us years of advantage, we still -- doubling down now will still give us years, even potentially decades of advantage in the future, as long as we actually manage it right. But if we don't, China is going to stay close and that will have catastrophic impacts for U.S. national security. Nick Schifrin: There's a debate over that, which will continue. But Jensen Huang's departure will empower advocates of stricter export controls, including a push on Capitol Hill to further restrict the world's leading technology from going to the U.S.' chief international competitor. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Nick Schifrin.

Some 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker.
The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel, Atlantic Asphalt.
The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".
The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference that all credit in the rescue effort went to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help".
"We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said.
Calls about the collision came in around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans Chief Melanie Montroll told the news conference.
There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to Port of New Orleans.
Passengers began disembarking from the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping on to its side, Mayor Moreno said.
Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help and officials shut down the Mississippi River for the search effort.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.
President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the rescue was an "incredible job".
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the US Coast Guard also supported local rescue operations.
Governor Jeff Landry also hailed the rescue as a "miracle on the Mississippi" given the "sheer number of people who were on that cruise ship" who were rescued.
Ships have operated safely on the Mississippi River for years, Landry said, pledging to investigate what happened.
Jamie Holford, a witness to the crash, told the BBC's US partner CBS that he saw the cruise ship hit the dock following the collision.
"It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like," he said. "It looked like something off the Titanic."
Holford added that he saw passengers and crew members "hollering" and "crying" as they tried to get off the ship while it was sinking.
The American Heritage can carry up to 150 guests and features a glass-enclosed restaurant, fitness centre and three guest lounges, according to its website.
Built in 2015, the vessel has at least four decks.

e52bde7bce92.text: Senate Democrats won back their majority last week, and now they’re fighting over who will lead it. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen has thrown his hat in the ring and says he will take on current Democratic leader Chuck Schumer. Congressional correspondent Lisa Desjardins reports on the first serious challenge Schumer has faced to his party leadership. Amna Nawaz: Well, Senate Democrats won back the majority last week. Now they're fighting over who will lead it. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has thrown his hat in the ring and says he spoke with current Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer before officially launching his challenge. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD): We understand that this will be a competition. I think it's important to give Senate Democrats a choice. That's what we just gave voters all over the country, a choice. They chose change. And I think that the Democratic Caucus needs to be open to new ideas, a different way of governing, and a different way of conducting and approaching politics. Amna Nawaz: Our congressional correspondent Lisa Desjardins is here with more on the first serious challenge Schumer has faced to his party leadership. Lisa, good to see you. Lisa Desjardins: Hi. Amna Nawaz: So why does Senator Van Hollen say he's running? Lisa Desjardins: First of all, this is a groundswell that has been developing outside of Washington, including from some in the Democratic base, especially progressives, for some time about Schumer. But Van Hollen says it is about the election results specifically. He said these new senators who were elected were part of a movement not just about new lawmakers, but about new leaders altogether. Van Hollen himself is 67 years old. He's been in Congress since 2003. But this is by far his most assertive move, going up against Chuck Schumer. Schumer has been the Democratic leader since President Trump first took office in 2017. He's a New Yorker. He knows how to kind of use the strength of leadership. And timing is everything. Schumer has been lining up these votes for some time. And he actually has some ideas that are the same as Van Hollen, including they both want to end funding for the Iraq War, perhaps even risking a shutdown. But Van Hollen is more progressive. He is someone who's openly saying it's time to end the filibuster. Amna Nawaz: So what are Van Hollen's actual chances here? Is this a real challenge for Schumer? Lisa Desjardins: It is a real challenge, but Schumer, as I'm saying, has a much greater advantage. And I want to go over exactly why. The math favors Schumer. First of all, these are 11 new senators who have so far been elected. There will be a 12 if Mary Peltola is also confirmed in Alaska. But take those 11 new senators, the majority of whom oppose Schumer, and compare them with the 44 members of the Senate now who will be voting on this leadership election there in yellow. You see one of them is Van Hollen, so he has that vote. But Schumer has been working on this crowd for months getting their votes. And timing is everything here. Van Hollen announced relatively late in the game. So let's look at exactly how many votes each one of them has so far. You see those opposing Schumer. There's a number especially of new senators, but he already has locked up all of those commitments. Schumer has the advantage. It is notable, of course. Schumer's the leader right now. He doesn't have a majority yet publicly pledged to him. But he says he has the votes. We will find out in December. Amna Nawaz: We will find out indeed. Lisa Desjardins, thank you so much. Lisa Desjardins: You're welcome.

For more on these numbers, we turn to John Sandweg, who served as acting ICE director under President Obama. John, very nice to have you back on the program. So these were individuals that were not arrested by ICE agents, but rather Border Patrol agents handed over to ICE, and then ICE executes the removal. William Brangham: And the administration argues it's only halfway there. It would like to notch up to a million deportations. Does our system have that capacity to do that? John Sandweg: You know, look, the administration's put a lot of resources in increasing the size of ICE. The majority of the immigrants that are in the interior of the United States -- at the border, there are ways to administratively what's called expedite a removal. If you have -- catch someone as they enter the United States, you can quickly serve them a deportation order without seeing an immigration judge. But for the population in the interior, where most of this work is now focused, most of these individuals are required to see an immigration judge. We have not seen significant -- we have seen the Trump administration put a lot of pressure on those courts to expedite cases, but we haven't seen them put significant resources in there. Unless and until we see a real expansion of the immigration courts so that these new handpicked judges by the Trump administration can issue those deportation orders more quickly, it's really hard to see -- even with all these new ICE resources coming online, really hard to see them getting up to a million deportations in a year. William Brangham: So, as you well know, ICE's actions on the interior have caused a great deal of blowback. We have seen children being arrested. We have seen U.S. citizens being arrested. Of course, several Americans were killed. There was a great deal of pushback against the administration. We saw some of that reflected in the midterm elections. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin was asked about whether or not he had been told by the administration to dial that back recently. Here's what he had to say. Laura Ingraham, FOX News Anchor: And my question to you tonight is, have you been given instructions to lighten up on enforcement? Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary: Not at all. Not at all. Laura Ingraham: Not at all? Markwayne Mullin: Not at all. We have changed our priorities from doing -- from doing, let's say, job site raids to doing warrant raids, meaning that we go into cities and we go after the worst of the worst. 27531f5cf26d.text: By — Doug Jacobson, The Conversation Doug Jacobson, The Conversation Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/what-to-know-about-microsofts-outage-and-why-it-takes-so-long-to-restore-email-services Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about Microsoft's outage and why it takes so long to restore email services Science Nov 13, 2026 6:33 PM EST This article originally appeared on The Conversation. The Microsoft services outage that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages. The failure affected the Microsoft 365 suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collaboration platform Teams, AI assistant Copilot and, significantly, the Outlook email service. Microsoft reported on Nov. 13 that the company is "continuing to see improvements in service availability" but that "some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery." Despite decades of predictions about its decline, email remains a central pillar of how organizations function. Password resets, invoices, legal notices and cybersecurity incident response coordination all depend on it. The Microsoft 365 outage affected businesses, governments and schools around the world. When most people think about cloud outages, they picture a broken website or a stalled app. When the service going down includes email, however, the mechanics of the failure and how to recover from it are different from those of almost every other cloud service. Unlike modern web apps or authentication gatekeepers, email wasn't designed to fail fast, meaning to immediately halt when a problem arises. Old architecture When a typical cloud service breaks, it acts like a closed door. If an authentication provider or a cloud application goes down, users are immediately locked out and see an error message. Access stops. When people cannot get into the system, they are not actively generating new work or adding heavy processing loads to the broken servers. Once engineers fix the underlying bug and unlock the door, traffic can resume and the service often recovers fairly quickly. Email does not have a closed door. It is built on an older, decentralized "store-and-forward" architecture designed to never lose a message, even when the destination is unreachable. Because email is a network of thousands of independent systems, an outage at one major provider does not stop users on other platforms from hitting "send." During major email disruptions like the one that hit Microsoft, millions of outside users on Gmail, corporate servers or other platforms could still compose and send emails to affected accounts without seeing an immediate error message. From the sender's perspective, everything works normally. Their email provider accepts the message, attempts to hand it off to the downed provider, realizes the destination isn't answering, and quietly holds onto the message in an outbound queue to try again later. Major highway crash One way to think about email traffic in outages is to imagine a multilane interstate highway where an accident blocks two lanes of traffic. Drivers miles away don't stop leaving their driveways just because there is a wreck up ahead; they keep entering the highway system. Soon, traffic backs up so severely that metered on-ramps have to stop letting new cars merge onto the interstate. Before long, that gridlock spills backward onto local feeder roads and city streets, choking traffic miles away from the actual crash site. In this analogy, a downed email provider is the crash. Every other email server around the world is an on-ramp or a feeder road. While the outage lasts, millions of messages continue to pile up in queues across the internet, with unaffected servers repeatedly resending email to see whether traffic is moving yet. When engineers finally fix the root cause of an email outage, it is the equivalent of tow trucks clearing the wreckage from the highway. The road is technically open again, but traffic does not instantly return to normal speed. First, the massive backlog of vehicles already stuck on the main highway has to start moving. Only after that congestion clears can the on-ramps start letting queued-up cars merge back in, which in turn slowly relieves the gridlock on the surrounding local roads. Similarly, when a major email provider comes back online, it is immediately hit with a tidal wave of pent-up messages and retry attempts from every other mail server on the internet. Processing those queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time – typically hours to days. Long, bumpy road to recovery Because organizations have largely outsourced their email to a small number of global providers, an outage doesn't just disrupt one company; it can stall entire sectors at once, cutting off the communication tool teams rely on to coordinate their emergency response. And for everyday users, this unique architecture explains why email failures feel so drawn out: Even hours after a provider officially announces a problem is fixed, messages can still arrive out of order or trickle in slowly as the digital traffic jam finally clears. 888380a2073f.text: David Brooks of The Atlantic and Ruth Marcus of The New Yorker join Amna Nawaz to discuss the week in politics, including the fallout of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and what the Trump administration knew, how Republicans are responding to their losses in the midterm elections, JD Vance's chances in 2028 and the Democratic leadership battle in the Senate. That's "The Atlantic"'s David Brooks and Ruth Marcus of "The New Yorker." Jonathan Capehart is away this evening. Welcome to you both. David Brooks: Good to see you. You have the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, essentially blaming the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, for not cracking down on those export controls for chips to China. David, I'm sort of less interested in the palace intrigue here and whether or not you think there's going to be accountability in the wake of these revelations. David Brooks: I'm super interested in the palace intrigue. Amna Nawaz: You go for it then. Ruth Marcus, "The New Yorker": Me too. (LAUGHTER) David Brooks: I know. When agencies go at each other, it's like popcorn for people like Ruth and I. Amna Nawaz: So Washington. Here we go. David Brooks: Yes, I -- right, at this stage, I have questions. What was Trump told about Huang's situation last month? Amna Nawaz: Yes. David Brooks: What was -- what did Howard Lutnick know? Why did Cantor Fitzgerald, Lutnick's old firm, which his kids now run, why did they cut their position in Nvidia by 50 percent? Why did we do nothing? What kind of chips were sold? There's a whole -- just a whole series of questions, that things look pretty bad. And the fact that one agency is going on for another makes you suspect that Scott Bessent isn't talking for nothing, that he knows something that is going to make this a bigger story. Amna Nawaz: Ruth? Ruth Marcus: I think we have a twist on the old Watergate question. What did the president know? When did he know it? And when did he forget it? (LAUGHTER) Ruth Marcus: Because we have been told that the president was briefed twice, including right before Jensen Huang hitched a ride with him on Air Force One to China, that Jensen Huang was having an affair with a Chinese asset. And what did the president do about this? Your questions are very serious and highfalutin. My question is, why is the president expressing condolences to Jensen Huang and he's been through hell, the president said, when, as an American citizen, I would like him to be worried more about what this might have -- what might have happened to our national security than what happened to his friend who couldn't keep his pants zipped. Sorry. Amna Nawaz: And lawmakers have questions. We're going to see if we get any answers. Let's talk about the continued fallout from these midterm election results, and specifically how Republicans, how this administration is responding. There is new reporting today that Vice President Vance is considering not running in 2028 after those terrible losses for Republicans. 8fdf466bb50f.text: Anthony Roth Costanzo cuts an unusual figure in the world of music. The leading international opera singer is performing in the Metropolitan Opera’s critically acclaimed and wildly popular “Lincoln at the Bardo,” which the Met will stream for free to the public on Saturday. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown has the story for our arts and culture series, CANVAS. Amna Nawaz: Anthony Roth Costanzo cuts an unusual figure in the world of music. A leading international opera singer, he also now heads an opera company. This unexpected voice is also now performing in the Metropolitan Opera's Wildly popular "Lincoln in the Bardo," which is being streamed free for the public tomorrow night on YouTube. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown has that story for our arts and culture series, Canvas. Jeffrey Brown: The Egyptian pharaoh Akhenaten in the opera by contemporary composer Philip Glass, a signature role for singer Anthony Roth Costanzo, sung in a high and highly distinctive voice, that of the countertenor. Anthony Roth Costanzo, General Director and President, Opera Philadelphia: You know, countertenor is just a guy who sings high. Jeffrey Brown: A guy who sings high. Anthony Roth Costanzo: That's me. But it's not your speaking voice. It's this other register. Jeffrey Brown: So, here's your speaking voice. Anthony Roth Costanzo: My speaking voice is like this, and I sing... (SINGING) Anthony Roth Costanzo: Up like that. Jeffrey Brown: The countertenor is a male singer with an unusually high range, a trained falsetto, reaching those of female singers. And that, says Costanzo, takes the emotions and for some the strangeness of opera up several notches. Anthony Roth Costanzo: We have to express an emotion, a feeling that goes so far beyond speaking. Beyond just the normal voice, the countertenor expresses the extraordinary. Jeffrey Brown: His new book and an accompanying recording, both titled "Countertenor," offer both a history of this voice and a personal history, a boy who spent his early years in Durham, North Carolina, and from the beginning loved to sing, eventually on national tours And Broadway by the time he was 13, and with the likes of Luciano Pavarotti, before becoming an opera star in his own right, performing on leading world stages. Anthony Roth Costanzo: When my voice started to slowly change, and I was just getting into opera, somebody said, maybe you're a countertenor, and I said, a what? And they said, oh, you know, it's this thing where you can keep singing high. And I said, well, sign me up. Jeffrey Brown: It's not that easy, of course. It requires very specialized vocal training, breath management, and technique to give the voice that kind of strength in such high registers. Earlier countertenor history, as Costanzo details, involved the castration of young boys before their voices changed. And some of these so-called castrati became world-famous figures. Major composers, including Mozart, Vivaldi, and Handel, wrote for them. Anthony Roth Costanzo: They became the rock stars of their era. There's a lot of connection to what Michael Jackson was doing. If you watch Michael Jackson hit his high notes, you see women faint. And women were fainting when the castrati were singing. So there's some connection between having men sing high, whether it's natural or unnatural, and people responding in an extreme way because it excites them. Jeffrey Brown: Think Prince, The Bee Gees, The Weeknd, and so many others. Falsetto has been exciting people forever, a big part of pop music history. In opera, there's an ongoing renaissance in roles for the countertenor, with Costanzo very much part of it. Here he is in the new production of "Lincoln in the Bardo" by composer Missy Mazzoli. But Costanzo is also eager to bring his sound beyond traditional classical music stages and to address contemporary cultural issues. That was seen in "Only an Octave Apart," a cabaret show alongside transgender performer Justin Vivian Bond, blending opera, standards and pop, with plenty of emphasis on gender subversion. Anthony Roth Costanzo: You know, you have someone who looks a very particular way and sings low, and someone who looks like me and sings high. It is so much fun, and it also brings into the foreground this question of what identity is. Jeffrey Brown: Costanzo's newest and perhaps most ambitious role is a highly unusual one for a leading singer. Anthony Roth Costanzo: I'm Anthony Roth Costanzo. I'm the general director and president here at Opera Philadelphia. Jeffrey Brown: In 2024, he became general director and president of a major opera company, Opera Philadelphia, his goal, to foster the art form's continuing relevance and accessibility. Anthony Roth Costanzo: Thank you for choosing opera. And I felt that opera wasn't changing quick enough. I felt like it wasn't adapting to our contemporary times. I think that the business model holds opera back. Jeffrey Brown: In addition to adventurous programming, one big experiment, $11 tickets, or pick your price. Costanzo says that's quickly brought in first-time and younger audiences, along with new funders excited to lend support. Opera has for a long time had this question of hanging out there, about accessibility, aging audiences, elitism. Anthony Roth Costanzo: It's just all the structures around it that keep people away, as well as their preconceptions. So it's not only about the price of the ticket. It's about the art you put on stage, but also the brand that you build. What I'm selling to people at Opera Philadelphia is an experience that's really fun. It costs less than a movie, but there's also a happy hour. And there's a whole way of branding it. We have put ads on the trash cans in Philadelphia. So, as you walk down the street, you encounter opera on a trash can, so that it doesn't feel so foreboding. Jeffrey Brown: "Try any and every thing," says the great pharaoh, "with every voice you have." For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Jeffrey Bro

Just before 5 p.m. on the last day of September, Jane Sellen and her colleagues at Californians for Pesticide Reform learned that regulators had to toss out nearly nine months’ worth of air-monitoring data for two deadly fumigants.
California’s Department of Pesticide Regulation, or DPR, said the state laboratory that analyzes its samples was “recalling and voiding” all the monitoring results for 1,3-dichloropropene, or 1,3-D, and methyl bromide from Oct. 24, 2025, through June 30, due to a quality-control problem.
How can pesticide regulators say they’re protecting anyone from 1,3-D or methyl bromide if they don’t know how much of these toxic gases entered the air? asked Sellen, development director for Californians for Pesticide Reform, a statewide coalition of public-interest groups.
Methyl bromide was one of the most widely used pesticides on California farms until the Environmental Protection Agency banned it for all but “critical uses” in 2005 to protect Earth’s ozone layer. A potent neurotoxin, the gas can also cause severe neurological disease, multisystem organ failure and death. Even so, California farmers have long received a critical use exemption, and apply about 1.6 million pounds of the noxious gas each year to fields that produce nut trees, berries and other crops.
Growers also apply more than 7 million pounds of drift-prone, cancer-causing 1,3-D each year on almonds, grapes, strawberries and other billion-dollar crops. The pesticide is banned in 40 countries to protect public health and the environment.
DPR collects air-monitoring samples and sends them to a laboratory at another state agency to keep track of how much of these and other pesticides escape from treated fields. To measure concentrations in a given sample, labs rely on what’s called a reference standard, a manufacturer-certified sample of a chemical of interest used to ensure accurate readings. The reference standards for methyl bromide and 1,3-D had “significantly degraded,” between 18 percent and 96 percent, over nine months, the agencies reported.
Losing the 1,3-D data is particularly vexing for pesticide-reform advocates. They say the data is critical for gauging the effects of a new rule regulators said would limit agricultural workers’ exposure to the dangerous chemical but health and environmental advocates believe is flawed.
“DPR muscled through regulations for 1,3-D that we don’t believe adequately protect communities,” said Sellen, whose organization has gone to court four times to compel state regulators to pass rules that are “consistent and effective” at protecting workers and their communities from 1,3-D.
Sellen said her conviction that DPR’s rules aren’t effective is reflected in Californians for Pesticide Reform’s lawsuits and the lab’s failure “to actually even partially characterize what communities are being exposed to.”
Double Standards
Over the past two years, state pesticide regulators enacted two different 1,3-D regulations, one for people who live near treated fields and another for those who work near them, even though most farmhands live and work in the same region.
The rule that went into effect in January 2024 says it’s safe for residents of farming communities, who are largely low-income and Latino, to be exposed to 1,3-D air concentrations that are 14 times higher than the level experts at the Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment, or OEHHA, say is safe. The other rule, for workers, which went into effect in January, set a safety target five times higher than OEHHA scientists said reduces a person’s lifetime cancer risk from exposure to the pesticide.
Pesticide regulators maintain that both rules mitigate the lifetime cancer risk for people living and working near 1,3-D treated fields.
Inside Climate News asked the Department of Pesticide Regulation and the California Department of Food and Agriculture, which analyzes the air samples, how it could take so long to notice a problem with the analytical results and if any ditched data could be salvaged. DPR spokesperson Amy MacPherson deferred to CDFA to explain the lab problems but did not address whether any data could be recovered.
A CDFA spokesperson was not able to provide an immediate response because its experts were traveling or on vacation.
Sellen is upset by the loss of so much air-monitoring data, which she says is an important way to audit the regulation’s effectiveness.
She’s worried that emissions increased, like they did after the residential bystander rule went into effect in 2024. A draft 1,3-D report DPR released in October shows that after that rule was implemented, both applications and emissions of the fumigant rose following a multi-year decline.
“DPR and CDFA have agreed on additional quality-control measures to make sure future air monitoring data is not compromised by similar problems,” DPR stated when it announced the problem.
Chemist Susan Kegley said such tests should be routine.
Good laboratory practice requires knowing the standards are correct, and there are several methods for doing that, said Kegley, principal scientist and CEO of the Pesticide Research Institute, an environmental consulting firm. “Running regular quality-control tests is the centerpiece of understanding how correct your method is.”
Caroline Cox, a retired pesticide scientist and former research director at the nonprofit Center for Environmental Health, doesn’t understand how it took state officials nine months to notice a problem with the standards. “It should be something that you notice virtually right away,” Cox said.
Even under the best circumstances, the agency typically releases air-monitoring results at least six months after collecting samples, Cox said. The delay is frustrating because it means she and others have to tell people in the community about potential risks months after they happened. “That just makes people really angry,” she said, “because what can they do?”

Cheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign.
One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory."
Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained.
The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire.
The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security".
This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests.
But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University.
"They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement."
The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online.
"It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations.
"The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority."
Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar.
In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms.
Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat.
Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun.
His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed".
"We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month.
Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly.
Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum.
CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar.
The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court.
Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders.
"We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer.
Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect.
"A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College.
The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP.
"Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order."
The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent.
Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence".
Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape.
Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress.
"Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added.
They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views.
Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India.
CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents.
Yet dissent has not been stamped out.
