A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.
For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.
With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.
But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.
Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.
Megaspeed is a case in point.
It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
The city-state has had some success in policing this.
It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.
They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.
In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.
The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.
Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.
But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.
Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.
In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.
Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.
Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.
In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.
Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.
Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.
On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".
China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.
How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.
In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.
For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.
But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.
Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.
BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.
In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.
Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.

7c79f553d94f.text: By — Larry Neumeister, Associated Press Larry Neumeister, Associated Press By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/u-s-wrongly-withheld-new-york-highway-funds-over-immigrant-licenses-appeals-court-rules Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. wrongly withheld New York highway funds over immigrant licenses, appeals court rules Politics Nov 13, 2026 5:55 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — The U.S. Transportation Department wrongly decided to withhold nearly $74 million in highway money from New York state after it refused to revoke nearly 33,000 questionable commercial driver's licenses for immigrants when an audit revealed problems last year, a federal appeals court said Friday. A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Manhattan concluded in a written decision that the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, an arm of the Transportation Department, acted in a manner that was "arbitrary, capricious, or contrary to law" when it penalized New York. WATCH: Duffy threatens to withhold millions in highway funds from New York over flaws in immigrant commercial driver's license system The appeals court said the state can't be faulted for failing to cancel licenses when a commercial driver lost legal status to stay in the United States because rules that would require a cancellation were not in place at the time. The driver's licenses pertain to commercial vehicles such as trucks, trailers, limousines and buses. New York Attorney General Letitia James complained when the lawsuit was filed in April that the federal government was unfairly holding back money the state needs to repair roads and bridges. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul in the spring called the federal cuts "devastating" and characterized them as "political payback." The Transportation Department said in a statement Friday that it makes no sense for states to let trucking licenses for foreign drivers stretch years beyond when they are legally in the U.S. "We've put a stop to the madness to keep the driving public safe," the statement said. The Transportation Department began enforcing existing English language requirements for truckers in the summer of 2025. Concerns about truck driver qualifications took on more urgency after an August 2025 crash in Florida, when a truck driver was accused of performing an illegal U-turn that killed three people. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that driver, who is from India, should never have been licensed in the first place. Audits conducted in every state uncovered numerous non-domiciled commercial driver's licenses that remained valid long after an immigrant's work permits had expired or were issued without properly verifying citizenship status. Since then, about 26,000 drivers have been pulled off the road for failing to demonstrate English proficiency, and the Transportation Department said 30,000 commercial licenses were canceled because they were issued illegally. Immigrants account for about 20% of all truck drivers while the non-domiciled licenses immigrants can receive represent about 5% of all commercial driver's licenses or about 200,000 drivers. Immigrant groups have said they believe that many drivers are being unfairly targeted. The dispute came after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy tightened rules governing when immigrants can obtain a commercial driver's license. Officials said they took actions against states like New York after learning that some licenses remained valid long after an immigrant was no longer authorized to be in the country. New York issued licenses valid for eight years regardless of how long a driver's visa remained valid, authorities said. A message seeking comment from the New York attorney general's office was not immediately returned. AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. 26fb447e524f.text: The Trump administration announced a six-month delay Friday in enforcing the Medicaid work requirements that were scheduled to take effect in January. Why it matters: The announcement pauses a set of rules that state officials have warned they're not ready to handle — and that could cause millions of people to lose their health coverage. Driving the news: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said there will be an "optional hold harmless period" through June 30 that will give states "a transition period to further modernize systems, improve processes, and streamline the applicant and beneficiary experience. Hospitals have been so worried about the impact of the work requirements that they've created their own outreach campaign to prepare people on Medicaid, per the New York Times . The concern is not that people will be kicked out of the program for not working, but that they'll be kicked out because they don't understand the reporting rules and won't be able to prove they've met the requirements. This is breaking news. Check back for updates.

e408e1ed5bec.text: An international health organization has determined that the United States has lost its measles elimination status, according to multiple news reports. Why it matters: It's an official recognition of how much the country's public health has deteriorated due to a rolling series of outbreaks since early last year. Increased public skepticism about the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, a barrage of distrust from federal officials like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and funding cuts for response efforts have all factored in the surge of cases, according to public health experts. The big picture: The Pan American Health Organization concluded there has been sustained transmission of the highly contagious virus for longer than 12 months, bringing the U.S. case count to its highest level in 35 years. The measles elimination status hinges on whether the same strain of measles stays in circulation for 12 months or longer without a break. The overwhelming majority of cases are in unvaccinated people. While overall measles vaccination rates remain relatively high, public health officials say they have to remain above 95% to maintain herd immunity. Driving the news: An expert panel convened by the Pan American Health Organization made the widely expected decision following a three-day meeting in Washington, D.C. What they're saying: "It is no surprise that the resurgence of measles has coincided with an administration that has inflicted significant damage to our health care system while spreading false claims about vaccines," said Richard Besser, president and CEO of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and a former acting director of the Centers for Disease Control. "It is unthinkable that people in the United States should be dying from measles in 2026," the Infectious Diseases Society said in comments prior to the decision. The group cited the potential long-term toll on infants infected this year, some of whom could develop serious neurologic disease years after the initial infection. By the numbers: There have been 5,412 confirmed cases so far this year, compared to 2,289 for all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's latest tally. The last time measles cases were higher was in 1991, when the U.S. had 9,643 cases. Pennsylvania is in the grip of an outbreak that has accounted for more than 1,500 cases so far and six measles-associated deaths. Those reports are widely considered to be an undercount, due to the lack of widespread testing and unreported instances of mild illness. While most measles cases aren't severe, they can have long-lasting effects because of the way the virus can suppress the body's immune responses, leaving people more susceptible to other infections. About 1 in 5 unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles is hospitalized, per the CDC. How it works: Experts rely on disease tracking by local health departments and genetic sequencing, and can also factor vaccination rates and surveillance efforts. Canada and the United Kingdom have both lost their measles elimination status over the past year. The determinations are largely symbolic, but mean the virus has become endemic and is spreading freely in pockets of unvaccinated people, according to Yale epidemiologist Katelyn Jetelina. Since early 2025, there have been large-scale outbreaks in West Texas, along the Utah-Arizona border and in South Carolina.

Stargazers are being treated to a diagonal parade of four planets in the pre-dawn sky throughout November.
Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will all be visible to the naked eye in the south-eastern to eastern sky.
Particularly notable will be the line-up on Monday 16 November when Mars and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together, according to the Royal Museums Greenwich.
From 24 November, a full Moon - the first of a run of four supermoons - will also join the planets in the morning sky.
Mercury
Mercury will be the hardest planet to spot in the parade.
As the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in our solar system, it is permanently locked in solar glare.
It is only visible in twilight and never in a fully dark sky. As always it will be dim and close to the horizon.
Try spotting it in a wide open sky with a flat horizon and look to the south-east.
Venus
Above Mercury and toward the right, you will spot Venus.
Venus is an easy planet to find as it is the brightest object in our night sky after the Moon. It has the highest albedo of any major planet in our solar system - that is reflects more sunlight back into space thus appearing brighter.
It is also usually the closest planet to Earth in its orbit - a mere 24 million miles away at times. It is a similar size too.
It will be higher in the sky than Mercury and visible earlier in the night in the hours before sunrise.
Don't mistake it with the bright star Spica which will be close to it. Stars twinkle while planets glow steadily.
Mars and Jupiter conjunction
Mars and Jupiter will appear to be very close to each other in the sky on the 15 and 16 November.
Mars is currently high in the eastern sky, with Jupiter below but appearing brighter.
"They will be separated by just 1.2 degrees, or roughly the width of a finger held at arm's length," according to Gideon Bendavid-Walker, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich.
The two planets will appear close to the bright star Regulus and may even look like a triple star.
If you have binoculars or a telescope then a few other bonus planets will also be visible this month.
At a similar time before sunrise, Uranus will be setting in the west. Then Saturn and Neptune will also be visible for a time in the evening rather than the morning sky.
What is the viewing forecast this weekend?
To view the parade, find a spot away from light pollution with a good view of the eastern horizon and let your eyes adjust to the dark for around twenty minutes.
The best time to view the planetary lineup is approximately 45-60 minutes before sunrise.
Saturday night will turn progressively more cloudy and windy with outbreaks of rain making their way eastwards.
An early frost could still be likely under clearer skies in the south and east, but even here the breeze and cloud will tend to increase.
Sunday night is forecast to be drier, as the day's rain and hill snow clear. However, wintry showers will pester northern Scotland with plenty of cloud.
Also the odd shower will pop up around north-west facing coasts.
Otherwise, the night looks mostly clear and dry, apart from the odd mist of fog patch.
Keep up with the weather where you are.

US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The Ukrainian president's comments on Saturday come after US envoys visited Moscow and an EU summit in Dublin as part of ongoing efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance as a condition of any peace deal to deter future threats, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.
Zelensky has also consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory, despite Moscow's demands for it to cede the Donbas.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky told reporters on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow the day prior.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.
Moscow has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
There have, however, been recent signs the two can find common ground: last month, US First Lady Melania Trump was able to broker a temporary ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky to allow for evacuations and aid deliveries.
US officials had previously said that Ukrainian Nato membership was off the table.
Zelensky said on Saturday that the US proposal made him believe that "Nato is back on the agenda".
But he cautioned: "You have also heard Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.
Ceding the small portions of land Ukraine still controls there would be a small concession in practical terms, but would be symbolically significant for Kyiv because it would constitute an acceptance of the Donbas being Russian.
Zelensky has previously spoken of retaking Russian-controlled territory in four of Ukraine's regions, as well as the Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.

For three decades, Montana voters had not elected a Democrat to the U.S. House of Representatives. That changed earlier this month when Sam Forstag, a former wildland firefighter and union leader, defeated Republican Aaron Flint in Montana’s 1st Congressional District.
During his congressional campaign, Forstag, 32, who as a leader in the National Federation of Federal Employees represented some 800 U.S. Forest Service workers in the Lolo, Bitterroot and Gallatin national forests, promised to strengthen federal land management agencies and improve wildfire preparedness.
In an interview with The Wild Idea Podcast before the election, Forstag called for simplifying the permitting process for prescribed burns and increasing wildland firefighters’ base pay to reduce their dependence on overtime. He argued that investing in measures such as prescribed burning and forest thinning could reduce the risk of destructive wildfires and save taxpayers money. He also proposed pursuing standalone legislation to fund those efforts.
Forstag has also expressed support for the Protecting the Right to Organize (PRO) Act, which would strengthen workers’ rights to form unions and bargain collectively. Democratic Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia introduced the bill in the House in March 2025, with a companion bill introduced by independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont. The legislation remains in committee and has not passed either chamber of Congress.
In a post-election email to supporters, Forstag outlined four priorities for his first term in Congress: affordable housing, healthcare, reducing the cost of living and campaign finance reform. Although wildfire preparedness and Forest Service staffing were central to his campaign, neither appeared among the four priorities listed in that email. But, in a separate message thanking supporters, Forstag reaffirmed his commitment to protecting Montana’s wild places for future generations.
Forstag has already begun challenging the Trump administration’s plans for federal public lands. In a Facebook video posted Nov. 12 from the U.S. Capitol, he criticized a new Interior Department proposal to reduce federal land holdings.
“They’re trying to sell off our public lands, but we won’t let them,” Forstag said. He also said he had reached out to Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke, whom he is replacing, hoping the outgoing congressman would oppose any effort to sell federal lands. Zinke’s office separately confirmed his opposition to federal land sales and transfers.
Forstag has also expressed interest in working with Republican Rep. Troy Downing, who represents eastern Montana. In a Facebook post, on Nov. 11, Forstag identified protecting public lands as an area where the two lawmakers could find common ground, despite their political differences. “”We can get so much more done for Montana when we work together in Congress,” he wrote.
Forstag said he would seek a position on the House Natural Resources Committee after taking office in January, giving him an opportunity to influence federal land policy. The Interior Department’s five-year strategic plan proposes selling some federal lands to states, tribes and local governments, although officials have not identified specific parcels. Whether Forstag can influence the administration’s plans will depend partly on congressional cooperation and the legal limits on such sales.
During freshman orientation in Washington, D.C. last week, Forstag said he was seeking congressional committee assignments that would give western Montana a stronger voice on housing and rebuilding federal public lands agencies. He also said he planned to join both the moderate Blue Dog Coalition and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, hoping to work across different wings of the Democratic Party to advance economic policies that benefit working people.
In a separate Facebook post, Forstag congratulated the newly elected members of Montana’s American Indian Caucus, which will have a record 14 Native American lawmakers into the state’s 2027 legislative session, and expressed support for tribal sovereignty, treaty rights, and Tribal water and land rights. He said the caucus would be an important voice for Native communities in the state Legislature.
Forstag’s victory marks a historic political shift in Montana, where Democrats have not won a U.S. House election since 1994. His win also brings a former firefighter to Washington at a time when federal workforce cuts have raised concerns about wildfire preparedness, Forest Service staffing and public lands management. During his campaign, Forstag pledged to restore staffing at federal land management agencies and expand fuels reduction crews as well as simplify the permitting process for prescribed burns and increase the use of such treatments to prevent costly wildfires.
While supporters hope his experience will help address those challenges, political observers caution that turning campaign promises into federal policy will not be easy for a first-term congressman.
“Forstag by himself cannot do much, of course,” said University of Montana political scientist Abhishek Chatterjee.
His ability to influence federal policy will depend on cooperation with other lawmakers, said Chatterjee. Other newly elected lawmakers may share Forstag’s goals to increase funding for wildfire prevention, he added, but presidential veto power and Senate filibusters could limit such efforts.
Chatterjee also expects Forstag to be a part of increased congressional opposition to certain proposals involving public land swaps or transferring federal lands to state governments.
The Forstag campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Where Forstag Won
According to unofficial results from the Montana Secretary of State, Forstag received 132,003 votes, or 50.34 percent, compared with Flint’s 122,694 votes, or 46.79 percent. Libertarian Nick Sheedy received 7,522 votes.

The growth of data centers and rapid electrification is driving Georgia Power toward another major expansion of its electric grid. The state’s largest utility is preparing to add between 2,000 and 6,000 megawatts of new capacity to its grid for 2032 and 2033. The utility is considering a mix of resources, including natural gas and battery storage, to meet its future electricity needs.
But how much each resource counts toward that expansion depends on a calculation called Effective Load Carrying Capability, or ELCC. It is the “critical renewable energy concept you’ve never heard of,” according to the Union of Concerned Scientists. And the way Georgia Power is using that calculation in its latest effort to secure new power generation is drawing scrutiny from renewable energy advocates across the state.
Prior to the rise of renewable energy, determining how much capacity a new power project added to the grid was relatively simple. Utilities projected peak electricity demand and ensured they had enough power plants available to meet it.
But because renewable resources like solar and wind are variable, planning grid expansions has become more complex. The sun is not always shining and the wind is not always blowing, making it more difficult to determine how much reliable capacity renewable projects actually add to the grid.
ELCC is a way of measuring how much capacity a power resource can reliably contribute to the grid. A resource with a 100 percent ELCC can be counted on for its full capacity when determining how much electricity the grid can reliably support. Natural gas typically has an ELCC near 60 to 80 percent, while solar and wind projects without battery storage can have ELCCs between 4 to 40 percent. With batteries, renewables can have ELCCs around 95 percent, but that value can fall as more batteries are added to the grid.
In its previous planning, Georgia Power assigned battery storage an ELCC of 95 percent for its first 3,000 megawatts of capacity, 75 percent for the next 3,000 megawatts and 50 percent for the next 3,000 megawatts. As more batteries are added, they become less valuable during peak demand because they increasingly compete to provide power at the same time.
Based on the amount of battery storage on the grid and planned for the future, the utility’s previous calculations suggest the current ELCC should be set at around 75 percent. The latest procurement, however, uses a much lower figure.
According to Bob Sherrier, an attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center and the Advanced Power Alliance, which both testified about the issue to Georgia regulators, Georgia Power is now using an ELCC of just 20 percent for battery storage in its upcoming procurement. That means a 1,000-megawatt battery project would count for just 200 megawatts toward the utility’s capacity needs. A 1,000-megawatt natural gas plant with an 80 percent ELCC, by comparison, would count for 800 megawatts.
ELCC calculations are based on modeling under different conditions and assumptions. Georgia Power did not provide details on the calculations but did tell Inside Climate News they have been consistent and are committed to accurate evaluations of all resources. In response to  additional questions about the request for proposal, a company representative said “the company is in the middle of several ongoing resource procurements and cannot comment on specifics of requests for proposals.”
The steep drop in ELCC from Georgia Power’s previous calculations could put battery storage at a disadvantage as the utility evaluates projects for its planned 2,000 to 6,000-megawatt expansion, Sherrier said. With a lower ELCC, developers would need to build more battery capacity to earn the same capacity credit as a natural gas project.
He called the change a “thumb on the scale for gas,” arguing that it makes battery storage artificially less valuable in the procurement.
“Batteries are going to look significantly more expensive than gas,” Sherrier said. “We know that is not the case anymore.”
Recent cost estimates show that utility-scale solar can be cheaper than new natural gas generation. Pairing solar with battery storage raises the cost, but can still make it competitive with gas while allowing electricity to be stored for use when it is needed.
If the ELCC for batteries remains unchanged, Sherrier fears the new expansion could once again be dominated by natural gas.
For its 2029-2031 expansion, Georgia Power planned nearly 10,000 megawatts of new capacity, including roughly 6,000 megawatts from natural gas, with the remainder coming from solar and battery projects. At the time of planning in 2024, the utility’s planning assigned battery storage an ELCC of 95 percent for its first 3,000 megawatts of capacity.
More than 6,000 megawatts of natural gas capacity, if operated at full output year-round, could produce an estimated 20 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent annually, roughly the same emissions as 4 million cars.
If the 2032-2033 procurement goes the way Sherrier expects, Georgia Power could lock in millions more tons of annual emissions.
Georgia Power is reviewing proposals for its 2032-2033 expansion, with battery storage still assigned an ELCC of 20 percent. But the issue is not settled. The utility and regulators are expected to discuss which projects to move forward with early next year.
According to Sherrier, however, some of the damage may already be done. By assigning batteries a lower capacity value, Georgia Power may have discouraged battery developers from submitting proposals in the first place. The impact of the ELCC calculation will become clearer when the utility’s selected projects are submitted for regulatory approval in mid-2027.
If the issue is not resolved in this procurement, SELC and the Advanced Power Alliance plans to push for a higher ELCC in the next round of expansion planning, which is expected to begin in 2028.

Leticia Gutierrez’s upset victory in a Houston-area congressional district means an environmental-health advocate will represent part of the country’s oil capital, and environmental groups say that could help communities choked for years by petrochemical pollution.
Gutierrez, who spent more than a decade as Air Alliance Houston’s government relations director, pledged to support policies to improve air quality and regulate AI data centers’ water consumption and electricity usage. The Democrat beat a vastly better-funded former oil-industry executive whose contributors included petrochemical companies and Elon Musk.
“There is now, dare I say it, a green Houston congressional contingent,” said Jennifer Hadayia, executive director of Air Alliance Houston. She counts Reps. Christian Menefee, Sylvia Garcia and Lizzie Fletcher, all of whom won re-election in their Houston-area districts, among that group.
“We know that they understand Houston is the energy capital of the world,” Hadayia said. “That also means we’re the pollution capital of the world, and I feel very confident that that group together is going to advocate for our best interests when it comes to things like efforts by the current EPA, [which] has been stripping the community of its rights to weigh in on pollution decisions.”
Gutierrez’s 9th Congressional District was among those redrawn by Texas Republicans in 2025 in an unsuccessful effort to maintain the party’s control of the U.S. House of Representatives. Instead, the blue-wave election last week swept numerous Republicans out of office in Texas and nationwide.
The redrawn district includes parts of Harris County and the Houston Ship Channel, a major source of pollution lined with hundreds of petrochemical facilities. During the campaign, Gutierrez pointed to the health consequences of living near those facilities. The Texas Department of State Health Services, studying part of east Harris County near the ship channel and other pollution sources, found higher-than-expected rates of certain cancers in 2015, and a 2025 update still found notably higher rates.
Advocates were heartened by her election because they say people in the region need representatives pushing for pollution control.
“I think a really big issue for Harris County and for District 9 is how we’re treating our national emission standards for hazardous air pollutants,” said Clara Goodwin, staff attorney at the Environmental Integrity Project.
Last year, the Trump administration invited companies to email requests for “presidential exemptions” to a number of rules designed to reduce Americans’ exposure to air pollution hazards, including cancer-causing chemicals. Goodwin estimated that 30 facilities in the district have sought such exemptions.
Hazardous material dredged from the Houston Ship Channel and moved to dump sites in the region also pose risks to residents in parts of Gutierrez’s district. In 2024, sample testing of dredge material from part of a channel expansion that began in 2022 found toxic substances, including high levels of cancer-causing arsenic. Despite this finding, current U.S. Environmental Protection Agency policy does not treat dredge material from ship channel expansions as dangerous, Goodwin said.
Gutierrez will join a Congress in January newly under Democratic control. New laws controlling pollution may be impossible for the next two years—President Donald Trump can veto them—but Hadayia said there will still be opportunities to act. The major rollbacks of EPA rules that began last year are an environmental injustice, because the harms fall unequally across the country, she added.
Democrats “can hold ethics investigations and expose some of the corruption that’s going on, including the destruction of the Environmental Protection Agency by the Trump administration,” said Josiah Rector, an associate professor and urban environmental historian at the University of Houston.

He also thinks there’s room for action on tax breaks for petrochemical companies along the Houston Ship Channel that contribute to local air pollution. Rector said those policies have left school districts and other public entities with inadequate funding while people, many of them lower income, pay with their health.
“Now with the defeat of [Gov.] Greg Abbott and the GOP in Texas, there’s a real opportunity for Democrats, both in the congressional delegation representing Harris County but also in the Texas state Legislature, to start phasing out these tax breaks for corporate polluters to incentivize renewable energy,” he said.
Some advocates are tempering their expectations about how quickly Gutierrez can act on her campaign promises.
“Obviously, she’ll be a freshman,” said Luke Metzger, executive director of Environment Texas, “and it’s difficult to be able to immediately have an impact when you’re a freshman, but I think I’m excited to see what committee she gets appointed to and what she does to hold the EPA’s feet to the fire.”

From our collaborating partner “Living on Earth,” public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by host Steve Curwood and Jenni Doering with U.S. Rep. Zoe Lofgren.
As Democrats prepare to take control of the House in January, they’re gearing up to advance a long list of priorities.
One key player in that effort will be the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, which oversees federal grants and research at the National Laboratories and agencies like NASA and NOAA. U.S. Rep. Zoe Lofgren represents California’s 18th district and, as the most senior Democrat on the committee, is in line to become its next chair. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
STEVE CURWOOD: What was your reaction on election day and after, as you understood that the Democrats would take control of both the House and Senate with sizable margins?
ZOE LOFGREN: It’s huge, and it’s a wonderful opportunity that we have to deliver for the American people on the things that matter to them. Obviously, the cost of living was top of mind for many, many voters. People are concerned about the corruption of this administration, which in many cases is related to the costs spiking. Everything from healthcare costs to energy costs and the like, and each committee in the Congress will have a piece of the remedy that we need to bring to bear as best we can.
JENNI DOERING: You are currently the ranking member of the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology in the House, and may become the chair in January. What issues fall under that committee?
LOFGREN: The entire science enterprise, primarily anything with the research, is related to the Science Committee. We have jurisdiction over the space program as well [as] some of the issues that we’ve worked on in fusion energy research and quantum computing. AI has been a focus of the committee, as well as just basic science research.
We do touch over into issues that relate to climate and in the science portfolio, it’s a broad jurisdiction. We’ve looked at some of the things that EPA has done, which have really been outrageous, as well as the Department of Energy. It’s a fun committee; my predecessor [U.S. Rep.] Eddie Bernice Johnson used to call it the committee of the future.
CURWOOD: What are your top priorities as you assume this position? The things that have been undone or moved ahead by the Trump administration—that list is fairly long. What’s at the top of yours?
LOFGREN: We need to do two main things. One is oversight—to put a spotlight, and in some cases, to uncover what the administration has done that has damaged the science enterprise in this country. We also need to do legislation to change policies that will better serve the American people.
The committee has a long history of bipartisanship, and it certainly has even in this Congress when it comes to legislation. I will say the Republicans have not been active in criticizing the administration, but we have worked collaboratively to pass a number of bills. I think all the bills that we passed were either unanimous or close to it, and so I’m hoping that that spirit of bipartisanship can continue on some of the bills that we need to enact in our subject area.
In terms of oversight, the administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency has done tremendous damage. Twenty percent of the agency’s workforce has quit, retired or been fired. They’ve shut labs down. The Office of Research and Development was completely wiped out. We’ve made multiple requests for records and documents, and they haven’t produced a single one.
Their science capacity has been gutted, and the science integrity is really impaired. It’s an industry-capture event, and climate denialism is rampant in the agency. It’s pathetic. Their basic mission is to use the best available science to protect health and the environment, and they’ve not done so.
We’re preparing our letters right now to [EPA Administrator Lee] Zeldin to renew our oversight requests. I sent a similar letter to the Department of Energy secretary, [Chris] Wright, last week. We need to know about their reorganization plans, the Endangerment Finding, and a number of other things. That’s first on the agenda.
DOERING: We wanted to ask you about what’s been happening at the National Science Foundation. We’ve reported in the past on how the Trump administration has targeted vital American science establishments by freezing and canceling grants, and also refusing to release obligated funds at the National Science Foundation. How might your committee go about investigating those missing funds and ensuring they’re returned?
LOFGREN: We’re going to get to the bottom of what has happened. The NSF was the crown jewel of our government’s support for discovery science across all fields of science and engineering. The president asked for a $3 billion cut in fiscal year ’25 and ’26, and it’s worth reminding ourselves that in a bipartisan way, Congress said no to that cut.
We enacted and funded the agency close to the fiscal year ’24 level, but as you mentioned, the money does not appear to be going out. There are whistleblower accounts that the administration is sort of taxing up to 30 percent of funds for some kind of slush fund [for] their politicized priorities, not science, but maybe funnel it into tech firms. We’re not sure. That would be in complete contravention of the law.
But looking forward, and I’ve discussed this with the incoming chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee, [Rep. Rosa DeLauro], I think Congress needs to consider and take a look at how we might be more prescriptive in the crafting of authorizations and appropriations so that the opportunity for mischief is severely curtailed, and the opportunity for court orders is significantly enhanced.

Gardeners in one of the most drought-hit parts of the UK have said they are adapting their planting strategies amid increasingly extreme weather.
West Sussex - like most of the country - experienced an unprecedented summer marked by record-breaking heatwaves and severe drought.
The conditions have put immense stress on many traditional plant species, with some seriously struggling or dying completely.
Iain Parkinson, head of landscape and horticulture at Kew Wakehurst near Ardingly, said he had seen a "big change" in climate over the some 40 years he has worked there.
"We've had trees die," he added.
Meanwhile, senior gardener at High Beeches near Haywards Heath, Elliot Chandler, said some rhododendrons had died off this year.
"That's probably going to continue," he said.
"We'll do what we can for the plants...but if they're not surviving, then we need to plant different things.
"That's the only way we can really maintain the garden and keep it full of interest and flowers."
Joe Whelan, head gardener at Nymans in Handcross, warned another year of drought could be "quite detrimental" on larger, more mature trees.
The gardeners said planting a greater diversity of species will be key to climate resilience, with plants from North America, southeastern Europe, central Asia, South Korea and Japan potentially faring better in future.
Chandler added it will not be a case of ripping out old plants and planting new species "in one go" but rather a gradual change over time with a "really diverse mix of things".
Whelan said it will be difficult to predict what will do well in the future.
It will be about "experimenting and accepting that some things probably aren't going to make it", he continued.

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.
The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.
It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing have yet to comment.
No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.
Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.
"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.
She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".
A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.
The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China, which has been building up its arsenal.
Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.
Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.
Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.
But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.
Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan.
The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.
Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.
Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory.
Eurovision, the pan-European competition famed for zany gimmicks, slick, sometimes over-the-top staging, the drama of its complex voting system and, occasionally, for outstanding music, celebrates its 70th birthday this year.
And to mark it, the European Broadcasting Union is trying out audiences in Asia.
It's an idea that's been talked about for two decades but never materialised, despite many false starts.
Until now - Eurovision Asia will hold its first grand final in Bangkok, starting at 20:30 ICT (13:30 GMT).
Transferring one of the most successful television formulas that has worked in Europe for 70 years to Asia has not been straightforward, says Sarun 'Note' Kungbunpot, a Eurovision enthusiast and Thai singer who has won several competitions in this region.
"It's still very new in Asia. I'm not sure many people have heard about it yet," he says, adding that he thinks it will take a bit of time for audiences to adjust.
"When we look at contests in Thailand, the Philippines and Korea, we actually compete based on the singer.
"It's all about popularity â fans are looking for their idols. But Eurovision is all about the song, not the singer. I think this needs to be communicated clearly."
Then there is the long history of Eurovision in Europe. It began in 1956 as a project to encourage greater cultural exchanges in a Europe which was trying to forge a common future after two world wars.
This was the very start of the age of mass television ownership, and Eurovision became such a fixture it is now an indelible piece of Europe's shared cultural heritage. It has no such resonance in Asia, and arrives in this region in the digital age, when traditional TV formats are struggling to cut through.
Only 11 countries are taking part in this first Eurovision Asia contest â host Thailand, along with Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, South Korea, Mongolia, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan.
Asian giants India, China, Japan and Indonesia are noticeably absent, although there are negotiations ongoing to try to get them into next year's contest, assuming there is one.
There have also been problems with the organisation of this event.
A sudden million-dollar (Â£760,000) budget cut just three weeks before the final meant many of the technicians familiar with staging Eurovision were not brought to Thailand, and there have been a number of staff resignations too.
Eurovision fans - and there are many passionate followers around the world - have noticed, criticising audio and lighting in rehearsal videos.
The contest's unusual voting system will be unfamiliar to Asian audiences. Like in Europe, Eurovision Asia will determine the winner through a 50/50 mix of public voting and national juries from each of the 11 contesting countries, as well as a 12th "rest of the world" category.
Anyone can vote - you get eight votes once you register - but you cannot vote for your own country's contestant and you must give your votes to at least three others.
The public and jury votes are then converted into points. The most popular song among the Bhutanese or Mongolians, for example, will get 12 points from those countries, while the song ranked last will get zero - the famous "nul points".
In Europe, there have long been reports of co-ordinated voting to back neighbours, for example the four Nordic countries voting for each other. This seems less likely in Eurovision Asia, but political differences, for example between Thailand and Cambodia after their border war last year, could influence how their audiences vote.
Filipinos, with their passion for singing, are expected to be enthusiastic participants and the 11 million who live overseas might make a difference. But as most live and work in countries which are not participating, their votes will only go into the "rest of the world" pool.
For Bhutan, with a population of less than a million, this is a rare chance to shine on a global stage, which puts some pressure on 24-year-old Thukten Nyendra, the singer representing the Himalayan kingdom in Bangkok with his song Lhayi Semo (The Angel). Before coming here he had never left his country or been on a plane before.
"I'm not a star. I'm just Nyendra over there," he told the BBC. "Nobody knows me. But Eurovision has given me a huge platform. Actually winning would mean the world to us... If I really make it through all of this, it would mean the entire freaking world to us."
The other characteristic of Eurovision is the song format â no more than three minutes, no more than six people on stage, and no backing band, only taped music.
This encourages performers to prepare elaborate, sometimes outrageous choreography and stunts to impress the audience â think Poland's My SÅowianie in 2014 with models in traditional costume churning butter on stage, or the Finnish heavy metal band Lordi donning flamboyant monster outfits in its 2006 entry.
There has also been a long association of Eurovision with LGBTQ+ artists. Eurovision Asia includes Malaysia and Bangladesh â where same-sex activity is illegal â and there are no visible LGBTQ+ elements this year.
Performers have been using the last days of rehearsals before the final to try to make their stage acts as striking as possible. Thinla from Laos has abandoned the short, sequinned dress she wore in the first video of her infectious reggaeton song Bae and is adopting Lao hill-tribe costume for her and her backing dancers.
Perhaps the most ambitious choreography is in Vietnamese singer TÃ³c TiÃªn's song Em TiÃªn ("Fairy Maiden").
It has been exhausting just watching her rehearse the elaborate moves and costume changes for more than an hour at a time.
The entry from Bangladesh's Beatmosphere, Tumi Ele ("You Came"), is unusual as an a cappella and beatboxing performance by six men with little backing music.
